arxiv_record.abstract:
Thompson sampling (TS) has emerged as a robust technique for contextual
bandit problems. However, TS requires posterior inference and optimization for
action generation, prohibiting its use in many online platforms where latency
and ease of deployment are of concern. We operationalize TS by proposing a
novel imitation-learning-based algorithm that distills a TS policy into an
explicit policy representation, allowing fast decision-making and easy
deployment in mobile and server-based environments. Using batched data
collected under the imitation policy, our algorithm iteratively performs
offline updates to the TS policy, and learns a new explicit policy
representation to imitate it. Empirically, our imitation policy achieves
performance comparable to batch TS while allowing more than an order of
magnitude reduction in decision-time latency. Buoyed by low latency and
simplicity of implementation, our algorithm has been successfully deployed in
multiple video upload systems for Meta. Using a randomized controlled trial, we
show our algorithm resulted in significant improvements in video quality and
watch time.
arxiv_record.authors: Hongseok Namkoong, Samuel Daulton, Eytan Bakshy
arxiv_record.title:
Distilled Thompson Sampling: Practical and Efficient Thompson Sampling
  via Imitation Learning

C1.justification: V1 principally claims comparable regret, reduced latency, and successful deployment. V3's abstract and introduction additionally claim experimentally demonstrated production benefits in video quality and engagement. The theoretical contribution is reframed around batch Thompson sampling, with the concrete Gaussian-process guarantee qualified by special initialization.

C2.justification: V3 adds substantive qualifications about prior misspecification, the impractical initialization needed for its concrete batch guarantee, and the absence of a corresponding guarantee without that initialization. It also explains why offline evaluation cannot replace online learning under costly randomization and nonstationarity, and attributes increased watch time to improved video quality. These changes materially refine interpretation and applicability.

D1.justification: The detailed architectures, RMSProp settings, 2,048 Monte Carlo samples, preprocessing, and latency hardware are retained across the experiment appendices. V3 newly documents deployment inputs such as device model and operating system, while omitting v1's explicit 117-dimensional encoded Mushroom representation and PharmGKB identification. Production-trial sample sizes and detailed procedures are not supplied.

E1.justification: Mushroom, Wheel, Warfarin, and the logged video-transcoding dataset are retained. V3 adds live randomized evaluations across Facebook Feed/Stories and Instagram Stories, including distinct iOS and Android populations. This substantially extends evaluation beyond the offline benchmarks and deployment statement in v1.

E2.justification: The offline comparisons retain Linear-TS, NeuralLinear-TS, Bootstrap-NN-TS, Neural-Greedy, UniformRandom, and the corresponding imitation methods. The new production trials compare against existing video-upload policies, adding a comparator family whose implementation is not specified.

E3.justification: V3 adds randomized online production evaluation with metrics for preservation of 1080p quality, watch time, and social interactions. The existing offline protocols retain their batch sizes, model configurations, preprocessing, and rejection-sampling evaluation. The major change is the additional production evaluation design.

E4.justification: The 50-action Warfarin analysis is retained from v1 Appendix F.4/Figure 2 in v3 Appendix E/Figure 3. No new ablation, sensitivity, robustness, or error analysis is reported; the production trials add outcome evaluations.

E5.justification: V3 newly states that the production findings are significant at the 95% level, without specifying test procedures or confidence intervals. Existing benchmark reporting remains two standard errors over 50 trials, or 100 for Wheel, and latency reporting retains 100,000 action-generation repetitions.

E6.justification: Existing benchmark findings and all Table 1 latency means and uncertainties are retained. V3 adds production results: up to fivefold improvement in 1080p preservation, watch-time increases of 1.1% for Facebook iOS Feed, 0.77% for Android Feed, 0.27% for Android Stories, and 0.45% for Instagram Stories, plus interaction gains. These are new trial outcomes, not improvements over v1 under the same benchmark settings.

M1.justification: The core posterior-sampling, policy-distillation, and online action-generation procedure is retained; batching was already described and evaluated in v1. However, v3 Section 5.2 introduces a special Gaussian-process initialization that selects action-context pairs by maximum posterior variance. This is a procedural addition for the theoretical guarantee, not a reported change to the benchmark implementations.

P1.justification: The introduction and theoretical exposition are extensively rewritten. Related work becomes a separate section, empirical evaluation moves before theory, Gaussian-process and generalization material moves from appendices into the main narrative, and the discussion expands. This is substantial restructuring beyond the addition of scientific content.

P2.justification: V3 adds an online/offline workflow diagram, changes typography and spacing throughout, enlarges existing result displays, and separates the latency table from the benchmark figure. Existing plots are retained and renumbered. The video panel's axis changes from average reward to 'Cumulative Regret', conflicting with v3's average-reward caption; this is a labeling inconsistency rather than evidence of a changed metric.

R1.justification: V3 substantially expands positioning around behavioral cloning, Bayesian dark knowledge, inverse and adversarial imitation learning, and technical debt. It also introduces literature supporting batch Gaussian-process analysis and localized complexity bounds. V1's explicit contrast with one-shot logged-feedback optimization and its associated references is removed.

T1.justification: V3 explicitly formalizes batch histories and substantially revises the regret decomposition and Gaussian-process analysis, adding a per-batch information assumption and initialization guarantee. Section 6 and Appendix D replace the earlier agnostic generalization bounds with faster localized-complexity bounds under realizability and add RKHS results. V1's generalized-linear theorem and separate explicit linear-bandit proof are removed.

improvement.justification: V3 addresses two important weaknesses in v1: deployment lacked measured production outcomes, and extension of the theory to batching was asserted without an explicit batch analysis. The added randomized-trial results and conditional batch guarantees substantially strengthen support for the paper's practical purpose, while expanded positioning and limitations clarify its contribution. These gains outweigh the loss of the separate generalized-linear analysis, although stronger theoretical assumptions, sparse trial documentation, and a figure-label inconsistency limit the improvement.

A1.justification: Both PDFs describe the same distilled Thompson sampling work. Their main text, equations, figures, tables, and complete appendices support reliable comparison despite substantial rewriting and reorganization.

after.justification: Section 4 and Appendix E retain the original experiments. The introduction additionally reports randomized production trials measuring video quality, watch time, and interactions.

before.justification: Section 5 and Appendix F report original benchmark, video-transcoding replay, and latency experiments, including the additional 50-action Warfarin experiment.

arxiv_record.abstract: In myriad statistical applications, data are collected from related but heterogeneous sources. These sources share some commonalities while containing idiosyncratic characteristics. One of the most fundamental challenges in such scenarios is to recover the shared and source-specific factors. Despite the existence of a few heuristic approaches, a generic algorithm with theoretical guarantees has yet to be established. In this paper, we tackle the problem by proposing a method called Heterogeneous Matrix Factorization to separate the shared and unique factors for a class of problems. HMF maintains the orthogonality between the shared and unique factors by leveraging an invariance property in the objective. The algorithm is easy to implement and intrinsically distributed. On the theoretic side, we show that for the square error loss, HMF will converge into the optimal solutions, which are close to the ground truth. HMF can be integrated auto-encoders to learn nonlinear feature mappings. Through a variety of case studies, we showcase HMF's benefits and applicability in video segmentation, time-series feature extraction, and recommender systems.
arxiv_record.authors: Naichen Shi and Raed Al Kontar and Salar Fattahi
arxiv_record.title: Heterogeneous Matrix Factorization: When Features Differ by Datasets

C1.justification: The abstract, introduction and conclusion broaden the contribution from linear shared/unique factor recovery to an extensible framework supporting incomplete observations and nonlinear autoencoders, with recommendation as an explicit application. Identifiability and local squared-error convergence remain central, but the claimed methodological and application scope expands substantially.

C2.justification: V2 interprets genre-aligned HAE embeddings and rating accuracy as evidence that genre-specific features capture useful preference information. It also emphasizes explicit orthogonality enforcement when explaining advantages over earlier decompositions. The stock-crash interpretation and limitations concerning unknown ranks and good initialization remain essentially unchanged.

D1.justification: V2 adds implementation guidance concerning Sparse FC backbones, AdamW, zero-padded inputs and differentiable folding/projection operations, including Appendix A's PyTorch guidance. V1's RTX 3080 hardware and approximate 0.1-second iteration-time disclosures are removed. Both PDFs link to the same code repository, so code access is not newly introduced.

E1.justification: V2 removes the European email-network task from v1 Section 6.3 and adds MovieLens-100K rating prediction. It also introduces incomplete-observation scenarios for synthetic matrices and the roundabout video. The original noiseless synthetic setting and stock-market coverage remain.

E2.justification: The pooled-SVD comparison disappears with the email experiment. V2 evaluates JIVE, RJIVE and perPCA against HMF on synthetic and video data, and matrix completion and Sparse FC on MovieLens. Table 4 additionally includes AutoSVD++, GHRS and GraphRec, explicitly using literature scores rather than newly run comparisons.

E3.justification: The video experiment now removes 40% of pixels, changes local rank from 100 to 30, and evaluates foreground/background MSE and PSNR. New synthetic tests remove 1%, 5%, 10% or 50% of entries, zero-fill comparator inputs and measure subspace error. MovieLens introduces ten genre-based clusters and a 90/10 split of observed ratings evaluated by RMSE.

E4.justification: V2 adds a missing-entry sensitivity study across four masking rates (Table 2) and a t-SNE comparison examining HAE versus standard-autoencoder representations (Figure 4). The email-network topology analysis is removed. These substantially change the robustness and representation analyses, while the original matrix-size convergence analysis and stock case study remain.

E5.justification: V1's eight-seed email results are removed. V2 specifies three seeds for synthetic missing-data tests and 80 seeds for matrix completion, HMF, Sparse FC and HAE on MovieLens. Mean-and-standard-deviation reporting is retained; these counts concern different experiments, not an established increase in runs for a retained experiment.

E6.justification: V1's email errors of 23.6 ± 0.3 for HMF and 24.7 ± 0.3 for pooled SVD disappear. V2 adds missing-data, video and recommendation results: for example, video background MSE is 0.001 for HMF versus 0.021 for perPCA, and MovieLens RMSE is 0.8800 ± 0.0006 for HAE versus 0.8838 ± 0.0006 for Sparse FC. These are new or replaced experiments; the original convergence and stock plots are unchanged.

M1.justification: V1 proposes linear HMF with squared-error fitting. V2 generalizes the objective to other losses, including projected squared error, and introduces heterogeneous autoencoders with shared and source-specific encoders, a common decoder, folded-embedding orthogonality and projection-based training (Section 3.2 and Appendix A). The original linear correction and averaging procedure is retained.

P1.justification: The abstract and introduction are extensively rewritten, and the separate contribution-summary subsection is absorbed into the narrative. Formulation joins the model section, while misalignment and identifiability move into convergence analysis with substantially shortened explanation. The appendices are reorganized from A–C to A–E, and the author block and author order change.

P2.justification: V2 removes the email table and graph, adds MovieLens results and a t-SNE figure, and introduces related-work, synthetic and video comparison tables. The video display is replaced and enlarged for masked inputs. Algorithm 1 gains client/server color coding and Algorithm 2 is added. Retained convergence and stock figures are relocated within the reformatted document.

R1.justification: V2 substantially expands positioning relative to JIVE, COBE, RJIVE, SLIDE, iNMF, BIDIFAC and perDL, alongside new recommendation literature. Table 1 explicitly compares distribution, orthogonality, convergence and incomplete-data capabilities. This replaces v1's much narrower discussion centered on conventional factorization and personalized PCA; the personalized-PCA publication update itself concerns the same work.

T1.justification: V2 adds a general-loss KKT and stationarity analysis with an O(1/T) squared-gradient bound, new supporting lemmas and formal Theorem 18 in Appendix D. That formal statement specifies bounded iterates and gradients and beta = 0. The original statistical-error and local-linear-convergence proofs are largely retained in Appendices B–C; v1's appendix Theorem 4 corresponds to v2's Theorem 15.

improvement.justification: V2 substantially strengthens v1's limited comparative validation through relevant decomposition baselines, controlled missing-data tests, quantitative video evaluation and repeated-run recommendation experiments (Tables 2–4). Expanded related work also gives the contribution a better-supported position. These gains outweigh removal of the email study and hardware/timing disclosure. Important qualifications remain: several MovieLens comparisons use literature scores, and the main general-loss theorem does not state the beta = 0 restriction present in its formal appendix version.

A1.justification: Both PDFs describe the same HMF research work. Their text, equations, figures, tables and complete appendices support comparison, including matching the original proofs across substantial reorganization and renumbering.

after.justification: V2 reports original synthetic, video, stock-market and MovieLens experiments, including repeated-run HMF and HAE results. Some additional MovieLens comparator scores are explicitly quoted from literature.

before.justification: V1 reports original synthetic convergence experiments, video segmentation, email-network prediction and stock-market analysis in Section 6.

arxiv_record.abstract: We present a novel Diffusion Offline Multi-agent Model (DOM2) for offline Multi-Agent Reinforcement Learning (MARL). Different from existing algorithms that rely mainly on conservatism in policy design, DOM2 enhances policy expressiveness and diversity based on diffusion model. Specifically, we incorporate a diffusion model into the policy network and propose a trajectory-based data-reweighting scheme in training. These key ingredients significantly improve algorithm robustness against environment changes and achieve significant improvements in performance, generalization and data-efficiency. Our extensive experimental results demonstrate that DOM2 outperforms existing state-of-the-art methods in all multi-agent particle and multi-agent MuJoCo environments, and generalizes significantly better to shifted environments {(in $28$ out of $30$ settings evaluated)} thanks to its high expressiveness and diversity. Moreover, DOM2 is ultra data efficient and requires no more than $5\%$ data for achieving the same performance compared to existing algorithms (a $20\times$ improvement in data efficiency).
arxiv_record.authors: Zhuoran Li, Ling Pan, Jiatai Huang, and Longbo Huang
arxiv_record.title: Improving Generalization and Data Efficiency with Diffusion in Offline Multi-agent RL

C1.justification: The central contributions remain diffusion-based DOM2 with value-guided training and trajectory replication, claiming improved performance, generalization and approximately 20-fold data efficiency. v2 quantifies generalization success as 28 of 30 settings and foregrounds the already-existing decentralized design, without introducing a materially different central claim.

C2.justification: Appendix A.4 newly attributes substantial data efficiency to diffusion itself and additional gains to reweighting, while discussing task-dependent thresholds and automated tuning as future work. Appendix A.3 adds explanations of MADIFF/DoF differences and acknowledges unequal training information and dataset usage. These substantially expand interpretation and applicability qualifications.

D1.justification: v2 provides a DOM2 code-access link, specifies dataset mixture proportions previously left unspecified, and documents hyperparameters for the added dataset qualities. It also supplies threshold-selection guidance and explicitly discloses that the main data-efficiency curves omit reweighting. These are reproducibility disclosures; they do not establish that corresponding earlier experiments changed or were rerun.

E1.justification: v2 adds random and random-medium behavior datasets across the retained MPE, HalfCheetah and 3-agent 6-landmark tasks. This substantially extends evaluation into low-quality training-data regimes beyond v1's four dataset qualities. The environment families and environmental-shift mechanisms are retained.

E2.justification: The original MA-CQL, OMAR and MA-SfBC comparisons remain. v2 Table 4 adds evaluated comparisons with MA-BRAC, MA-IQL, MA-Diffusion-QL, both MA-EDP variants, OMAC, OMIGA, CFCQL, MADIFF and DoF. Appendix A.3 additionally compares MADIFF and DoF across MPE tasks and computational costs.

E3.justification: The data-efficiency plots change from averaging three dataset qualities to five and revise the sample-size grid. The regularization sweep extends from 25 to 100. New protocols include component-removal controls, return-above-400 policy counts, threshold tests and computational measurements over 10,000 training steps with scheduled episode evaluations.

E4.justification: Beyond v1's regularization and diffusion-step sweeps, v2 adds component ablations testing policy improvement, diffusion loss, reweighting and noise-network architecture. Appendix analyses add trajectory visualizations and good-policy counts, reweighting-threshold sensitivity, and data-efficiency comparisons with versus without reweighting.

E5.justification: Both versions specify five random seeds and report means and standard deviations, with uncertainty already displayed in v1. The existing K=1 and K=10 landmark evaluations are retained. Additional results do not introduce a different uncertainty-estimation practice, confidence intervals or significance tests.

E6.justification: All 48 original benchmark-table result rows are retained unchanged, but v2 adds substantial results for new dataset qualities, comparators and analyses. For example, random Predator Prey reports DOM2 at 208.7±57.3 versus OMAR at 14.3±9.5 (Table 1). Table 9 also introduces settings where MADIFF or DoF outperform DOM2. Revised data-efficiency curves use different aggregation and are not same-setting performance changes.

M1.justification: The diffusion policy, residual noise network, DPM-Solver sampling, actor/critic objectives and trajectory-replication procedure are retained. 'Data augmentation' becomes 'data reweighting,' and the two algorithms are combined into one listing, without changing their operations.

P1.justification: The main narrative and section sequence remain recognizable. Changes include the title and author information, consistent reweighting terminology, expanded introductory and method explanations, a dedicated ablation subsection, and reorganized appendices. Much of the original prose and mathematical exposition is retained.

P2.justification: v2 adds a conceptual schematic, component-ablation charts and trajectory visualizations, and expands the introductory diversity display. It restructures benchmark tables, merges the HalfCheetah tables and the sensitivity figures, adds several analysis tables, and redraws data-efficiency axes and panels. The publication template and page layout also change substantially.

R1.justification: v2 expands positioning to newer diffusion and offline MARL work, including IDQL, DAC, MADIFF, DoF, CFCQL, OMAC and OMIGA. Sections 2 and 4.4 and Appendix A.3 develop substantial comparisons between DOM2's decentralized policy diffusion and centralized trajectory or joint-policy approaches, beyond v1's mainly single-agent diffusion comparisons.

T1.justification: Section 3 corrects the stated score-function definition from -sigma_t times the gradient of log q_t to the gradient of log q_t; Section 4.1 correspondingly calls the network target a scaled score. The substantive diffusion equations and appendix derivations remain, with no new theorem or proof.

improvement.justification: v2 substantially strengthens evidence that was limited in v1: component ablations and direct diversity analyses test why DOM2 works, while broader baseline and low-quality-data evaluations test its comparative value. Dataset-construction disclosures, a code link and computational measurements improve reproducibility and practical assessment. Some superiority language exceeds Table 9, and Appendix A.3 acknowledges comparison confounds, but these qualifications do not outweigh the substantial evidential gains.

A1.justification: Despite the changed title, both PDFs describe DOM2 and retain matching methods and experiments. All 20 pages of v1 and 27 pages of v2, including appendices, equations, tables and figures, support reliable comparison.

after.justification: v2 retains these original experiments and adds low-quality-data evaluations, further baseline comparisons, component ablations, diversity measurements and computational-efficiency results.

before.justification: v1 reports original DOM2 experiments on MPE, multi-agent HalfCheetah and the 3-agent 6-landmark task, including generalization, data-efficiency and hyperparameter results.

arxiv_record.abstract: The entity resolution problem requires finding pairs across datasets that belong to different owners but refer to the same entity in the real world. To train and evaluate solutions (either rule-based or machine-learning-based) to the entity resolution problem, generating a ground truth dataset with entity pairs or clusters is needed. However, such a data annotation process involves humans as domain oracles to review the plaintext data for all candidate record pairs from different parties, which inevitably infringes the privacy of data owners, especially in privacy-sensitive cases like medical records. To the best of our knowledge, there is no prior work on privacy-preserving ground truth dataset generation, especially in the domain of entity resolution. We propose a novel blind annotation protocol based on homomorphic encryption that allows domain oracles to collaboratively label ground truths without sharing data in plaintext with other parties. In addition, we design a domain-specific easy-to-use language that hides the sophisticated underlying homomorphic encryption layer. Rigorous proof of the privacy guarantee is provided and our empirical experiments via an annotation simulator indicate the feasibility of our privacy-preserving protocol (f-measure on average achieves more than 90\% compared with the real ground truths).
arxiv_record.authors: Yixiang Yao, Weizhao Jin, Srivatsan Ravi
arxiv_record.title: Labeling without Seeing? Blind Annotation for Privacy-Preserving Entity Resolution

C1.justification: V2 frames novelty more specifically around pairwise entity annotation and replaces the simulator contribution with an implemented protocol. Efficient, independent encrypted computation becomes an explicit contribution. The central HE-based privacy, DSL and annotation-quality claims remain.

C2.justification: V1's unmeasured assurance that HE overhead would not threaten feasibility is replaced by discussion of measured costs, BinFHE constraints, limited parallelization and future optimizations. V2 also explains the preference for HE over MPC, Febrl's missing-value relaxation effects and the mechanisms illustrated by the new case studies.

D1.justification: Beyond v1's simulator/parser description, v2 documents OpenFHE/BinFHE, public-key STD128 configuration, OpenMP, Linux hardware with an 8-core 3.60 GHz CPU and 32 GB RAM, bit-level representation, implementation pseudocode and GUI workflows. These substantially expand implementation and reproducibility information.

E1.justification: V2 adds synthetic Febrl person-record linkage to the retained e-commerce and bibliographic tasks. Its census-like attributes, missing values and textual corruption substantially broaden coverage toward biomedical-style records, although these are not actual patient data.

E2.justification: The new overhead evaluation introduces plaintext storage as a reference for ciphertext size and serial HE execution as a reference for parallel execution (Section 5.3). These are internal efficiency comparisons; no competing annotation system, PSI method or PIR method is experimentally evaluated.

E3.justification: V1 evaluates annotation through simulation and explicitly excludes execution-time benchmarking. V2 adds a 2,500-comparison encrypted benchmark using representative token/record lengths, serial and parallel execution, and computation/communication metrics. The original tasks retain their 50 sampled matches and accuracy metrics.

E4.justification: V2 adds resource-cost analyses, a serial-versus-parallel comparison, token-length analysis, DSL familiarization assessment and two disagreement-resolution case studies. The earlier annotation-round and feature-importance analyses remain; the latter moves from Section 5.3 to Appendix D.2.

E5.justification: Neither version reports random seeds, repeated-run counts, confidence intervals, error bars or statistical tests. Annotation rounds are protocol iterations, not repeated trials estimating uncertainty.

E6.justification: The original four tasks' plotted accuracy results are retained, while Febrl curves and substantial new cost results are added. Examples include approximately 32 KB per encrypted character and Abt-Buy benchmark times of 540,000 seconds serial versus 160,000 parallel (Figure 7). V2 also newly reports roughly 30 minutes of DSL/GUI familiarization.

M1.justification: The annotation protocol and DSL remain intact. Algorithm 1 corrects is_in's initial accumulator from True to False, and v2 introduces parallel execution of its BinFHE implementation. However, the new Algorithm 2 displays XOR-based byte_equal logic inconsistent with equality.

P1.justification: V2 substantially reorganizes existing material into appendices covering HE background, DSL/functions, security and feature importance. It also revises the introduction and contribution statements, expands protocol explanations, and restructures the experimental narrative around H1–H3 and HE overheads.

P2.justification: The paper changes from a two-column ACM layout to a single-column TMLR layout, redraws explanatory diagrams, expands benchmark panels and adds cost plots, a missing-value table, GUI screenshots, a token-length histogram and case-study displays. V1's Figure 7 is retained unchanged as v2's Figure 12.

R1.justification: V2 adds substantive positioning against PSI, weighted PSI and PIR, including possible HE-based integration, and acknowledges additional privacy-preserving crowdsourcing methods. New HE/PPER references support this expanded context and the more specific pairwise-annotation novelty claim; Lindell's MPC reference is removed.

T1.justification: The adversary and security definitions and simulation argument move from v1 Section 4.6 to v2 Appendix B.2 without substantive revision. The homomorphic-encryption definitions and derivations are retained; no new theorem or proof is supplied.

improvement.justification: V1 explicitly defers real encrypted implementation and benchmarking; v2 supplies an OpenFHE implementation description and measured resource costs, substantially addressing that central evidential gap. Febrl evaluation and concrete cases further strengthen applicability and transparency. Algorithm 2's apparent XOR/equality error limits confidence in the implementation documentation, but the added empirical and reproducibility evidence provides a substantial net improvement.

A1.justification: Both PDFs describe the same blind annotation research. Their text, equations, tables and figures are readable, including v2's Appendices A–E; v1 has no appendices.

after.justification: V2 retains those experiments and adds Febrl results, encrypted computation and communication measurements, and annotation case studies.

before.justification: V1 reports original annotation-simulator experiments on four matching tasks, including accuracy, agreement across rounds and feature-importance results.

arxiv_record.abstract: In this work, we address the challenge of multi-domain translation, where the objective is to learn mappings between arbitrary configurations of domains within a defined set (such as $(D_1, D_2)\rightarrow{}D_3$, $D_2\rightarrow{}(D_1, D_3)$, $D_3\rightarrow{}D_1$, etc. for three domains) without the need for separate models for each specific translation configuration, enabling more efficient and flexible domain translation. We introduce Multi-Domain Diffusion (MDD), a method with dual purposes: i) reconstructing any missing views for new data objects, and ii) enabling learning in semi-supervised contexts with arbitrary supervision configurations. MDD achieves these objectives by exploiting the noise formulation of diffusion models, specifically modeling one noise level per domain. Similar to existing domain translation approaches, MDD learns the translation between any combination of domains. However, unlike prior work, our formulation inherently handles semi-supervised learning without modification by representing missing views as noise in the diffusion process. We evaluate our approach through domain translation experiments on BL3NDT, a multi-domain synthetic dataset designed for challenging semantic domain inversion, the BraTS2020 dataset, and the CelebAMask-HQ dataset.
arxiv_record.authors: Tsiry Mayet and Simon Bernard and Romain Herault and Clement Chatelain
arxiv_record.title: Multiple Noises in Diffusion Model for Semi-Supervised Multi-Domain Translation

C1.justification: The central contribution remains flexible, semi-supervised multi-domain diffusion. V2's abstract narrows the novelty positioning: arbitrary-domain translation is acknowledged as shared with prior approaches, while inherent semi-supervised handling is emphasized. Its conclusion also adds an explicit claim of superior information fusion across modalities.

C2.justification: V2 expands explanations of noisy-conditioning failures, segmentation behavior and diversity–fidelity tradeoffs. Its new limitations section discusses the shared fusion bottleneck, parameter scaling, difficulties with heterogeneous modalities and absent human evaluation. These substantially extend v1's bridge-error discussion and brief future-work remarks.

D1.justification: Appendix A substantially expands reproducibility information, documenting optimizer parameters, EMA, training budgets, early stopping, preprocessing, ControlNet training and architecture/time-embedding details. Appendix B.5 identifies timing hardware and measurement procedures. V2 also replaces v1's 'code will be made available' footnote with a concrete repository address.

E1.justification: V1 evaluates only the synthetic cube/pyramid/icosphere dataset. V2 retains it under the name BL3NDT and adds CelebAMask-HQ face, sketch and segmentation tasks and BraTS 2020 MRI modality completion and tumor segmentation. The supplement also evaluates unconditional joint face/sketch/mask generation.

E2.justification: V2 adds evaluated ControlNet[N] comparisons on all three datasets (Appendix B.6), substantially broadening the comparison methods. V1's NoisyCond-O and UMM-CSGM-O variants using −1 for missing views disappear. NoisyCond becomes MSDM†, while the noise-filled adaptations remain under revised names; these renamings are not new baselines.

E3.justification: For the retained synthetic experiments, the reported batch size changes from 32 to 128 and plateau-based learning-rate reduction by 0.5 becomes decay by 0.75 every ten epochs. V2 adds 0% fully supervised training examples, dataset-specific sampling protocols, LPIPS/SSIM/PSNR/Jaccard evaluations, and sampler/step-count comparisons. These extend and revise the evaluation design.

E4.justification: V1's condition-noise sweep is retained in Appendix B.1. V2 adds MDD[NOISY] and MDD[RAND] component ablations, diversity–fidelity analysis, scheduler sensitivity, generation-trajectory comparisons, and tests reducing available MRI inputs from four to one (Section 4.5.2 and Appendices B.2–B.4). These investigate mechanisms and robustness beyond the original analyses.

E5.justification: Appendix B.5 newly specifies that generation times are averaged over 100 runs. This adds repeated-measurement reporting for computational results, not evidence of increased training repetitions. Accuracy results in both versions lack reported seed variation, confidence intervals or significance tests.

E6.justification: Synthetic results are replaced: MDD's fully supervised MAE changes from 0.06096 in v1 Table II to 0.0316 in v2 Table 2 after accounting for its scale, under revised training settings. Extensive real-data and diagnostic results are added. The new BraTS T1 P50% comparison is mixed: ControlNet[N] has higher PSNR than MDD (23.968 versus 22.928), but lower SSIM (0.832 versus 0.892; Table 11).

M1.justification: The central independent per-domain noise formulation and conditional inference procedure remain. V2 Algorithm 1 adds a random conditional mask that keeps selected domains clean during training; removing this step defines MDD[RAND]. This is a bounded training refinement, distinct from the expanded implementation description.

P1.justification: The abstract, introduction, related work and method explanations are extensively rewritten. Existing implementation material moves into Appendix A, the original noise-strategy study moves into Appendix B.1, and the experimental narrative is reorganized by dataset. Dedicated limitations and broader-impact sections further change the document structure.

P2.justification: V2 replaces the two-column presentation with a single-column layout, restructures comparison tables and adds architecture, generation-trajectory, diversity and medical-result displays. Existing figures are also revised or relocated: v1's noise-strategy Figures 6–7 become v2 Figures 12–13, rather than new analyses.

R1.justification: V2 substantially broadens positioning beyond the original clean/noisy diffusion comparison, adding discussions of StarGAN, fixed-direction ControlNet, diffusion-inpainting mechanisms and mixture-of-experts fusion for scalability. It also refines the novelty attribution toward inherent semi-supervision. Publication-year and venue updates for retained references do not constitute these changes.

T1.justification: The Introduction corrects P(D) from 'partitions' to the power set and explicitly identifies 2^L source/complement configurations. This is a limited formal correction. The basic diffusion mathematics remains, and neither version supplies theorems or proofs; v2's additional displayed equations largely unpack existing algorithmic operations.

improvement.justification: V2 addresses v1's principal evidential weakness—validation confined to synthetic data—through face translation and medical modality-completion experiments. Component ablations, robustness analyses and fuller implementation details substantially strengthen support and reproducibility. Reporting problems remain, notably the apparent interchange of T1 baseline rows between Tables 4 and 13 and absent accuracy uncertainty estimates, but they do not outweigh the substantial gains in validation and explanatory depth.

A1.justification: Both PDFs describe the same MDD framework and retain the original synthetic translation task. Text, equations, tables and figures are readable throughout. V1 has no appendix; v2 includes complete supplementary Appendices A–B.

after.justification: V2 reports original synthetic, face-translation and medical-imaging experiments, with additional ablations, sampling analyses, diversity measurements and computational results in its supplement.

before.justification: V1 reports original synthetic translation experiments, including supervision-dependent MAE results in Table II, bridge translation examples and condition-noise sensitivity results.

arxiv_record.abstract:
Biological and artificial information processing systems form representations
of the world that they can use to categorize, reason, plan, navigate, and make
decisions. How can we measure the similarity between the representations formed
by these diverse systems? Do similarities in representations then translate
into similar behavior? If so, then how can a system's representations be
modified to better match those of another system? These questions pertaining to
the study of representational alignment are at the heart of some of the most
promising research areas in contemporary cognitive science, neuroscience, and
machine learning. In this Perspective, we survey the exciting recent
developments in representational alignment research in the fields of cognitive
science, neuroscience, and machine learning. Despite their overlapping
interests, there is limited knowledge transfer between these fields, so work in
one field ends up duplicated in another, and useful innovations are not shared
effectively. To improve communication, we propose a unifying framework that can
serve as a common language for research on representational alignment, and map
several streams of existing work across fields within our framework. We also
lay out open problems in representational alignment where progress can benefit
all three of these fields. We hope that this paper will catalyze
cross-disciplinary collaboration and accelerate progress for all communities
studying and developing information processing systems.

C1.justification: Both versions claim an interdisciplinary unifying framework, a survey connecting cognitive science, neuroscience and machine learning, and an agenda of open problems. Recasting the paper as a Perspective does not materially change these core contributions.

C2.justification: v3 adds substantive qualifications about implementation-dependent alignment scores, confounded versus controlled stimuli, and stimulus timing and presentation order (Sections 3.3.5, 5.1 and 5.2). Conversely, it removes v1's detailed interpretability faithfulness/scalability caveats and robotics proxy-task tradeoffs. Practical interpretations and limitations are substantially revised, while the warning that representational alignment need not imply behavioral alignment remains.

D1.justification: New Section 3.3.5 documents implementation choices needed to specify CKA reproducibly, including the HSIC estimator and score transformations, and mentions a Python package for standardizing similarity implementations. This adds practical reproducibility guidance without introducing experiment-specific hardware, training records or a new code release for this paper.

E1.justification: Neither version conducts training or evaluation on datasets. The additional modalities and systems cataloged in v3 Table 2 expand literature coverage, not datasets or tasks evaluated by this work.

E2.justification: Neither version evaluates a proposed method against baselines. Tables 1 and 2 classify alignment functions and published studies; their expanded membership is not an experimental comparator change.

E3.justification: No evaluation protocol is introduced or revised for this work. Settings in the retained worked examples remain substantively unchanged. The new discussion of CKA implementations does not report adopting a different metric in an experiment.

E4.justification: The same nine literature examples are retained. Neither version contributes original ablations, robustness tests or supplementary empirical analyses; added discussion of confounds and distribution shifts describes prior research and methodological concerns.

E5.justification: Neither version reports its own repeated runs, uncertainty intervals or significance tests. The new biased/unbiased HSIC discussion explains estimator properties rather than changing statistical estimation or uncertainty reporting for an analysis performed here.

E6.justification: Reported literature findings change: v3 Section 2.1.2 adds the cited U-shaped relationship between alignment and few-shot transfer, while omitting v1 Section 4.2.1's approximately five-second speaker–listener lag. These are secondary findings, not new experiments. Quantities in the central worked examples, including Hebart et al.'s 1.46 million judgments, 1,854 categories and 49 dimensions, remain unchanged.

M1.justification: The five-component framework and the measuring, bridging and increasing objectives remain. Explicit measurement mappings refine the formal description of existing stages; no new algorithm, architecture or training/inference procedure is proposed.

P1.justification: The background review moves from Section 4 to Section 2, preceding the framework; worked examples move from Section 3 to Section 4. The abstract, introduction and substantial background passages are rewritten. Existing cross-cultural and communication material receives separate subsections, and the Section 5.2 subsections are reordered.

P2.justification: Figure 2 is redrawn with interfaces, measurement mappings and mathematical labels, plus a much fuller caption. arxiv_record.abstract: We suggest the use of hash functions to cut down the communication costs when counting subgraphs under edge local differential privacy. While various algorithms exist for computing graph statistics, including the count of subgraphs, under the edge local differential privacy, many suffer with high communication costs, making them less efficient for large graphs. Though data compression is a typical approach in differential privacy, its application in local differential privacy requires a form of compression that every node can reproduce. In our study, we introduce linear congruence hashing. With a sampling rate of $s$, our method can cut communication costs by a factor of $s^2$, albeit at the cost of increasing variance in the published graph statistic by a factor of $s$. The experimental results indicate that, when matched for communication costs, our method achieves a reduction in the $\ell_2$-error for triangle counts by up to 1000 times compared to the performance of leading algorithms.
arxiv_record.authors: Quentin Hillebrand, Vorapong Suppakitpaisarn and Tetsuo Shibuya
arxiv_record.title: Communication Cost Reduction for Subgraph Counting under Local Differential Privacy via Hash Functions

arxiv_record.abstract: We introduce a framework for joint grounded scene graph - image generation, a challenging task involving high-dimensional, multi-modal structured data. To effectively model this complex joint distribution, we adopt a factorized approach: first generating a grounded scene graph, followed by image generation conditioned on the generated grounded scene graph. While conditional image generation has been widely explored in the literature, our primary focus is on the generation of grounded scene graphs from noise, which provides efficient and interpretable control over the image generation process. This task requires generating plausible grounded scene graphs with heterogeneous attributes for both nodes (objects) and edges (relations among objects), encompassing continuous attributes (e.g., object bounding boxes) and discrete attributes (e.g., object and relation categories). To address this challenge, we introduce DiffuseSG, a novel diffusion model that jointly models the heterogeneous node and edge attributes. We explore different encoding strategies to effectively handle the categorical data. Leveraging a graph transformer as the denoiser, DiffuseSG progressively refines grounded scene graph representations in a continuous space before discretizing them to generate structured outputs. Additionally, we introduce an IoU-based regularization term to enhance empirical performance. Our model outperforms existing methods in grounded scene graph generation on the VG and COCO-Stuff datasets, excelling in both standard and newly introduced metrics that more accurately capture the task's complexity. Furthermore, we demonstrate the broader applicability of DiffuseSG in two important downstream tasks: 1) achieving superior results in a range of grounded scene graph completion tasks, and 2) enhancing grounded scene graph detection models by leveraging additional training samples generated by DiffuseSG.
arxiv_record.authors: Bicheng Xu, Qi Yan, Renjie Liao, Lele Wang, Leonid Sigal
arxiv_record.title: Joint Generative Modeling of Grounded Scene Graphs and Images via Diffusion Models

arxiv_record.abstract: Generative Flow Networks (GFlowNets) are a family of probabilistic generative models that learn to sample compositional objects proportional to their rewards. One big challenge of GFlowNets is training them effectively when dealing with long time horizons and sparse rewards. To address this, we propose Evolution guided generative flow networks (EGFN), a simple but powerful augmentation to the GFlowNets training using Evolutionary algorithms (EA). Our method can work on top of any GFlowNets training objective, by training a set of agent parameters using EA, storing the resulting trajectories in the prioritized replay buffer, and training the GFlowNets agent using the stored trajectories. We present a thorough investigation over a wide range of toy and real-world benchmark tasks showing the effectiveness of our method in handling long trajectories and sparse rewards. We release the code at http://github.com/zarifikram/egfn.
arxiv_record.authors: Zarif Ikram, Ling Pan, Dianbo Liu
arxiv_record.title: Evolution Guided Generative Flow Networks

arxiv_record.abstract: Deep learning is providing a wealth of new approaches to the problem of novel view synthesis, from Neural Radiance Field (NeRF) based approaches to end-to-end style architectures. Each approach offers specific strengths but also comes with limitations in their applicability. This work introduces ViewFusion, an end-to-end generative approach to novel view synthesis with unparalleled flexibility. ViewFusion consists in simultaneously applying a diffusion denoising step to any number of input views of a scene, then combining the noise gradients obtained for each view with an (inferred) pixel-weighting mask, ensuring that for each region of the target view only the most informative input views are taken into account. Our approach resolves several limitations of previous approaches by (1) being trainable and generalizing across multiple scenes and object classes, (2) adaptively taking in a variable number of pose-free views at both train and test time, (3) generating plausible views even in severely underdetermined conditions (thanks to its generative nature) -- all while generating views of quality on par or even better than comparable methods. Limitations include not generating a 3D embedding of the scene, resulting in a relatively slow inference speed, and our method only being tested on the relatively small Neural 3D Mesh Renderer dataset. Code is available at https://github.com/bronemos/view-fusion.

arxiv_record.abstract: Label smoothing loss is a widely adopted technique to mitigate overfitting in deep neural networks. This paper studies label smoothing from the perspective of Neural Collapse (NC), a powerful empirical and theoretical framework which characterizes model behavior during the terminal phase of training. We first show empirically that models trained with label smoothing converge faster to neural collapse solutions and attain a stronger level of neural collapse. Additionally, we show that at the same level of NC1, models under label smoothing loss exhibit intensified NC2. These findings provide valuable insights into the performance benefits and enhanced model calibration under label smoothing loss. We then leverage the unconstrained feature model to derive closed-form solutions for the global minimizers for both loss functions and further demonstrate that models under label smoothing have a lower conditioning number and, therefore, theoretically converge faster. Our study, combining empirical evidence and theoretical results, not only provides nuanced insights into the differences between label smoothing and cross-entropy losses, but also serves as an example of how the powerful neural collapse framework can be used to improve our understanding of DNNs.

arxiv_record.abstract: A common theoretical approach to understanding neural networks is to take an infinite-width limit, at which point the outputs become Gaussian process (GP) distributed. This is known as a neural network Gaussian process (NNGP). However, the NNGP kernel is fixed and tunable only through a small number of hyperparameters, thus eliminating the possibility of representation learning. This contrasts with finite-width NNs, which are often believed to perform well because they are able to flexibly learn representations for the task at hand. Thus, in simplifying NNs to make them theoretically tractable, NNGPs may eliminate precisely what makes them work well (representation learning). This motivated us to understand whether representation learning is necessary in a range of graph tasks. We develop a precise tool for this task, the graph convolutional deep kernel machine. This is very similar to an NNGP, in that it is an infinite width limit and uses kernels, but comes with a ``knob'' to control the amount of flexibility and hence representation learning. We found that representation learning gives noticeable performance improvements for heterophilous node classification tasks, but less so for homophilous node classification tasks.
arxiv_record.authors: Ben Anson, Edward Milsom, Laurence Aitchison
arxiv_record.comments: Major revision. Title and abstract updated. Added new analysis section on linear models and additional datasets. Paper accepted to TMLR

arxiv_record.abstract: We introduce Tune without Validation (Twin), a simple and effective pipeline for tuning learning rate and weight decay of homogeneous classifiers without validation sets, eliminating the need to hold out data and avoiding the two-step process. Twin leverages the margin-maximization dynamics of homogeneous networks and an empirical scaling law that links training and test losses across hyper-parameter configurations. This mathematical modeling yields a regime-dependent, validation-free selection rule: in the non-separable regime, training loss is monotonic in test loss and therefore predictive of generalization, whereas in the separable regime, the parameters' norm becomes a reliable indicator of generalization due to margin maximization. Across 37 dataset-architecture configurations for image classification, we demonstrate that Twin achieves a mean absolute error of 1.28% compared to an Oracle baseline that selects HPs using test accuracy. We demonstrate Twin's benefits in scenarios where validation data is scarce, such as small-data regimes, or difficult and costly to collect, as in medical imaging. Code available at https://github.com/lorenzobrigato/twin.
arxiv_record.authors: Lorenzo Brigato and Stavroula Mougiakakou
arxiv_record.title: Twin: Tuning Learning Rate and Weight Decay of Deep Homogeneous Classifiers without Validation

V2 makes a regime-dependent generalization predictor connecting margin maximization and empirical loss scaling a central contribution, and explicitly scopes the title, abstract, and conclusion to homogeneous classifiers. C2.justification: V2 replaces the earlier small-data/IID-versus-OOD explanation with separability and optimization-regime interpretations. Transfer-learning failures are further interpreted through noisy scaling relationships and weakened norm-loss monotonicity. Appendices C and F add substantive qualifications about stochasticity, approximate homogeneity, smoothed margins, and the lack of direct theoretical applicability to regression or alternative losses.

D1.justification: Appendix D supplies batch sizes, training budgets, normalization and augmentation recipes, the natural-image 80/20 validation split, transformer warmup, and label-smoothing settings. V1 instead refers readers to an appendix absent from the supplied file. V2 also adds pseudocode and a code-availability statement with a repository link. These are substantial documentation additions; the PDFs do not establish corresponding changes to the underlying retained training settings.

E1.justification: The original small-data, MedMNIST, CIFAR, TinyImageNet, and transfer-learning coverage is retained. V2 adds a bounded FashionMNIST classification experiment using LeNet300-100, also testing selection over learning rate and initialization scale. The reported increase from 34 to 37 configurations does not itself establish additional dataset coverage.

E2.justification: V2 adds an evaluated worst-case m-sharpness selection baseline across eight dataset-model settings in Section 4.1 and Table 1. It removes the standalone minimum-training-loss baseline SelTS from the benchmark tables and overview comparison. Oracle and SelVS remain principal comparators, substantially changing the validation-free comparison set.

E3.justification: New protocols include m-sharpness evaluation using 2,048 training examples, batches of 128, 20 ascent steps, perturbation radius 0.05, and a 15% training-accuracy filter. The FashionMNIST experiment uses full-batch gradient descent and an initialization-scale sweep. Grid robustness changes from regular interval slicing to randomly removing 20–80% of configurations. Newly supplied settings for retained benchmarks are documentation additions, not evidence that those experiments were rerun.

E4.justification: V1's Quickshift-parameter ablation disappears, while v2 adds separability-threshold sensitivity and replaces regular grid-density tests with random-sparsity analysis. It also adds scaling-law goodness-of-fit analyses, configuration-wise accuracy distributions, and transfer-learning loss/norm diagnostics. Early-stopping and optimizer analyses are retained with revisions; transfer learning is partly relocated rather than newly introduced.

E5.justification: V2 explicitly repeats random grid removal across 50 seeds and displays the resulting MAE distributions in Figure 6, adding uncertainty reporting to the grid-robustness analysis. This is a localized addition; neither PDF supplies comparable repeated-training uncertainty estimates for the principal benchmark tables.

E6.justification: Under the retained reported small-data settings, Twin's EN-B0 average changes from 71.3% to 69.5%, RN50 from 75.5% to 76.2%, and RNX101 from 75.4% to 75.6%. Medical accuracy changes from 82.9% to 83.1%. V2 adds sharpness-comparison, FashionMNIST, threshold, sparsity, and scaling-fit results. The natural-image table omits two RN20 rows, preventing direct comparison of its aggregate means. V2 also changes RNX101's Oracle EuroSAT score from 88.6% to 90.0% while retaining an inconsistent 75.9% average.

M1.justification: V1 selects the minimum-norm model within a training-loss region identified using outlier filtering, normalization, and Quickshift segmentation. V2 replaces this central procedure with an accuracy-based rule: select the minimum-norm model among configurations exceeding 99% training accuracy, or select minimum training loss if none qualifies. Section 3.3 and Algorithm 1 therefore describe an actual algorithm change.

P1.justification: The abstract, introduction, method narrative, experimental interpretations, and conclusion are extensively rewritten. V2 introduces a separate problem-definition section, moves related work after experiments, organizes evaluations by comparison type, and relocates most transfer-learning discussion to Appendix E. The title and terminology also change substantially.

P2.justification: V2 redraws the overview diagram, replaces the segmentation-pipeline presentation with Algorithm 1, and introduces numerous scaling, sensitivity, and distribution plots. Benchmark tables gain model-class, win-count, or difference fields and lose SelTS entries. The transfer-learning figure is relocated and updated. Wider pages and text wrapping around figures and tables substantially alter the layout.

R1.justification: The primary grounding shifts from Liu et al.'s learning-phase framework to Lyu and Li's margin-maximization results and research on optimization regimes and loss-to-loss scaling. V2 substantially expands positioning against generalization-gap prediction, sharpness-based selection, and validation-free early stopping in Sections 2 and 5, replacing much of v1's image-classification-centered related-work discussion.

T1.justification: V2 adds a formal HPO formulation, homogeneous-network margin definitions and bounds, an assumed train-test power-law relationship, and derivative and critical-point analyses in Sections 2–3. These substantially replace v1's qualitative learning-phase rationale. improvement.justification: V2 substantially improves reproducibility and scrutiny of the selection rule through Algorithm 1, the implementation details missing from the supplied v1, the sharpness comparison, and threshold, sparsity, and scaling-fit analyses. A1.justification: Both PDFs describe the same Twin research and provide readable methods, experiments, equations, and figures. V2 includes Appendices A–G; the unavailable earlier supplemental details limit that part of the comparison.

after.justification: V2 reports original benchmark results, a FashionMNIST experiment, sharpness comparisons, sensitivity analyses, and scaling-law fits in the main text and appendices.

arxiv_record.abstract: Federated Learning (FL) has garnered increasing attention due to its unique characteristic of allowing heterogeneous clients to process their private data locally and interact with a central server, while being respectful of privacy. A critical bottleneck in FL is the communication cost. A pivotal strategy to mitigate this burden is Local Training, which involves running multiple local stochastic gradient descent iterations between communication phases. Our work is inspired by the innovative Scaffnew algorithm, which has considerably advanced the reduction of communication complexity in FL. We introduce FedComLoc (Federated Compressed and Local Training), integrating practical and effective compression into Scaffnew to further enhance communication efficiency. Extensive experiments, using the popular TopK compressor and quantization, demonstrate its prowess in substantially reducing communication overheads in heterogeneous settings.
arxiv_record.authors: Kai Yi, Georg Meinhardt, Laurent Condat, Peter Richt\'arik
arxiv_record.comments: Accepted version at Transactions on Machine Learning Research (TMLR)
arxiv_record.title: FedComLoc: Communication-Efficient Distributed Training of Sparse and Quantized Models

arxiv_record.abstract: Unitarity is a useful principle for stabilizing deep neural networks, but in graph neural networks (GNNs) instability is induced not only by learnable parameters but also by the graph propagation operator. Motivated by this distinction, we propose Graph Unitary Message Passing (GUMP), a message-passing framework that uses a unitary propagation operator on a transformed graph to avoid graph-induced exponential decay under repeated propagation. GUMP combines (i) a graph transformation that maps an input graph to an Eulerian line-graph construction admitting unitary adjacency matrices, and (ii) a practical unitary projection procedure based on Newton-Schulz iteration. Theoretical analysis clarifies that, under standard analysis assumptions, unitary propagation keeps the graph-propagation term depth-stable, while vanilla normalized propagation exhibits exponential decay in its non-trivial spectral components. Across synthetic long-range tasks, TUDataset benchmarks, and LRGB datasets, GUMP improves over vanilla message passing and achieves competitive or superior performance against strong baselines. Code is available at https://github.com/ucker/gump_code.
arxiv_record.authors: Haiquan Qiu, Quanming Yao
arxiv_record.title: Graph Unitary Message Passing

C2.justification: v2 explicitly states that row-energy conservation guarantees neither individual source-target influence nor a depth-invariant full Jacobian. It qualifies the Jacobian plots as directionally consistent with the theory rather than direct validation of its quantity. Limitations now analyze degree-sensitive expansion costs and the exact-theory/finite-iteration gap, supported by numerical diagnostics and runtime evidence, substantially extending v1's brief computational caveats.

D1.justification: v2 adds a code-availability URL and specifies the previously abstract Scatter operation as an incoming-edge mean, with zero output for isolated nodes. It supplies synthetic-task hyperparameters, numerical-diagnostic initialization and tolerance, CPU information, and training-time/batching details. Shared benchmark hyperparameter rows largely persist. The iteration budget used for the main accuracy results remains unspecified.

E1.justification: v2 adds CrossedRing, Ring, and CliquePath synthetic tasks, ogbg-molhiv molecular classification, and Cora/Citeseer node classification. E3.justification: New protocols include synthetic distances 4–28 with depth tied to distance, official scaffold-split ROC-AUC evaluation on ogbg-molhiv, block diagnostics at tolerance 10^-7 with five versus ten projection iterations, and runtime comparisons with matched propagated-node budgets. LRGB now references the Tönshoff evaluation protocol and flags Kiani et al.'s different setup; common TU split proportions and listed hyperparameters are retained.

E4.justification: Appendix D.1 adds substantial tests of block rank, conditioning, and finite-step projection accuracy using random continuous representations. v2 also adds synthetic distance stress tests, extends depth/Jacobian analyses, compares ADGN and Drew's Jacobian behavior, and measures computational overhead under two batching controls. arxiv_record.abstract: Compound identification from tandem mass spectrometry (MS/MS) data is a critical step in the analysis of complex mixtures. Typical solutions for the MS/MS spectrum to compound (MS2C) problem involve comparing the unknown spectrum against a library of known spectrum-molecule pairs, an approach that is limited by incomplete library coverage. Compound to MS/MS spectrum (C2MS) models can improve retrieval rates by augmenting real libraries with predicted MS/MS spectra. Unfortunately, many existing C2MS models suffer from problems with mass accuracy, generalization, or interpretability. We develop a new probabilistic method for C2MS prediction, FraGNNet, that can efficiently and accurately simulate MS/MS spectra with high mass accuracy. Our approach formulates the C2MS problem as learning a distribution over molecule fragments. FraGNNet achieves state-of-the-art performance in terms of prediction error and surpasses existing C2MS models as a tool for retrieval-based MS2C.

arxiv_record.abstract:
Unstructured pruning is a popular compression method for efficiently reducing model parameters. However, while it effectively decreases the number of parameters, it is commonly believed that unstructured pruning cannot shorten the computational critical path, i.e., the maximum number of layers traversed during forward propagation.
  In this paper, we study when and how unstructured pruning can yield structural effects. For rectifier-activated networks, we introduce the notion of neuron entropy, which quantifies the degree of nonlinearity utilization. We show that magnitude-based pruning naturally lowers this entropy, sometimes down to zero-entropy layers that become linearizable and can thus be removed. Building on this insight, we propose a method that leverages "unstructured" pruning to favor sparsity in low-entropy layers, enabling their complete removal. We validate the phenomenon across CNNs, Vision Transformers, and NLP models: unstructured pruning can induce effective layer removal with little or no performance degradation in over-parameterized networks.
arxiv_record.authors: Zhu Liao, Victor Qu\'etu, Van-Tam Nguyen, Enzo Tartaglione
arxiv_record.title: Layer Collapse Can be Induced by Unstructured Pruning

arxiv_record.abstract:
We propose Soft Preference Optimization (SPO), a method for aligning
generative models, such as Large Language Models (LLMs), with human
preferences, without the need for a reward model. SPO optimizes model outputs
directly over a preference dataset through a natural loss function that
integrates preference loss with a regularization term across the model's entire
output distribution rather than limiting it to the preference dataset. Although
SPO does not require the assumption of an existing underlying reward model, we
demonstrate that, under the Bradley-Terry (BT) model assumption, it converges
to a softmax of scaled rewards, with the distribution's "softness" adjustable
via the softmax exponent, an algorithm parameter. We showcase SPO's
methodology, its theoretical foundation, and its comparative advantages in
simplicity, computational efficiency, and alignment precision.

Arsalan Sharifnassab, Saber Salehkaleybar, Sina Ghiassian, Surya
  Kanoria, Dale Schuurmans

C1.justification: The abstract drops v1's claim of comparative computational efficiency. The central abstract and introduction claims remain: reward-model-free alignment, global regularization, and adjustable softmax convergence under the BT assumption. The technical extensions do not substantially rewrite this central framing.

C2.justification: V4 Section 9 explicitly identifies unexamined dependence on dataset size and preference-label noise, and learning from implicit preferences as future work. Computational overhead from online sampling and the token-wise KL bias–variance tradeoff were already discussed in v1 Section 5 and Appendix B.

D1.justification: V4 newly documents accelerator configurations, including four H100 GPUs for AlpacaFarm and A100 GPUs for TinyStories, gradient accumulation, method-specific hyperparameter ranges, ranking-weight decay settings, and four-story labeling and filtering instructions (Appendices D–E). The existing practice of generating 32 regularization samples every eight steps is retained for TinyStories.

E1.justification: V1 evaluates pairwise preference alignment on TinyStories-derived stories. V4 adds AlpacaFarm question answering evaluated through AlpacaEval 2, and replaces the pairwise story experiment with four-story ranking and best-of-n alignment tasks (Sections 7.1–7.2).

E2.justification: Beyond v1's DPO comparison, v4 evaluates IPO, KTO, CPO, R-DPO, and SimPO alongside DPO on AlpacaFarm (Table 1). The story comparisons add S-DPO and Best-response-SFT; Table 2 evaluates a ranking adaptation of DPO, while Table 3 does not include DPO.

E3.justification: The story experiments change from GPT3.5-Turbo labeling and evaluation to GPT4o-2024-08-06, approximately 100,000 retained pairs to 5,000 four-story groups, and batches of 128 pairs to 32 groups. The win-rate opponent changes from the pretrained model to Best-response-SFT. The new question-answering protocol uses Llama2-7B, four training epochs, GPT4-Turbo evaluation, and both conventional and length-controlled win rates.

E4.justification: V1 Figure 1 compares weighting choices and DPO regularization coefficients over training. V4 removes those trajectories and adds a controlled comparison of global KL against three dataset-restricted regularizers (Table 4). Weighting analyses extend to question answering, ranking, and best-of-n alignment, including a reported lack of benefit for ranking.

E5.justification: V1 averages story win rates over 1,000 pairs without quantifying their estimation uncertainty. E6.justification: V1's 72% SPO versus 68% DPO peak win rates and subsequent training trajectories are replaced by results under different settings. arxiv_record.abstract: We present a generative model that amortises computation for the field and potential around e.g.~gravitational or electromagnetic sources. Exact numerical calculation has either computational complexity $\mathcal{O}(M\times{}N)$ in the number of sources $M$ and evaluation points $N$, or requires a fixed evaluation grid to exploit fast Fourier transforms. Using an architecture where a hypernetwork produces an implicit representation of the field or potential around a source collection, our model instead performs as $\mathcal{O}(M + N)$, achieves relative error of $\sim\!4\%-6\%$, and allows evaluation at arbitrary locations for arbitrary numbers of sources, greatly increasing the speed of e.g.~physics simulations. We compare with existing models and develop two-dimensional examples, including cases where sources overlap or have more complex geometries, to demonstrate its application.
arxiv_record.authors: Berian James and Stefan Pollok and Ignacio Peis and Elizabeth Louise Baker and Jes Frellsen and Rasmus Bj{\o}rk
arxiv_record.title: Scalable physical source-to-field inference with hypernetworks

arxiv_record.abstract: In this work, we propose Salient Sparse Federated Learning (SSFL), a streamlined approach for sparse federated learning with efficient communication. SSFL identifies a sparse subnetwork prior to training, leveraging parameter saliency scores computed separately on local client data in non-IID scenarios, and then aggregated, to determine a global mask. Only the sparse model weights are trained and communicated each round between the clients and the server. On standard benchmarks including CIFAR-10, CIFAR-100, and Tiny-ImageNet, SSFL consistently improves the accuracy sparsity trade off, achieving more than 20\% relative error reduction on CIFAR-10 compared to the strongest sparse baseline, while reducing communication costs by $2 \times$ relative to dense FL. Finally, in a real-world federated learning deployment, SSFL delivers over $2.3 \times$ faster communication time, underscoring its practical efficiency.

C2.justification: V2 develops structural alignment as a stronger explanation for shared-mask performance, adds minibatch-sufficiency and warmup/client-drift interpretations, and extensively argues for hardware-acceleration compatibility. D1.justification: V2 adds a code-access link, the K=100 benchmark-client count, layer-specific Kaiming initialization details, explicit communication-accounting assumptions, and baseline adaptation information. E1.justification: The CIFAR-10, CIFAR-100 and TinyImageNet datasets and existing non-IID scenarios remain. V2 adds a bounded new scenario within CIFAR-10: training initially on classes 0–7, then admitting clients with previously unseen classes 8–9 (Appendix A.6). This extends coverage to novel-class arrival without adding another dataset or domain.

E2.justification: V2 Table 1 adds evaluated SparsyFed and Flash comparisons on CIFAR-10/100 Dirichlet partitions. FedPM is added to the CIFAR-100 comparison, including Figure 2(b), while its CIFAR-10 pathological result from v1 Table 1 is omitted. FedAvg and Random also gain entries in corresponding benchmark tables. These substantially expand and revise the actual comparator set.

E3.justification: V2 introduces ResNet-50 evaluation across 50–95% sparsity, an oracle-mask comparison using 1–400 minibatches, and a warmup control with 10 dense rounds evaluated at the same total 500 rounds. Its OOD protocol introduces held-out-class clients at round 225. These are substantial new evaluation designs; the original benchmark partition parameters and core training hyperparameters are retained.

E4.justification: V2 adds analyses testing minibatch sufficiency against a full-training-set oracle, sensitivity to initialization versus dense warmup, and adaptation after distribution shift. The earlier permutation, global/local random-mask, longer-training and heterogeneous-client analyses are largely retained or rearranged. However, v1 Appendix A.3's separate saliency-based local-mask experiment reporting 70.22% accuracy is removed.

E5.justification: V1's main accuracy tables contain point estimates. V2 adds explicit five-run reporting, ± quantities in Tables 1–2, random-seed information, and error bars or standard-deviation bands in mask analyses. TinyImageNet FOMO is identified as a single run that failed to converge. V1 already reported uncertainty for communication times. The new run-count disclosures do not establish that more runs were performed than in v1.

E6.justification: V2 adds substantial results for ResNet-50, oracle-mask estimation, warmup and OOD adaptation; Table 3 reports 47.53% for SSFL versus 12.04% for DisPFL at 95% sparsity. Original headline SSFL benchmark accuracies remain unchanged. FedPM's reported CIFAR-10 Dirichlet accuracy changes from 57.30% to 46.44%, and SubFedAvg's CIFAR-10 communication figure changes from 278.8 to 346.6 MB. Deployment timing values are also revised, rather than merely replotted.

M1.justification: V2 adds one-shot OOD adaptation: clients recompute saliency using trained active weights and original initializations for inactive weights, then refresh the shared mask and resume training (Section 4.3, Algorithm 2). This substantially extends v1's fixed-mask procedure. The stated Algorithm 1 also changes initialization from averaging client initializations to server initialization, and model aggregation from equal averaging to data-size weighting.

P1.justification: The introduction, contribution list, method exposition and conclusion are extensively rewritten. The standalone preliminaries section disappears, much of the original related work moves to Appendix B, and experiments are reorganized into explicit benchmark and analysis subsections. The title and publication formatting also change. The narrative restructuring is substantial independently of added scientific content.

P2.justification: V2 redraws Figure 1, reorganizes the original dataset tables into partition-based tables, and replaces the communication-time table with a model-size plot. Existing convergence plots are merged, and client-performance plots move into a composite main-text figure. New oracle/OOD plots and ResNet-50, warmup and cost-analysis tables substantially change the visual presentation beyond numerical updates.

R1.justification: V2 substantially updates positioning around dynamic, structured and initialization-pruning FL, discussing additional work such as SparsyFed, FedPaI and HeteroFL. Appendix B retains much of v1's historical survey while expanding sparse language-model coverage and acknowledging earlier related gradient-aggregation and neuroimaging work. This goes well beyond relocating references or updating bibliographic metadata.

T1.justification: The connection-saliency derivation remains mathematically equivalent despite substantial rewriting. V2 Appendices A.3–A.4 add computational-complexity and communication-cost derivations, including fixed-mask 4sP-byte transmission versus 8sP for COO and 4sP+P/8 for bitmasks. This is a limited analytical extension; the new oracle-mask convergence evidence is empirical, not a convergence proof.

improvement.justification: V1 provided little direct validation of minibatch sufficiency or the decision to avoid warmup, and omitted run counts for benchmark accuracies. V2 substantially addresses these gaps through oracle-mask and warmup experiments, uncertainty reporting, and broader baseline and larger-model comparisons. These strengthen support for the central design. The gains outweigh shortcomings, including removal of the local-saliency-mask experiment, absence of a no-refresh OOD control, and new numerical inconsistencies such as Table 3's 23.21-point gap being described as 24.39 points in the text.

A1.justification: Both PDFs describe SSFL despite the changed title. Their complete main texts, equations, tables, figures and appendices are readable and support reliable matching of retained, revised and added material.

after.justification: V2 retains original benchmark experiments and adds ResNet-50, oracle-mask estimation, warmup and distribution-shift results in Section 4 and Appendix A.

before.justification: V1 reports original federated classification experiments, mask analyses and geographically distributed communication-time measurements in Section 5 and Appendix A.

arxiv_record.abstract: When applying deep learning models in open-world scenarios, active learning (AL) strategies are crucial for identifying label candidates from a nearly infinite amount of unlabeled data. In this context, robust out-of-distribution (OOD) detection mechanisms are essential for handling data outside the target distribution of the application. However, current works investigate both problems separately. In this work, we introduce SISOM as the first unified solution for both AL and OOD detection. By leveraging feature space distance metrics SISOM combines the strengths of the currently independent tasks to solve both effectively. We conduct extensive experiments showing the problems arising when migrating between both tasks. In these evaluations SISOM underlined its effectiveness by achieving first place in two of the widely used OpenOOD benchmarks and second place in the remaining one. In AL, SISOM outperforms others and delivers top-1 performance in three benchmarks
arxiv_record.authors: Sebastian Schmidt, Leonard Schenk, Leo Schwinn, Stephan G\"unnemann
arxiv_record.title: A Unified Approach Towards Active Learning and Out-of-Distribution Detection
