arxiv_record.abstract: Traditional offline reinforcement learning (RL) methods predominantly operate in a batch-constrained setting. This confines the algorithms to a specific state-action distribution present in the dataset, reducing the effects of distributional shift but restricting the policy to seen actions. In this paper, we alleviate this limitation by introducing state-constrained offline RL, a novel framework that focuses solely on the dataset's state distribution. This approach allows the policy to take high-quality out-of-distribution actions that lead to in-distribution states, significantly enhancing learning potential. The proposed setting not only broadens the learning horizon but also improves the ability to combine different trajectories from the dataset effectively, a desirable property inherent in offline RL. Our research is underpinned by theoretical findings that pave the way for subsequent advancements in this area. Additionally, we introduce StaCQ, a deep learning algorithm that achieves state-of-the-art performance on the D4RL benchmark datasets and aligns with our theoretical propositions. StaCQ establishes a strong baseline for forthcoming explorations in this domain.

arxiv_record.abstract: Deep learning models benefit from rich (e.g., multi-modal) input features. However, multimodal models might be challenging to deploy, because some inputs may be missing at inference. Current popular solutions include marginalization, imputation, and training multiple models. Marginalization achieves calibrated predictions, but it is computationally expensive and only feasible for low dimensional inputs. Imputation may result in inaccurate predictions, particularly when high-dimensional data, such as images, are missing. Training multiple models, where each model is designed to handle different subsets of inputs, can work well but requires prior knowledge of missing input patterns. Furthermore, training and retaining multiple models can be costly. We propose an efficient method to learn both the conditional distribution using full inputs and the marginal distributions. Our method, Knockout, randomly replaces input features with appropriate placeholder values during training. We provide a theoretical justification for Knockout and show that it can be interpreted as an implicit marginalization strategy. We evaluate Knockout across a wide range of simulations and real-world datasets and show that it offers strong empirical performance.
arxiv_record.authors: Minh Nguyen, Batuhan K. Karaman, Heejong Kim, Alan Q. Wang, Fengbei Liu, Mert R. Sabuncu
arxiv_record.title: Knockout: A simple way to handle missing inputs

P2.justification: v3 changes typography, author layout, spacing, and table organization throughout. Regression plots expand to three panels with larger comparator legends; the tree table gains backbone groups. New summary, ablation, and Food-101 displays are added, Buffalo's table is removed, and the Gaussian illustration and placeholder sweep move into the main text.

R1.justification: v3 substantially expands positioning against imputation theory and supervised missing-data research, including Josse, Bertsimas, Le Morvan, and Ipsen. T1.justification: v3 corrects reversed mask states in Section 2.2's marginalization identity and Appendix A.2's derivation. improvement.justification: v3 substantially strengthens evaluation of the unchanged method: its much broader regression comparisons address v1's limited comparator coverage, while controlled MNAR, training-size, and augmentation controls directly examine important assumptions. A1.justification: Both PDFs describe the same Knockout method and corresponding experiments. Their text, equations, tables, figures, and complete appendices are readable and support reliable comparison, including identifying relocated material.

after.justification: v3 retains original empirical results and adds further simulations, ablations, model configurations, and text-image classification experiments on UPMC Food-101.

before.justification: v1 reports original regression and classification simulations and experiments on Alzheimer's forecasting, noisy-label learning, tumor segmentation, tree classification, and prostate cancer detection, including appendix results.

arxiv_record.abstract: Adapting models to dynamic, real-world environments characterized by shifting data distributions and unseen test scenarios is a critical challenge in deep learning. In this paper, we consider a realistic and challenging Test-Time Adaptation setting, where a model must continuously adapt to test samples that arrive sequentially, one at a time, while distinguishing between known and unknown classes. Current Test-Time Adaptation methods operate under closed-set assumptions or batch processing, differing from the real-world open-set scenarios. We address this limitation by establishing a comprehensive benchmark for {\em Open-set Single-image Test-Time Adaptation using Vision-Language Models}. Furthermore, we propose ROSITA, a novel framework that leverages dynamically updated feature banks to identify reliable test samples and employs a contrastive learning objective to improve the separation between known and unknown classes. Our approach effectively adapts models to domain shifts for known classes while rejecting unfamiliar samples. Extensive experiments across diverse real-world benchmarks demonstrate that ROSITA sets a new state-of-the-art in open-set TTA, achieving both strong performance and computational efficiency for real-time deployment. Our code can be found at the project site https://manogna-s.github.io/rosita/
arxiv_record.authors: Manogna Sreenivas, Soma Biswas
arxiv_record.title: Efficient Open Set Single Image Test Time Adaptation of Vision Language Models

E2.justification: V1's main comparisons use ZS-Eval, TPT, TPT-C, and the MaPLe-based PAlign variants. V2 Tables 1–3 additionally evaluate (K+1)PC, UniEnt, TDA, and DPE on retained benchmarks. arxiv_record.abstract: Recurrent neural networks (RNNs) are a widely used tool for sequential data analysis; however, they are still often seen as black boxes. Visualizing the internal dynamics of RNNs is a critical step toward understanding their functional principles and developing better architectures and optimization strategies. Prior studies typically emphasize network representations only after training, overlooking how those representations evolve during learning. Here, we present Multiway Multislice PHATE (MM-PHATE), a graph-based embedding method for visualizing the evolution of RNN hidden states across the multiple dimensions spanned by RNNs: time, training epoch, and units. Across controlled synthetic benchmarks and real RNN applications, MM-PHATE preserves hidden-representation community structure among units and reveals training-phase changes in representation geometry. In controlled synthetic systems spanning multiple bifurcation families and smooth state-space warps, MM-PHATE recovers qualitative dynamical progression while distinguishing family-level differences. In task-trained RNNs, the embedding identifies information-processing and compression-related phases during training, and time-resolved geometric and entropy-based summaries align with linear probes, time-step ablations, and label--state mutual information. These results show that MM-PHATE provides an intuitive and comprehensive way to inspect RNN hidden dynamics across training and to better understand how model architecture and learning dynamics relate to performance.

C1.justification: The abstract, contributions, and conclusion add claims about recovering bifurcation progression, distinguishing dynamical families under tested warps, and agreement with independent task-information diagnostics. Broad uniqueness and information-bottleneck conclusions are narrowed toward empirical geometric findings within the studied settings.

C2.justification: v2 explicitly interprets embedding entropy as geometric dispersion rather than direct representation information. It develops explanations distinguishing early-step label-irrelevant variability from later task-relevant structure, and adds substantive qualifications about non-invariance to smooth warps, descriptive clustering, and entropy distances not uniquely measuring representation quality.

D1.justification: Appendices A.1–A.10 substantially expand dataset statistics, preprocessing, sampling, embedding parameters, synthetic generation, and diagnostic procedures. Examples include t-SNE perplexity 50 and 2000 iterations, LLE/UMAP configurations, and explicit synthetic integration settings. These disclosures do not establish reruns of existing experiments. v1's promised future code release is removed without replacement access information.

E1.justification: v2 retains Area2Bump and HAR but adds controlled Hopf and Pitchfork synthetic datasets, dynamic-versus-static controls, and clean-versus-warped scenarios (Section 5.1; Appendix A.5). Label-corruption and sequence-masking experiments also introduce new test conditions on Area2Bump.

E2.justification: The Area2Bump comparisons expand from PCA, t-SNE, and Isomap to include LLE and UMAP in visualizations, entropy analyses, and quantitative comparisons. Appendix A.4 additionally evaluates a final-time-step baseline labeled M-PHATE, which v1 discussed but did not experimentally compare.

E3.justification: v2 adds neighborhood-overlap evaluation on shared sampling grids, time-resolved logistic-regression probes, fixed-weight sequence masking around time-step 350, and per-unit label-MI estimation. New experiments include 10–50-unit LSTM comparisons and 100-unit label-shuffling models. These are additional protocols; the retained main LSTM training configurations are unchanged.

E4.justification: New analyses test whether embeddings recover known bifurcations, tolerate smooth warps and tanh readouts, preserve neighborhoods, and reflect task-relevant information through probes, masking, and MI. Random-label stress tests, network-size sensitivity, and quantitative HAR geometry analyses substantially extend v1's entropy, clustering, and architecture comparisons.

E5.justification: Appendix A.10 specifies 10 independent class-permutation configurations per shuffle level, and Figures A.35–A.36 add regression fits, R-squared values, and p-values. Fixed-seed information is also newly provided for some embedding procedures. Statistical reporting remains localized rather than extending repeated-run uncertainty to the retained main comparisons.

E6.justification: v2 adds numerical neighborhood scores and findings from synthetic controls, probes, ablations, label corruption, and HAR geometry. Table 1 reports intra-step k=5 preservation of 0.621 for MM-PHATE versus 0.417 for PCA; LLE instead leads inter-step k=5, 0.812 versus 0.794. Table 3 also places t-SNE above MM-PHATE at intra-step k=15. The original Area2Bump and HAR validation accuracies, 74% and 84%, are retained.

M1.justification: The MM-PHATE procedure remains the same: standardized activation tensors, intra-step and same-unit inter-step affinities, kernel symmetrization, row normalization, and PHATE embedding. Added diagnostics and implementation explanations do not establish a change to the embedding algorithm.

P1.justification: The abstract, introduction, and retained empirical discussions are extensively rewritten. Results adopt a synthetic-validation-then-application narrative, limitations are integrated into the conclusion, and the supplement is reorganized into thematic appendices with expanded explanations and a notation section.

P2.justification: v2 adds extensive synthetic, diagnostic, and statistical figures plus quantitative tables. Existing Area2Bump comparison panels expand to include LLE and UMAP; the kernel schematic and dataset-PCA figure move to the appendix. Retained architecture figures are relocated, and typography, author layout, and figure sizing change substantially.

R1.justification: v2 adds targeted literature on LLE, UMAP, conditional entropy bottlenecks, and smooth dynamical comparisons, including Chen et al., Friedman et al., and Sagodi and Park in Appendix A.5, while removing several references. The central positioning as an extension of M-PHATE for joint time-step and epoch visualization remains intact.

T1.justification: v2 removes v1's mathematical argument linking the analyzed entropy directly to retained input information through determinism. It adds formal synthetic-system and warp definitions and constructs unit-balanced temporal trajectories, bounded signed-flow alignment, and a composite epoch-change metric (Appendices A.5 and A.14). The core kernel equations remain unchanged, and no invariance theorem is established.

improvement.justification: v2 substantially addresses v1's reliance on visual impressions and insufficiently justified entropy interpretations through controlled simulations, quantitative neighborhood comparisons, and independent probes and ablations. Clearer conceptual qualifications and implementation documentation strengthen validity and reproducibility. These gains outweigh new reporting problems, including Table 3's exception to the claimed unchanged rankings and Figure A.23's contradictory interpretation of latent versus embedded entropy transitions.

A1.justification: Both PDFs describe the same MM-PHATE work and contain readable main texts, equations, figures, and appendices. Retained methods and experiments can be matched despite extensive additions, rewriting, and renumbering.

after.justification: v2 retains original empirical results and adds synthetic dynamical-system simulations, quantitative embedding comparisons, probes, ablations, and robustness experiments.

before.justification: v1 reports original Area2Bump and HAR experiments, including trained-network visualizations, entropy analyses, cluster-based subnetworks, and supplementary GRU and vanilla-RNN results.

arxiv_record.abstract: Machine unlearning offers effective solutions for revoking the influence of specific training data on pre-trained model parameters. While existing approaches address unlearning for classification and generative models, they overlook an important category of machine learning models: contrastive learning (CL) methods. This paper addresses this gap by introducing the Machine Unlearning for Contrastive Learning (MUC) framework and adapting existing methods. We identify limitations in current approaches, noting that several methods perform inadequately as unlearners and that existing evaluation tools insufficiently validate unlearning effects in contrastive learning. To address these issues, we propose Alignment Calibration (AC), a novel method that explicitly considers contrastive learning properties and optimizes towards new auditing metrics for easy verification of unlearning. Through empirical comparisons with baseline methods on SimCLR, MoCo, and CLIP, we demonstrate that AC: (1) achieves state-of-the-art performance, approximating exact unlearning (retraining); (2) enables data owners to clearly visualize unlearning effects through black-box evaluation. The code is available at https://github.com/EhanW/Alignment-Calibration.
arxiv_record.authors: Yihan Wang, Yiwei Lu, Guojun Zhang, Franziska Boenisch, Adam Dziedzic, Yaoliang Yu, Xiao-Shan Gao

arxiv_record.abstract: Autoregressive language models have demonstrated a remarkable ability to extract latent structure from text. The embeddings from large language models have been shown to capture aspects of the syntax and semantics of language. But what should embeddings represent? We connect the autoregressive prediction objective to the idea of constructing predictive sufficient statistics to summarize the information contained in a sequence of observations, and use this connection to identify three settings where the optimal content of embeddings can be identified: independent identically distributed data, where the embedding should capture the sufficient statistics of the data; latent state models, where the embedding should encode the posterior distribution over states given the data; and discrete hypothesis spaces, where the embedding should reflect the posterior distribution over hypotheses given the data. We then conduct empirical probing studies to show that transformers encode these three kinds of latent generating distributions, and that they perform well in out-of-distribution cases and without token memorization in these settings.
arxiv_record.authors: Liyi Zhang, Michael Y. Li, R. Thomas McCoy, Theodore R. Sumers, Jian-Qiao Zhu, Thomas L. Griffiths
arxiv_record.title: What Should Embeddings Embed? Autoregressive Models Represent Latent Generating Distributions

C1.justification: V1's central claim concerns predictive sufficient statistics demonstrated through simple synthetic processes. V2's abstract and introduction extend the contribution to topic structure embedded in partially exchangeable sequences and pretrained language models on natural corpora. This materially broadens the claimed applicability while retaining the original framework.

C2.justification: V2 revises the HMM interpretation to acknowledge current-state sufficiency and explain next-state preference through output-layer computations. It adds interpretations concerning embedding parsimony, semantic proportion and masked-objective expressivity. V1's explicit limitations concerning simple likelihoods and hierarchical extensions are replaced by broader applications and future directions.

D1.justification: V2 adds a code-availability link, new generative-process descriptions, corpus split sizes, model parameter counts, GPU assignments and tuning ranges with selected settings in Tables 9–12. Reproducibility information is substantially expanded, although Section 4.3's 100-word topic documents are not reconciled with Appendix A.3's general 500-token statement.

E1.justification: V2 retains the original synthetic tasks and adds LDA-generated documents, partially exchangeable HMM-LDA sequences, and topic-mixture recovery on 20Newsgroups and WikiText-103. This substantially extends coverage to mixed semantic/syntactic generation and natural language.

E2.justification: V2 adds explicit comparisons against BERT-tiny, LDA and a supervised word embedder in Table 3, plus comparisons among pretrained GPT-2, Llama 2 and BERT variants with a randomly initialized GPT-2 control. The retained HMM target comparisons are unchanged despite their new connection to belief-state inference.

E3.justification: The original three-layer toy-model configuration is retained. New protocols include a four-layer transformer for synthetic topics, pretrained-model evaluation with 20 or 100 LDA topics, total-variation loss, averaged versus last-token embeddings, and corpus-specific splits. Architecture sweeps additionally vary embedding width, depth and attention heads.

E4.justification: V2 adds cross-topic-model controls testing whether probes alone explain recovery, reverse prediction testing embedding parsimony, architecture sensitivity, Gamma-Exponential memorization tests, and layer/pooling analyses. It also examines semantic proportion in HMM-LDA and the topic–perplexity relationship while controlling for token position. Existing posterior-moment and Gaussian memorization analyses are retained.

E5.justification: The retained HMM and rectangle tables switch from standard deviations to standard errors while still reporting ten seeds. New topic experiments and architecture sweeps report three-seed summaries. Appendix A.4 adds mixed-effects estimation with standard errors, degrees of freedom, p-values and a collinearity diagnostic, substantially expanding statistical analysis.

E6.justification: The HMM and rectangle table means remain unchanged, but v2 adds extensive results. Table 3 reports 70.5% AT versus 46.6% BERT accuracy at alpha = 1; Table 6 reports 28.4–84.6% embedding variance explained. Natural-corpus results and updated conjugate-model curves further expand the evidence. These are newly reported or replaced results, not established v1-to-v2 performance gains.

M1.justification: The central autoregressive representation-learning and probing procedure is retained, including linear-softmax probes and nonlinear variants already present in v1. Topic applications, different model configurations and the auxiliary reverse-prediction MLP expand the experiments without revising the core learning or inference method.

P1.justification: The abstract, introduction, related work and discussion are extensively rewritten. Discrete hypotheses become a subsection of exchangeable models, their experiments merge into Section 4.1, Gaussian posterior-moment material moves to the appendix, and the conclusion becomes a separate section. This is substantial restructuring of retained material as well as expansion.

P2.justification: V2 merges rectangle schematics and selected PCA panels into Figure 3, relocates and rearranges v1's Gaussian-moment Figure 3 as appendix Figure 8, and redraws retained plots. New heatmaps, topic-mixture plots, an HMM-LDA illustration and numerous result/settings tables substantially change the visual presentation, alongside the journal layout.

R1.justification: V2 substantially expands positioning relative to mechanistic interpretability, information-bottleneck theory, belief-state inference, mixed-membership concept extraction and concurrent Bayesian accounts. It adds discussions of Shai et al., Wang et al. and Ye et al., among others. V1's citation to Zhang et al. (2023), Deep de Finetti, is absent.

T1.justification: The original exchangeability proposition and proof remain. V2 Section 3.2 additionally establishes current-state posterior sufficiency alongside next-state posterior sufficiency through Equation 3. Appendix A.1 supplies Bayesian derivations for autoregressive and masked-language-model objectives, substantially extending the mathematical treatment.

improvement.justification: V2 addresses an important limitation of v1's entirely synthetic validation by testing pretrained models on natural corpora and adding controls for probe-driven explanations. Reverse prediction, the position-controlled statistical analysis and the HMM theoretical clarification strengthen the argument. These gains outweigh reporting weaknesses, including inconsistent topic-sequence lengths, the loss of explicit limitations, and Table 7's autoregressive-superiority caption conflicting with some accuracy entries.

A1.justification: Both PDFs describe the same predictive-sufficiency framework and share identifiable experiments. All pages, including appendices, equations, tables and figures, are readable and support comparison despite substantial expansion and reorganization.

after.justification: V2 retains these empirical studies and adds original topic-model experiments, natural-corpus evaluations, controls, architecture sweeps and statistical analyses.

before.justification: V1 reports original transformer-probing experiments on conjugate distributions, hidden Markov models and rectangle hypothesis spaces, including posterior-moment, distribution-shift and memorization analyses.

arxiv_record.abstract: The design of image and video quality assessment (QA) algorithms is extremely important to benchmark and calibrate user experience in modern visual systems. A major drawback of the state-of-the-art QA methods is their limited ability to generalize across diverse image and video datasets with reasonable distribution shifts. In this work, we leverage the denoising process of diffusion models for generalized image QA (IQA) and video QA (VQA) by understanding the degree of alignment between learnable quality-aware text prompts and images or video frames. In particular, we learn cross-attention maps from intermediate layers of the denoiser of latent diffusion models (LDMs) to capture quality-aware representations of images or video frames. Since applying text-to-image LDMs for every video frame is computationally expensive for videos, we only estimate the quality of a frame-rate sub-sampled version of the original video. To compensate for the loss in motion information due to frame-rate sub-sampling, we propose a novel temporal quality modulator. Our extensive cross-database experiments across various user-generated, synthetic, low-light, frame-rate variation, ultra high definition, and streaming content-based databases show that our model can achieve superior generalization in both IQA and VQA.
arxiv_record.authors: Shankhanil Mitra, Diptanu De, Shika Rao, Rajiv Soundararajan
arxiv_record.comments: Accepted to Transactions on Machine Learning Research
arxiv_record.title: Image and Video Quality Assessment using Prompt-Guided Latent Diffusion Models for Cross-Dataset Generalization

C1.justification: The abstract, introduction, and conclusion expand the central contribution from generalized IQA to a unified image/video framework. A novel temporal quality modulator and computationally practical video assessment become explicit contributions. v1's separate contribution emphasizing adaptation with very few parameters is no longer stated.

C2.justification: v2 adds explanations of motion loss from subsampling, temporal correction, video query-weight learning, paired-prompt behavior, and preservation of distortion information through resizing and the VAE. It removes v1's explicit aspect-ratio limitation and adds edge-device and higher-resolution compute limitations. The difficulty of assessing PIPAL images remains acknowledged.

D1.justification: v2 adds a repository pointer, SlowFast pretraining and feature-dimension details, temporal-modulator implementation information, the number of diffusion cross-attention blocks, and dataset metadata tables. It also reports video runtime and parameter counts. Conversely, v1's explicit LoRA adaptation description disappears; the PDFs do not explain whether that implementation was abandoned.

E1.justification: v2 adds video assessment using LSVQ training and eleven cross-database evaluation datasets covering camera captures, frame-rate variation, Ultra-HD, gaming, and streaming. IQA coverage additionally includes SPAQ, TID2013, KADID-10K, and AIGIQA-20K. The three generated-image evaluation datasets from v1 remain represented.

E2.justification: Table 1 adds ARNIQA, QCN, and partial DP-IQA/PFD-IQA comparisons. Intra-database IQA adds LIQE, ARNIQA, QPT, QCN, LoDA, and DSMix; Appendix A.4 also directly compares LIQE under matched training data. New video comparisons include VSFA, DOVER, and ModularVQA, while generated-image comparisons add CLIP-IQA+ and IPCE.

E3.justification: The reported IQA training budget changes from 15 to 10 epochs, and inference changes from averaging eight sampled timesteps to using fixed t=50. Generated-image evaluation changes from within-dataset 80:20 splits to AIGIQA-20K training and external-dataset testing. New video protocols specify six training epochs, sparse frame processing, LSVQ training, and dataset-specific finetuning. These descriptions do not establish that retained results were rerun.

E4.justification: v2 adds controlled tests of SlowFast features versus motion cross-attention, video query-weight learning, Stable Diffusion v1.5 versus v2, distortion separability after resizing/VAE processing, and two video correction case studies. Existing prompt, resolution, denoising-step, and IQA component analyses are largely retained or relocated rather than newly introduced.

E5.justification: v1 Appendix B explicitly uses ten random splits for generated-image evaluation; its replacement in v2 Appendix A.5 specifies an official training split without reporting repeated-run estimation. Retained intra-dataset IQA still reports medians over ten splits, and video finetuning follows that existing practice. Neither version supplies confidence intervals, seed variability, or significance tests.

E6.justification: v2 adds extensive video, LIQE, backbone, and generated-image cross-database results. Reported intra-database GenzIQA SRCC/PLCC changes from 0.916/0.932 to 0.936/0.950 on KonIQ and from 0.613/0.718 to 0.627/0.728 on FLIVE. Original Table 1 dataset scores and many ablation values remain unchanged. Revised training/inference descriptions and replacement generated-image protocols prevent treating all numerical differences as same-setting improvements.

M1.justification: v2 retains the core GenzIQA attention, prompt-learning, and pooling design but introduces GenzVQA. Section 3.3 adds one-frame-per-second quality estimation and a temporal quality modulator combining diffusion features with SlowFast features. Video training also updates query weights, which remain frozen for IQA.

P1.justification: The introduction, contribution list, method narrative, and conclusion are extensively rewritten around image and video assessment. Related work is reorganized into IQA/VQA sections, analyses are consolidated under Section 4.4, and several studies move between the main text and appendices. The title and author information also change.

P2.justification: v2 redraws the main architecture diagram, adds a temporal-modulator diagram and distortion-specific visualizations, expands benchmark tables, and introduces video, efficiency, and dataset-summary tables. Existing figures and tables are also relocated or reformatted, including rearranging the noise plots and correcting the fixed-prompt column labels from v1 Table 10.

R1.justification: Related work expands substantially into video quality assessment and positions GenzVQA against feature-based, transformer, and vision-language approaches. IQA positioning now explicitly discusses recent diffusion methods such as DP-IQA, PFD-IQA, and DiffV2IQA, including differences in adaptation and computational cost.

T1.justification: Section 3.3 adds mathematical definitions for sparse-video averaging, motion cross-attention, temporal modulation, and the final video score. The underlying diffusion and IQA mathematics remains equivalent, while v1's LoRA factorization is omitted. The additions formulate the new procedure without introducing theoretical guarantees or proofs.

improvement.justification: v2 substantially strengthens validation of the central generalization claim: it supplies the previously missing LIQE comparison, replaces within-dataset generated-image testing with cross-dataset evaluation, and examines the video extension through component ablations and computational comparisons. These address important gaps in comparative and mechanistic evidence. The gains outweigh lost LoRA documentation and reporting weaknesses, including unexplained Table 1 averages and broad superiority wording that overlooks dataset-specific losses such as LIVE-IQA and LIVE-YT-Gaming.

A1.justification: Both PDFs describe the same GenzIQA research, with v2 extending it to video quality assessment. Their main text, equations, tables, figures, and appendices are readable and support a reliable comparison.

after.justification: v2 retains original IQA experiments and reports additional video-quality benchmarks, temporal-modulator ablations, backbone comparisons, and cross-database generated-image results.

before.justification: v1 reports original cross-database and intra-database IQA results, component ablations, and generated-image experiments, including those in the appendices.

arxiv_record.abstract: The rapid development of time series forecasting research has brought many deep learning-based modules in this field. However, despite the increasing amount of new forecasting architectures, it is still unclear if we have leveraged the full potential of these existing modules within a properly designed architecture. In this work, we propose a novel hierarchical neural architecture search approach for time series forecasting tasks. With the design of a hierarchical search space, we incorporate many architecture types designed for forecasting tasks and allow for the efficient combination of different forecasting architecture modules. Results on long-term-time-series-forecasting tasks show that our approach can search for lightweight high-performing forecasting architectures across different forecasting tasks.
arxiv_record.authors: Difan Deng and Marius Lindauer
arxiv_record.title: Optimizing Time Series Forecasting Architectures: A Hierarchical Neural Architecture Search Approach

C1.justification: V1 presents DARTS-TS as a proposed differentiable NAS framework. V2 centers novelty on the hierarchical search space and describes DARTS-TS as architectures obtained by applying existing DARTS-PT. Its contribution list also adds the claim that this search space has distinctive properties and challenges relative to CNN-based NAS spaces. The lightweight, competitive forecasting claim remains.

C2.justification: V2 adds substantive interpretations linking heterogeneous operations to weak zero-cost proxies, dataset-dependent architecture performance to task-specific search and transferable priors, and mixed operations to efficiency without explicitly optimizing latency. Appendix D qualifies TimesFM comparisons through reported training-data overlap. New ablation discussions address overfitting and component dependence; the original distribution-shift limitation remains.

D1.justification: V2 newly documents optimizer hyperparameters, search/training epoch budgets, gradient clipping, learning-rate restarts, and per-stage GPU costs in Appendix B. It clarifies rolling-origin evaluation and exclusion of test data from search, and provides foundation-model checkpoints, hardware, runtime limits, and sampling settings. The project repository link remains, while v1's separate baseline-license list is removed.

E1.justification: Both versions evaluate the same twelve datasets: four ETT datasets, ECL, Traffic, Weather, Exchange, and four PEMS datasets. New analyses and foundation-model comparisons reuse this coverage; they do not introduce a new forecasting domain or task.

E2.justification: V2 adds actual accuracy and efficiency comparisons against TimesFM and Moirai-MoE in Appendix D, Tables 11-12, and Figure 11. The original seven forecasting baselines remain. The component comparison also gains DARTS-TS CV and Concat Seq First controls in Table 13.

E3.justification: New protocols include sampling 3,000 architectures, a five-fold cross-validation control, horizon and optimization-epoch sweeps, and batch-one foundation-model timing. Appendix B also reports PEMS look-back windows of 96 instead of v1's 336 and specifies AdamW for small-dataset retraining rather than v1's blanket Adam description. V2 Section 6.1 still states 336 for all models, so the PEMS implementation and whether existing experiments were rerun remain unresolved.

E4.justification: Beyond v1's window-size and macro-component ablations, v2 adds search-space performance distributions, cross-dataset architecture comparisons, zero-cost-proxy correlations, and operation-presence analyses. Appendix E adds horizon transfer, cross-validation, reversed component ordering, optimization-duration sensitivity, operation removal, RevIN removal, and matched versus mixed encoder-decoder controls.

E5.justification: V1 already reports five-seed means and standard deviations and marks statistical comparability through underlining. V2 substantially expands this reporting with explicit statistics and p-values against selected best baselines in Tables 9-10 and a stated 0.05 significance threshold. The test itself is not named. Existing five-run counts remain unchanged; the new foundation-model evaluations explicitly use one seed.

E6.justification: All numerical entries in Tables 1-2 and the corresponding detailed benchmark tables are retained. V2 adds substantial new results for search-space analyses, foundation models, statistical comparisons, and ablations. Existing ECL efficiency entries also change: v1 Figure 4 reports DARTS-TS inference at 29 ms and 145 MB with 1.21 million parameters; v2 Figure 8 reports 20 ms and 119 MB with 0.831 million parameters. These are revised measurements, not an established gain for an unchanged model.

M1.justification: The proposed hierarchical search space, operation sets, forecasting heads, weighted Flat/Seq combination, differentiable search, and perturbation-based hierarchical pruning remain unchanged. Newly evaluated ablation variants and expanded implementation disclosures do not establish a revision to the proposed method.

P1.justification: The main section sequence and most retained explanatory prose persist. V2 copyedits grammar and terminology, switches to author-year citations, revises the contribution list, inserts new analytical subsections, and reorganizes the appendices. The broader-impact and license sections are removed; the existing narrative is largely preserved.

P2.justification: V2 adds distribution plots, proxy-correlation and horizon heatmaps, operation analyses, epoch-sensitivity plots, and foundation-model and encoder-decoder comparisons, alongside new cost, hyperparameter, significance, and ablation tables. The journal format changes the title block, headers, sizing, and placement. Existing architecture examples and the window-size heatmap are retained. Expanded Table 13 contains duplicated Flat Only metric columns.

R1.justification: V2 substantially expands positioning around NAS benchmarks and zero-cost proxies, adding works such as NAS-Bench-Suite-Zero, SNIP, and SynFlow. It also introduces references concerning operation importance, prior-informed search, multi-objective NAS, and Moirai-MoE. Together with the revised contribution framing, these additions position the work more explicitly as a heterogeneous search-space contribution using existing optimization methods.

T1.justification: The forecasting formulation, bilevel optimization problem, weighted prediction equation, operation definitions, and forecasting-loss formulas retain their mathematical content. V2's additional proxy and architecture discussions are empirical or intuitive; no new theorem, proof, or substantive formal derivation is introduced.

improvement.justification: V2 substantially strengthens the evidence for the central heterogeneous search-space contribution through systematic architecture sampling and targeted operation, encoder-decoder, and search-setting controls. Detailed hyperparameters, search costs, and explicit statistical results also address important reproducibility and evidential gaps in v1. The conflicting PEMS window descriptions, unspecified statistical test, and Table 13 formatting error limit clarity, but the stronger validation and technical documentation provide a substantial net quality improvement.

A1.justification: Both PDFs describe the same DARTS-TS research. Their complete main texts and appendices are readable, including equations, tables, and figures, and retained content can be matched across renumbering and relocation.

after.justification: V2 retains those empirical results and adds sampled-architecture analyses, foundation-model comparisons, statistical results, and further ablations.

before.justification: V1 reports original forecasting experiments on twelve datasets, efficiency measurements, architecture examples, and window-size and component ablations.

arxiv_record.abstract:
Frontier Large Language Models (LLMs) can be socially discriminatory or
sensitive to spurious features of their inputs. Because only well-resourced
corporations can train frontier LLMs, we need robust test-time strategies to
control such biases. Existing solutions, which instruct the LLM to be fair or
robust, rely on the model's implicit understanding of bias. Causality provides
a rich formalism through which we can be explicit about our debiasing
requirements. Yet, as we show, a naive application of the standard causal
debiasing strategy, counterfactual data augmentation, fails under standard
assumptions to debias predictions at an individual level at test time. To
address this, we develop a stratified notion of debiasing called stratified
invariance, which can capture a range of debiasing requirements from population
level to individual level through an additional measurement that stratifies the
predictions. We present a complete observational test for stratified
invariance. Finally, we introduce a data augmentation strategy that guarantees
stratified invariance at test time under suitable assumptions, together with a
prompting strategy that encourages stratified invariance in LLMs. We show that
our prompting strategy, unlike implicit instructions, consistently reduces the
bias of frontier LLMs across a suite of synthetic and real-world benchmarks
without requiring additional data, finetuning or pre-training.
arxiv_record.authors: Leonardo Cotta and Chris J. Maddison
arxiv_record.title: Test-Time Fairness and Robustness in Large Language Models

C1.justification: The central contribution shifts from OOC as a route to counterfactual-invariant predictions to a stratified-invariance framework with an observational test and test-time augmentation guarantee. The abstract, introduction, and conclusion now distinguish population guarantees from approaching individual invariance and claim empirical support for that relationship. This substantially revises the scope of the original guarantee.

C2.justification: v2 interprets the retained benchmark improvements as stratified rather than individual counterfactual invariance. It expands the existing proxy-S caveat, makes exact context recovery explicit, and identifies counterfactual conditional generation as a particularly strong LLM assumption. Section 5.2 attributes imperfect and nonmonotonic invariance to imperfect conditional sampling and explicitly distinguishes approaching individual invariance from satisfying it.

D1.justification: v2 specifies which model families use transformation temperatures 0.7 and 0.8, lists the synthetic variables in Appendix D, and adds completion and data-generation prompts in Appendix F. These are localized documentation additions. Conversely, Table 4 drops the earlier task-specific Z_list column although Prompt 13 still requires it. The temperature clarification does not establish a change to retained experimental settings.

E1.justification: The five earlier datasets remain, several under shortened names. Section 5.2 adds three controlled semantic-leakage tasks: animal preferences versus food completions, and color or food preferences versus occupation completions. Known exogenous variables and explicitly generated counterfactual inputs introduce a distinct testing scenario for individual invariance beyond the retained classification benchmarks.

E2.justification: Matched benchmark comparisons retain Default/Standard, CoT, and the same six safety prompts, including the same Amazon exclusions. The Qwen scaling study retains Default/Standard, CoT, and Precog. The new semantic-leakage study uses existing Standard and Unbiased comparators; it introduces no new comparison method.

E3.justification: Section 5.2 introduces a controlled design covering combinations of three binary exogenous variables and multiple contexts, with Claude 3.5 Sonnet generating inputs and gpt-4o-mini predicting answers. It adds CI Probability, measuring prediction agreement across counterfactual groups. The existing 200-example bias and F1 protocols remain; renaming CI_delta to SI-bias leaves their numerical computation unchanged.

E4.justification: v2 adds a direct stratification ablation comparing OOC without supplied exogenous variables and with U1, (U1,U2), and (U1,U2,U3). Figure 4 tests whether finer conditioning approaches individual counterfactual invariance and reveals an intermediate nonmonotonic result. The earlier Qwen model-size analysis is retained in Appendix E rather than newly introduced.

E5.justification: v1 explicitly identifies OOC results as means and standard deviations over three independent executions. v2 retains the same ± values but omits that explanation and run count. It additionally reports fixing seeds for the synthetic experiment. These are reporting changes, without evidence that the retained experiments used more or fewer runs.

E6.justification: All matched means and uncertainty values in Tables 1–3 are unchanged. v2 adds substantive counterfactual-invariance results: fully stratified OOC achieves CI Probability 0.75, 0.75, and 0.50 on Animal/Food, Color/Work, and Food/Work, respectively, with nonmonotonic intermediate behavior on Food/Work. It also newly summarizes the retained benchmark scores as improvements over Default in 23/27 settings.

M1.justification: v1 Algorithm 1 begins by estimating S with the LLM; v2 accepts S directly, retains estimation as a fallback, and uses supplied exogenous variables in Section 5.2. This generalizes the conditioning inputs. The obfuscation and context-addition prompts, randomized context selection, and majority-vote pipeline remain substantially unchanged.

P1.justification: The title, abstract, contribution statements, theoretical exposition, method explanation, and conclusion are extensively rewritten. Results are divided into real-world and synthetic studies; scaling moves to an appendix; the appendices are reorganized around proofs, adjustment choices, synthetic tasks, results, and prompts. Terminology also changes from explicit to implicit safety instructions and from Default to Standard prompting.

P2.justification: v2 redraws the introductory OOC diagram, replaces main-text result tables with stacked improvement plots, and replaces dataset-specific F1 scatterplots with model-specific boxplots. Retained tables and scaling plots are relocated and reformatted. It adds the stratification-results plot and causal DAG figure, and converts the earlier prompt-parameter figure into Table 4.

R1.justification: v2 substantially repositions the work around distinctions between observational, stratified, and counterfactual fairness. It adds substantive engagement with Fawkes and Evans, Silva, Quinzan and colleagues, and Plecko and Bareinboim, and revises its interpretation of Veitch and colleagues. Earlier proxy-measurement references are removed, while semantic-leakage literature supports the new experimental direction.

T1.justification: v1 Proposition 1 treats conditional independence as sufficient for almost-sure counterfactual invariance, while Proposition 2 uses a counterfactual adjustment-set assumption. v2 replaces this foundation with stratified invariance, an observational equivalence under adjustment assumptions in Lemma 1, and an augmentation guarantee under context recoverability and exact conditional sampling in Theorem 1. Appendix A supplies replacement proofs; Appendix B adds graphical adjustment reasoning.

improvement.justification: v1's Proposition 1 and Appendix A treat distributional evidence as establishing almost-sure counterfactual invariance. v2 corrects this central mismatch through stratified invariance and appropriately scoped observational and augmentation results with proofs. The controlled stratification study and clearer assumptions strengthen the connection between claims and evidence. Losing the three-run uncertainty explanation and Z_list parameter values weakens reproducibility, but these limited losses do not outweigh the substantial improvement in the validity and calibration of the central guarantee.

A1.justification: Both PDFs describe the same OOC prompting research, despite the changed title and theoretical framework. The complete main texts and appendices, including equations, figures, tables, and prompts, support reliable comparison.

after.justification: v2 retains those empirical results and adds original synthetic semantic-leakage experiments testing the effect of stratification in Section 5.2 and Figure 4.

before.justification: v1 reports original OOC-versus-baseline experiments on five datasets, including Tables 1–3 and predictive-performance and model-scaling results.

arxiv_record.abstract: Foundational Vision-Language Models (VLMs) excel across diverse tasks, but adapting them to new domains without forgetting prior knowledge remains a critical challenge. Continual Learning (CL) addresses this challenge by enabling models to learn sequentially from new data while mitigating the forgetting of prior information, typically under supervised settings involving label shift. Nonetheless, abrupt distribution shifts can still cause substantial forgetting, potentially nullifying the benefits of supervised updates, especially when storing or replaying past data is infeasible. In this work, we propose leveraging unlabeled testtime data in an unsupervised manner to reinforce prior task performance without requiring replay or stored examples. Unlike traditional Test Time Adaptation (TTA), which primarily focuses on domain shift or corruption, our method improves performance on earlier tasks by exploiting representative test samples encountered during deployment. We introduce a simple Teacher-Student framework with gradient-based sparse parameter updates, and show that it effectively mitigates forgetting in class-incremental CL for VLMs, offering a memory-free alternative to episodic replay with strong empirical results.
arxiv_record.authors: Vaibhav Singh, Rahaf Aljundi, Eugene Belilovsky
arxiv_record.title: Dual-Phase Continual Learning: Supervised Adaptation Meets Unsupervised Retention

E1.justification: The five evaluated datasets, class-incremental sequences, Aircraft-to-Cars sequence and imbalanced-stream scenario remain. v2 adds Gaussian-corrupted CIFAR100 adaptation and evaluation scenarios (Table 9). E2.justification: v2 adds evaluated SPU+Du, SPU+RMT and SparsCL+RMT comparisons (Table 4), plus FLYP, ZSCL, SLCA and SPU comparators within the existing imbalance experiment (Table 3). The standalone SL row disappears from Table 2. Finetune becoming FLYP is a matched rename, not a new baseline.

E3.justification: The reported forgetting metric changes from decline relative to accuracy immediately after learning each task to decline relative to its best earlier accuracy. v2 adds controlled data-fraction, sparsity, TTL-removal and full-test-set evaluations. E4.justification: v2 adds controls isolating dual momentum without mask union, teacher-only pseudo-labels and the TTL phase itself. New analyses examine corruption, unlabeled-data quantity, sparsity, per-task forgetting, evaluation-set choice and runtime (Table 6, Tables 9–16 and Figure 3). Momentum sensitivity and class imbalance were already studied in v1.

E5.justification: The uncertainty values accompanying long-sequence accuracies in v1 Table 3 disappear from v2 Table 5; for example, 45.01 ± 0.31 becomes 45.01. Both appendices retain averaging over five random seeds, so this is reduced uncertainty reporting, not evidence of fewer runs.

E6.justification: The main DoSAPP Table 2 scores remain unchanged, but v2 adds substantial comparison and ablation results. M1.justification: Algorithm 1 retains gradient-selected sparse updates, teacher-student pseudo-label selection, accumulated task masks, dual-momentum EMA and the CLIP loss. v2 clarifies which parameters remain frozen. P1.justification: The title, abstract, introduction, related work, method explanations and results narrative are extensively rewritten. P2.justification: v2 adds a CTTA comparison matrix, numerous experimental tables and a three-panel forgetting heatmap. R1.justification: v2 substantially expands positioning against TTA and CTTA through Table 1 and rewritten related work, including NOTE, EATA, EcoTTA, RMT, PSMT and DSS. T1.justification: The mathematical definition of forgetting changes substantively in the evaluation section, from post-learning-versus-final accuracy to best-previous-versus-final accuracy. The dual-momentum derivation is otherwise retained from Appendix A.1 as Appendix 8.1, without a new theorem or substantive proof revision.

improvement.justification: v2 addresses important gaps in v1's validation by isolating the contribution of TTL and pseudo-label selection and comparing against CL methods combined with test-time adaptation (Tables 4 and 12–14). Together with corruption and sensitivity analyses, these controls substantially strengthen support for the central retention mechanism. These gains outweigh the removed long-sequence uncertainty values and remaining reporting problems, including the inconsistent forgetting-sign explanation in Appendix 8.7.

A1.justification: Despite the changed title, both PDFs describe DoSAPP with the same authors, algorithm and core experiments. Both documents, including their appendices, are readable and support reliable comparison.

after.justification: v2 retains original DoSAPP experiments and adds adaptation-method comparisons, corruption tests, controlled ablations and computational measurements.

arxiv_record.abstract: Discrete audio tokens have recently gained considerable attention for their potential to bridge audio and language processing, enabling multimodal language models that can both generate and understand audio. However, preserving key information such as phonetic content, speaker identity, and paralinguistic cues remains a major challenge. Identifying the optimal tokenizer and configuration is further complicated by inconsistent evaluation settings across existing studies. To address this, we introduce the Discrete Audio and Speech Benchmark (DASB), a comprehensive framework for benchmarking discrete audio tokens across speech, general audio, and music domains on a range of discriminative and generative tasks. Our results show that discrete representations are less robust than continuous ones and require careful tuning of factors such as model architecture, data size, learning rate, and capacity. Semantic tokens generally outperform acoustic tokens, but a gap remains between discrete tokens and continuous features, highlighting the need for further research. DASB codes, evaluation setup, and leaderboards are publicly available at https://poonehmousavi.github.io/DASB-website/.
arxiv_record.authors: Pooneh Mousavi, Jarod Duret, Darius Petermann, Artem Ploujnikov, Luca Della Libera, Anastasia Kuznetsova, Cem Subakan, Mirco Ravanelli
arxiv_record.title: DASB - Discrete Audio and Speech Benchmark

C1.justification: v3 broadens the central contribution from a speech benchmark to evaluation across speech, music and general audio. It adds prominent claims that direct token evaluation isolates quantization loss and that discrete representations require careful scaling and tuning because of weaker robustness. The general semantic-token advantage and gap relative to continuous representations remain central.

C2.justification: v3 substantially expands explanations of codebook redundancy, optimization instability, data/model scaling and SQ-Codec failure conditions. Appendices E-H discuss initialization confounds, decoder strength and sampling-error propagation. Rankings are qualified as high-level summaries, and uncontrolled tokenizer training differences are acknowledged. The earlier speech-only limitation is removed following the actual coverage expansion.

D1.justification: v3 newly documents TPE/Orion tuning over 20 trials, embedding initialization, ASR tokenization choices, TTS best-of-ten selection using Whisper Large, and sampling-search settings. Tokenizer metadata, checkpoint links, licenses and resource descriptions are expanded or revised. Access instructions shift toward a project website, but the public-availability claim conflicts with a footnote promising release with the camera-ready version.

E1.justification: v3 retains the speech suite and adds ESC-50 and UrbanSound8K sound classification, GTZAN genre and music-versus-speech classification, NSynth pitch classification, MUSDB music separation, FUSS general-sound separation and LibriTTS multi-speaker TTS. These substantially expand the represented domains and task requirements beyond v1's speech-only evaluations.

E2.justification: v3 retains the six original tokenizers and adds Mimi, SQ-Codec and WavTokenizer to the speech comparisons. New-domain evaluations introduce BEATs, MERT, DEMUCS and TDCN++ baselines. Generative tables also add unprocessed-mixture controls, while the reconstruction comparison replaces v1's continuous-SSL reference with ground-truth audio.

E3.justification: The reported English-ASR training split changes from train-clean-100 to 'train-clean-960'; Branchformer replaces ContextNet and the low-resource linear head, and character-only outputs gain BPE alternatives. Multi-speaker TTS introduces phoneme inputs and a different architecture and dataset. Reconstruction evaluation changes from DNSMOS/dWER to UTMOS/WER, and Appendix H adds a 100-sample inference-parameter search.

E4.justification: v1 already analyzes bitrate, downstream architectures and reconstruction. v3 adds random-versus-encoder-based embedding initialization experiments for ASR and keyword spotting (Table 12), TTS top-k and temperature sensitivity experiments (Figures 4-5), and revised reconstruction diagnostics (Appendix F). These substantially expand the questions investigated beyond the original analyses.

E5.justification: v1 reports point estimates without run counts or uncertainty estimates. v3 states that evaluations use three random seeds and presents averaged results with widespread ± values, alongside discussion of training variability. This is newly documented repeated-run evidence, not an established increase from a known v1 run count; the meaning of ± is not explicitly defined.

E6.justification: Many speech scores are replaced, and extensive new-domain, tokenizer, initialization and sampling results are added. For six-codebook Discrete WavLM with the BiLSTM ASR head, test-clean WER changes from 8.52 in v1 Table 9 to 4.32 ± 0.23 in v3 Table 2. The changed training split and protocol prevent interpreting this as a same-setting performance gain.

M1.justification: The frozen encoder, attention-based combination, downstream model and decoder framework remains. v3 adds a localized SQ-Codec adaptation using ternary-matrix dequantization and concatenated group embeddings, and introduces a VALL-E-based TTS path with residual prediction. These extend the retained framework rather than replace its central procedure.

P1.justification: The abstract, introduction, related work and results narrative undergo extensive rewriting. v3 separates tokenizer selection from encoding, reorganizes results around domains, scaling, rankings and category trade-offs, and restructures the appendices around second-head results and additional analyses. Terminology also changes from 'compression' to 'acoustic' tokens.

P2.justification: Result tables are reorganized from bitrate blocks into tokenizer groups with codebook-count columns, and first-head results replace the main-text best-of-two summaries. Tokenizer metadata tables are redesigned, Figure 2 is redrawn, and new domain and ablation tables are added. Radar plots replace the earlier ranking table, while Figures 4-5 introduce TTS sensitivity plots.

R1.justification: Related work is substantially expanded with ESPnet-Codec, VERSA, HEAR, newer tokenizers and broader speech, music and multimodal-model literature. The comparison with the already-cited Codec-SUPERB is rewritten around direct token evaluation versus waveform reconstruction, giving DASB a more explicit and stronger methodological novelty position.

T1.justification: The bitrate definition and attention equations are retained. Neither version supplies theoretical propositions or proofs, and v3's additional mechanism explanations and ranking descriptions do not introduce substantive mathematical reasoning or formal guarantees.

improvement.justification: v3 resolves v1's acknowledged speech-only coverage limitation and materially strengthens assessment of benchmark stability through three-seed reporting, explicit tuning procedures and initialization/sampling analyses. These additions substantially improve usefulness and transparency. Undefined ± statistics, conflicting code-release statements and scaling arguments that mix datasets and languages remain weaknesses, but the gains in empirical support and diagnostic depth are substantial overall.

A1.justification: Both PDFs describe DASB, retaining its core benchmark design and overlapping speech experiments. The text, equations, figures, tables and complete appendices are readable and support reliable comparison despite substantial expansion.

after.justification: v3 reports original speech, music and general-audio evaluations, embedding-initialization experiments and TTS sampling analyses in Tables 2-4 and 9-12 and Appendix H.

before.justification: v1 reports original downstream speech experiments and audio reconstruction evaluations in Tables 2-4 and Appendices D-E.

arxiv_record.abstract: Learning a world model for model-free Reinforcement Learning (RL) agents can significantly improve the sample efficiency by learning policies in imagination. However, building a world model for Multi-Agent RL (MARL) can be particularly challenging due to the scalability issue in a centralized architecture arising from a large number of agents, and also the non-stationarity issue in a decentralized architecture stemming from the inter-dependency among agents. To address both challenges, we propose a novel world model for MARL that learns decentralized local dynamics for scalability, combined with a centralized representation aggregation from all agents. We cast the dynamics learning as an auto-regressive sequence modeling problem over discrete tokens by leveraging the expressive Transformer architecture, in order to model complex local dynamics across different agents and provide accurate and consistent long-term imaginations. As the first pioneering Transformer-based world model for multi-agent systems, we introduce a Perceiver Transformer as an effective solution to enable centralized representation aggregation within this context. Results on Starcraft Multi-Agent Challenge (SMAC) show that it outperforms strong model-free approaches and existing model-based methods in both sample efficiency and overall performance.
arxiv_record.authors: Yang Zhang, Chenjia Bai, Bin Zhao, Junchi Yan, Xiu Li, Xuelong Li
arxiv_record.comments: Accepted by Transactions on Machine Learning Research
arxiv_record.title: Decentralized Transformers with Centralized Aggregation are Sample-Efficient Multi-Agent World Models

arxiv_record.abstract: The intrinsic capability to continuously learn a changing data stream is a desideratum of deep neural networks (DNNs). However, current DNNs suffer from catastrophic forgetting, which interferes with remembering past knowledge. To mitigate this issue, existing Continual Learning (CL) approaches often retain exemplars for replay, regularize learning, or allocate dedicated capacity for new tasks. This paper investigates an unexplored direction for CL called Retrospective Feature Estimation (RFE). RFE learns to reverse feature changes by aligning the features from the current trained DNN backward to the feature space of the old task, where performing predictions is easier. This retrospective process utilizes a chain of small feature mapping networks called retrospector modules. Empirical experiments on several CL benchmarks, including CIFAR10, CIFAR100, and Tiny ImageNet, demonstrate the effectiveness and potential of this novel CL direction compared to existing representative CL methods, motivating further research into retrospective mechanisms as a principled alternative for mitigating catastrophic forgetting in CL. Code is available at: https://github.com/mail-research/retrospective-feature-estimation.

C2.justification: v2 adds a specific limitation concerning weaker CIFAR10 performance and possible instability in recovering fine-grained features. It develops retention/privacy tradeoffs among RFE variants and distinguishes training from inference resource costs. v1's discussion of previous-task-data dependence and GAN remedies disappears, while long-chain overhead and class-incremental confidence concerns remain.

D1.justification: v2 adds a project code-availability statement, gated-module dimensions, parameter accounting, implementation names for hyperparameters, ViT training details and execution-time measurements. It also documents auxiliary backbones and float32 memory accounting. Conversely, v1's eight-RTX-A5000 hardware disclosure, per-dataset selected-hyperparameter table and GAN training recipe are removed; these are substantive changes in reproducibility information.

E1.justification: The three underlying benchmarks remain CIFAR10, CIFAR100 and Tiny ImageNet. v2 Table 3 extends class-incremental evaluation to Tiny ImageNet, whereas v1 Table 2 reports that task only on CIFAR100. Longer task sequences and different backbones primarily change protocols within this retained coverage.

E2.justification: The controlled comparisons become rehearsal-focused: o-EWC and LwF.mc disappear from the main task-incremental table, and ER-MKD is added. ER and AGEM also enter the CIFAR100 class-incremental comparison, where they were absent in v1. Appendix B.6 adds indirect comparisons with non-rehearsal methods using cited results under different configurations.

E3.justification: Auxiliary-network training changes from 50 epochs at 5e-4 to 40 epochs at 5e-3, and stated hyperparameter search ranges change substantially. The 5,000-sample setting disappears, while longer-sequence evaluations and a pretrained ViT protocol with 30 epochs at 1e-5 are added. v2 also resolves the standard Tiny ImageNet split description to 10 tasks, already specified in v1's appendix despite its conflicting main text.

E4.justification: v1's cosine-loss/regularization ablation and GAN-alignment comparison are removed. v2 adds gated-versus-MLP and end-to-end ablations, taskwise forgetting heatmaps, longer-chain accuracy and representation-error analyses, and timing/memory analyses. The existing PCA investigation is revised from CIFAR10 to CIFAR100 and augmented with quantitative RMSE measurements.

E5.justification: Both versions report results with plus/minus values. v2 Appendix A.4 newly specifies averaging over three runs with different random seeds. This discloses the repetition procedure but does not establish an increase in runs relative to v1; neither version clearly defines the plus/minus statistic.

E6.justification: The principal result tables change extensively. For example, CIFAR100 task-incremental accuracy with 1,000 previous-task samples changes from ILR's 78.53±0.25 in v1 Table 1 to RFE-P's 80.64±0.59 in v2 Table 2, under revised architecture and training rather than identical conditions. RFE-B, Tiny ImageNet class-incremental, ViT, timing and longer-chain results are added; GAN and 5,000-sample results are removed.

M1.justification: Beyond renaming, v2 replaces ILR's compression-and-concatenation architecture with multiplicative projections and sigmoid gates, and replaces squared-L2-plus-cosine alignment with squared L2. Training incorporates current-data feature regularization; the new RFE-B variant also updates earlier retrospectors using replay. The GAN option disappears, while Appendix B.3 introduces an end-to-end training alternative.

P1.justification: The title and terminology change throughout from ILR/rectifiers to RFE/retrospectors. Training-data explanations, contribution statements and experimental narration are substantially rewritten and reorganized. A new experimental appendix restructures the supplementary material; the existing versatility discussion moves from Appendix B to C, and the societal-impacts section disappears.

P2.justification: Figure 2 is redrawn for the gated architecture, the PCA display is replaced and augmented with RMSE, and new forgetting heatmaps and accuracy curves appear. Main tables are redesigned to distinguish training/inference parameters and expand class-incremental comparisons. Hyperparameter presentation and the overall journal layout also change substantially.

R1.justification: The existing related-work taxonomy remains, but v2 adds references including ER-MKD, HAT, winning subnetworks, HyperNet and ViT, while removing several GAN-related references. It adds positioning against frozen pretrained-model adaptation and supplementary comparisons with non-rehearsal approaches. Publication and title updates for retained references are not treated as new works.

improvement.justification: v2 substantially strengthens evidence for the central mechanism through longer-chain accuracy and RMSE analyses, architectural alternatives and a second backbone. A1.justification: Both PDFs describe the same continual-learning research, with ILR renamed and revised as RFE. All pages, including equations, figures, tables and appendices, are readable and support comparison.

arxiv_record.abstract: Entanglement is a key property of quantum states that acts as a resource for a wide range of tasks in quantum computing. Entanglement detection is a key conceptual and practical challenge. Without adaptive or joint measurements, entanglement detection is constrained by no-go theorems (Lu et al. [Phys. Rev. Lett., 116, 230501 (2016)]), necessitating full state tomography. Batch entanglement detection refers to the problem of identifying all entangled states from amongst a set of $K$ unknown states, which finds applications in quantum information processing. We devise a method for performing batch entanglement detection by measuring a single-parameter family of entanglement witnesses, as proposed by Zhu, Teo, and Englert [Phys. Rev. A, 81, 052339, 2010], followed by a thresholding bandit algorithm on the measurement data. The proposed method can perform batch entanglement detection conclusively when the unknown states are drawn from a practically well-motivated class of two-qubit states $\mathcal{F}$, which includes Depolarised Bell states, Bell diagonal states, etc. Our key novelty lies in drawing a connection between batch entanglement detection and a Thresholding Bandit problem in classical Multi-Armed Bandits (MAB). The connection to the MAB problem also enables us to derive theoretical guarantees on the measurement/sample complexity of the proposed technique. We demonstrate the performance of the proposed method through numerical simulations and an experimental implementation. More broadly, this paper highlights the potential for employing classical machine learning techniques for quantum entanglement detection.

arxiv_record.abstract: Spuriousness arises when there is an association between two or more variables in a dataset that are not causally related. In this work, we propose an explainability framework to preemptively disentangle the nature of such spurious associations in a dataset before model training. We leverage a body of work in information theory called Partial Information Decomposition (PID) to decompose the total information about the target into four non-negative quantities, namely unique information (in core and spurious features, respectively), redundant information, and synergistic information. Our framework helps anticipate when the core or spurious feature is indispensable, when either suffices, and when both are jointly needed for an optimal classifier trained on the dataset. Next, we leverage this decomposition to propose a novel measure of the spuriousness of a dataset. We arrive at this measure systematically by examining several candidate measures, and demonstrating what they capture and miss through intuitive canonical examples and counterexamples. Our framework Spurious Disentangler consists of segmentation, dimensionality reduction, and estimation modules, with capabilities to specifically handle high-dimensional image data efficiently. Finally, we also perform empirical evaluation to demonstrate the trends of unique, redundant, and synergistic information, as well as our proposed spuriousness measure across $6$ benchmark datasets under various experimental settings. We observe an agreement between our preemptive measure of dataset spuriousness and post-training model generalization metrics such as worst-group accuracy, further supporting our proposition. The code is available at https://github.com/Barproda/spuriousness-disentangler.

snapshot_arxiv_record.abstract: Spuriousness arises when there is an association between two or more variables in a dataset that are not causally related. In this work, we propose an explainability framework to preemptively disentangle the nature of such spurious associations in a dataset before model training. We leverage a body of work in information theory called Partial Information Decomposition (PID) to decompose the total information about the target into four non-negative quantities, namely unique information (in core and spurious features, respectively), redundant information, and synergistic information. Our framework helps anticipate when the core or spurious feature is indispensable, when either suffices, and when both are jointly needed for an optimal classifier trained on the dataset. Next, we leverage this decomposition to propose a novel measure of the spuriousness of a dataset. We arrive at this measure systematically by examining several candidate measures, and demonstrating what they capture and miss through intuitive canonical examples and counterexamples. Our framework Spurious Disentangler consists of segmentation, dimensionality reduction, and estimation modules, with capabilities to specifically handle high-dimensional image data efficiently. Finally, we also perform empirical evaluation to demonstrate the trends of unique, redundant, and synergistic information, as well as our proposed spuriousness measure across $6$ benchmark datasets under various experimental settings. We observe an agreement between our preemptive measure of dataset spuriousness and post-training model generalization metrics such as worst-group accuracy, further supporting our proposition. The code is available at https://github.com/Barproda/spuriousness-disentangler.
