C1.justification: The central claim changes from unique spurious-feature information being the spuriousness measure to a broader explanation of four dependency types and a signed measure incorporating core information and synergy. v2 emphasizes anticipating optimal-classifier feature preferences and removes v1's asserted superiority of its autoencoder estimator over classical estimators.

C2.justification: v2 develops substantive interpretations of redundancy as allowing either feature and synergy as enabling spurious features to denoise core features. It explicitly distinguishes Bayes-optimal predictions from actual trained-model accuracy. Appendix A expands limitations to subjective feature categorization, sample-complexity and optimization difficulties, unresolved estimation error and interactions among multiple spurious-feature groups.

D1.justification: v2 adds algorithm pseudocode, segmentation prompts and pretrained-model details, estimator choices, runtime measurements, cluster-selection guidance and a code-access link. Conversely, v1's layer-by-layer architecture table and detailed Waterbird architecture diagram disappear, along with explicit 70/30 splitting, weighted-sampling and numerical stopping-threshold disclosures. These are substantial changes in reproducibility information, not necessarily changes to every underlying procedure.

E1.justification: Waterbird and both Dominoes variants are retained. v2 adds Adult income prediction, CelebAMask-HQ hair-color classification, Spawrious dog-breed classification, and binary/ten-class Colored MNIST. Coverage also expands to unavailable segmentation masks and non-spatial color biases, substantially broadening domains and input conditions.

E2.justification: v2 adds focused numerical comparisons against I(Y;B) and I(Y;B)-I(Y;F) in Table 2, plus DIT versus Liang et al. PID estimators on binary CMNIST in Figure 24. v1 does not report corresponding comparisons; its stated PCA comparison is not accompanied by identifiable comparative results.

E3.justification: v2 adds class-balanced and additional random-split Waterbird evaluations, IoU measurement, cluster-count sweeps and CMNIST flip-rate protocols. Waterbird autoencoder training changes from 150 pretraining plus 50 training epochs to 50 plus 100. The reported Dominoes 2.0 Group 11 training count changes from 3,000 to 300. v2 also describes worst-group evaluation across groups, replacing v1's explicit fixed-minority/averaging description. These are reported revisions, not proof that every retained experiment was rerun.

E4.justification: Beyond retained balancing, background-mixing and Grad-CAM analyses, v2 adds quantitative mask alignment using IoU, cluster-count sensitivity and runtime/convergence analysis, and sensitivity to PID-estimator choice (Tables 1, 3–4; Figures 16 and 24). These directly examine localization validity, representation stability and computational limitations absent from v1.

E5.justification: v2 introduces +/- reporting for worst-group accuracies in Tables 7–8 and Pearson correlations with p-values in Figures 7 and 14; v1 reports point estimates and descriptive trends. This statistical reporting remains limited: v2 does not identify what +/- represents or specify repetition counts or seeds, so additional runs cannot be inferred.

E6.justification: v2 adds Msp values, results for four additional datasets and new diagnostic analyses. Earlier accuracy summaries also change: unbalanced Waterbird is 29.75% in v1 Table 1 and 45.92 +/- 1.43% in v2 Table 7. Most earlier PID components recur with rounding in v2 Table 6, while v1's mean-accuracy panel is removed. Revised settings and reporting prevent treating changed accuracies as controlled performance gains.

M1.justification: v2 replaces unique spurious-feature information alone with Msp = Uni(Y:B|F) - Uni(Y:F|B) - Syn(Y:F,B). It adds automatic CLIPSeg/FPN segmentation and alternative estimation routes, including multiclass PID estimation. The autoencoder reconstruction/clustering objective and Waterbird bottleneck already existed in v1 and are not new components.

P1.justification: The title, abstract, introduction and conclusion are extensively rewritten around dataset explainability and the revised measure. v1's combined main-results section becomes separate theory and methodology sections; experiments are reorganized around feature-availability scenarios, and limitations and broader impacts receive dedicated appendices. This substantially changes the narrative structure.

P2.justification: v2 switches the main text from two columns to one, redraws and separates the framework diagrams, and adds an algorithm box and canonical-dependency illustration. Experimental displays are reorganized with Msp axes, logarithmic PID scales and expanded tables; new diagnostic plots appear. Earlier detailed architecture displays are removed, not merely relocated.

R1.justification: The central positioning of applying PID to dataset spuriousness remains. v2 adds focused connections to feature-separation and Gaussian-separability research, dataset documentation, and PID-estimation limitations and alternatives. It also explicitly attributes the retained stochastic-matrix lemma to Bertschinger et al. (2014), refining attribution and positioning.

T1.justification: Section 3 and Appendix C add the Msp definition, candidate measures and counterexamples, Gaussian redundancy/synergy lemmas, a noisy-feature information bound and Bayes-classifier derivations. v2 also proves feature-transfer monotonicity. The earlier Blackwell-equivalence argument is retained, including its stochastic-matrix proof as Lemma 7, rather than newly introduced.

improvement.justification: v2 substantially strengthens conceptual justification through explicit counterexamples and treatment of core information, redundancy and synergy. Evaluations beyond v1's two image datasets, quantitative localization checks and estimator/cluster sensitivity analyses address important validation gaps. Clearer applicability limits also improve interpretation. Lost architecture detail and undefined uncertainty notation weaken reproducibility, but the gains in justification and empirical scrutiny outweigh those losses.

A1.justification: Both PDFs describe the same PID-based Spuriousness Disentangler research, retaining identifiable theory and Waterbird/Dominoes experiments despite substantial revision. Text, equations, figures, tables and appendices are readable and support reliable comparison.

after.justification: v2 reports original evaluations across six datasets, including new tabular and multiclass experiments, quantitative localization results and sensitivity analyses in Section 5 and Appendix D.

before.justification: v1 reports original PID estimates, classification accuracies and Grad-CAM results for Waterbird and two Dominoes variants in Section 4 and Appendix B.

arxiv_record.abstract: Existing studies have shown that Message-Passing Graph Neural Networks (MPNNs) are highly susceptible to adversarial attacks. In contrast, despite the increasing importance of Graph Transformers (GTs), their robustness properties are unexplored. We close this gap and design the first adaptive attacks for GTs. In particular, we provide general design principles for strong gradient-based attacks on GTs w.r.t. structure perturbations and instantiate our attack framework for five representative and popular GT architectures. Specifically, we study GTs with specialized attention mechanisms and Positional Encodings (PEs) based on pairwise shortest paths, random walks, and the Laplacian spectrum. We evaluate our attacks on multiple tasks and perturbation models, including structure perturbations for node and graph classification, and node injection for graph classification. Our results reveal that GTs can be catastrophically fragile in many cases. Addressing this vulnerability, we show how our adaptive attacks can be effectively used for adversarial training, substantially improving robustness.

C2.justification: v2 adds explanations connecting adversarial-training success to flexible learned attention, Polynormer's Reddit difficulties to missing positional encodings, and homophily results to injection unnoticeability. It discusses adversarial-training overhead and implementation limitations. However, v1's explicit caveat that attacks provide no guarantee of proximity to the optimal adversarial example is omitted.

D1.justification: v2 adds a reproduction-code link, configuration-file instructions, model-specific hyperparameter Tables 4–12, adversarial-training pseudocode, and numerical settings for spectral gradients and attention. These substantially expand documentation without establishing changes to retained experiments. Conversely, v1's GPU/timing information and explicit CLUSTER block-size disclosure are omitted.

E1.justification: v2 retains CLUSTER and both UPFD datasets, adds featureless Reddit Threads graph classification under structure attacks, and evaluates local single-victim CLUSTER attacks. These additions broaden the represented graph data and attack tasks beyond v1's global node-classification and graph-level node-injection evaluations.

E2.justification: v2 adds a single-random-perturbation baseline alongside the retained random-search attack, expands transfer comparisons with GPS and Polynormer and with GPS-GCN on CLUSTER, and evaluates Nettack in the local CLUSTER comparison (Figure 26). Nettack was cited but not evaluated in v1.

E3.justification: Reported attack-budget ranges expand from 15% to 50% on CLUSTER and from 50% to 100% on UPFD. New protocols include Reddit's stratified 75/12.5/12.5 split, local attack constraints, homophily measurement, and adversarial-training budgets and replay settings. The original datasets' splits, first-50-test-graph evaluation, and 125 attack steps remain.

E4.justification: The original component ablations and constrained CLUSTER analysis remain. v2 adds comparisons of SAN spectral-gradient alternatives, detailed transferability analyses, tests of whether injected graphs preserve node-centric homophily, and local-attack evaluations with different constraints (Appendix C). These address substantial additional questions about attack effectiveness and meaningfulness.

E5.justification: Both versions report attack averages and standard deviations over four random seeds, including the component-ablation tables. The added experiments and result rows do not introduce a different uncertainty-reporting practice, increased run count, confidence intervals, or formal significance tests.

E6.justification: v2 adds extensive architecture, Reddit Threads, transfer, local-attack, homophily, and adversarial-training results. Figure 7 newly reports much greater adversarial-training benefits for Graphormer than GCN. Table 3 adds SAN eigen-backpropagation results, including 54.4 ± 0.6% unconstrained CLUSTER accuracy with attention relaxation. Existing Graphormer/GRIT ablations are retained; rounding of old SAN values is not a result change.

M1.justification: v2 adds attack adaptations for GPS's gated message passing and Polynormer's sparse attention, plus an alternative eigenvalue-separation procedure enabling spectral backpropagation (Appendix F.2). It also introduces modified free adversarial training with separate attack/model passes and discrete perturbations (Section 7, Appendix D), substantially extending v1's attack framework.

P1.justification: The title, abstract, introduction, and methodological exposition are extensively rewritten. Architecture descriptions move from v1's Appendix B into the main preliminaries, and v2 separates evaluation, attack results, adversarial training, related work, and conclusion into distinct sections. The narrative is substantially reorganized beyond the added scientific content.

P2.justification: The main text changes from two-column to single-column layout. Retained attack plots are redrawn with revised panels, axes, styling, and legends, and duplicated main-text ablations are consolidated in the appendix. New displays include the node-probability illustration, defense and transfer plots, homophily distributions, local-attack plots, and hyperparameter tables.

R1.justification: The central positioning as the first adaptive GT robustness study remains. v2 adds focused connections to free adversarial training, prior work on MPNN flexibility, Polynormer, and homophily-based unnoticeability, while removing several earlier positional-encoding and certification references. The existing related-work argument remains largely recognizable.

T1.justification: v1 states spectral perturbation approximations and refers readers elsewhere for repeated eigenvalues. v2 adds a discontinuity counterexample and explicit eigenspace-basis construction, derives a minimum-norm eigenvalue-separation optimization (Appendix F), and supplies architecture-specific complexity reasoning (Appendix G.3). Principle II also explicitly requires differentiability almost everywhere.

improvement.justification: The new hyperparameter tables and numerical procedures substantially reduce v1's reproducibility gaps, while broader architecture/task comparisons and local-attack and homophily checks strengthen validation. Section 7 and Figure 7 also add an empirically tested defense. These gains outweigh the loss of hardware/timing details and the explicit optimality caveat, although the broad robust-learning interpretation remains supported chiefly by Graphormer-versus-GCN experiments.

A1.justification: Both PDFs describe the same graph-transformer robustness work, with matching core relaxations, node-injection formulation, and retained experiments. Their main texts, figures, tables, equations, and appendices support reliable comparison despite the changed title and substantial expansion.

after.justification: v2 retains original experiments and adds results for further architectures, Reddit Threads, local attacks, homophily analyses, and adversarial training in Sections 6–7 and Appendix C.

before.justification: v1 reports original attack results on CLUSTER and both UPFD datasets, including accuracy curves and component ablations in Section 5 and Appendix E.

arxiv_record.abstract:
Assessing the quality of outputs generated by generative models, such as
large language models and vision language models, presents notable challenges.
Traditional methods for evaluation typically rely on either human assessments,
which are resource-intensive, or automatic metrics that often show a low
correlation with human judgment. Another common approach is to use deep
learning systems, which not only consume a substantial amount of compute and
time but also require extensive training data. In this study, we introduce a
tuning-free framework called ReFeR, designed to evaluate generative outputs,
including both text and images, by leveraging a 2-level hierarchy of LLMs and
VLMs themselves. We rigorously evaluate our framework, ReFeR, across four
diverse evaluation tasks. The framework not only improves the accuracy of these
evaluations, surpassing previous benchmarks but also generates constructive
feedback. Interestingly, the framework is also applicable to reasoning tasks.
Experiments on four reasoning tasks demonstrate superior collective reasoning
abilities of the framework. We present two variants of the framework:
ReFeR-Turbo, optimized for accelerated performance, and ReFeR-Lite, offering a
more cost-effective solution. ReFeR-Lite is $\sim7.7\times$ more efficient
while being comparably accurate to ReFeR-Turbo. We make code, data and PIP
package publicly available. See this PIP URL
https://pypi.org/project/refer-agents/ and this Git URL
https://github.com/yaswanth-iitkgp/ReFeR_Code .

Turbo/Lite and approximately 7.7-fold efficiency become headline claims. Fine-tuning remains in an appendix but loses its central contribution status, and the earlier specific SummEval and GPT-3.5/GPT-4 improvement claims are replaced.

C2.justification: V2 adds explanations for task-dependent differences between hierarchy and debate, guidance on peer count and chair strength, and interpretations of chair dependence on correct peers. Appendix G newly argues that SummEval's skewed ratings undermine its suitability. Limitations shift toward computational cost, weaker chairs, missing inter-peer discussion and untested modalities, while several configuration questions left open in v1 receive empirical discussion.

D1.justification: V2 adds API-provider information, task-specific generation limits, an AutoPrompt worked example, expanded task prompts and repository/PyPI links claiming public access. V1 only promised code after review. Conversely, v1's explicit fine-tuning split details and A100 hardware statement disappear. V2 also retains a future-release statement in Section 11, leaving its availability wording inconsistent.

E1.justification: V2 retains SummEval, TopicalChat, GSM8k and CSQA, adds ICQD caption evaluation and AGIQA image-generation evaluation, and adds AQuA multiple-choice algebra and BBH-DU date reasoning. StrategyQA is removed. Multimodal evaluation, only proposed as future work in v1 Appendix C, is now actually tested.

E2.justification: The reasoning comparison replaces ReConCile and GPT-4 rows with zero-shot CoT, Self Correction, Multi-Agent Debate and Multi-Agent Peer Review. arxiv_record.abstract: We introduce Proximal Policy Distillation (PPD), a novel policy distillation method that integrates student-driven distillation and Proximal Policy Optimization (PPO) to increase sample efficiency and to leverage the additional rewards that the student policy collects during distillation. To assess the efficacy of our method, we compare PPD with two common alternatives, student-distill and teacher-distill, over a wide range of reinforcement learning environments that include discrete actions and continuous control (ATARI, Mujoco, and Procgen). For each environment and method, we perform distillation to a set of target student neural networks that are smaller, identical (self-distillation), or larger than the teacher network. Our findings indicate that PPD improves sample efficiency and produces better student policies compared to typical policy distillation approaches. Moreover, PPD demonstrates greater robustness than alternative methods when distilling policies from imperfect demonstrations. The code for the paper is released as part of a new Python library built on top of stable-baselines3 to facilitate policy distillation: `sb3-distill'.

arxiv_record.abstract: Decision Transformer (DT) has emerged as a promising class of algorithms in offline reinforcement learning (RL) tasks, leveraging pre-collected datasets and Transformer's capability to model long sequences. Recent works have demonstrated that using parts of trajectories from training tasks as prompts in DT enhances its performance on unseen tasks, giving rise to Prompt-DT methods. However, collecting data from specific environments can be both costly and unsafe in many scenarios, leading to suboptimal performance and limited few-shot prompt abilities due to the data-hungry nature of Transformer-based models. Additionally, the limited datasets used in pre-training make it challenging for Prompt-DT type of methods to distinguish between various RL tasks through prompts alone. To address these challenges, we introduce the Language model-initialized Prompt Decision Transformer (LPDT) framework, which leverages pretrained language models providing rich prior knowledge for RL tasks and fine-tunes the sequence model using Low-rank Adaptation (LoRA) for meta-RL problems. We further incorporate prompt regularization to effectively differentiate between tasks based on prompt feature representations. Comprehensive empirical studies demonstrate that initializing with a pre-trained language model provides the prior knowledge and achieves a similar performance with Prompt-DT under only $10\%$ data in some MuJoCo control tasks. We also provide a thorough ablation study to validate the effectiveness of each component, including sequence modeling, language models, prompt regularizations, and prompt strategies.

arxiv_record.abstract: Neural-network processing in machine learning applications relies on layer synchronization. This is practiced even in artificial Spiking Neural Networks (SNNs), which are touted as consistent with neurobiology, in spite of processing in the brain being in fact asynchronous. A truly asynchronous system however would allow all neurons to evaluate concurrently their threshold and emit spikes upon receiving any presynaptic current. Omitting layer synchronization is potentially beneficial, for latency and energy efficiency, but asynchronous execution of models previously trained with layer synchronization may entail a mismatch in network dynamics and performance. We present and quantify this problem, and show that models trained with layer synchronization either perform poorly in absence of the synchronization, or fail to benefit from any energy and latency reduction, when such a mechanism is in place. We then explore a potential solution direction, based on a generalization of backpropagation-based training that integrates knowledge about an asynchronous execution scheduling strategy, for learning models suitable for asynchronous processing. We experiment with two asynchronous neuron execution scheduling strategies in datasets that encode spatial and temporal information, and we show the potential of asynchronous processing to use less spikes (up to 50%), complete inference faster (up to 2x), and achieve competitive or even better accuracy (up to 10% higher). Our exploration affirms that asynchronous event-based AI processing can be indeed more efficient, but we need to rethink how we train our SNN models to benefit from it. (Source code available at: https://github.com/RoelMK/asynctorch)

arxiv_record.abstract: Reinforcement learning policies parametrized by deep neural networks have achieved strong performance for continuous control, yet even small input perturbations may lead to unpredictable behavior. This sensitivity limits their use in safety-critical domains, where robustness guarantees are required. Our work addresses this gap between state-of-the-art adversarial training methods and formal verification to train verifiably robust agents. Previous works train networks with individual adversarial perturbations, making them only robust against the specific adversarial attacks used. In contrast, our approach propagates entire perturbed input sets, enclosing all possible adversarial attacks within a single network pass. We leverage this to explicitly penalize the size of the output set (minimizing closed-loop uncertainty) and thereby make the actor robust against all possible attacks. This is realized by the use of set-based policy gradients, where each output within the set has a different gradient, thereby balancing the accuracy and robustness of the network. Doing so, we achieve formal verifiability across different verification frameworks for up to 9 times larger input perturbations compared to standard reinforcement learning and improve certified worst-case performance.
arxiv_record.authors: Manuel Wendl, Lukas Koller, Tobias Ladner, Matthias Althoff
arxiv_record.title: Training Verifiably Robust Agents Using Set-Based Reinforcement Learning

C1.justification: The central contribution remains set-based reinforcement learning for verifiably robust control. v2 additionally claims verifiability across different frameworks and quantifies perturbation tolerance as up to nine times that of standard reinforcement learning. It also explicitly claims empirical scalability to more complex locomotion tasks, extending rather than replacing the original contribution.

C2.justification: v1 discusses conservative policies and computational costs. v2 adds substantive qualifications: training alone does not guarantee robustness, Hopper results lack formal certification, verification requires known dynamics and bounded uncertainties, and model mismatch can invalidate safety guarantees. Appendix C also interprets how critic regularization affects contraction and convergence, expanding the explanation of the robustness-performance trade-off.

D1.justification: v2 newly specifies benchmark time horizons, averaging over the last five agents in each training run, Hopper evaluation details and hardware, and code/video access pointers. The existing architecture and training-parameter table are retained. These additions improve documentation without demonstrating changes to the corresponding retained experimental settings.

E1.justification: v2 adds MuJoCo Hopper-v2 locomotion, substantially extending evaluation to more complex dynamics and larger state/action spaces. The original navigation, inverted-pendulum, and 1D/2D quadrocopter tasks remain; 'quadrotor' is a renaming, and the 2D task was already evaluated in v1's appendix.

E2.justification: v1 compares against PA-PC, Naive, and Grad. v2 adds evaluated MAD and RORL comparators in Figure 5, broadening comparison to maximum-action-difference attacks and conservative smoothing. RORL is explicitly excluded from the TD3 comparison; the appendix's 2D quadrotor plot retains the original comparator set.

E3.justification: v2 introduces verification across four toolboxes and empirical Hopper evaluation using 50 MAD-attacked trajectories and 200 trajectories with uniform perturbations. It also adds noiseless learning-curve evaluations. The reported verified-return formula changes its negative-reward sign convention from v1 Equation 30 to v2 Equation 12. Existing network sizes and tabulated training hyperparameters remain unchanged; newly stated horizons do not establish changed settings.

E4.justification: Beyond the existing weighting-factor comparisons and quadrocopter attack analysis, v2 adds actor/critic regularization sweeps with convergence histories, learning curves, verification-toolbox dependence tests, and attack-specific results for the inverted pendulum. These examine parameter sensitivity, training stability, and whether improved verifiability extends beyond CORA.

E5.justification: v1 states that experiments use five seeds and displays shaded bands without defining their statistical meaning. v2 explicitly reports means and 95% confidence intervals across five seeds. This improves uncertainty reporting without establishing an increase in the number of runs.

E6.justification: v2 adds MAD/RORL results, Hopper returns and runtimes, sensitivity and convergence results, and multi-toolbox verification outcomes. Table 1 reports CORA verification times of 423.45 seconds for the standard agent and 1.99 seconds for the set-based agent. The retained attack-return plots are also revised between v1 Figure 6 and v2 Figure 7. The original training-time values remain unchanged in v2 Table 2.

M1.justification: The SA-SC and SA-PC procedures retain zonotope propagation, the center-error plus diameter regression loss, weighted set-based policy gradients, and the actor-only simplification. The gradient factors are rearranged equivalently, and the expanded exposition does not establish a new method component or training procedure.

P1.justification: v2 extensively rewrites the abstract, introduction, method explanations, and evaluation narrative. It moves the probabilistic derivations into Appendix B, consolidates benchmark descriptions in Appendix C, brings the regression-loss proof into the main text, and introduces dedicated related-work and limitations sections. The presentation now emphasizes gradient sets and verified performance.

P2.justification: The paper changes from a two-column layout to a predominantly single-column journal layout. v2 adds set-propagation and gradient illustrations, verification and Hopper runtime tables, and numerous sensitivity and learning-history plots. Existing experimental figures are enlarged or restructured, while the probability-density illustration and 2D quadrotor results are relocated and relabeled.

R1.justification: The basic positioning against pointwise adversarial training remains. v2 adds discussion and citations concerning conservative smoothing, randomized smoothing, model-based certification, alternative verification tools, and reachset-conformant modeling. Much of the dedicated related-work section relocates earlier introductory material; Koller et al.'s preprint-to-publication update is the same underlying work.

T1.justification: The central loss derivations and expectation-preservation proof are retained, largely in v2 Appendix B. v2 adds a polynomial runtime bound and proof in Proposition 4, formulates the objective using adversary-dependent state visitation, explicitly restricts the expectation-preservation proposition to ReLU networks, and revises the sign in the verified-return expression. These are bounded additions and corrections to the existing theoretical framework.

improvement.justification: v2 substantially strengthens support for the central verifiability claim through additional robust-RL baselines, verification across four toolboxes, and sensitivity and convergence studies. Explicit confidence intervals and substantive limitations make the evidence easier to assess, especially the distinction between empirical Hopper robustness and formal certification. The Hopper runtime caption understates overhead—Table 4 reports 343.56 versus 44.70 seconds for SA-PC and PA-PC—but this limited weakness does not outweigh the substantial gains in validation and qualification.

A1.justification: Both PDFs describe the same set-based reinforcement learning work. Their text, equations, figures, tables, and complete appendices are readable, allowing content to be matched despite substantial reorganization and formatting changes.

after.justification: v2 retains original control experiments and reports additional baseline comparisons, verification-toolbox evaluations, Hopper-v2 experiments, and hyperparameter studies.

arxiv_record.abstract: In the last few years, due to the broad applicability of deep learning to downstream tasks and end-to-end training capabilities, increasingly more concerns about potential biases to specific, non-representative patterns have been raised. Many works focusing on unsupervised debiasing usually leverage the tendency of deep models to learn ``easier'' samples, for example by clustering the latent space to obtain bias pseudo-labels. However, the interpretation of such pseudo-labels is not trivial, especially for a non-expert end user, as it does not provide semantic information about the bias features. To address this issue, we introduce ``Say My Name'' (SaMyNa), the first tool to identify biases within deep models semantically. Unlike existing methods, our approach focuses on biases learned by the model. Our text-based pipeline enhances explainability and supports debiasing efforts: applicable during either training or post-hoc validation, our method can disentangle task-related information and proposes itself as a tool to analyze biases. Evaluation on traditional benchmarks demonstrates its effectiveness in detecting biases and even disclaiming them, showcasing its broad applicability for model diagnosis.
arxiv_record.authors: Massimiliano Ciranni, Luca Molinaro, Carlo Alberto Barbano, Attilio Fiandrotti, Vittorio Murino, Vito Paolo Pastore, Enzo Tartaglione
arxiv_record.title: Say My Name: a Model's Bias Discovery Framework

arxiv_record.abstract:
Generative Flow Networks (GFlowNets) are a class of generative models that
sample objects in proportion to a specified reward function through a learned
policy. They can be trained either on-policy or off-policy, needing a balance
between exploration and exploitation for fast convergence to a target
distribution. While exploration strategies for discrete GFlowNets have been
studied, exploration in the continuous case remains to be investigated, despite
the potential for novel exploration algorithms due to the local connectedness
of continuous domains. Here, we introduce Adapted Metadynamics, a variant of
metadynamics that can be applied to arbitrary black-box reward functions on
continuous domains. We use Adapted Metadynamics as an exploration strategy for
continuous GFlowNets. We show several continuous domains where the resulting
algorithm, MetaGFN, accelerates convergence to the target distribution and
discovers more distant reward modes than previous off-policy exploration
strategies used for GFlowNets.
arxiv_record.authors: Dominic Phillips and Flaviu Cipcigan
arxiv_record.title:
MetaGFN: Exploring Distant Modes with Adapted Metadynamics for
  Continuous GFlowNets

arxiv_record.abstract:
Learning new tasks by leveraging prior experience is a fundamental trait of intelligent systems. While Model-Agnostic Meta-Learning (MAML) is a leading approach, it suffers from significant computational and memory overhead due to the requirement of computing second-order meta-gradients. We propose \textbf{FO-B-MAML}, a novel first-order variant of MAML derived from a bi-level optimization perspective. Our framework introduces a new expression of the meta-gradient, defined as the derivative of the solution of a perturbed optimization problem. This formulation allows the meta-gradient to be estimated using various finite difference methods; in this work, we propose and analyze two simple yet effective estimators: a forward and a symmetric approximation.
  Unlike existing first-order methods like FO-MAML and Reptile, which suffer from irreducible bias, we prove that FO-B-MAML converges to a stationary point of the meta-objective. Notably, the symmetric estimator achieves an improved $\mathcal{O}(\delta^{2/3})$ bias rate, strictly enhancing previous first-order theory. Furthermore, we demonstrate that the MAML objective violates standard smoothness assumptions; we show instead that its smoothness constant grows with the norm of the meta-gradient. This property theoretically justifies the use of normalized or clipped-gradient methods (SNGDM) over vanilla gradient descent.
  Our empirical results validate these advancements: FO-B-MAML achieves high accuracy, closely following second-order MAML performance. Crucially, our method bypasses the ``activation bottleneck'' of second-order approaches, maintaining a flat memory footprint even when scaling to deep, activation-heavy CNNs and Transformers.

arxiv_record.abstract:
Recent approaches in text-to-image customization have primarily focused on
preserving the identity of the input subject, but often fail to control the
spatial location and size of objects. We introduce GroundingBooth, which
achieves zero-shot, instance-level spatial grounding on both foreground
subjects and background objects in the text-to-image customization task. Our
proposed grounding module and subject-grounded cross-attention layer enable the
creation of personalized images with accurate layout alignment, identity
preservation, and strong text-image coherence. In addition, our model
seamlessly supports personalization with multiple subjects. Our model shows
strong results in both layout-guided image synthesis and text-to-image
customization tasks. The project page is available at
https://groundingbooth.github.io.

arxiv_record.abstract: Vision-language models (VLMs) such as CLIP are trained via contrastive learning between text and image pairs, resulting in aligned image and text embeddings that are useful for many downstream tasks. A notable drawback of CLIP, however, is that the resulting embedding space seems to lack some of the structure of its purely text-based alternatives. For instance, while text embeddings have long been noted to satisfy analogies in embedding space using vector arithmetic, CLIP has no such property. In this paper, we propose an approach to natively train CLIP in a contrastive manner to reason about differences in embedding space. We finetune CLIP so that text descriptions of differences between images correspond to their difference in image embedding space, using synthetically generated data with large language models on image-caption paired datasets. We first demonstrate that our approach yields significantly improved capabilities in ranking images by a certain attribute (e.g., elephants are larger than cats), which is useful in retrieval or constructing attribute-based classifiers, and improved zeroshot classification performance on many downstream image classification tasks. In addition, our approach enables a new mechanism for inference that we refer to as comparative prompting, where we leverage prior knowledge of text descriptions of differences between classes of interest, achieving even larger performance gains in classification. Finally, we illustrate that the resulting embeddings obey a larger degree of geometric properties in embedding space, such as in text-to-image generation.
arxiv_record.authors: Dylan Sam, Devin Willmott, Joao D. Semedo, J. Zico Kolter

arxiv_record.abstract:
The creation of manufacturable and editable 3D shapes through Computer-Aided
Design (CAD) remains a highly manual and time-consuming task, hampered by the
complex topology of boundary representations of 3D solids and unintuitive
design tools. While most work in the 3D shape generation literature focuses on
representations like meshes, voxels, or point clouds, practical engineering
applications demand the modifiability and manufacturability of CAD models and
the ability for multi-modal conditional CAD model generation. This paper
introduces GenCAD, a generative model that employs autoregressive transformers
with a contrastive learning framework and latent diffusion models to transform
image inputs into parametric CAD command sequences, resulting in editable 3D
shape representations. Extensive evaluations demonstrate that GenCAD
significantly outperforms existing state-of-the-art methods in terms of the
unconditional and conditional generations of CAD models. Additionally, the
contrastive learning framework of GenCAD facilitates the retrieval of CAD
models using image queries from large CAD databases, which is a critical
challenge within the CAD community. Our results provide a significant step
forward in highlighting the potential of generative models to expedite the
entire design-to-production pipeline and seamlessly integrate different design
modalities.

arxiv_record.abstract: Broadcast operations are widely used in scientific computing libraries, yet their mathematical formulation is often implicit and inconsistently represented in machine learning literature. This problem frequently leads to invalid equations when element-wise products are written despite mismatched tensor shapes. In this paper, we formalize such operations by introducing the broadcast product $\boxdot$, which explicitly extends the Hadamard product through shape-aligned element duplication. We provide a rigorous definition of the broadcast product, analyze its algebraic properties, and show how it can be expressed using standard linear algebra. Building on this framework, we formulate least-squares problems and sketch a proof-of-concept broadcast decomposition. As a preliminary illustration, we show that the formalism enables a new family of decompositions with distinct structural properties from conventional tensor decompositions. This work establishes a mathematical foundation for broadcast-aware tensor operations, connecting practical implementations with rigorous tensor analysis.
arxiv_record.authors: Yusuke Matsui and Tatsuya Yokota
arxiv_record.title: Broadcast Product: Redefining Shape-aligned Element-wise Multiplication and Beyond

arxiv_record.abstract: Existing causal inference (CI) models are often restricted to data with low-dimensional confounders and singleton actions. We propose an autoregressive (AR) CI framework capable of handling complex confounders and sequential actions commonly found in modern applications. Our approach accomplishes this using {\em sequencification}, which transforms data from an underlying causal diagram into a sequence of tokens. Sequencification not only accommodates training with data generated from a large class of DAGs, but also extends existing CI capabilities to estimate multiple causal quantities using a {\em single} model. We can directly compute probabilities from interventional distributions, simplifying inference and improving outcome prediction accuracy. We demonstrate that an AR model adapted for CI is efficient and effective in various complex applications such as navigating mazes, playing chess endgames, and evaluating the impact of certain keywords on paper acceptance rates, where we consider causal queries beyond standard reinforcement learning-type questions.
arxiv_record.authors: Daniel Jiwoong Im, Kevin Zhang, Nakul Verma, Kyunghyun Cho
arxiv_record.title: Deep Autoregressive Models as Causal Inference Engines

arxiv_record.abstract: When solving inverse problems, one increasingly popular approach is to use pre-trained diffusion models as plug-and-play priors. This framework can accommodate different forward models without re-training while preserving the generative capability of diffusion models. Despite their success in many imaging inverse problems, most existing methods rely on privileged information such as derivative, pseudo-inverse, or full knowledge about the forward model. This reliance poses a substantial limitation that restricts their use in a wide range of problems where such information is unavailable, such as in many scientific applications. We propose Ensemble Kalman Diffusion Guidance (EnKG), a derivative-free approach that can solve inverse problems by only accessing forward model evaluations and a pre-trained diffusion model prior. We study the empirical effectiveness of EnKG across various inverse problems, including scientific settings such as inferring fluid flows and astronomical objects, which are highly non-linear inverse problems that often only permit black-box access to the forward model. We open-source our code at https://github.com/devzhk/enkg-pytorch.

arxiv_record.abstract: Vision-language Models (VLMs) are essential for contextual understanding of both visual and textual information. However, their vulnerability to adversarially manipulated inputs presents significant risks, leading to compromised outputs and raising concerns about the reliability in VLM-integrated applications. Detecting these malicious prompts is thus crucial for maintaining trust in VLM generations. A major challenge in developing a safeguarding prompt classifier is the lack of a large amount of labeled benign and malicious data. To address the issue, we introduce VLMGuard, a novel learning framework that leverages the unlabeled user prompts in the wild for malicious prompt detection. These unlabeled prompts, which naturally arise when VLMs are deployed in the open world, consist of both benign and malicious information. To harness the unlabeled data, we present an automated maliciousness estimation score for distinguishing between benign and malicious samples within this unlabeled mixture, thereby enabling the training of a binary prompt classifier on top. Notably, our framework does not require extra human annotations and is robust to realistic prompt variations, offering strong flexibility and practicality for real-world applications. Extensive experiments show that VLMGuard achieves superior detection results, improving AUROC by 5.39% on average over the state-of-the-art method. Disclaimer: This paper may contain offensive examples; reader discretion is advised. Code is available at: https://github.com/radiolab-ntu/vlmguard.

arxiv_record.abstract: Recent methods aim to merge neural networks (NNs) with identical architectures trained on different tasks into a single multi-task model. While most works focus on the simpler setup of merging NNs initialized from a common pre-trained network, we target the harder problem of merging large transformers trained on different tasks from distinct initializations. We show that traditional merging methods fail catastrophically in this setup, while Knowledge Distillation (KD) achieves much better results, though at a higher cost. However, KD is data-inefficient, as it does not exploit the original models' weights. To solve this, we introduce "Foldable SuperNet Merge" (FS-Merge), which trains a SuperNet containing the original models (with frozen weights) using a feature reconstruction objective. After training, the SuperNet is folded back to the size of a single original model. FS-Merge is simple, data-efficient, has a computational cost comparable to KD, and is proven to have superior expressiveness compared to traditional merging methods on MLP models. It achieves SOTA results when tested on MLPs and transformers across various sizes, tasks, modalities, and distribution shifts, especially in low-data scenarios.
arxiv_record.authors: Edan Kinderman, Itay Hubara, Haggai Maron, Daniel Soudry
arxiv_record.title: Foldable SuperNets: Scalable Merging of Transformers with Different Initializations and Tasks

arxiv_record.abstract:
Scaling the input context length of a large language model (LLM) incurs a
significant increase in computation cost and memory footprint to maintain the
attention key-value (KV) cache. Existing KV cache compression methods suffer
from inefficient compression strategies and limited memory reduction effects,
making it difficult for LLMs to conduct long-context inference on
consumer-grade devices, especially when inferring long-context stream input.
Such obstacles prevent consumer-grade devices from supporting more complex
applications, creating challenges for the democratization of LLMs. To overcome
this, we propose Locret, the first framework to create an eviction policy
compatible with chunked prefill. By evaluating the causal importance of KV
cache units by learnable retaining heads, Locret enables precise eviction of
cache units, facilitating efficient long-context inference. In our extensive
empirical studies, Locret outperforms the recent popular and competitive
approaches in terms of memory efficiency and generation quality -- Locret
achieves up to 20x of KV cache compression ratio within less than 10%
performance loss. Furthermore, Locret achieves 128K+ long-context inference on
a single NVIDIA 4090 GPU without compromising generation quality and only costs
<1 GPU hour of additional training.
arxiv_record.authors: Yuxiang Huang, Binhang Yuan, Xu Han, Chaojun Xiao, Zhiyuan Liu

Locret: Enhancing Eviction in Long-Context LLM Inference with Trained
  Retaining Heads on Consumer-Grade Devices

arxiv_record.abstract: Federated learning is a decentralized collaborative training paradigm preserving stakeholders' data ownership while improving performance and generalization. However, statistical heterogeneity among client datasets degrades system performance. To address this issue, we propose Adaptive Normalization-free Feature Recalibration (ANFR), a model architecture-level approach that combines weight standardization and channel attention to combat heterogeneous data in FL. ANFR leverages weight standardization to avoid mismatched client statistics and inconsistent averaging, ensuring robustness under heterogeneity, and channel attention to produce learnable scaling factors for feature maps, suppressing inconsistencies across clients due to heterogeneity. We demonstrate that combining these techniques boosts model performance beyond their individual contributions, by improving class selectivity and channel attention weight distribution. ANFR works with any aggregation method, supports both global and personalized FL, and adds minimal overhead. Furthermore, when training with differential privacy, ANFR achieves an appealing balance between privacy and utility, enabling strong privacy guarantees without sacrificing performance. By integrating weight standardization and channel attention in the backbone model, ANFR offers a novel and versatile approach to the challenge of statistical heterogeneity. Extensive experiments show ANFR consistently outperforms established baselines across various aggregation methods, datasets, and heterogeneity conditions. Code is provided at https://github.com/siomvas/ANFR.

arxiv_record.abstract: While conventional wisdom holds that policy gradient methods are better suited to complex action spaces than action-value methods, foundational work has shown that the two paradigms are equivalent in small, finite action spaces (O'Donoghue et al., 2017; Schulman et al., 2017a). This raises the question of why their computational applicability and performance diverge as the complexity of the action space increases. We hypothesize that the apparent superiority of policy gradients in such settings stems not from intrinsic qualities of the paradigm but from universal principles that can also be applied to action-value methods, enabling similar functions. We identify three such principles and provide a framework for incorporating them into action-value methods. To support our hypothesis, we instantiate this framework in what we term QMLE, for Q-learning with maximum likelihood estimation. Our results show that QMLE can be applied to complex action spaces at a computational cost comparable to that of policy gradient methods, all without using policy gradients. Furthermore, QMLE exhibits strong performance on the DeepMind Control Suite, even when compared to state-of-the-art methods such as DMPO and D4PG.
arxiv_record.authors: Arash Tavakoli, Sina Ghiassian, Nemanja Raki\'cevi\'c
arxiv_record.title: Learning in complex action spaces without policy gradients

C2.justification: Section 5.3 adds practical interpretations connecting amortization to tolerance of small sampling budgets and reduced inference costs. Appendix D interprets the new scalability findings, while footnote 5 qualifies the MLE analogy by explaining that the reframed likelihood gradient alone does not define a meaningful optimization problem.

D1.justification: Appendix B.3 replaces a future code-release promise with a declared release and concrete repository link, adding Stable Baselines provenance and licensing information. Appendix D documents new ablation configurations. One ambiguity remains: D.3 retains Table 1's uniform ratio of 0.9 while specifying a categorical ratio of 1.

E1.justification: v1 already tests discrete and curriculum variants on Cartpole SwUp, Hopper Hop, and Walker Run. v2 substantially extends discrete-action coverage with three-bin versions of Finger Spin, Walker Walk, Quadruped Run, Humanoid Walk, and Dog Walk, reaching 38 dimensions and approximately 1.35 quintillion actions (Figure 10). E2.justification: v2 adds DQN as an evaluated comparator in the discrete-control architecture study (Figure 10), with its results attributed to Seyde et al. (2023) in Table 2. The original main-text and appendix comparator sets remain unchanged.

E3.justification: Appendix D adds experimental designs comparing sampling budgets of 2 and 1000, controlling target and greedy budgets at 2 while removing learned predictors, and comparing sampled maximization against DQN's exact maximization on discretized tasks. These are new protocols; the original benchmark settings and Table 1 remain unchanged.

E4.justification: New Section 5.3 and Appendix D systematically examine sampling sensitivity, the contribution of amortization, and architecture-related scalability. These substantially extend the retained bandit and appendix analyses. The DQN comparison jointly removes several principles, rather than isolating architecture alone.

E5.justification: Table 2 replaces QMLE's unspecified task-dependent '5 or 10' seeds with five for Dog and Humanoid tasks and ten elsewhere, and adds ten seeds for DQN. This clarifies reporting without establishing increased repetitions. Mean returns with one standard error were already reported in v1.

E6.justification: New Figures 8–10 report sampling-budget sensitivity, substantial degradation without amortization, and discrete QMLE performance alongside DQN's learning curves or computational failures. These substantially expand the empirical findings. All nine original figure graphics are retained unchanged, so the additions do not represent improved scores on the original comparisons.

M1.justification: Section 4, Algorithm 1, and the main architecture in Appendix B retain the same sampling, amortized maximization, Q-learning, and predictor-training procedures. The new ablation variants evaluate existing components without revising the proposed method.

P1.justification: The abstract, introduction, and selected explanations are revised, including clarification of complex action spaces and the illustrative experiment. Section 5.3 and an ablation appendix are inserted, but most existing prose and the overall argument sequence remain intact.

P2.justification: v2 adopts a comprehensive journal layout with different typography, margins, headers, and author formatting. It adds three multipanel ablation figures, expands Figure 3's caption and the seed table, and relocates the original Figures 8–9 as Figures 11–12 without changing their graphics.

R1.justification: v2 adds Bellemare et al. (2017) for distributional learning and Hill et al. (2018) for Stable Baselines. It sharpens DDPG's role as the closest comparison, while retaining the positioning relative to QT-Opt, AQL, and earlier sampling-based maximization work.

T1.justification: The mathematical definitions and derivations remain substantively unchanged, with no new theorem or proof. Equation 14 adds an indicator for positive additional-sample counts, explicitly expressing the already-stated zero-sample reduction; it does not change the estimator under the usual empty-sum convention.

improvement.justification: Section 5.3 and Appendix D substantially address v1's limited direct testing of the principles through controlled sampling and amortization studies and broader discrete-action evidence. A1.justification: Both PDFs describe the same QMLE work and provide readable text, equations, figures, tables, and appendices. The original material can be matched reliably, including v1 Appendix D, which becomes Appendix E in v2.

after.justification: v2 retains those original results and adds sampling-budget, amortization, and architecture comparisons in Appendix D.

before.justification: v1 reports original QMLE control benchmarks, bandit experiments, and appendix demonstrations involving multiagent coordination and action-space curricula.

arxiv_record.abstract: Over-parameterized models are typically vulnerable to membership inference attacks, which aim to determine whether a specific sample is included in the training of a given model. Previous Weight regularizations (e.g., L1 regularization) typically impose uniform penalties on all parameters, leading to a suboptimal tradeoff between model utility and privacy. In this work, we first show that only a small fraction of parameters substantially impact the privacy risk. In light of this, we propose Privacy-aware Sparsity Tuning (PAST), a simple fix to the L1 Regularization, by employing adaptive penalties to different parameters. Our key idea behind PAST is to promote sparsity in parameters that significantly contribute to privacy leakage. In particular, we construct the adaptive weight for each parameter based on its privacy sensitivity, i.e., the gradient of the loss gap with respect to the parameter. Using PAST, the network shrinks the loss gap between members and non-members, leading to strong resistance to privacy attacks. Extensive experiments demonstrate the superiority of PAST, achieving a state-of-the-art balance in the privacy-utility trade-off.
arxiv_record.authors: Hengxiang Zhang, Qiang Hu, Hongxin Wei
arxiv_record.title: Defending Membership Inference Attacks via Privacy-aware Sparsity Tuning

C1.justification: The central claims remain that privacy sensitivity is concentrated in relatively few parameters and that adaptive sparsity tuning improves privacy-utility trade-offs. Compatibility with trained and already-defended models was already claimed and tested in v1. v2 foregrounds broader validation without replacing these core scientific contributions.

C2.justification: v2 replaces an unexplored-white-box limitation with measured residual vulnerabilities, explicitly distinguishes PAST's empirical protection from differential-privacy guarantees, and adds a hypothesized limitation concerning pretrained LLM knowledge. It also explains privacy-sensitivity migration and revises the sparsity interpretation from decreasing to increasing Gini, substantially refining mechanisms and applicability boundaries.

D1.justification: Appendix F/Table 3 supplies model-specific hyperparameter ranges, Section 5 documents Opacus and the DP-SGD search grid, and CIFAR-10 split sizes become explicit. The basic optimizer, training budgets and hardware information are retained. Conversely, v1's instruction to detach adaptive weights from backpropagation is omitted.

E1.justification: The five datasets and classification tasks are retained. v2 Section 5 adds white-box gradient attacks and evaluation on especially vulnerable canary samples, substantially extending adversary-access and evaluated-population coverage. Additional model architectures alone do not constitute new dataset coverage.

E2.justification: v2 adds MIST and SELENA to the CIFAR defense comparisons and evaluates DP-SGD in Figure 8a. Conversely, v1 Appendix B's direct loss-gap optimization comparator disappears. CCL is retained from v1's combined-defense experiment rather than newly introduced.

E3.justification: New evaluations introduce SqueezeNet/MobileViT configurations, LiRA/RMIA with 32 inference models, AUC and low-FPR metrics, and a canary test with 500 members and 500 non-members. Cross-dataset P1 changes from using maximum attack advantage in v1 to average attack advantage in v2. Appendix F also describes lambda-then-alpha tuning, unlike v1's stated alpha-only tuning.

E4.justification: v2 adds inference-set size/composition sensitivity, shared-hyperparameter tests across architectures, alternative privacy proxies, within-layer sensitivity, privacy migration and an RMIA regularization ablation. Earlier CIFAR-100 and alpha/epoch analyses remain under new numbering. The direct-loss-gap ablation is removed, rather than relocated.

E5.justification: v1 provides no repeated-seed uncertainty analysis. v2 Appendix J and Table 4 report nine seeds and means with standard deviations for accuracy, attack AUC and P1 on CIFAR-10/ResNet-18, including P1 of 0.791 ± 0.006. This introduces explicit uncertainty reporting without establishing how many runs underlay v1.

E6.justification: v2 reports substantial new attack, architecture, DP-SGD, canary and robustness results. Its new white-box comparison reports gradient-mean attack AUC of 0.981 without defense versus 0.796 with PAST. Figure 2b changes from a decreasing to an increasing Gini trajectory. Revised cross-dataset P1 results use different aggregation and cannot establish same-setting performance gains.

M1.justification: Both retain module-normalized weighted L1 regularization and post-convergence tuning. However, v1's adaptive-weight equation uses an undefined G-tilde and gradients without absolute-value signs, whereas v2 Equation (6) explicitly normalizes gradient magnitudes. The PDFs do not establish whether this changes the procedure or corrects the earlier notation.

P1.justification: The abstract, introduction, method exposition and results narrative undergo extensive rewriting and reorganization. Related work moves from the main text to Appendix A, a substantial Discussion section is introduced, and retained appendix material is reorganized alongside separate theory, settings and analysis sections.

P2.justification: The earlier P1 tables are replaced by Figure 5 bar charts, the CIFAR-10 comparison moves to Appendix H, and the dense module-level plot is regrouped into Figures 15-16. Numerous new plots and tables accompany extensive changes to axes, legends, captions and publication layout. Several retained results are therefore redisplayed rather than newly added.

R1.justification: The positioning around overparameterization, pruning and regularization remains largely intact. v2 adds references and targeted discussion concerning LiRA/RMIA, MIST/SELENA, differential privacy and worst-case privacy evaluation, and supplies attribution for CCL. Related work's relocation to Appendix A does not itself change the research positioning.

T1.justification: Unlike v1, v2 Appendices B-C contain formal propositions, a theorem and proofs. These include a Gaussian-loss argument relating the mean loss gap to attack advantage at fixed FPR, a Bayesian optimal-membership-inference derivation following cited prior work, and a posterior-distribution derivation. These additions substantially expand the mathematical rationale.

improvement.justification: v2 substantially strengthens the assessment of privacy protection through LiRA/RMIA, vulnerable-canary and white-box evaluations, including explicit evidence of remaining weaknesses. Seed statistics, formal rationale and clearer applicability limits improve credibility and assessability. These gains outweigh losing the direct-loss-gap comparison and replacing precise P1 tables with bar charts. The changed P1 aggregation is not evidence of a performance improvement.

A1.justification: Both PDFs describe the same PAST research. Their main text, equations, figures, tables and appendices are readable and support comparison, including matching material moved or renumbered in v2.

after.justification: v2 retains original experimental results and adds attack evaluations, architecture comparisons, robustness analyses and repeated-seed measurements.

before.justification: v1 reports original membership-inference defense experiments on five datasets, privacy-sensitivity measurements, ablations and runtime results, including appendix experiments.

arxiv_record.abstract: As LLM-based agents become increasingly autonomous and will more freely interact with each other, studying the interplay among them becomes crucial to anticipate emergent phenomena and potential risks. In this work, we provide an in-depth analysis of the interactions among agents within a simulated hierarchical social environment, drawing inspiration from the Stanford Prison Experiment. Leveraging 2,400 conversations across six LLMs (i.e., LLama3, Orca2, Command-r, Mixtral, Mistral2, and gpt4.1) and 240 experimental scenarios, we analyze persuasion and anti-social behavior between a guard and a prisoner agent with differing objectives. We first document model-specific conversational failures in this multi-agent power dynamic context, thereby narrowing our analytic sample to 1,600 conversations. Among models demonstrating successful interaction, we find that goal setting significantly influences persuasiveness but not anti-social behavior. Moreover, agent personas, especially the guard's, substantially impact both successful persuasion by the prisoner and the manifestation of anti-social actions. Notably, we observe the emergence of anti-social conduct even in absence of explicit negative personality prompts. These results have important implications for the development of interactive LLM agents and the ongoing discussion of their societal impact.
arxiv_record.authors: Gian Maria Campedelli, Nicol\`o Penzo, Massimo Stefan, Roberto Dess\`i, Marco Guerini, Bruno Lepri, Jacopo Staiano

C1.justification: The four research questions and central claims remain: goal difficulty principally affects persuasion, guard personas strongly influence anti-social behavior, undesirable behavior can emerge without negative persona prompts, and some models fail role adherence. The expanded model sample and supplementary checks do not replace these headline contributions.

C2.justification: V3 adds model safeguards as an alternative explanation for unattempted escapes, whereas v1 emphasizes anticipated difficulty. It explicitly limits its agents to role-playing LLMs without memory or environmental interaction, discusses the prison scenario's realism, and interprets stricter scoring as showing that persuasion is harder to establish. Most existing limitations and persona-based interpretations remain.

D1.justification: V3 Table 1 specifies the GPT-4.1 snapshot and context length, and the text identifies annotator affiliations and roles. The code reference changes to an anonymized repository described as providing code and generated conversations. V1's separate reproducibility statement, including installation, database, and analysis-script guidance, is removed; existing prompts and open-model hyperparameters remain documented.

E1.justification: Both versions evaluate the same prison environment, escape and additional-yard-time goals, five personality pairings, and risk/oversight conditions. V3's additional conversations extend model configurations within this coverage. Information-protection and policing scenarios are proposed future work, not evaluated tasks.

E2.justification: V3 adds GPT-4.1 to the evaluated roster of Llama3, Command-r, Orca2, Mixtral, and Mistral v0.2. The original five remain, and Mixtral and Mistral are still excluded from downstream behavioral analyses because of conversational failures, leaving four analyzed models instead of three.

E3.justification: V3 Appendix F.2 introduces an additional evaluation protocol that re-annotates previously successful conversations using clearer commitment requirements, excluding vague promises and unconfirmed supervisor referrals. The main permissive labels remain. The experimental total increases from 2,000 to 2,400 conversations, and the reported annotator panel increases from 13 to 15; the 19-message format and original decoding settings are retained.

E4.justification: V3 adds scenario-specific failure analyses (Tables 3–6), separates persuasion attempts from success conditional on attempting across personalities (Tables 8–12), and tests sensitivity to success definitions (Table 13). It also adds fractional-logit robustness checks for the bounded anti-social behavior outcomes, beyond v1's OLS analyses and existing temporal and Granger analyses.

E5.justification: V3 Table 7 adds Cohen's kappa for outcome and turn annotations, plus the mean and standard deviation of absolute turn disagreements, beyond v1 Table 3's disagreement counts. Fractional-logit checks add an alternative estimation procedure. Both versions already report ten repetitions per configuration, confidence intervals, standard deviations, and significance tests; no increase in repetitions is reported.

E6.justification: V3 adds GPT-4.1 outcomes and updates pooled estimates: the yard-time persuasion odds ratio changes from 9.31 to 35.07 after expanding the model pool, not as a same-setting performance gain. New Table 13 reports that stricter coding retains only 44 of 111 Llama3 yard-time successes and 4 of 118 GPT-4.1 successes. Detailed failure, conditional-success, and robustness results are also newly reported.

M1.justification: The toolkit architecture, shared/private prompt templates, role assignments, and conversation-generation procedure remain unchanged (v1 Appendices A–B; v3 Appendices B–C). Adding GPT-4.1 as an evaluated model and changing supplementary outcome scoring do not introduce a new simulation method.

P1.justification: The abstract, introduction, related work, and substantial portions of the results and conclusions are rewritten. Conclusions move before limitations, the ethics statement becomes a broader-impact statement, the standalone reproducibility section disappears, and a new persuasion-results appendix reorganizes the supporting narrative.

P2.justification: V3 introduces ten additional tables and six fractional-logit figures, expands the annotation table with agreement statistics, and adds GPT-4.1 panels or series throughout existing displays. Figures and tables are extensively resized and relocated, and tighter line spacing changes the document layout beyond simple renumbering.

R1.justification: V3 substantially expands positioning around multi-agent security, emergent misalignment, social conventions, and agent definitions, citing works such as Hammond et al. (2025), de Witt (2025), and Ashery et al. (2025). It sharpens the distinction between hierarchical interactions and interactions among equals, engages SPE criticism through Le Texier (2019), and removes some older general AI background references.

T1.justification: The OLS specification, Granger restricted model, F-statistic, and stationarity discussion are mathematically equivalent across versions. V3 adds empirical estimation and annotation checks, but no new mathematical definitions, derivations, theorems, or proofs.

improvement.justification: V1 leaves the sensitivity of its permissive persuasion labels untested. V3 directly quantifies that important weakness: only 44 of 111 Llama3 yard-time successes survive stricter coding. Together with annotation-agreement statistics and fractional-logit checks, this substantially strengthens evidential transparency and robustness. The improvement is tempered by reporting inconsistencies, notably GPT-4.1 yard-time attempts disagreeing between Figure 2 and Table 8, and the removal of reproducibility setup guidance.

A1.justification: Both PDFs describe the same zAImbardo study of guard–prisoner LLM interactions. Their main text, figures, tables, equations, and complete appendices are readable and can be matched across the revision.

after.justification: V3 reports 2,400 conversations across six LLMs, retaining the original empirical analyses and adding persuasion re-annotation, detailed outcome breakdowns, and robustness analyses.

before.justification: V1 reports original simulations comprising 2,000 conversations across five LLMs, with human persuasion annotations, anti-social behavior measurements, and statistical analyses.

arxiv_record.abstract: Recent literature has effectively leveraged diffusion models trained on continuous variables as priors for solving inverse problems. Notably, discrete diffusion models with discrete latent codes have shown strong performance, particularly in modalities suited for discrete compressed representations, such as image and motion generation. However, their discrete and non-differentiable nature has limited their application to inverse problems formulated in continuous spaces. This paper presents a novel method for addressing linear inverse problems by leveraging generative models based on discrete diffusion as priors. We overcome these limitations by approximating the true posterior distribution with a variational distribution constructed from categorical distributions and continuous relaxation techniques. Furthermore, we employ a star-shaped noise process to mitigate the drawbacks of traditional discrete diffusion models with absorbing states, demonstrating that our method performs comparably to continuous diffusion techniques with a lower GPU memory consumption. Our code is available at https://github.com/sony/g2d2.

C1.justification: The principal method, comparable-reconstruction-quality claim, and training-free motion claim remain. v2 removes the explicit first-use claim for image inverse problems and adds prominent memory/accessibility claims, including up to 77% lower memory and suitability for 8 GiB GPUs. Its conclusion further asserts an order-of-magnitude memory reduction, exceeding the unchanged table's evidence.

C2.justification: v2 adds substantive interpretations of prompt dependence, possible decoder effects in prior selection, and persistent errors when prompts mismatch target faces. It acknowledges motion-quality versus path-accuracy tradeoffs and the limited ImageNet FID reference size. These provide specific applicability boundaries beyond v1's general speed, performance, and future-domain limitations.

D1.justification: v1 promises a future code release; v2 reports public code and supplies its repository link. v2 also documents revised optimization parameters, an alternative prior source, and clean-fid features, preprocessing, and reference statistics. Hardware reporting gains an unresolved inconsistency: Section 4.1 says all experiments use RTX 3090, while Appendix E.5 retains A6000 measurements.

E1.justification: ImageNet/FFHQ super-resolution and Gaussian deblurring remain. Motion evaluation changes substantially: v1 illustrates hand-designed forward and zigzag paths, whereas v2 evaluates HumanML3D test motions with sparse conditioning at 5 of 196 frames. This introduces a distinct sparse-control scenario; the earlier motion demonstrations are no longer reported.

E2.justification: v2 adds OmniControl and Guided Motion Diffusion (GMD) as quantitative motion comparators in Table 3, providing external comparisons absent from v1's motion demonstration. The image comparison methods remain DPS, DDRM, PSLD, ReSample, and the Markov-process variant.

E3.justification: The main image evaluations expand from 100 to 1,000 images per dataset. Reported optimization settings change, including Adam to RAdam, learning rates, schedules, and the ImageNet super-resolution KL weight. v2 also introduces SSIM/FID/KID evaluation, quantitative sparse-motion protocols, and prompt/prior controls; the prior comparison uses 100 FFHQ images.

E4.justification: Appendices E.7-E.9 add tests of text conditioning, VQDiff-ITHQ versus CVQDiff-FFHQ priors, and prompt-related failure cases. Figure 2 expands the early-structure analysis through multiple conditional samples. The existing Markov-process and forgetting-coefficient analyses are retained, with revised examples.

E5.justification: Neither version reports repeated-run counts, random seeds, confidence intervals, error bars, or significance tests for its results. Larger evaluation sets and additional metrics do not change the uncertainty-reporting practice.

E6.justification: Tables 1-2 replace the image scores: for example, G2D2 ImageNet super-resolution changes from LPIPS/PSNR 0.349/23.20 to 0.340/23.82. Changed samples and optimization settings prevent interpreting this as a same-setting gain. v2 adds motion, prompt/prior, and SSIM/FID/KID results. The memory/time values in v1 Table 4 and v2 Table 5 remain identical.

M1.justification: The reported inner optimization changes from Adam to RAdam in Section 4.1 and Appendix E.2. The variational objective, Gumbel-Softmax relaxation, star-shaped sampling, and initialization strategy remain fundamentally unchanged. The star-decomposed distribution corresponds to v1's qsampling, rather than a newly introduced sampler.

P1.justification: The introduction and methodological exposition are extensively rewritten. Section 3 separates star-shaped noise, the decomposed distribution, and variational inference more explicitly, with expanded explanations and revised terminology. Ethics and reproducibility statements move into appendices, and the appendix structure is reorganized.

P2.justification: v2 substantially redraws Figures 2-3, adds prompt/prior/failure figures and motion/expanded-metric tables, and removes v1's motion Figures 6 and 14. Several retained image grids are relocated and enlarged. Typography, headings, and page layout also change throughout.

R1.justification: The existing related-work framework is retained. v2 adds a focused distinction from Feynman-Kac steering, a paragraph on applications across domains, and references supporting the motion comparators, alternative prior, optimizer, metrics, and prompt tuning. This extends the positioning without replacing its central relationship to continuous inverse solvers and discrete guidance.

T1.justification: Appendix D corrects important reasoning: the KL proof uses the decomposed joint, and Lemma D.1 replaces v1 Lemma B.3's unjustified Kronecker-delta return argument with successive marginalization. These substantively repair support for the retained method. However, v2's new transition-normalization condition uses (K-1)beta despite Eq. 2 containing K beta contributions per non-mask column.

improvement.justification: v2 repairs an important marginal-preservation proof and substantially strengthens validation through broader image sampling, quantitative motion comparisons, and analyses exposing prompt/prior dependencies and failures. These address weaknesses in v1's theoretical support and largely illustrative motion evidence. The gains outweigh new reporting defects, including the transition-normalization inconsistency, conflicting hardware statements, and an unsupported order-of-magnitude memory claim: Table 5 shows 4.7 versus at most 20.9 GiB. The improvement rests on stronger justification and more informative evidence, rather than the changed performance scores alone.

A1.justification: Both PDFs describe G2D2 and have readable text, equations, tables, figures, and appendices. The expanded and reorganized material in v2 can be matched reliably to v1.

after.justification: v2 reports original image reconstruction experiments, quantitative HumanML3D motion results, prompt and prior-model ablations, and failure cases.

before.justification: v1 reports original ImageNet and FFHQ reconstruction experiments, graphical-model and forgetting-coefficient analyses, resource measurements, and qualitative motion-generation results.

arxiv_record.abstract: Causal learning from data has received much attention recently. Bayesian networks can be used to capture causal relationships. There, one recovers a weighted directed acyclic graph in which random variables are represented by vertices, and the weights associated with each edge represent the strengths of the causal relationships between them. This concept is extended to capture dynamic effects by introducing a dependency on past data, which may be captured by the structural equation model. This formalism is utilized in the present contribution to propose a score-based learning algorithm. A mixed-integer quadratic program is formulated and an algorithmic solution proposed, in which the pre-generation of exponentially many acyclicity constraints is avoided by utilizing the so-called branch-and-cut (``lazy constraint'') method. Comparing the novel approach to the state-of-the-art, we show that the proposed approach turns out to produce more accurate results when applied to small and medium-sized synthetic instances containing up to 80 time series. Lastly, two interesting applications in bioscience and finance, to which the method is directly applied, further stress the importance of developing highly accurate, globally convergent solvers that can handle instances of modest size.
arxiv_record.authors: Pavel Rytir, Ales Wodecki, Georgios Korpas, Jakub Marecek
arxiv_record.title: ExDBN: Learning Dynamic Bayesian Networks using Extended Mixed-Integer Programming Formulations
