C1.justification: The abstract expands the claimed demonstrated scale from 25 to 80 time series. The introduction shifts from finding global solutions to near-global solutions, and the conclusion replaces the finance claim of two-minute global optimality with a 20% gap in 30 minutes. These substantially revise scalability and attained-exactness claims while retaining eventual global convergence.

C2.justification: V3 introduces a substantive limitation concerning normalization and suitability for data with meaningful original scales. It interprets baseline weaknesses through their non-Gaussian or nonlinear modeling assumptions and discusses variability as dependent on computation time. The new finance interpretation explicitly acknowledges that preferring ExDBN's network is subjective because ground truth is unknown.

D1.justification: V3 newly identifies Gurobi and the main benchmark's 32 GB memory limit, and specifies autoregressive order two for the financial networks. Conversely, the numerical regularization settings supplied in v1's plot legends disappear from v3's redesigned plots. These are localized additions and losses in reproducibility information.

E1.justification: V3 adds ER-3-1-var, with Gaussian noise variances sampled separately for each variable from (0.6, 1.2). The ER/SF graph families, Krebs-cycle task, and 16-CDS dataset remain. V1's ER2-1-1 corresponds to v3's renamed ER-2-2, so that naming change does not add coverage.

E2.justification: V1's synthetic experiments directly compare only with DYNOTEARS. V3 adds evaluated LiNGAM and NTS-NOTEARS comparisons in Figures 1–2 and the scalability study. It also adds DYNOTEARS as an actual comparator within the finance application, displaying both methods' learned networks in Figures 6–7.

E3.justification: The evaluation changes from selecting the best ground-truth-based threshold separately for each method to using a fixed threshold of 0.15. G-score evaluation is dropped. New experiments include a runtime–accuracy study with 25 variables and 250 samples, and scaling to 30–80 variables with n = 5d, a 22-hour limit, and 128 GB memory. The main benchmark's 7200-second cap is retained.

E4.justification: V3 quantifies the three lazy-constraint variants already discussed in v1 through Table 2, and adds runtime–SHD curves and constraint-count diagnostics in Figures 3 and 5. It also reports a qualitative normalization-sensitivity test and substantially expands the finance case study through analysis of recovered graph structures.

E5.justification: Both versions specify ten seeds per synthetic experiment. V3 adds standard deviations and uncertainty bands to the earlier mean-and-worst-case reporting, and reports runtime means with standard deviations in Table 1. This expands uncertainty reporting without establishing an increase in repetitions.

E6.justification: V3 replaces and expands the synthetic results, removes G-score results, and adds runtime, scalability, and financial-network findings. Table 2 reports mean MIP gaps of 0.335, 0.344, and 0.346 for all-cycle, shortest-cycle, and first-cycle variants. The finance result changes from global optimality within two minutes to a 20% gap after 30 minutes; identical experimental settings are not established.

M1.justification: The documented L2 penalty changes from sums of edge indicators and unsquared lag weights in v1 Equation 11 to squared intra- and inter-slice weights in v3 Equation 13. This revises one objective component; the structural model and lazy cycle-cut algorithm remain. The PDFs do not establish whether implementation changed.

P1.justification: The introduction and problem formulation are extensively rewritten, with expanded variable definitions and a new MIQP tutorial. Data generation moves into the experiments section, the applications are reordered, and the title and regularization terminology change. These constitute substantial narrative restructuring beyond the added experiments.

P2.justification: V1's three full-page figures organized by graph ensemble are replaced by SHD and F1 grids organized across ensembles and sample sizes. V3 adds runtime and scaling plots, constraint-count plots, two tables, and paired financial-network heatmaps. The author block, typography, and placement of figures within the text are also redesigned.

R1.justification: V3 substantially expands connections to optimization-based DAG learning through Manzour, Xu, and Jaakkola, and adds literature on scale-sensitive causal benchmarks, DBN history, and mixed-integer optimization foundations. The introduction consequently provides a broader account of competing approaches and their limitations than v1's predominantly application-oriented framing.

T1.justification: The mathematical definition of L2 regularization is substantively corrected between v1 Equation 11 and v3 Equation 13. The identifiability remark and underlying cycle-exclusion and convergence reasoning remain. The new MIQP and MIP-gap section mainly supplies standard background rather than new theorems or proofs.

improvement.justification: V3 substantially strengthens the evidence needed to assess ExDBN's accuracy–computation tradeoff through measured runtimes, standard deviations, time-budget analyses, and quantified lazy-constraint comparisons, which v1 largely lacked. It also supplies meaningful applicability limitations and qualifies the finance optimality claim. Missing per-setting regularization values and lingering L1/L0 terminology inconsistencies weaken reproducibility, but the expanded empirical support and more explicit qualifications provide a substantial net quality improvement.

A1.justification: Both PDFs describe ExDBN and retain the same core research problem and algorithm. All 12 pages of v1 and 16 pages of v3, including equations, plotted results, and end matter, support comparison. Neither supplied PDF contains an appendix.

after.justification: V3 reports original synthetic comparisons, scalability and runtime experiments, lazy-constraint evaluations, and learned financial networks, alongside the retained biomedical result.

before.justification: V1 reports original synthetic comparisons with DYNOTEARS in Figures 1–3 and ExDBN runtime and optimality-gap results for the finance and biomedical examples.

arxiv_record.abstract: Generative adversarial networks (GANs) learn a latent space whose samples can be mapped to real-world images. Such latent spaces are difficult to interpret. Some earlier supervised methods aim to create an interpretable latent space or discover interpretable directions, which requires exploiting data labels or annotated synthesized samples for training. However, we propose using a modification of vector quantization called space-filling vector quantization (SFVQ), which quantizes the data on a piece-wise linear curve. SFVQ can capture the underlying morphological structure of the latent space, making it interpretable. We apply this technique to model the latent space of pre-trained StyleGAN2 and BigGAN networks on various datasets. Our experiments show that the SFVQ curve yields a general interpretable model of the latent space such that it determines which parts of the latent space correspond to specific generative factors. Furthermore, we demonstrate that each line of the SFVQ curve can potentially refer to an interpretable direction for applying intelligible image transformations. We also demonstrate that the points located on an SFVQ line can be used for controllable data augmentation.
arxiv_record.authors: Mohammad Hassan Vali and Tom B\"ackstr\"om
arxiv_record.title: Unsupervised Panoptic Interpretation of Latent Spaces in GANs Using Space-Filling Vector Quantization

C1.justification: The central claims about latent-space interpretation, editing directions, and controllable augmentation remain. v2 extends its introduction/conclusion superiority claims to SeFa and removes v1's explicit claim that joint interpretable directions had never previously been found.

C2.justification: v1 inferred latent-space class proportions from codeword fractions. v2's Section 5.1 and Appendix A.1 show that diversity alone does not explain the horse class's roughly 25% allocation and that initialization with 8 or 16 codewords changes it, materially qualifying that interpretation. v2 also expands the geometric/MSE explanation and drops the assertion that a larger image pool alone establishes greater statistical significance.

D1.justification: v2 documents uniform dithering and the training loss, supplies SeFa semantic indices and layer ranges in Table 3, and updates the repository address. Conversely, v1's detailed reproducibility statement and code inventory disappear, although codebook-access statements remain. The PDFs do not establish that the underlying resources became unavailable.

E1.justification: Both versions use FFHQ, AFHQ, LSUN Cars, CIFAR10, ImageNet, and the same synthetic distribution domains. The added human ratings and initialization/sensitivity experiments evaluate retained data and editing tasks rather than introducing new application coverage.

E2.justification: SeFa, previously only cited, becomes an evaluated comparator across seven face-editing directions in Tables 1–2 and Figure 11, alongside GANSpace and LatentCLR. It also participates in the new human-ranking comparison, substantially extending the central comparative evaluation.

E3.justification: v2 introduces a 20-participant ranking study using 100 latent vectors, five per participant, with seven editing positions at sigma=2.67. It adds analyses using 10,000 vectors per CIFAR10 class and initialization/hyperparameter sweeps. The main qualitative illustration changes sigma from 2.5 to 4. The existing automatic evaluation retains 1,000 vectors and 41-image trajectories.

E4.justification: v2 adds random-versus-proposed initialization comparisons on 3D moons (Figure 4), CIFAR10 class-diversity and initial-codebook-size analyses (Appendix A.1), and systematic bitrate, batch-size, and learning-rate sensitivity tests (Appendix A.8). The earlier bitrate, class-transfer, and traveling-salesman analyses are retained.

E5.justification: Both versions average automatic scores over 1,000 latent vectors without reporting repeated-training seeds, confidence intervals, or significance tests. New human-rank frequencies and class-diversity variances are descriptive results, not uncertainty estimates.

E6.justification: All existing SFVQ, GANSpace, and LatentCLR numerical rows in Tables 1–2 are unchanged. New SeFa rows alter some rankings: its smile correlation is 0.46 versus SFVQ's retained 0.40. Figure 10 adds human-ranking outcomes favoring SFVQ on five directions, with comparable performance on rotation and gender. New appendix results document initialization-dependent class allocation and hyperparameter sensitivity.

M1.justification: The proposed norm-ordered initialization, 0.99/0.01 codebook expansion, adjacent-codeword editing directions, and BigGAN latent-space transfer remain unchanged. v2 explains existing SFVQ training more explicitly; alternative initial codebook sizes are experimental configurations rather than a replacement algorithm.

P1.justification: The introduction's contribution bullets become an integrated narrative, the method explanation expands into separate why/how subsections, and qualitative and quantitative comparisons receive separate sections. The reproducibility section is removed and appendices are reorganized. These changes substantially revise the exposition beyond routine language editing.

P2.justification: v2 adds Hilbert-curve, dithering, initialization, and geometric diagrams; human-ranking, class-diversity, and sensitivity plots; and a SeFa configuration table. Comparison tables expand and the qualitative comparison figure is replaced. Existing displays are reorganized within the journal layout, while the earlier ten-example gallery is no longer embedded.

R1.justification: Section 2 expands substantially beyond the earlier three-category overview, explaining supervised, linear/nonlinear, GAN-inversion, and diffusion-editing approaches and their relationship to this work. Numerous relevant works are added, including StyleSpace, Song et al.'s methods, and recent diffusion research, with an explicit distinction between the paper's GAN focus and diffusion editing.

T1.justification: Section 3.1 adds explicit mathematical definitions of the dithered codebook and nearest-sample quantization map, including uniform interpolation, in Equation (1). v1 described curve mapping verbally. This adds limited formal specification without introducing a theorem, proof, or new theoretical guarantee.

improvement.justification: v2 substantially strengthens validation of the retained method through human rankings, a substantive SeFa comparison, and tests of previously asserted hyperparameter robustness. Its initialization analysis also qualifies an important overinterpretation of codeword proportions, while fuller method explanations improve assessability. Losing the detailed reproducibility inventory and moving qualitative examples to an unavailable supplement reduces self-containment, but these drawbacks are outweighed by the stronger evidence and more informative analysis of central claims.

A1.justification: Both PDFs describe the same SFVQ study, and all included pages and appendices are readable. However, v1 includes ten qualitative comparison plates, while v2 references a separate 50-example supplement that is not supplied. Those galleries cannot be fully matched; the remaining material supports reliable comparison.

after.justification: v2 retains original experimental results and adds SeFa comparisons, human rankings in Figure 10, and initialization and sensitivity analyses in Appendices A.1 and A.8.

before.justification: v1 reports original SFVQ experiments, quantitative face-editing results in Tables 1–2, and appendix experiments on class transfer, bitrates, and synthetic distributions.

arxiv_record.abstract: Node representations, or embeddings, are low-dimensional vectors that capture node properties, typically learned through unsupervised structural similarity objectives or supervised tasks. While recent efforts have focused on explaining graph model decisions, the interpretability of unsupervised node embeddings remains underexplored. To bridge this gap, we introduce DiSeNE (Disentangled and Self-Explainable Node Embedding), a framework that generates self-explainable embeddings in an unsupervised manner. Our method employs disentangled representation learning to produce dimension-wise interpretable embeddings, where each dimension is aligned with distinct topological structure of the graph. We formalize novel desiderata for disentangled and interpretable embeddings, which drive our new objective functions, optimizing simultaneously for both interpretability and disentanglement. Additionally, we propose several new metrics to evaluate representation quality and human interpretability. Extensive experiments across multiple benchmark datasets demonstrate the effectiveness of our approach.
arxiv_record.authors: Simone Piaggesi, Andr\'e Panisson, Megha Khosla
arxiv_record.title: Disentangled and Self-Explainable Node Representation Learning

arxiv_record.abstract: Multi-objective learning (MOL) aims to learn under multiple potentially conflicting objectives and strike a proper balance. While recent preference-guided MOL methods often rely on additional optimization objectives or constraints, we consider the classic Tchebycheff scalarization (TCH) that naturally allows for locating solutions with user-specified trade-offs. Due to its minimax formulation, directly optimizing TCH often leads to training oscillation and stagnation. In light of this limitation, we propose an adaptive online mirror descent algorithm for TCH, called (Ada)OMD-TCH. One of our main ingredients is an adaptive online-to-batch conversion that significantly improves solution optimality over traditional conversion in practice while maintaining the same theoretical convergence guarantees. We show that (Ada)OMD-TCH achieves a convergence rate of $\mathcal O(\sqrt{\log m/T})$, where $m$ is the number of objectives and $T$ is the number of rounds, providing a tighter dependency on $m$ in the offline setting compared to existing work. Empirically, we demonstrate on both synthetic problems and federated learning tasks that (Ada)OMD-TCH effectively smooths the training process and yields preference-guided, specific, diverse, and fair solutions.
arxiv_record.authors: Meitong Liu, Xiaoyuan Zhang, Chulin Xie, Kate Donahue, Han Zhao
arxiv_record.title: Adaptive Online Mirror Descent for Tchebycheff Scalarization in Multi-Objective Learning

R1.justification: New Table 1 and Section 3.4 substantially expand positioning against prior OMD, gradient-manipulation, and preference-guided methods. arxiv_record.abstract: We study offline off-dynamics reinforcement learning (RL) to utilize data from an easily accessible source domain to enhance policy learning in a target domain with limited data. Our approach centers on return-conditioned supervised learning (RCSL), particularly focusing on Decision Transformer (DT) type frameworks, which can predict actions conditioned on desired return guidance and complete trajectory history. Previous works address the dynamics shift problem by augmenting the reward in the trajectory from the source domain to match the optimal trajectory in the target domain. However, this strategy can not be directly applicable in RCSL owing to (1) the unique form of the RCSL policy class, which explicitly depends on the return, and (2) the absence of a straightforward representation of the optimal trajectory distribution. We propose the Return Augmented (REAG) method for DT type frameworks, where we augment the return in the source domain by aligning its distribution with that in the target domain. We provide the theoretical analysis demonstrating that the RCSL policy learned from REAG achieves the same level of suboptimality as would be obtained without a dynamics shift. We introduce two practical implementations REAG$_\text{Dara}^{*}$ and REAG$_\text{MV}^{*}$ respectively. Thorough experiments on D4RL datasets and various DT-type baselines demonstrate that our methods consistently enhance the performance of DT type frameworks in off-dynamics RL.
arxiv_record.authors: Ruhan Wang, Yu Yang, Zhishuai Liu, Dongruo Zhou, Pan Xu
arxiv_record.comments: 26 pages, 11 tables, 8 figures. Published in Transactions on Machine Learning Research (TMLR)
arxiv_record.title: Return Augmented Decision Transformer for Off-Dynamics Reinforcement Learning

E1.justification: The three locomotion environments remain, but reported coverage contracts substantially. Random evaluations and all morphology-shift evaluations disappear. E2.justification: v2 adds evaluated Reinformer and QT baselines and their augmented variants, plus DFDT, H2O, and IGDF in Tables 8–10. The conventional algorithms and their DARA variants remain. Within the consistency ablation, the unaugmented DT control shown in v1 Figure 7 is absent from v2 Figure 5.

E3.justification: The reported Walker2D-Medium clipping interval changes from 0.9–2 to 0.9–1.25. The consistency ablation changes from backward reconstruction within context windows to reconstruction from an augmented initial return. New protocols compare Q predictions with 100 rollout trajectories and vary CQL regularization and target sample counts. Figure 1 also replaces summed ranks with normalized average ranks. These changes do not establish that retained experiments were rerun.

E4.justification: v2 adds Q-value accuracy checks, sensitivity to critic training, and empirical checks of the Gaussian approximation in Figures 6–8. Clipping and consistency analyses extend to three backbones. Conversely, v1's target-return sweep and empirical-statistics augmentation comparison disappear, alongside several dynamics stress tests. This substantially changes the questions investigated.

E5.justification: Five-seed averaging remains. v2 identifies the seeds, explicitly labels standard deviations, and adds 95% confidence intervals for the principal comparisons in Table 7. Figure 6 reports means and variances over 100 trajectories. These refine uncertainty reporting without establishing an increase in repeated training runs.

E6.justification: v2 adds extensive results for additional backbones, comparators, and diagnostics while removing earlier evaluation entries. Retained scores also change: Walker2D Medium-Replay 1T BCQ changes from 62.567 to 60.638, and HalfCheetah Medium-Expert 1T AWR changes from 901.68 to 90.168 (v1 Table 1; v2 Table 8). Revised aggregate ranks use a different comparison pool and cannot be interpreted as direct performance gains.

M1.justification: The augmentation procedures remain DARA-based return relabeling and Gaussian mean–variance matching through Equations 4.1–4.4. CQL-based estimation and variance-ratio clipping already appear in v1. v2 renames the framework and applies it to Reinformer and QT without specifying a new augmentation mechanism.

P1.justification: The introduction, related work, experimental narrative, and ablation discussion are extensively rewritten around DT-type frameworks. Terminology changes throughout from RADT to REAG. Detailed theory moves into the main text, references move before the appendices, and the appendix structure is reorganized with separate failure-analysis and additional-theory sections.

P2.justification: v2 adopts journal formatting and substantially redesigns the displays. Comparisons are organized around multiple backbones, v1's landscape results table is replaced by separate portrait tables, and several plots become grouped panels. Confidence-interval tables, Q-value curves, and histograms are added; earlier plots and the consistency pseudocode are removed.

R1.justification: Section 2 substantially expands beyond DARC/DARA to discuss filtering, representation alignment, cross-domain optimization, and model-based approaches, including H2O, VGDF, BOSA, IGDF, SRPO, and MOBODY. v2 also cites DFDT and positions the earlier RADT study as a precursor to the broader REAG framework.

T1.justification: The original detailed sample-complexity result largely moves from v1 Appendix A into v2 Section 4.4, with its proof retained in Appendix A. Separately, new Appendix E introduces distinct source and target behavior policies, mixture-policy definitions, revised coverage assumptions, and Theorems E.4–E.6 with proofs. This materially extends the theoretical scope.

improvement.justification: v2 substantially strengthens validation beyond the single DT backbone through additional architectures and relevant comparators, checks key estimation assumptions, and explicitly analyzes cases where augmentation hurts. Appendix E also extends the analysis to differing behavior policies used in practice. These gains improve the support and qualification of the paper's conclusions, despite the loss of Random and morphology evaluations, several earlier ablations, and self-contained DT training details.

A1.justification: Both PDFs describe the same return-augmentation research, with RADT renamed REAG in v2. Their main text, equations, tables, figures, and appendices support reliable comparison, including the rotated results table in v1.

after.justification: v2 retains original experiments and adds evaluations involving Reinformer, QT, additional baselines, value-function diagnostics, and empirical return distributions in Section 5 and Appendix C.

before.justification: v1 reports original MuJoCo experiments comparing DT, RADT, and baseline algorithms, together with dynamics-shift and component ablations in Section 5 and Appendix D.

arxiv_record.abstract: The rapid discovery of new chemical compounds is essential for advancing global health and developing treatments. While generative models show promise in creating novel molecules, challenges remain in ensuring the real-world applicability of these molecules and finding such molecules efficiently. To address this challenge, we introduce Conditional Latent Space Molecular Scaffold Optimization (CLaSMO), which integrates a Conditional Variational Autoencoder (CVAE) with Latent Space Bayesian Optimization (LSBO) to strategically modify molecules while preserving similarity to the original input, effectively framing the task as constrained optimization. Our LSBO setting improves the sample-efficiency of the molecular optimization, and our modification approach helps us to obtain molecules with higher chances of real-world applicability. CLaSMO explores substructures of molecules in a sample-efficient manner by performing BO in the latent space of a CVAE conditioned on the atomic environment of the molecule to be optimized. Our extensive evaluations across diverse optimization tasks, including rediscovery, docking score, and multi-property optimization, show that CLaSMO efficiently enhances target properties, delivers remarkable sample-efficiency crucial for resource-limited applications while considering molecular similarity constraints, achieves state of the art performance, and maintains practical synthetic accessibility. We also provide an open-source web application that enables chemical experts to apply CLaSMO in a Human-in-the-Loop setting.
arxiv_record.authors: Onur Boyar, Hiroyuki Hanada, Ichiro Takeuchi
arxiv_record.comments: Published in Transactions on Machine Learning Research
arxiv_record.title: Conditional Latent Space Molecular Scaffold Optimization for Accelerated Molecular Design

arxiv_record.abstract: Reliable confidence estimation is essential for enhancing the trustworthiness of large language models (LLMs), especially in high-stakes scenarios. Despite its importance, accurately estimating confidence in LLM responses remains a significant challenge. In this work, we propose using an auxiliary learning model to assess response correctness based on the self-consistency of multiple outputs generated by the LLM. Our method builds a consistency graph to represent the agreement among multiple responses and uses a graph neural network (GNN) to estimate the likelihood that each response is correct. Experiments demonstrate that this method has strong calibration performance on various benchmark datasets and generalizes well to out-of-domain cases.

arxiv_record.abstract:
Language agents based on large language models (LLMs) have demonstrated great
promise in automating web-based tasks. Recent work has shown that incorporating
advanced planning algorithms, e.g., tree search, is advantageous over reactive
planning for web agents. However, unlike simulated sandbox environments,
real-world environments such as the web are rife with irreversible actions.
This undermines the feasibility of backtracking, a cornerstone of (tree)
search. Overly relying on test-time search also hurts efficiency. We advocate
model-based planning for web agents that employs a world model to simulate and
deliberate over the outcome of each candidate action before committing to one.
We systematically explore this paradigm by (1) Proposing a model-based planning
framework, WebDreamer, which employs LLMs to serve as both world models and
value functions; (2) Training specialized LLMs as world models with a scalable
data synthesis pipeline. Empirical results demonstrate that WebDreamer achieves
substantial performance improvements over reactive baselines. It is
competitive, while being 4-5 times more efficient, with tree search in sandbox
environments (VisualWebArena) and also works effectively on real-world websites
(Online-Mind2Web and Mind2Web-Live). Furthermore, our trained world model,
Dreamer-7B, performs comparable to GPT-4o, highlighting the potential of
specialized world models for efficient and effective planning in complex web
environments.

arxiv_record.abstract: We consider the approximation of functions by 2-layer neural networks with a small number of hidden weights based on the squared loss and small datasets. Due to the highly non-convex energy landscape, gradient-based training often suffers from local minima. As a remedy, we initialize the hidden weights with samples from a learned proposal distribution, which we parameterize as a deep generative model. To train this model, we exploit the fact that with fixed hidden weights, the optimal output weights solve a linear equation. After learning the generative model, we refine the sampled weights with a gradient-based post-processing in the latent space. Here, we also include a regularization scheme to counteract potential noise. Finally, we demonstrate the effectiveness of our approach by numerical examples.

arxiv_record.title: Generative Feature Training of Thin 2-Layer Networks

snapshot_arxiv_record.abstract: We consider the approximation of functions by 2-layer neural networks with a small number of hidden weights based on the squared loss and small datasets. Due to the highly non-convex energy landscape, gradient-based training often suffers from local minima. As a remedy, we initialize the hidden weights with samples from a learned proposal distribution, which we parameterize as a deep generative model. To train this model, we exploit the fact that with fixed hidden weights, the optimal output weights solve a linear equation. After learning the generative model, we refine the sampled weights with a gradient-based post-processing in the latent space. Here, we also include a regularization scheme to counteract potential noise. Finally, we demonstrate the effectiveness of our approach by numerical examples.

C1.justification: The abstract, contribution paragraph and discussion retain the same central claims: learned feature proposals, analytically solved output weights, latent refinement and regularization improve training of thin two-layer networks on small datasets. The additional evidence does not redefine the main contribution.

C2.justification: v2 replaces the categorical minibatching prohibition with a discussion of batch-dependent output weights and explicitly states the squared-loss restriction. Appendix B explains why jointly sampled output weights underperform. Section 4.2 qualifies support recovery by acknowledging off-support features, while Remark 1 discusses extension to vector-valued outputs.

D1.justification: Appendix C supplies settings that v1 left to the code: learning rates of 1e-4 for GFT/refinement and 1e-3 for neural networks, 100000 neural-network steps, epsilon=1e-7 and 1000 regularization samples. These are newly documented details; the code address, GPU and reported runtime remain unchanged.

E1.justification: Both versions evaluate g1–g3, f1–f3, h1–h3 and the same six UCI datasets: Propulsion, Galaxy, Airfoil, CCPP, Telemonit and Skillkraft. The new appendices vary feature counts and training procedures on existing tasks, without adding data domains or test scenarios.

E2.justification: v2 adds F-Opt and Gaussian kernel ridge regression to each of Tables 1–3. Figure 1 additionally evaluates conventional neural-network training, previously absent from that comparison. Appendix B introduces fully sampled weights and noisy-gradient controls, substantially expanding the evaluated alternatives.

E3.justification: New settings include N=50 and N=200 in Appendix A, joint feature/output-weight sampling and noisy SGD with noise strength 0.1 times the step size in Appendix B, and a median-rule Gaussian kernel. Existing experiments retain their splits, metrics, regularization search and stated GFT training budget; Appendix C's disclosures do not establish reruns.

E4.justification: Beyond v1's refinement comparisons and feature visualization, v2 tests direct feature optimization, sensitivity to feature count, replacing the analytic output-weight solve with joint sampling, and adding gradient noise. Appendices A–B and the expanded Figure 1 provide substantial new evidence about component necessity and optimization behavior.

E5.justification: Both versions report five-run mean test MSEs. Tables 4–6 extend the same reporting practice, without adding seed information, dispersion estimates, confidence intervals, significance tests or an increased repeat count.

E6.justification: Matched scores in Tables 1–3 and retained Figure 1 panels are unchanged. v2 adds F-Opt, kernel-ridge and neural-network visualization results, plus extensive width and ablation results in Tables 4–6. These also expose sensitivity: Table 5 reports Fourier GFT-r MSE 1.82 for f3 with d=10, M=200 and N=200, an added setting rather than a revised original score.

M1.justification: The proposed pipeline retains the linear output-weight solve, learned feature distribution, latent-space Adam refinement and total-variation regularization. GFT-p is renamed GFT-r. F-Opt's direct reduced-loss optimization was already described in v1; the new experimental controls do not revise the proposed GFT procedure.

P1.justification: v2 edits prose, replaces GFT-p/post-processing terminology with GFT-r/feature refinement, converts Example 1 into bullets and expands the explanation of compared methods. It adds Appendices A–C and updates author/publication information, while retaining the main section sequence and narrative.

P2.justification: Figure 1 expands from nine to twelve panels through a new neural-network row. Tables 1–3 gain comparator rows and are reflowed, while three new tables present appendix experiments. Best-score highlighting gains boldface, and publication headers are added.

R1.justification: Section 2 adds connections to extreme learning machines, Dunbar et al.'s adaptive random-feature work and implicit kernel learning, while sharpening distinctions from sparse feature selection and alternating updates. Kernel-regression and UCI references are also added. Publication updates for existing references do not represent new related works.

T1.justification: Section 3.1 newly states that the regularized solution of equation (6) converges to the minimum-norm solution of equation (5) as epsilon approaches zero. This adds a limited mathematical property; the core derivations remain unchanged and no new theorem or proof is supplied.

improvement.justification: The F-Opt comparisons and Appendix B controls address an important gap in v1 by directly testing the roles of learned proposals and analytically solved output weights. Width experiments and explicit implementation settings further strengthen empirical scrutiny and reproducibility. These are substantial gains, although five-run means still lack dispersion estimates and the newly exposed width-dependent failures receive little interpretation.

A1.justification: Both PDFs are complete, readable versions of the same research work. Their methods, equations, experiments, figures and tables can be matched reliably. v1 ends with references; v2 additionally contains Appendices A–C.

after.justification: v2 retains the original experiments and adds numerical baseline comparisons, feature-count experiments and ablations, including original results in Tables 4–6.

before.justification: Sections 4.2–4.4 report original feature visualizations, synthetic function approximation and UCI regression results in Figure 1 and Tables 1–3, alongside baseline results attributed to prior work.

arxiv_record.abstract: Despite rapid advancements in TTS models, a consistent and robust human evaluation framework is still lacking. For example, MOS tests fail to differentiate between similar models, and CMOS's pairwise comparisons are time-intensive. The MUSHRA test is a promising alternative for evaluating multiple TTS systems simultaneously, but in this work we show that its reliance on matching human reference speech unduly penalises the scores of modern TTS systems that can exceed human speech quality. More specifically, we conduct a comprehensive assessment of the MUSHRA test, focusing on its sensitivity to factors such as rater variability, listener fatigue, and reference bias. Based on our extensive evaluation involving 492 human listeners across Hindi and Tamil we identify two primary shortcomings: (i) reference-matching bias, where raters are unduly influenced by the human reference, and (ii) judgement ambiguity, arising from a lack of clear fine-grained guidelines. To address these issues, we propose two refined variants of the MUSHRA test. The first variant enables fairer ratings for synthesized samples that surpass human reference quality. The second variant reduces ambiguity, as indicated by the relatively lower variance across raters. By combining these approaches, we achieve both more reliable and more fine-grained assessments. We also release MANGO, a massive dataset of 246,000 human ratings, the first-of-its-kind collection for Indian languages, aiding in analyzing human preferences and developing automatic metrics for evaluating TTS systems.

C1.justification: The central claims about reference-matching bias, judgement ambiguity, and the benefits of NMR/DG remain. The corpus contribution is revised from 47,100 ratings and 471 listeners to 246,000 Hindi/Tamil ratings and 492 listeners; Section 7 reports 255,000 annotations including English. These revise the stated contribution's scale without redefining its central scientific claims.

C2.justification: v3 adds explanations for near-tied Tamil rankings and inflated anchor scores, discusses objective metrics' perceptual and language limitations, and uses survey responses to interpret rater behavior. Section 7 explicitly acknowledges no significant English variance reduction. Limitations now discuss missing demographics and additional biases, although Appendix A.8 inconsistently retains the statement that English was not evaluated.

D1.justification: v3 adds an explicit MANGO dataset-access link and identifies TorchAudio-Squim for objective measurements. It also documents rater demonstration calls, iterative guideline development, demographic nonresponse, and institutional ethics approval. XTTS training information is relocated rather than newly introduced.

E1.justification: v1 evaluates Hindi and Tamil using IndicTTS. v3 adds English systems trained on LJSpeech and evaluations by native US English speakers, substantially extending language, corpus, and listener-population coverage (Section 7).

E2.justification: Standard MUSHRA and CMOS remain the comparison protocols, with FS2, ST2, and VITS as the principal evaluated systems. XTTSv2 and duplicated VITS already appeared in v1's extended test; its table is moved into v3's main text. The new objective metrics assess alignment with conventional MUSHRA rather than introduce additional baselines against the proposed variants.

E3.justification: Table 1 increases DG panels from 14 Hindi and 15 Tamil listeners to 20 each, and DG-NMR panels from 15 to 20 each. New protocols include English evaluations with 30 listeners rating 30 utterances, English CMOS with 15 listeners, and a focused Tamil FS2-versus-VITS CMOS test. Section 4.7 also introduces PESQ, STOI, and SI-SDR measurements.

E4.justification: v3 adds objective-metric alignment analysis, CMOS-derived preference breakdowns, an 89-participant post-evaluation survey, and Tamil and English fault-isolation analyses (Section 4.7; Appendices A.2, A.5, A.7). A focused Tamil CMOS comparison investigates the FS2/VITS ranking discrepancy. Existing sensitivity, rejection-rule, and extended-system analyses are retained.

E5.justification: Both versions report means, standard deviations, and 95% confidence intervals and use 1,000 subsampling trials for ranking sensitivity. v3 does not specify a revised uncertainty-estimation, seed, or significance-testing procedure. Larger listener panels and changed interval values affect settings and results.

E6.justification: DG and DG-NMR results are revised alongside the enlarged panels: Hindi DG-NMR ST2/VITS means change from 89.55/89.33 in v1 Table 4 to 84.97/85.68 in v3 Table 6, reversing their order. Original MUSHRA, CMOS, NMR, and extended-test scores are retained. v3 additionally reports English, objective-metric, preference, survey, and diagnostic results; these are added or revised findings, not same-setting TTS performance improvements.

M1.justification: The NMR, DG, and combined procedures remain unchanged, including the six error counts, three perceptual dimensions, and scoring weights and caps. Section 5 newly describes iterative development, but the documented procedures and appendix guidelines do not establish a method revision.

P1.justification: v3 substantially expands explanatory material through a new MUSHRA background subsection and extended discussions of scoring and results. It adds dedicated English and Future Work sections and reorganizes the appendices, including moving the extended-test material into the main text. Much of the original introduction and method wording remains.

P2.justification: v3 adds objective-metric, English-comparison, and preference tables; a survey display; Tamil/English diagnostic plots; and English rating distributions. Several existing distribution plots are redrawn, Figure 5 is revised, and the extended-test table moves from the appendix to the main text. These changes substantially expand and reorganize the visual presentation.

R1.justification: v3 adds supporting literature on naturalness, expressive evaluation, anchor limitations, objective metrics, and perceptual biases, including Shirali-Shahreza and Penn, Merritt et al. (2018), Kumar et al. (2023a), and Zielinski. The existing positioning as a critique and refinement of MUSHRA remains.

T1.justification: The scoring formulas in v1 Appendix A.3 and v3 Appendix A.6 are algebraically identical. Reordering the arguments of min(7, SP) and changing notation or equation layout do not change the mathematics. No new theorem, proof, or substantive derivation is introduced.

improvement.justification: The English study directly addresses v1's explicit lack of English validation, while larger DG panels and targeted diagnostic analyses substantially strengthen assessment of the proposed protocols. Reporting the absence of significant English variance reduction also clarifies their limits. These gains outweigh incomplete editorial integration: Appendix A.8 still denies English evaluation, and Appendix A.5's 22% difficulty claim conflicts with Figure 9's 12% difficult plus 3% very difficult.

A1.justification: Both PDFs describe the same MUSHRA evaluation study and proposed variants. Their text, tables, figures, scoring formula, and complete appendices are readable and support reliable matching despite substantial additions in v3.

after.justification: v3 retains original empirical results and adds English evaluations, objective-metric results, a participant survey, and further diagnostic analyses.

before.justification: v1 reports original Hindi and Tamil listening experiments, including MUSHRA and CMOS scores, proposed-variant evaluations, and listener-sensitivity analyses.

arxiv_record.abstract: Spiking Neural Networks (SNNs) with their bio-inspired Leaky Integrate-and-Fire (LIF) neurons inherently capture temporal information. This makes them well-suited for sequential tasks like processing event-based data from Dynamic Vision Sensors (DVS) and event-based speech tasks. Harnessing the temporal capabilities of SNNs requires mitigating vanishing spikes during training, capturing spatio-temporal patterns and enhancing precise spike timing. To address these challenges, we propose TSkips, augmenting SNN architectures with forward and backward skip connections that incorporate explicit temporal delays. These connections capture long-term spatio-temporal dependencies and facilitate better spike flow over long sequences. The introduction of TSkips creates a vast search space of possible configurations, encompassing skip positions and time delay values. To efficiently navigate this search space, this work leverages training-free Neural Architecture Search (NAS) to identify optimal network structures and corresponding delays. We demonstrate the effectiveness of our approach on four event-based datasets: DSEC-flow for optical flow estimation, DVS128 Gesture for hand gesture recognition and Spiking Heidelberg Digits (SHD) and Spiking Speech Commands (SSC) for speech recognition. Our method achieves significant improvements across these datasets: up to 18% reduction in Average Endpoint Error (AEE) on DSEC-flow, 8% increase in classification accuracy on DVS128 Gesture, and up to 8% and 16% higher classification accuracy on SHD and SSC, respectively.
arxiv_record.authors: Prajna G. Malettira, Shubham Negi, Wachirawit Ponghiran, Kaushik Roy
arxiv_record.title: TSkips: Efficiency Through Explicit Temporal Delay Connections in Spiking Neural Networks

C1.justification: The abstract, enumerated contributions, headline performance claims, and conclusion retain their substantive message. However, v2 removes the introduction's assertion that learnable synaptic delays capture only short-window patterns, narrowing the comparative claim motivating TSkips.

C2.justification: v2 interprets the skip-removal results as evidence that TSkips improve learned representations during training, and discusses differences between forward and backward spike activity. New discussion addresses historical-state storage, memory and energy costs, neuromorphic routing constraints, and deployment without delayed states. Section 4.6 also acknowledges the parameter-efficiency advantage of competing transformers.

D1.justification: v2 documents the zero-tensor inference control, its treatment of alpha on DSEC-flow, and per-run NAS-selected delays and positions. Existing hardware, optimizer schedules, neuron initialization, dropout, and detailed architecture tables are retained. Corresponding CIFAR10-DVS-specific skip placements and delays are not supplied.

E1.justification: v2 retains the four original datasets and adds CIFAR10-DVS object classification in Section 4.6. This extends coverage to a distinct recognition task and event streams with artificially generated temporal information from repeated camera movements.

E2.justification: DVS-Gesture Table 2 adds Streaming rollout SNN, cited as Kugele et al. (2021), with 0.8M parameters and 95.56% accuracy. The new CIFAR10-DVS comparison adds NDA ResNet18/VGG11 baselines, alpha-SSA, and SpikingResformer, alongside Spikingformer. The original optical-flow and speech comparator sets remain unchanged.

E3.justification: v2 adds evaluation using large spiking ResNet18/VGG11 models with NDA augmentation, and controlled inference tests that replace delayed-state inputs with zeros. Table 12 additionally evaluates NAS searches producing seed-dependent delay and connection choices. The original datasets' stated splits, metrics, sequence lengths, and training schedules are retained.

E4.justification: Section 4.5 and Figure 8 add spike-activity analyses for two SHD examples. Appendices B.2 and C.2 test whether gains survive disabling temporal skips at inference, while Appendix D.2 examines robustness across NAS seeds. The earlier delay, placement, depth, energy, convergence, and operator analyses are retained.

E5.justification: v1 provides benchmark point estimates without reported seed counts or dispersion. v2 explicitly reports additional DSEC-flow NAS experiments across three random seeds, with mean AEE and standard deviation in Table 12. This introduces uncertainty reporting for that evaluation, without establishing repeated-run reporting for all benchmarks.

E6.justification: The original headline scores are retained, but v2 adds substantial results: CIFAR10-DVS backward-TSkips ResNet18 reaches 82.93% versus its 78.00% baseline; SHD backward-TSkips-1 scores 92.78% with skips disabled versus 93.64% enabled; and Table 12 reports seed-aggregated AEE. These are new evaluations, not improvements over v1 under unchanged conditions. New Table 6 reverses Mini/Micro labels relative to Table 1.

M1.justification: The core delayed connections, adaptive LIF neurons, alpha mixing, NAS procedure, and training algorithm are retained. Sections 4.5 and 5 introduce an optional deployment procedure that disables delayed-state propagation at inference. For DSEC-flow, Appendix B.2 explains retaining the alpha-weighted current-state contribution while zeroing the delayed contribution.

P1.justification: Most existing prose and the order of the original methodological and experimental material are retained. v2 makes targeted explanatory rewrites, introduces Observations, Scalability, and Discussion sections, and reorganizes the supplement into Appendices A-D. Author information, citation style, terminology, and cross-references are also updated.

P2.justification: The document changes from a two-column format to a predominantly single-column journal layout, extensively resizing and relocating figures and tables. v2 adds the spike-activity Figure 8 and Tables 4, 6, 9, and 12. Existing plots and supplementary tables remain identifiable despite renumbering and reformatting.

R1.justification: Section 2 adds substantive discussion of streaming rollouts, SCTT temporal skips, and TTFS delayed connections. It replaces the blanket short-window characterization with distinctions involving configuration-search expense, synchronization, and evaluation scope. Section 4.4 also positions TSkips as complementary to DCLS-Delays. These changes materially refine the relationship to closely related research.

T1.justification: Section 3.3 changes the formal temporal constraint from t < Delta t < T to 0 < t - Delta t < T and explicitly specifies discrete time indices. This revises the admissible delayed-time condition. The principal equations and search-space calculation remain unchanged; no new theorem or proof appears.

improvement.justification: v2 addresses important validation gaps through inference-removal controls, three-seed NAS results, and evaluation on standard architectures for CIFAR10-DVS. Closer engagement with prior temporal-skip methods and explicit hardware limitations also improve scientific positioning and qualification of the claims. These are substantial gains beyond the retained headline scores. The inconsistent Mini/Micro labels in Table 6 and missing CIFAR10-DVS skip configurations limit precision and reproducibility, but do not outweigh the overall improvement.

A1.justification: Both PDFs describe the same TSkips research. Their complete main texts, figures, tables, equations, and supplementary sections are readable and support reliable comparison despite substantial reformatting.

after.justification: v2 retains those original results and adds CIFAR10-DVS experiments, inference-time skip-removal analyses, spike-activity observations, and experiments across random seeds.

before.justification: v1 reports original optical-flow and classification experiments on DSEC-flow, DVS128 Gesture, SHD, and SSC, alongside ablations, convergence analyses, and energy estimates.

arxiv_record.abstract: Referring Image Segmentation (RIS) is an advanced vision-language task that involves identifying and segmenting objects within an image as described by free-form text descriptions. While previous studies focused on aligning visual and language features, exploring training techniques, such as data augmentation, remains underexplored. In this work, we explore effective data augmentation for RIS and propose a novel training framework called Masked Referring Image Segmentation (MaskRIS). We observe that the conventional image augmentations fall short of RIS, leading to performance degradation, while simple random masking significantly enhances the performance of RIS. MaskRIS uses both image and text masking, followed by Distortion-aware Contextual Learning (DCL) to fully exploit the benefits of the masking strategy. This approach can improve the model's robustness to occlusions, incomplete information, and various linguistic complexities, resulting in a significant performance improvement. Experiments demonstrate that MaskRIS can easily be applied to various RIS models, outperforming existing methods in both fully supervised and weakly supervised settings. Finally, MaskRIS achieves new state-of-the-art performance on RefCOCO, RefCOCO+, and RefCOCOg datasets. Code is available at https://github.com/naver-ai/maskris.
arxiv_record.authors: Minhyun Lee, Seungho Lee, Song Park, Dongyoon Han, Byeongho Heo, Hyunjung Shim

C1.justification: The introduction explicitly extends the contribution beyond RIS to REC and positions holistic masking with pixel-level DCL against architecture-dependent, CLS-based alternatives. This broadens the claimed applicability and sharpens the novelty claim, while the abstract's original RIS performance claims and the conclusion remain substantially unchanged.

C2.justification: v2 adds explanations about preserving semantic anchors during text masking and the unfavorable accuracy/computation tradeoff of cross-distillation. It also interprets RefClef and REC results as supporting broader applicability. The existing limitations concerning ambiguous descriptions and difficult visual scenes are retained.

D1.justification: v2 describes the additional linguistic masking variants and acknowledges use of the NSML platform. However, it removes v1's two-A6000 hardware disclosure and measured 18.4-hour CARIS versus 16.7-hour MaskRIS training comparison. Appendix C's core implementation settings and the code-access link remain unchanged.

E1.justification: v2 adds segmentation evaluation on RefClef, extending beyond the three COCO-derived datasets, and adds Referring Expression Comprehension on RefCOCO (Table 3). These expand both represented data and task requirements beyond v1's segmentation coverage.

E2.justification: Table 1 adds CM-MaskSD and MagNet. Table 2 adds DETRIS and a ReMamber-with/without-MaskRIS comparison; ReMamber previously appeared only in other comparisons. New REC comparisons evaluate EEVG, SimVG and C3VG, substantially broadening the comparator set.

E3.justification: The established RIS splits, metrics, image resolution and training recipe remain unchanged. Added experiments introduce REC evaluation using DetAcc and additional encoder configurations, plus comparisons varying masking regions, linguistic masking schemes and auxiliary distillation. These extend the protocol without replacing the existing RIS evaluation.

E4.justification: v2 adds object-centric versus context versus holistic image masking (Table 5), whole-word/span/POS-based text masking (Appendix Table C), and cross-distillation (Appendix Table D). Figure 8 adds three qualitative ablation examples. Earlier component, masking-ratio, patch-size and training-loss analyses are retained, sometimes relocated.

E5.justification: Neither version reports seed counts, repeated-run uncertainty, confidence intervals or statistical significance tests. Both present point estimates and training curves without uncertainty estimates.

E6.justification: v2 adds RefClef results (75.21 oIoU for CARIS and 76.06 with MaskRIS), REC results, additional architecture comparisons and new ablation outcomes. Table 1 revises combined-training CARIS scores, including RefCOCO testA from 79.40 to 79.85 and RefCOCOg test from 69.75 to 68.73; corresponding MaskRIS scores remain unchanged. The earlier measured training times are removed.

M1.justification: The proposed random image masking, BERT-style text masking and shared-weight clean/masked prediction distillation remain unchanged. The corrected loss-weight equation preserves the default lambda of 0.5. Alternative masking and distillation schemes are evaluated as ablations; no changed core procedure is documented for the REC applications.

P1.justification: The contribution list, compatibility discussion and computational-cost discussion are revised, and a dedicated comparison section is added. The masking-ratio discussion moves into a reorganized appendix; affiliations, acknowledgments and citation style also change. Most existing prose and the main section sequence are retained.

P2.justification: The document changes from a two-column format to a single-column journal layout with extensively repositioned displays. v2 adds a comparison diagram and several tables, expands Tables 1–2 and the qualitative masking figure, rearranges the augmentation plots side by side, and moves the masking-ratio table into the appendix.

R1.justification: v2 substantially expands positioning against masking-based RIS research, especially CM-MaskSD and MagNet, through the introduction, related work, new Figure 2 and Section 4.4. It also adds literature supporting REC comparisons, RefClef and alternative text masking strategies.

T1.justification: Appendix Equation 5 changes from lambda times Ldist plus (1-lambda) times Lce to (1-lambda) times Ldist plus lambda times Lce. This resolves v1's contradiction with its statement that lambda=1 recovers CARIS. Other mathematical definitions and equations remain unchanged.

improvement.justification: v2 substantially strengthens the paper by addressing v1's missing comparisons with closely related masking methods and adding targeted evidence about masking choices, distillation and applicability beyond the original RIS benchmarks. Correcting Equation 5 also removes a concrete mathematical inconsistency. These gains outweigh the loss of measured runtime and hardware information, although the added experiments remain sparsely specified and some Table 1 commentary is stale after the comparator and score updates.

A1.justification: Both PDFs describe MaskRIS. Their main text, equations, tables, figures and appendices are readable and can be matched despite substantial reformatting.

after.justification: v2 retains those original experiments and adds RefClef results, referring expression comprehension experiments and further masking and distillation analyses.

before.justification: v1 reports original segmentation results, robustness evaluations, component ablations and training analyses in Section 4 and Appendix A.

arxiv_record.abstract: Graph federated learning is of essential importance for training over large graph datasets while protecting data privacy, where each client stores a subset of local graph data, while the server collects the local gradients and broadcasts only the aggregated gradients. Recent studies reveal that a malicious attacker can steal private image data from the gradient exchange of neural networks during federated learning. However, the vulnerability of graph data and graph neural networks under such attacks, i.e., reconstructing both node features and graph structure from gradients, remains largely underexplored. To answer this question, this paper studies the problem of whether private data can be reconstructed from leaked gradients in both node classification and graph classification tasks and proposes a novel attack named Graph Leakage from Gradients (GLG). Two widely used GNN frameworks are analyzed, namely GCN and GraphSAGE. The effects of different model settings on reconstruction are extensively discussed. Theoretical analysis and empirical validation demonstrate that, by leveraging the unique properties of graph data and GNNs, GLG achieves more accurate reconstruction of both nodal features and graph structure from gradients.
arxiv_record.authors: Divya Anand Sinha, Ruijie Du, Yezi Liu, Athina Markopolou, Yanning Shen
arxiv_record.title: Gradient Inversion Attack on Graph Neural Networks

C1.justification: The abstract and conclusion add a central comparative claim of more accurate feature and graph-structure reconstruction, beyond v1's feasibility claim that graph data can leak. The research question shifts toward exploiting graph properties, while the introduction narrows the novelty claim from the first work to among the first.

C2.justification: V2 adds explanations linking DLG's difficulties to feature–topology interdependencies. Appendix H attributes difficult feature reconstruction to absent direct node-level supervision and interprets higher multi-hop scores as successful topology reconstruction despite imperfect features. Most existing limitations and sensitivity interpretations remain.

D1.justification: Appendix H adds technical documentation that GSM-k evaluation aggregates neighborhoods using a randomly initialized GCN with at least k layers. Existing GLG optimizer, initialization, width, and regularization details are retained; moving pseudocode to Appendix A does not change their substance.

E1.justification: V2 extends evaluation to citation-network data through OGBN-Arxiv for Node Attacker 1 and adds Tox21 molecular graph reconstruction in Appendix H. The existing social, synthetic, MUTAG, COIL-RAG, and FRANKENSTEIN coverage is retained.

E2.justification: V1 discusses competing attacks without directly benchmarking them. V2 adds DLG comparisons across all seven attack settings in Tables 3–9. Tox21 comparisons additionally include GRAIN, TabLeak, DLG+A, and TabLeak+A in Tables 19–20.

E3.justification: The new Tox21 evaluation introduces GSM-0, GSM-1, GSM-2, and FULL metrics alongside RNMSE, AUC, and AP, including comparisons with adjacency information supplied to baselines. Settings for retained experiments, including model width, optimizer, batch sizes, and matching procedures, remain unchanged.

E4.justification: Table 19 adds a limited side-information analysis comparing DLG and TabLeak with their adjacency-informed +A variants. The existing regularization, network-width, batch-size, initialization, threshold, and graph-size/density analyses are retained, often relocated to appendices.

E5.justification: V2 Table 19 introduces asymmetric upper/lower uncertainty margins without defining their statistical meaning. Existing standard-deviation reporting and run counts remain: generally 20 runs and 10 for minibatch experiments. V2 explicitly calls the 20 runs independent, without reporting an increase.

E6.justification: V2 adds extensive baseline, OGBN-Arxiv, and Tox21 results. Some retained values also change: GCN/GitHub joint node reconstruction AUC changes from 0.96±0.01 in v1 Table 4 to 0.99±0.04 in v2 Table 6. The PDFs do not explain whether these revisions reflect corrections or reruns; existing batch and TU-dataset results are retained.

M1.justification: The gradient-matching objectives, regularizers, projection and sampling procedures, and Algorithms 1–3 remain unchanged. The algorithms move to Appendix A; attacker suffixes a/b/c become G/N/GN. Molecular initialization and thresholding strategies already appeared in v1.

P1.justification: V2 substantially reorganizes the narrative: related work becomes Section 2, algorithms move to Appendix A, and neighborhood, batch, and sensitivity studies move to Appendix F. TU-dataset discussion is consolidated in Appendix G. Extensive prose revisions standardize reconstruction terminology and attacker names.

P2.justification: Seven main result tables gain separate DLG blocks, and the target-node table gains an OGBN-Arxiv column. New tables summarize method differences, threat models, and Tox21 results. Existing figures are retained but several move to appendices; TU adjacency-table panels change from stacked to side-by-side.

R1.justification: The new Related Work section substantively positions GLG against concurrent GRAIN, emphasizing their different requirements for node-degree information, and adds DAGER and graph-privacy literature. Table 1 provides a new method comparison, replacing v1's positioning as the sole first graph-gradient attack.

T1.justification: Propositions 1–6, their stated conditions, the label-extraction derivation, and proofs in Appendices B–E retain the same mathematical substance. V2 adds no theorem, proof, or substantive correction; the additional GSM metrics serve empirical evaluation.

improvement.justification: V2 addresses an important validation gap through systematic DLG comparisons and additional GRAIN/TabLeak benchmarks, substantially strengthening evidence for GLG's comparative value. Its treatment of concurrent work also improves novelty positioning. Some superiority statements exceed the results—GRAIN has higher GSM-0, and DLG wins certain GitHub feature comparisons—and Table 19's uncertainty margins are undefined. These limitations temper, but do not outweigh, the substantial gain in comparative validation.

A1.justification: Both PDFs describe the same GLG research and provide readable text, equations, figures, tables, and appendices. Renamed attackers and relocated material can be matched reliably.

after.justification: Section 6 and Appendices F–H retain original experiments and add baseline comparisons and results on OGBN-Arxiv and Tox21.

before.justification: Section 5 and Appendix F report original feature and adjacency reconstruction experiments, including batch, sensitivity, and initialization studies.

arxiv_record.abstract: Vision-Language Models (VLMs) have great potential in medical tasks, like Visual Question Answering (VQA), where they could act as interactive assistants for both patients and clinicians. Yet their robustness to distribution shifts on unseen data remains a key concern for safe deployment. Evaluating such robustness requires a controlled experimental setup that allows for systematic insights into the model's behavior. However, we demonstrate that current setups fail to offer sufficiently thorough evaluations. To address this gap, we introduce a novel framework, called SURE-VQA, centered around three key requirements to overcome current pitfalls and systematically analyze VLM robustness: 1) Since robustness on synthetic shifts does not necessarily translate to real-world shifts, it should be measured on real-world shifts that are inherent to the VQA data; 2) Traditional token-matching metrics often fail to capture underlying semantics, necessitating the use of large language models (LLMs) for more accurate semantic evaluation; 3) Model performance often lacks interpretability due to missing sanity baselines, thus meaningful baselines should be reported that allow assessing the multimodal impact on the VLM. To demonstrate the relevance of this framework, we conduct a study on the robustness of various Fine-Tuning (FT) methods across three medical datasets with four types of distribution shifts. Our study highlights key insights into robustness: 1) No FT method consistently outperforms others in robustness, and 2) robustness trends are more stable across FT methods than across distribution shifts. Additionally, we find that simple sanity baselines that do not use the image data can perform surprisingly well and confirm LoRA as the best-performing FT method on in-distribution data. Code is provided at https://github.com/IML-DKFZ/sure-vqa.
arxiv_record.authors: Kim-Celine Kahl, Selen Erkan, Jeremias Traub, Carsten T. L\"uth, Klaus Maier-Hein, Lena Maier-Hein, Paul F. Jaeger
arxiv_record.title: SURE-VQA: Systematic Understanding of Robustness Evaluation in Medical VQA Tasks

C1.justification: v2 adds the conclusion that medical and non-medical base models perform similarly after fine-tuning. The three framework requirements, strong language-only baselines, LoRA's in-distribution advantage and absence of a consistent robustness winner remain. Greater abstract emphasis on shift-versus-method variability restates a conclusion already present in v1.

C2.justification: v2 adds specific qualifications about medical-knowledge and demographic biases in LLM judges, the predominantly radiological scope, and the framework's status as a research tool rather than a clinically deployable benchmark. Appendix E further explains generalization through related question patterns and recommends greater training-data diversity.

D1.justification: v2 supplies separate selected hyperparameters for the non-medical model, revised evaluator prompts, and explicit identification of LLaVA-Med with (IA)3 for the retained multimodal ablation. Dataset-processing instructions and code-access information remain substantially unchanged.

E1.justification: Both versions use English SLAKE, OVQA and MIMIC-CXR-VQA with the same medical VQA coverage. The new swapped-shift study changes which existing SLAKE modalities and question categories are held out, rather than introducing new data or task types. Corruption and combined OVQA shifts already appear in v1.

E2.justification: v2 adds LLaVA 1.6 as a non-medical comparator to LLaVA-Med 1.5 throughout the robustness experiments. Appendix B.1 also expands the evaluator comparison beyond Mistral and traditional metrics to models including Phi-3, Gemma, Qwen, LLaMA, Granite, Biomistral and Prometheus. The original fine-tuning and sanity-baseline sets remain.

E3.justification: Evaluation switches from Mistral to Gemma with revised closed-ended grading prompts, and the human study increases from 50 to 100 questions per dataset. New protocols evaluate LLaVA 1.6 and hold out MRI or Position categories in SLAKE instead of X-Ray or Size. Original dataset sizes, preprocessing and hyperparameter-search ranges are retained.

E4.justification: v2 adds per-question image/no-image win-tie-loss analysis, comparisons among LLM judges, and a SLAKE ablation testing sensitivity to held-out categories. Appendix C.5.1 adds statistical examinations of robustness rankings and variability. The corruption study and multimodal-shift ablation are retained, not newly introduced.

E5.justification: New Appendix C.5.1 reports 100 bootstrapped robustness estimates per experiment, pairwise Welch tests with multiple-testing correction, and ANOVA F-values and p-values. These substantially extend v1's robustness uncertainty reporting. The existing three-seed PEFT means and standard deviations remain; no increase in training seeds is established.

E6.justification: Tables 14-19 revise scores and add non-medical-model results, alongside new evaluator, swapped-shift and statistical findings. For example, OVQA LoRA's open-ended question-type OoD score changes from 1.72 to 1.98 in Table 16. Because the evaluator changes from Mistral to Gemma, this is a replaced measurement, not a same-setting performance gain.

M1.justification: The framework's evaluator component changes from Mistral to Gemma. Appendix A.2 also revises closed-ended prompts to explicitly accept synonymous answers and additional irrelevant detail. The three requirements, hybrid exact-match/LLM scoring structure and fine-tuning methods remain.

P1.justification: The former framework-setup and separate fine-tuning-study sections become a unified Empirical Study with explicit R1-R3 validation subsections. Results discussion and conclusions are rewritten, and appendix dataset details move before hyperparameter searches. This substantially reorganizes the narrative beyond merely appending experiments.

P2.justification: v2 adds win-tie-loss charts, an expanded evaluator heatmap, non-medical-model plots, a significance matrix, a corruption-pipeline diagram and swapped-shift panels. Tables gain medical/non-medical subdivisions, qualitative examples move to the appendix, and the publication template changes typography and page layout.

R1.justification: v2 adds Gemma, Bahri et al. and Jeong et al., positioning its fine-tuned medical/non-medical comparison against Jeong's zero- and few-shot findings. Some contextual references, including Yoon et al. and Ma et al., disappear. The central positioning around three evaluation pitfalls remains.

T1.justification: The relative-robustness definition is unchanged, and neither version introduces theoretical propositions or proofs. The new bootstrap, Welch-test and ANOVA procedures are empirical statistical analyses rather than new mathematical theory.

improvement.justification: v2 substantially strengthens validation by comparing multiple judges on a larger human-rated sample, checking robustness findings with a second base model, and testing alternative held-out categories. These address v1's dependence on one evaluator and one backbone. Added statistical analyses and explicit applicability limitations improve assessability, although changed scoring prevents interpreting cross-version numerical differences as performance gains.

arxiv_record.abstract: Grounding the instruction in the environment is a key step in solving language-guided goal-reaching reinforcement learning problems. In automated reinforcement learning, a key concern is to enhance the model's ability to generalize across various tasks and environments. In goal-reaching scenarios, the agent must comprehend the different parts of the instructions within the environmental context in order to complete the overall task successfully. In this work, we propose CAREL (Cross-modal Auxiliary REinforcement Learning) as a new framework to solve this problem using auxiliary loss functions inspired by video-text retrieval literature and a novel method called instruction tracking, which automatically keeps track of progress in an environment. The results of our experiments suggest superior sample efficiency and systematic generalization for this framework in multi-modal reinforcement learning problems. Our code base is available here.

arxiv_record.abstract: Edge-attributed multigraphs, in which multiple edges with distinct attributes connect the same pair of nodes, arise naturally in many real-world systems. In these graphs, effective learning requires preserving information from repeated interactions while distinguishing contributions from different neighbors. Existing neural network solutions for edge-attributed multigraphs remain limited: some lose information from repeated interactions, while others break permutation equivariance. To address this, we introduce \emph{neighbor-aware aggregation}, an operator that first combines multi-edge features for each neighbor and then aggregates across neighbors. This operator captures per-neighbor statistics that standard single-stage aggregation cannot represent. Building on this operator, we present MEGA-GNN, a model-agnostic message-passing framework for edge-attributed multigraphs. We show that MEGA-GNN is permutation equivariant and has the same asymptotic complexity as standard GNNs with edge updates. We evaluate our approach on datasets from social networks and financial transaction networks. Neighbor-aware aggregation consistently improves GNN performance and matches or surpasses state-of-the-art methods.
arxiv_record.authors: H. \c{C}a\u{g}r{\i} Bilgi, Kubilay Atasu
arxiv_record.title: MEGA: Message Passing Neural Networks for Multigraphs with EdGe Attributes

E5.justification: Both versions report means and standard deviations across different seeds: five runs in v1 and at least five in v3, without establishing an increase for retained experiments. v3 adds a focused set of two-sided Wilcoxon signed-rank tests across six paired AML dataset scores (Appendix E.4, Table 21). These are limited procedural extensions; the neighbor-aware terminology itself does not establish a new method.

P1.justification: The abstract, introduction and method exposition are extensively rewritten around neighbor-aware aggregation. Related work moves from Section 5 to Section 2, while detailed limitations of existing methods move to Appendix A. Experiments are reorganized into diagnostic, social, financial, ablation and scalability sections, and the appendices are restructured. The title, authorship listing and publication header also change.

P2.justification: v3 redraws the aggregation illustration and introduces detailed layer diagrams and relational-model diagrams. The AML presentation shifts from v1's colored result table to main-text comparison plots with expanded appendix tables. Existing Multi-GNN/ADAMM illustrations are combined and relocated to the appendix.

R1.justification: Related work expands substantially to DIAM, FraudGT, JODIE, relational architectures and their expressiveness, aggregation theory, and financial-crime applications. Appendix A develops the distinction and complementarity between relation-aware and neighbor-aware processing. Earlier universality/random-initialization and subgraph-method discussions are reduced. This changes the research positioning beyond bibliographic updates or moving the related-work section.

T1.justification: v1's conditional-universality theorem, unique-node-ID lemma and BFS proof construction are removed. v3 introduces formal single-stage and neighbor-aware operators and a new expressiveness theorem for sum/raw-moment aggregators, whose proof assumes a constant edge-feature coordinate. Its complexity analysis includes linear transformations and node activations, extending v1's aggregation-focused analysis. The permutation-equivariance proof and port-number proposition/counterexample are also revised.

improvement.justification: v3 substantially strengthens the empirical explanation of why the method works. Random-grouping, edge-collapse and capacity-matched controls address important alternatives left unresolved by v1's benchmark and component comparisons. arxiv_record.abstract: In this paper, we introduce Modality-Inconsistent Continual Learning (MICL), a new continual learning scenario for Multimodal Large Language Models (MLLMs) that involves tasks with inconsistent modalities (image, audio, or video) and varying task types (captioning or question-answering). Unlike existing vision-only or modality-incremental settings, MICL combines modality and task type shifts, both of which drive catastrophic forgetting. To address these challenges, we propose MoInCL, which employs a Pseudo Targets Generation Module to mitigate forgetting caused by task type shifts in previously seen modalities. It also incorporates Instruction-based Knowledge Distillation to preserve the model's ability to handle previously learned modalities when new ones are introduced. We benchmark MICL using a total of six tasks and conduct experiments to validate the effectiveness of our MoInCL. The experimental results highlight the superiority of MoInCL, showing significant improvements over representative and state-of-the-art continual learning baselines.

arxiv_record.abstract: 2D concept art generation for 3D scenes is a crucial yet challenging task in computer graphics, as creating natural intuitive environments still demands extensive manual effort in concept design. While generative AI has simplified 2D concept design via text-to-image synthesis, it struggles with complex multi-instance scenes and offers limited support for structured terrain layout. In this paper, we propose a Training-free Triplet Tuning for Sketch-to-Scene (T3-S2S) generation after reviewing the entire cross-attention mechanism. This scheme revitalizes the ControlNet model for detailed multi-instance generation via three key modules: Prompt Balance ensures keyword representation and minimizes the risk of missing critical instances; Characteristic Priority emphasizes sketch-based features by highlighting TopK indices in feature channels; and Dense Tuning refines contour details within instance-related regions of the attention map. Leveraging the controllability of T3-S2S, we also introduce a feature-sharing strategy with dual prompt sets to generate layer-aware isometric and terrain-view representations for the terrain layout. Experiments show that our sketch-to-scene workflow consistently produces multi-instance 2D scenes with details aligned with input prompts.
