arxiv_record.abstract: Humans possess a remarkable ability to acquire knowledge efficiently and apply it across diverse modalities through a coherent and shared understanding of the world. Inspired by this cognitive capability, we introduce a concept-centric multi-modality learning framework built around a modality-agnostic concept space that captures structured, abstract knowledge, alongside a set of modality-specific projection models that map raw inputs onto this shared space. The concept space is decoupled from any specific modality and serves as a repository of universally applicable knowledge. Once learned, the knowledge embedded in the concept space enables more efficient adaptation to new modalities, as projection models can align with existing conceptual representations rather than learning from scratch. This efficiency is empirically validated in our experiments, where the proposed framework exhibits faster convergence compared to baseline models. In addition, the framework's modular design supports seamless integration of new modalities, since projection models are trained independently yet produce unified outputs within the shared concept space. We evaluate the framework on two representative downstream tasks. While the focus is not on task-specific optimization, the framework attains comparable results with a smaller training footprint, no task-specific fine-tuning, and inference performed entirely within a shared space of learned concepts that offers interpretability. These findings point toward a promising direction for developing learning systems that operate in a manner more consistent with human cognitive processes.
arxiv_record.authors: Yuchong Geng, Ao Tang
arxiv_record.comments: Published in Transactions on Machine Learning Research (TMLR), 2026. Official version: https://openreview.net/forum?id=8WAAPP32c7

arxiv_record.abstract: In many practical applications, large language models (LLMs) need to acquire new knowledge not present in their pre-training data. Efficiently leveraging this knowledge usually relies on supervised fine-tuning or retrieval-augmented generation (RAG). Although RAG has emerged as the industry standard for knowledge injection, fine-tuning has not yet achieved comparable success. This paper proposes utilizing prompt distillation, a self-distillation-based method previously explored primarily for style alignment and instruction tuning, to internalize new factual knowledge from free-form documents. Unlike prior methods, our approach requires neither larger teacher models nor structured knowledge formats. Across multiple LLM sizes and model families, we show that prompt distillation outperforms standard supervised fine-tuning and can even surpass RAG. We analyze the key factors contributing to prompt distillation's effectiveness and examine how it scales.

arxiv_record.abstract: Large language models (LLMs) demonstrate an impressive ability to utilise information within the context of their input sequences to appropriately respond to data unseen by the LLM during its training procedure. This ability is known as in-context learning (ICL). Humans and non-human animals demonstrate similar abilities, however their neural architectures differ substantially from LLMs. Despite this, a critical component within LLMs, the attention mechanism, resembles modern associative memory models, widely used in and influenced by the computational neuroscience community to model biological memory systems. Using this connection, we introduce an associative memory model capable of performing ICL. We use this as inspiration for a novel residual stream architecture which allows information to directly flow between attention heads. We test this architecture during training within a two-layer Transformer and show its ICL abilities manifest more quickly than without this modification. We then apply our architecture in small language models with 8 million and 1 billion parameters, focusing on attention head values, with results also indicating improved performance at these larger and more naturalistic scales.

arxiv_record.comments: 35 pages, 14 figures, 6 tables; accepted and published in TMLR

C2.justification: v2 adds explanations involving auto- versus hetero-association, preservation of representations across layers, and strong IOI differences despite similar training losses. It proposes specific hippocampal ablation hypotheses and explicitly qualifies broader applicability through task-specific gains and unresolved scalability and cost trade-offs (Sections 6.1–6.3).

D1.justification: Section 5 adds substantial architecture, tokenizer, precision, optimizer, training-schedule, and IOI-Hard generation details. The code-access disclosure is retained. Some new schedule information conflicts internally: the prose specifies 500 warmup and 5,000 cooldown steps, while Table 4 gives 1% and 10% of a 40,000-step run.

E1.justification: Section 5 adds pretraining on English Nemotron-CC-HQ documents and evaluation on ARC, PIQA, OpenBookQA, and HellaSwag. IOI-Hard adds a distinct contextual retrieval scenario involving 25 sentences and multiple name, place, and object associations. The original synthetic tasks and TinyStories/IOI coverage remain.

E2.justification: The matched synthetic comparisons retain the classic Transformer and query/key residual variants. Language-model comparisons still use the classic architecture against residual values, including at 1B scale. Appendix B introduces separate architectural controls without expanding these head-to-head comparator sets.

E3.justification: New experiments use 1B-parameter models trained for 40,000 iterations on approximately 84 billion tokens, with batch size 512 and context length 4,096. Evaluation adds single- and five-shot benchmark accuracy and 1,000 generated IOI-Hard prompts. Appendix B also introduces one-layer control configurations; the original experiments' stated settings remain substantially unchanged.

E4.justification: New Appendix B tests four one-layer architectures without learned value projections, varying ReLU depth and placement. These controls examine whether that simpler AMICL-inspired construction supports ICL and how architecture affects learning trajectories. The existing AMICL parameter sweeps and accuracy-threshold analyses are retained.

E5.justification: Section 5.2 adds a paired t-test using benchmark accuracies across training checkpoints, alongside correlation reporting. The original four-seed synthetic experiments and three-instance language-model reporting remain unchanged. Independent repeated-training uncertainty is not reported for the new 1B comparison.

E6.justification: New 1B results show gains concentrated on ARC and OpenBookQA, little change on PIQA and HellaSwag, and a clearer IOI-Hard advantage (Figures 5, 6, and 14). Original numerical tables are unchanged, but Figure 3's IC2 loss changes from rising above 12 to falling near zero. The unchanged IOI table also receives inaccurate new percentage summaries of approximately 590% improvement and 60% reduction.

M1.justification: The AMICL assignments and layer-to-layer query, key, and value residual operations remain unchanged. The 1B model applies the existing residual-values method in another model configuration; the value-projection removals are control experiments rather than revisions to the proposed method.

P1.justification: Previously continuous sections are reorganized into named subsections separating setup, architecture, evaluation, interpretation, limitations, and conclusions. P2.justification: v2 adds training and benchmark plots, four control-experiment figures, and two hyperparameter tables. Figure 3's loss panel is revised, including its vertical scale. R1.justification: New Appendix A substantially expands the neuroscience background and positioning of associative memory models. arxiv_record.abstract: In this paper, we introduce a novel method for extending Ricci flow to hypergraphs by defining probability measures on the edges and transporting them on the line expansion. This approach yields a new weighting on the edges, which proves particularly effective for community detection. We extensively compare this method with a similar notion of Ricci flow defined on the clique expansion, demonstrating its enhanced sensitivity to the hypergraph structure, especially in the presence of large hyperedges. The two methods are complementary and together form a powerful and highly interpretable framework for community detection in hypergraphs.

arxiv_record.title: Hypergraph clustering using Ricci curvature: an edge transport perspective

arxiv_record.abstract: Large language models (LLMs) possess vast semantic knowledge but often struggle with complex reasoning tasks, particularly in relational reasoning problems such as kinship or spatial reasoning. In this paper, we present Path-of-Thoughts (PoT), a novel framework for solving relation reasoning that decomposes the task into three key stages: graph extraction, path identification, and reasoning. Unlike previous approaches, PoT efficiently extracts a reasoning graph that identifies crucial entities, relations, and attributes within the context. Subsequently, PoT identifies query-relevant reasoning paths within the graph, facilitating downstream reasoning of potential answers. Experimental evaluations across four datasets of relational reasoning demonstrate that PoT surpasses state-of-the-art baselines by a significant margin (up to 21.3%) without requiring fine-tuning or extensive LLM calls. Furthermore, unlike prior neuro-symbolic methods, PoT exhibits improved resilience against LLM extraction errors and input ambiguity by leveraging the compositional nature of graphs.

C1.justification: The introduction narrows the graph's stated role from a task-agnostic foundation illustrated by planning to downstream relational reasoning. It also reframes the novelty claim from handling hallucinations and ambiguities through path identification to identifying query-relevant subgraphs before reasoning. The three-stage contribution and up-to-21.3% improvement claim remain.

C2.justification: v2 expands the limitations beyond dataset-label quality to untested non-relational generalization, manual symbolic-rule construction, and latency/accuracy tradeoffs, with recommendations for choosing the two variants. New analyses distinguish path identification's benefits for LLM reasoning from its small effect on symbolic benchmark accuracy, and interpret multiple-path selection and computational efficiency.

D1.justification: v2 specifies depth-first search and documents new model settings and module-level resource consumption. It consolidates v1's conflicting temperature statements of 0 and 0.3 into 0.3, with GPT-5 defaults, without establishing that retained experiments changed. It removes the statement that code and datasets accompany supplementary materials and omits the full SPARTUN label-mapping list.

E1.justification: Both versions use StepGame, CLUTRR, SPARTUN Find Relation questions, and the Chinese kinship dataset, together with the synthetic extraction test and seven graph-noise scenarios. Additional backbones and analyses operate within this retained coverage.

E2.justification: The external baseline roster remains IO/Zero-shot, Few-shot, CoT, CoT-SC, and LLM-ASP. v2 adds internal comparison variants: PoT with path identification removed in Table 6 and shortest-path-only reasoning in Table 7. Figure 2 retains the earlier noise comparison under symbolic-reasoner-with/without-path-identification labels.

E3.justification: v2 substantially expands model configurations with Llama3-70B-Instruct, o1-mini, Claude-3.7-Sonnet, and GPT-5 at minimal and medium reasoning effort. It adds module-level latency and token measurements on GPT-4o StepGame k=3, plus path-removal and shortest-path controls. Existing benchmark sizes, preprocessing, and accuracy definitions are retained; these additions do not establish reruns of the earlier results.

E4.justification: New Table 6 directly tests removing path identification from both PoT variants. Appendix A.2/Table 7 analyzes path-count distributions and compares multiple paths against the shortest path alone. Table 25 adds an extraction-error example, and Table 26 introduces reasoning-error cases. The earlier extraction-prompt comparison and synthetic-noise analysis remain.

E5.justification: Tables 1–2 introduce paired McNemar significance annotations comparing the highest and second-highest accuracies, absent from v1. Single-trial reporting remains, with no newly reported repeated-run uncertainty or confidence intervals. The captions do not specify the significance threshold.

E6.justification: The earlier GPT-3.5, GPT-4-turbo, GPT-4o, extraction, and noise results are retained. v2 adds substantial backbone, cost, ablation, and error-analysis results. The new findings include exceptions to superiority: on o1-mini CLUTRR, PoT-LLM scores 58.5 versus CoT-SC's 64.6, while PoT-Symbolic scores 65.9 versus LLM-ASP's 20.2 (Table 2). These are newly reported configurations, not same-setting improvements over v1.

M1.justification: The default graph-extraction, path-identification, and reasoning pipeline is unchanged, as are the appendix prompt templates. Section 4.2 newly identifies the path-finding algorithm as depth-first search; this specifies an existing component rather than establishing a procedural change. Shortest-path and path-removal variants are experimental controls.

P1.justification: The document is substantially reorganized: dataset and backbone descriptions move into Section 5.1, the noise taxonomy moves to Appendix A.1, and appendix topics and prompt collections are reordered. The limitations are rewritten and placed before the conclusion. The introduction, problem definition, and results narrative are edited, and the title loses its Path-of-Thoughts prefix.

P2.justification: The two-column presentation becomes a single-column layout with a redesigned author block. Table 1 incorporates the former appendix GPT-3.5 results and adds Llama3; new tables display reasoning-model results, costs, ablations, and errors. Prompt tables are reordered and sometimes split. Figure 2 changes from stacked to side-by-side panels with revised legends while retaining its plotted results.

R1.justification: v2 adds references for Llama 3, o1, SymBa, and hierarchical cooperative task allocation, including limited discussion of automated rule generation and task decomposition. It refines the introduction's novelty positioning, while the substantive related-work comparison with prompting and neuro-symbolic approaches remains largely unchanged.

T1.justification: Section 2 introduces clearer notation for the context, question, and queried entities but retains the same problem definition and composition assumptions. Graph and path definitions remain substantively unchanged. Neither version supplies formal theorems or proofs.

improvement.justification: Tables 6–7 substantially strengthen evaluation of the central path-identification contribution by directly testing its removal and restricting path selection, revealing both benefits and settings with little benefit. A1.justification: Both PDFs describe the same Path-of-Thoughts (PoT) research. Their main text, figures, tables, and complete appendices support reliable comparison despite substantial reformatting and relocation of material.

arxiv_record.abstract: Offline reinforcement learning (RL) enables policy learning from pre-collected offline datasets, relaxing the need to interact directly with the environment. However, limited by the quality of offline datasets, it generally fails to learn well-qualified policies in suboptimal datasets. To address datasets with insufficient optimal demonstrations, we introduce Goal-cOnditioned Data Augmentation (GODA), a novel goal-conditioned diffusion-based method for augmenting samples with higher quality. Leveraging recent advancements in generative modelling, GODA incorporates a novel return-oriented goal condition with various selection mechanisms. Specifically, we introduce a controllable scaling technique to provide enhanced return-based guidance during data sampling. GODA learns a comprehensive distribution representation of the original offline datasets while generating new data with selectively higher-return goals, thereby maximizing the utility of limited optimal demonstrations. Furthermore, we propose a novel adaptive gated conditioning method for processing noisy inputs and conditions, enhancing the capture of goal-oriented guidance. We conduct experiments on the D4RL benchmark and real-world challenges, specifically traffic signal control (TSC) tasks, to demonstrate GODA's effectiveness in enhancing data quality and superior performance compared to state-of-the-art data augmentation methods across various offline RL algorithms.
arxiv_record.authors: Xingshuai Huang, Di Wu, and Benoit Boulet
arxiv_record.title: Goal-Conditioned Data Augmentation for Offline Reinforcement Learning

C1.justification: The abstract and three principal contributions retain their central novelty and performance claims. Section 7 adds qualifications that GODA cannot synthesize expert-level performance from nonexpert data alone and requires latent representations for visual applications. These narrow the stated applicability without replacing the main contribution.

C2.justification: v2 adds substantive explanations for return-prior superiority, dataset-dependent scaling benefits and Pen-Human failure, together with explicit expert-data and visual-input limitations. It also introduces a Maze2D explanation involving direct spatial-goal conditioning, although the documented conditioning remains RTG and timestep; this is an unsupported interpretive addition rather than an established input change.

D1.justification: v2 documents substantial implementation information for its extensions: 84×84×3 observations encoded into 50-dimensional representations, encoder freezing and head fine-tuning, and online augmentation of 1M samples per 10K interactions with a 1:1 real/synthetic ratio and changing goal parameters. Sensitivity-analysis procedures and weights are also supplied. Original denoiser hyperparameters, hardware and timing information are retained in Appendix B.

E1.justification: v2 adds Medium-Expert locomotion datasets, pixel-based V-D4RL Cheetah-Run at four data-quality levels, and online interaction scenarios for three Gym tasks. These expand represented data quality, observation modality and interaction conditions. The original Gym, Maze2D, Adroit and traffic-control coverage is retained.

E2.justification: The external augmentation baselines TATU, SynthER and DiffStitch remain unchanged in corresponding experiments. Table 6 adds four internal comparison variants removing either gated connection or only its gating, beyond v1's AdaLN/in-context comparisons. BC, DMG and SAC otherwise serve as new evaluation backbones using familiar unaugmented/SynthER controls.

E3.justification: Section 5 revises the reported diversity metric from L2 distance to average nearest-neighbor Min L2 Distance, with corresponding changes to Equation 11 and results. Added protocols include latent-space BC evaluation, DMG evaluation and online SAC over 100K interactions. The online experiment uses update-to-data ratios of 1 for vanilla SAC and 20 for both augmented methods, so that comparison has unequal update budgets.

E4.justification: v2 adds separate connection/gating ablations (Table 6), a reward-sensitivity investigation of Adroit failures (Appendix C.3, Table 10), and scaling-factor experiments across additional dataset-quality levels (Figure 10). These investigate component contributions and failure conditions beyond v1's analyses. Existing mixed-dataset and traffic-data-size studies are retained in Appendices C.5–C.6.

E5.justification: Appendix C.3 adds weighted-least-squares reward-sensitivity estimation and 95th-percentile statistical summaries. These are diagnostic estimates, not confidence intervals. The principal benchmark's five-seed declaration and existing ± and error-band reporting practices remain unchanged; no increase in runs or new significance testing is documented.

E6.justification: Original task-level Gym/Maze2D, Adroit and traffic-control scores are retained, but v2 adds substantial results for the new settings and analyses. For example, visual BC averages are 39.9±4.8 with GODA versus 37.5±3.5 with SynthER (Table 4). The Gym IQL GODA average changes from 54.7 to 66.2 because Medium-Expert rows are added, not because retained task scores improve. Distance values also change under the revised metric.

M1.justification: The original offline denoiser, loss and RTG/timestep conditioning remain unchanged. However, v2 adds a visual pipeline using BC pretraining, frozen encoders, latent-space augmentation and output-head fine-tuning (Section 4.1.2), plus an online procedure with periodic diffusion retraining, hybrid replay and changing goal schedules (Appendix C.2, Algorithm 2). These substantially extend the procedure.

P1.justification: v2 substantially reorganizes the paper, moving related work, implementation details and selected existing analyses into appendices. Method explanations expand to distinguish training from sampling, provide worked goal-selection examples and explain algorithm stages. Experimental sections are reorganized around the expanded evaluations, beyond routine wording edits.

P2.justification: The document changes from a two-column to a single-column layout and substantially redistributes figures and tables. v2 adds a workflow diagram, goal-selection examples, new result tables and online/scaling plots, and redraws the diversity-distance panel. Several original ablation plots are retained unchanged but relocated; the mixed-dataset table's previously incorrect caption is corrected.

R1.justification: v2 adds references supporting visual offline RL, DMG, SAC and image-generation conditioning, and updates several introductory application citations. Its central positioning against SynthER and DiffStitch remains unchanged. Moving the largely retained related-work discussion to Appendix A is organizational rather than a substantive positioning change.

T1.justification: Section 3.3 corrects v1's RTG-offset reasoning: adding a constant to every RTG changes the terminal reward, not the first reward. v2 also revises the distance definition and introduces a Lipschitz-based reward-sensitivity definition and composite measure in Appendix C.3. The central method equations remain unchanged, and no theorem or proof is added.

improvement.justification: Where v1 left individual gating contributions and the Pen-Human failure largely unexamined, v2 supplies component controls, sensitivity analysis and broader scaling tests. The explicit nearest-neighbor metric, clearer procedures and concrete applicability limits substantially improve scrutiny of the central claims. Unequal SAC update budgets and the unsupported spatial-goal explanation weaken parts of the added interpretation, but do not outweigh these gains.

A1.justification: Both PDFs describe the same GODA research. Their text, equations, tables and figures support reliable comparison, including material relocated into v2's Appendices A–C. v1 has no separately labelled appendices.

after.justification: v2 retains original empirical results and adds visual-observation, DMG, online SAC, component-ablation and reward-sensitivity results.

before.justification: v1 reports original GODA data-quality measurements, policy evaluations, ablations and traffic-control simulation results, alongside some baseline results attributed to prior work.

arxiv_record.abstract: Scientific problems require resolving multi-scale phenomena across different resolutions and learning solution operators in infinite-dimensional function spaces. Neural operators provide a powerful framework for this, using tensor-parameterized layers to capture complex, multi-dimensional relationships. However, scaling neural operators to high-resolution problems leads to significant computational demands, making the training of industrial-scale models prohibitive. In this work, we introduce \textbf{TensorGRaD}, a novel method that directly addresses the memory challenges associated with optimizing large tensor-structured weights. Our approach, based on a \texit{robust tensor decomposition}, factorizes gradients as the sum of a low-rank tensor and a sparse one to efficiently capture information within optimizer states, including outliers. Additionally, we provide a recipe for mixed precision training of TensorGRaD, achieving further memory savings without sacrificing accuracy. We showcase the effectiveness of TensorGRaD on Fourier Neural Operators, a class of models crucial for solving partial differential equations (PDE). We provide theoretical guarantees for TensorGRaD, demonstrating its fundamental advantage over matrix-based gradient compression methods. We empirically demonstrate large improvements across various PDE tasks, including the challenging turbulent Navier-Stokes case at a Reynolds number of $10^5$. TensorGRaD reduces total memory usage by over $50\%$ while maintaining and sometimes even improving accuracy.
arxiv_record.authors: Sebastian Loeschcke, David Pitt, Robert Joseph George, Jiawei Zhao, Cheng Luo, Yuandong Tian, Jean Kossaifi, Anima Anandkumar
arxiv_record.title: TensorGRaD: Tensor Gradient Robust Decomposition for Memory-Efficient Neural Operator Training

C1.justification: V1 centers its contribution on structure-preserving low-rank tensor-gradient compression and optimizer-memory savings up to 75%. V2 makes combined sparse-plus-low-rank compression and a mixed-precision recipe central contributions, emphasizing highly turbulent PDE evaluation and total-memory savings exceeding 50%. This substantially redefines the claimed contribution and its supporting scope.

C2.justification: V2 adds explanations linking sparse entries to localized outliers, low-rank factors to global structure, and sparse-first ordering to improved factor estimation. It also interprets update-frequency effects and half-precision optimizer degradation. Beyond v1's decomposition-overhead and rank-selection limitations, v2 discusses sparse-index costs, joint rank/sparsity selection and the need for full-precision optimizer states.

D1.justification: V2 substantially expands implementation and reproducibility information: COO storage and scatter reconstruction, precision allocation, dataset-pair construction, decomposition-update frequencies, detailed NS1024 training configurations, and A100/H100/H200 hardware. Appendix F adds profiling warmup, collection and allocation-classification details. The stated code location changes from an anonymous repository to the named TensorGRaD repository.

E1.justification: V2 adds highly turbulent Kolmogorov flow, described at approximately Re = 2×10^5 in Appendix A and labeled 10^5 in the main results. V1's Re = 10^3 Navier–Stokes data and the other PDE datasets remain. This substantially extends the dynamical regime tested; 1024×1024 resolution itself was already present in v1.

E2.justification: Beyond v1's uncompressed and matrix-GaLore comparisons, v2 evaluates GRASS-inspired structured-sparse tensor methods, including top-k, probability and random selection, and a randomized-SVD low-rank variant. The earlier tensor method becomes an explicit low-rank-only control for the hybrid method. These comparators appear in reported results, especially Tables 1–4 and 11.

E3.justification: V2 introduces full, Mixed-1 and Mixed-2 precision controls, sparse-density and composition experiments, and a new high-Re evaluation protocol. Appendix A specifies 1,577 training and 279 test pairs with temporal offset 256 and stride 4; Table 13 specifies a staged 256-to-1024 training schedule. These are new experimental settings, not evidence that retained benchmark results were rerun.

E4.justification: V2 retains earlier rank, matricization and timing analyses while adding gradient-reconstruction error distributions, sparse-versus-low-rank ordering and residual/additive comparisons, precision sensitivity, projection-update frequency and sparse-mask selection ablations. Figures 3 and 7 and Tables 2, 3 and 11 test substantial new questions about the hybrid method's behavior.

E5.justification: V1 Table 6 already contains ± values without specifying their interpretation or run count. V2 Tables 1 and 4 explicitly report means ± one standard error over three seeds, and Appendix F discloses three profiling repeats. Reporting remains uneven: Table 11 promises standard deviations but displays only point estimates. No increase in runs for retained results is established.

E6.justification: Earlier benchmark values are retained under Tensor low-rank labels in v2 Tables 5–10 and 12. Substantial new results include high-Re test L2 values of 16.82±0.18 for full-precision TensorGRaD versus 17.02±0.18 for Adam, both ×10^-2 (Table 1), and precision-dependent degradation in Table 3. These are newly reported conditions and findings, not same-setting improvements over v1's Navier–Stokes scores.

M1.justification: V1 uses Tucker-based low-rank gradient projection. V2 Algorithm 1 adds an unstructured sparse branch, compresses the residual with the low-rank branch, maintains separate Adam moments and combines their updates with scaling parameters. The earlier method remains as the low-rank-only component; the hybrid is a substantive procedural extension.

P1.justification: The abstract, introduction, method exposition and results narrative are extensively rewritten around TensorGRaD. Setup and results are combined, substantial background and dataset descriptions move to appendices, and standalone implicit-regularization and applications sections disappear. Explicit limitations and broader-impact passages are added. This is substantial narrative restructuring beyond the method's renaming.

P2.justification: V2 adds a hybrid-method schematic, reconstruction-error plots, turbulent-flow snapshots and new precision/composition tables, while redesigning the main memory–accuracy displays. Existing material is also relocated: v1 Figure 2 becomes v2 Figure 8, and v1 Table 1 becomes v2 Table 6. Typography, spacing and table placement change substantially throughout.

R1.justification: V2 substantially expands positioning around GRASS, robust PCA, robust tensor decomposition and low-rank-plus-sparse recovery. It also distinguishes gradient compression from SLTrain's weight decomposition and Scatterbrain's attention decomposition. V1 primarily positioned its contribution against matrix GaLore and tensor-weight compression; several earlier citations and their associated discussion are removed.

T1.justification: V2 adds mathematical definitions of sparse supports, structured Cartesian-product masks and projection/back-projection operations in Section 2.2 and Appendix E. The principal stable-rank, FNO-reversibility and fixed-projection convergence results remain essentially unchanged across v1 Appendices H–J and v2 Appendices K–M. No corresponding new convergence proof for the full hybrid update is supplied.

improvement.justification: V2 substantially strengthens validation through sparse and low-rank controls, precision and composition ablations, a harder turbulent benchmark, explicit three-seed uncertainty and fuller reproduction details. These make the memory–accuracy trade-off considerably more assessable than in v1. Important qualifications remain: Table 1's 52-to-29 GB reduction is approximately 44%, despite the accompanying 55% claim, and the retained proofs address the low-rank component rather than the full hybrid method. These shortcomings limit the headline claims but do not outweigh the substantial validation gains.

A1.justification: Both PDFs describe the same research lineage, with Tensor-GaLore extended and renamed TensorGRaD. Their complete main texts, figures, tables, equations and appendices support comparison, including matching retained experiments and proofs across relocation and renaming.

after.justification: V2 retains original experiments and adds high-Reynolds-number Navier–Stokes results, sparse/low-rank comparisons, precision experiments and additional ablations.

before.justification: V1 reports original FNO training experiments on Burgers, Darcy flow, Navier–Stokes and electromagnetic propagation, including accuracy, memory, rank ablations and execution times.

arxiv_record.abstract: Autoregressive construction approaches generate solutions to vehicle routing problems in a step-by-step fashion, leading to high-quality solutions that are nearing the performance achieved by handcrafted operations research techniques. In this work, we challenge the conventional paradigm of sequential solution construction and introduce an iterative search framework where solutions are instead deconstructed by a neural policy. Throughout the search, the neural policy collaborates with a simple greedy insertion algorithm to rebuild the deconstructed solutions. Our approach matches or surpasses the performance of state-of-the-art operations research methods across three challenging vehicle routing problems of various problem sizes.
arxiv_record.authors: Andr\'e Hottung, Paula Wong-Chung, Kevin Tierney
arxiv_record.title: Neural Deconstruction Search for Vehicle Routing Problems

E3.justification: V2 adds original-stopping-rule versus wall-time comparisons and BQ beam-width-16 evaluations alongside the retained beam-width-64 setting. E5.justification: Neither version reports repeated-seed uncertainty estimates, confidence intervals, error bars, or significance tests. E6.justification: V2 adds baseline scores and substantial runtime, sensitivity, ablation, and transfer results while retaining the main NDS scores. before.justification: Section 4 reports original routing benchmarks, component ablations, generalization tests, and scalability measurements. Appendices A and B provide training curves and policy-rollout visualizations.

arxiv_record.abstract: Designing a reinforcement learning from human feedback (RLHF) algorithm to approximate a human's unobservable reward function requires assuming, implicitly or explicitly, a model of human preferences. A preference model that poorly describes how humans generate preferences risks learning a poor approximation of the human's reward function. In this paper, we conduct three human studies to asses whether one can influence the expression of real human preferences to more closely conform to a desired preference model. Importantly, our approach does not seek to alter the human's unobserved reward function. Rather, we change how humans use this reward function to generate preferences, such that they better match whatever preference model is assumed by a particular RLHF algorithm. We introduce three interventions: showing humans the quantities that underlie a preference model, which is normally unobservable information derived from the reward function; training people to follow a specific preference model; and modifying the preference elicitation question. All intervention types show significant effects, providing practical tools to improve preference data quality and the resultant alignment of the learned reward functions. Overall we establish a novel research direction in model alignment: designing interfaces and training interventions to increase human conformance with the modeling assumptions of the algorithm that will learn from their input.

C1.justification: The central interface-influence contribution remains, but v3 expands its main claims to three preference models and cross-domain/stochastic settings. The introduction explicitly focuses applicability on sequential decisions, distinguishing single-step LLM RLHF. Introduction and conclusion add model-dependent transfer failures and unintended influence, qualifying the earlier practical-success narrative.

C2.justification: v3 introduces cognitive load and limited remaining improvement over control as explanations for unsuccessful regret transfer. It discusses intuitive rather than explicit computation, unintended influence toward regret, and environment-dependent benefits of question wording. These add substantive mechanisms and applicability boundaries; the earlier partial-return identifiability explanation remains.

D1.justification: v3 documents the space-domain rewards, transfer procedure, tunnel dynamics, and additional survey questions. Conversely, it removes v1 Appendix J.4's hardware specifications and PyTorch/scikit-learn versions. Existing learning hyperparameters, partition seeds, and the shared code/data access link remain.

E1.justification: v1 evaluates interventions within the deterministic delivery domain. v3 adds transfer from delivery-domain training to preference elicitation in a space domain with different rewards, and a delivery environment with stochastic tunnel transitions. These test cross-domain generalization and decisions with uncertain outcomes, substantially expanding scenario coverage.

E2.justification: The added stochastic study evaluates change-in-expected-return alongside regret, expanding the compared preference/reward-learning models beyond v1's partial-return/regret pairing. Comparator membership in the original studies is retained: full comparisons removed from the main plots remain in v3 Appendix K.4.

E3.justification: v3 adds separate training and elicitation domains and a stochastic evaluation, each with 10 subjects per condition. Section 5.1 changes normalized return from (Vpi - VU)/V* to (Vpi - VU)/(V* - VU). Reported PRIVILEGED counts change from 64/65/50 to 39/43/42 for partial return/regret/control, but appendix collection totals and subsampling remain unchanged; this does not establish an actual dataset reduction or rerun.

E4.justification: v3 adds generalization tests under domain and transition changes, cognitive-load survey analyses explaining unsuccessful regret transfer (Appendix E.3), and analysis of unintended preference-model influence (Appendix I). The synthetic-preference identifiability experiment was already present in v1 Appendix J.6 and is retained in v3 Appendix K.6.

E5.justification: The ten partition seeds and original statistical analyses are retained. Whether accuracy testing changes is unresolved: v3 Table 1 specifies Wilcoxon tests outside PRIVILEGED, whereas Appendix J still specifies Fisher's exact test and retains earlier p-values. The table also marks transfer accuracy as p < 0.01, while Appendix J reports p = 0.049.

E6.justification: Substantial new results accompany the added studies. Transfer accuracy is 86.29% versus 60.0% for partial return and 72.58% versus 72.92% for regret, comparing intervention with control (Table 7). Stochastic-study accuracies are 69.4% versus 67.8% for change-in-expected-return and 61.2% versus 65.9% for regret (Table 9). Original accuracy tables and full learning curves remain unchanged. v3 Figure 13 also corrects v1 Figure 9's significance caption to partial return, p < 0.05.

M1.justification: The three intervention mechanisms and original deterministic procedures remain. v3 adds a QUESTION variant targeting change-in-expected-return in stochastic environments, using the new question 'Which path do you prefer to start with?' and the corresponding reward-learning likelihood. This is a limited adaptation rather than a replacement of the intervention framework.

P1.justification: The introduction and conclusion are substantially expanded and rewritten around sequential decisions, transfer, and conditional effectiveness. Related work becomes two subsections, the experimental narrative gains nested follow-up studies, and the appendices are reorganized. The standalone practicality appendix disappears as cross-domain applicability receives direct experimental treatment.

P2.justification: v3 adds an experiment-summary table, new task illustrations, learning and likelihood plots, and accuracy tables. Figure 2 becomes a deterministic/stochastic comparison. Main reward-learning plots are simplified to target-versus-control displays, while the original full comparisons move to Appendix K.4. These are substantial display and layout changes beyond renumbering.

R1.justification: New Section 2.2 substantially broadens positioning around preference measurement, survey design, annotator discretion, and normative aggregation, citing works including Treiman, Buyl, and D'Alonzo. Section 3.2 also relates change-in-expected-return to Marklund and Van Roy's bootstrapped-return model. This exceeds a limited citation update.

T1.justification: v1 presents regret through a deterministic-transition derivation. v3 defines general regret using the sum of V* - Q*, separately defines change-in-expected-return and its preference distribution, and distinguishes these models under stochastic transitions (Section 3.2 and Figure 2). This substantially extends the formal framework, although it adds no theorem or proof. The normalized-return definition is also corrected.

improvement.justification: v3 directly tests the cross-domain practicality question left as future work in v1 Appendix A, revealing both successful transfer and an important failure boundary. The stochastic study further tests whether interventions distinguish outcomes from decision quality. These additions substantially strengthen assessment of applicability, supported by clearer scope and corrected reporting. Conflicting participant counts and summary-table statistics, an overbroad claim that all training interventions improve reward learning, and removed hardware/software details remain weaknesses, but do not outweigh the stronger empirical examination.

A1.justification: Both PDFs describe the same research on influencing human preferences for RLHF. Their text, equations, figures, tables, and complete appendices support comparison, including matching results moved between the main text and appendices.

after.justification: v3 retains those empirical results and adds cross-domain training, stochastic-environment experiments, and participant-survey analyses.

before.justification: v1 reports three human-subject experiments, analyses of collected preferences, reward-learning evaluations, and supplementary analyses.

arxiv_record.abstract: Mixture of Vision Encoders (MoVE) has emerged as a powerful approach to enhance the fine-grained visual understanding of multimodal large language models (MLLMs), improving their ability to handle tasks such as complex optical character recognition and scene understanding. Despite these advances, effectively combining diverse encoders and their visual tokens, while also scaling to high-resolution inputs, remains an open challenge. In this work, we conduct a systematic study of fusion designs for MoVE-based MLLMs, highlighting principles for token-level integration across complementary encoders. Our study shows that a lightweight recipe consisting of post-adaptation fusion with independent projectors, tile-level sequence interleaving, and dynamic tiling with global context delivers strong performance on diverse benchmarks. We integrate these principles into a simple and effective architecture that we call LEO. Extensive evaluation on 11 vision-language benchmarks demonstrates that LEO achieves better results on the majority of tasks compared to existing MoVE-based approaches. Furthermore, LEO adapts effectively to the specialized domain of autonomous driving without altering its architecture or training recipe, achieving competitive performance against established baselines and thereby highlighting its ability to generalize. The code is available at https://github.com/Mozhgan91/LEO.
arxiv_record.authors: Mozhgan Nasr Azadani, James Riddell, Sean Sedwards, Krzysztof Czarnecki
arxiv_record.title: Rethinking the Mixture of Vision Encoders Paradigm for Enhanced Visual Understanding in Multimodal LLMs

E1.justification: v2 adds MathVista evaluation for visually grounded mathematical reasoning. The original 13 general benchmarks remain represented in Appendix Table 13, and LingoQA remains included. E2.justification: v2 substantially revises the comparison sets: Table 4 adds DeepSeek-VL, SPHINX, MoME-X3, MouSi-X3, and Eagle-X3, while Table 7 introduces RADIO, RADIO2.5, and MoVE-KD-v1.1. E4.justification: The limited v1 ablations expand into systematic tests of four tiling strategies, four merging strategies, and pre/post-adaptation fusion across encoder pairs. v2 also adds training-data scaling, efficiency tradeoffs, and explicit failure cases in Appendix A.5–A.7. E5.justification: Neither version reports repeated-run counts, random seeds, confidence intervals, significance tests, or uncertainty estimates for its experimental results. v2's added averages aggregate benchmark scores rather than repeated trials.

E6.justification: v2 adds extensive fusion, tiling, efficiency, scaling, and qualitative results, including LEO's MathVista score of 37.2. The original 13 LEO benchmark scores and LingoQA scores are retained. Instruct-BLIP's VizWiz value changes from 45.5 in v1 Table 1 to 34.5 in v2 Table 13. The separate MMMU test score and LingoQA no-tiling results disappear.

M1.justification: The final LEO architecture retains InternViT-300M and SAM-L, dynamic tiling with global context, pixel unshuffling, independent MLP projectors, tile-level token interleaving, and InternLM2-7B. v2 formalizes and evaluates these existing components; its expanded experimental variants do not establish a redesign of the proposed model.

P1.justification: The title, abstract, introduction, related work, and conclusion are extensively rewritten around three investigative directions. A dedicated empirical-study section now precedes the LEO description. General-model comparisons and detailed ablations move into a new multipart appendix, substantially changing the narrative and document organization.

P2.justification: v2 adopts a single-column journal layout, redraws the overview and fusion diagrams, and reorganizes comparison tables. Main-text averages are paired with full appendix tables, and new efficiency and success/failure displays are added. R1.justification: v2 broadens related work to knowledge-distilled encoders and newer visual-understanding approaches, adding works such as RADIO, RADIOv2.5, MoVE-KD, and MoME. improvement.justification: v2 substantially strengthens support for the central fusion-design claims. arxiv_record.abstract: We introduce BN-Pool, the first clustering-based pooling method for Graph Neural Networks that adaptively determines the number of supernodes in a coarsened graph. BN-Pool leverages a generative model based on a Bayesian nonparametric framework for partitioning graph nodes into an unbounded number of clusters. During training, the node-to-cluster assignments are learned by combining the supervised loss of the downstream task with an unsupervised auxiliary term, which encourages the reconstruction of the original graph topology while penalizing unnecessary proliferation of clusters. By automatically discovering the optimal coarsening level for each graph, BN-Pool preserves the performance of soft-clustering pooling methods while avoiding their typical redundancy by learning compact pooled graphs. The code is available at https://github.com/NGMLGroup/Bayesian-Nonparametric-Graph-Pooling.
arxiv_record.authors: Daniele Castellana, Filippo Maria Bianchi
arxiv_record.title: BN-Pool: Bayesian Nonparametric Pooling for Graphs

C1.justification: The central claim of the first adaptive soft-clustering pooling operator remains. The abstract shifts from broadly superior benchmark performance to preserving performance while producing compact representations. The conclusion extends the stated contribution to graph regression and sparse O(E) reconstruction, without replacing the principal adaptive-pooling claim.

C2.justification: v1 proposes heterophilic adaptation as future work; v2 documents underperformance on Multipartite and explains it through the model's homophilic architectural and loss biases. v2 also interprets hyperparameter sensitivity and explains dense/sparse memory and runtime tradeoffs, including reduced sampling efficiency as graph density increases. These substantially develop the applicability boundaries and limitations.

D1.justification: v2 adds dataset-specific selected hyperparameters in Table 11, hardware and timing information in Section 5.3, expanded forward-pass pseudocode, and GPU negative-sampling and dense-enumeration details in Appendix A. It also reports access through Torch Geometric Pool, supplementing the repository already linked in v1.

E1.justification: v2 adds Peptides-struct graph regression and Multipartite classification under explicitly heterophilic, adversarial connectivity. These materially extend task and environmental coverage. The earlier datasets remain covered; GCB-H, IMDB, and DD results move to Appendix C, Table 12.

E2.justification: Compared with v1 Table 2, v2 Tables 3 and 12 add evaluated graph-level comparators SEP, EigenPooling, and HOSC. Table 3 also adds a GNN without hierarchical pooling. The four node-clustering comparators remain unchanged.

E3.justification: Reported graph-level settings change substantially: early-stopping patience falls from 500 to 100 epochs, learning-rate plateau patience from 200 to 30, and KL annealing from 300 to 50 epochs. MolHiv changes from one 32-unit MP layer before and after pooling to two 64-unit layers on each side with dropout and batch normalization. v2 also expands the prior-hyperparameter grid and introduces additional pooling-ratio evaluations.

E4.justification: v2 adds prior-hyperparameter sensitivity experiments on Enzymes and Colors3, comparator pooling-ratio sweeps, and analyses of memory, epoch time, and training duration, including dense versus sparse BN-Pool. Multipartite provides an explicit heterophilic stress test. The earlier Cora and GCB-H qualitative analyses are largely relocated rather than newly introduced.

E5.justification: Both versions report means and standard deviations. v2 newly specifies averaging over 10 folds for Table 5 and identifies dataset folds and weight initializations as sources of variation in Table 8. This adds limited statistical documentation; an increase in repetitions for retained results or a formal significance-testing procedure is not established.

E6.justification: The node-clustering scores are unchanged, but BN-Pool graph-level scores are revised: Colors3 changes from 93±1 to 99±0 and MUTAG from 91±8 to 88±7. Because reported settings also change, these are not controlled same-setting gains or losses. v2 adds substantial results, including Peptides-struct MAE of 0.255±0.001, Multipartite accuracy of 58±2, and new sensitivity, cluster-count, and resource measurements.

The reported dense auxiliary-loss normalization also changes from 1/N in v1 Equation 10 to 1/N² in v2 Equation 12. These change the training objective and computation while retaining the DP/SBM foundation.

P2.justification: The main text changes from two columns to one, with widespread figure and table relocation. v2 adds overview and GNN/SRC diagrams, redraws the BN-Pool schematic, expands the cluster-distribution display, and introduces several analysis tables. R1.justification: v2 adds references supporting additional pooling comparators, broader graph applications, KL annealing, and software availability. However, Section 4 retains essentially the same positioning relative to DiffPool, DGVAE, SB-VAE, and the IBP-based overlapping SBM. Publication updates to existing references do not constitute new related work.

T1.justification: v2 Equation 3 restores the missing alpha_DP multiplier on the base-distribution term in v1 Appendix A, Equation 15, correcting the DP predictive distribution. Section 3.4.1 also supplies the sparse-loss expression and its 2E-term complexity argument. Most DP background and the underlying variational derivation are retained.

improvement.justification: v2 substantially strengthens validation through additional comparators, a no-pooling control, pooling-ratio sweeps, an explicit heterophilic failure case, and measured dense/sparse computational costs. These address important gaps in v1's evidence, while dataset-specific settings and clearer exposition improve auditability. arxiv_record.abstract: Collaborative learning (CL) enables multiple participants to jointly train machine learning (ML) models on decentralized data sources without raw data sharing. While the primary goal of CL is to maximize the expected accuracy gain for each participant, it is also important to ensure that the gains are fairly distributed: no client should be negatively impacted, and gains should reflect contributions. Most existing CL methods require central coordination and focus only on gain maximization, overlooking fairness. In this work, we first show that the existing measure of collaborative fairness based on the correlation between accuracy values without and with collaboration has drawbacks because it does not account for negative collaboration gain. We argue that maximizing mean collaboration gain (MCG) while simultaneously minimizing the collaboration gain spread (CGS) is a fairer alternative. Next, we propose the CYCle protocol that enables individual participants in a private decentralized learning (PDL) framework to achieve this objective through a novel reputation scoring method based on gradient alignment between the local cross-entropy and distillation losses. We further extend the CYCle protocol to operate on top of gossip-based decentralized algorithms such as Gossip-SGD. We also theoretically show that CYCle performs better than standard FedAvg in a two-client mean estimation setting under high heterogeneity. Empirical experiments demonstrate the effectiveness of the CYCle protocol to ensure positive and fair collaboration gain for all participants, even in cases where the data distributions of participants are highly skewed.
arxiv_record.authors: Nurbek Tastan, Samuel Horvath, Karthik Nandakumar
arxiv_record.title: CYCle: Choosing Your Collaborators Wisely to Enhance Collaborative Fairness in Decentralized Learning

arxiv_record.abstract: Learned optimization has emerged as a promising alternative to hand-crafted optimizers, with the potential to discover stronger learned update rules that enable faster, hyperparameter-free training of neural networks. A critical element for practically useful learned optimizers, that can be used off-the-shelf after meta-training, is strong meta-generalization: the ability to apply the optimizers to new tasks. Recent state-of-the-art work in learned optimizers, VeLO (Metz et al., 2022), requires a large number of highly diverse meta-training tasks along with massive computational resources, 4000 TPU months, to achieve meta-generalization. This makes further improvements to such learned optimizers impractical. In this work, we identify several key elements in learned optimizer architectures and meta-training procedures that can lead to strong meta-generalization. We also propose evaluation metrics to reliably assess quantitative performance of an optimizer at scale on a set of evaluation tasks. Our proposed approach, Celo, makes a significant leap in improving the meta-generalization performance of learned optimizers and also outperforms tuned state-of-the-art optimizers on a diverse set of out-of-distribution tasks, despite being meta-trained for just 24 GPU hours.
arxiv_record.authors: Abhinav Moudgil, Boris Knyazev, Guillaume Lajoie, Eugene Belilovsky
arxiv_record.title: Celo: Training Versatile Learned Optimizers on a Compute Diet

arxiv_record.abstract: Overparameterized deep networks that generalize well have been key to the dramatic success of deep learning in recent years. The reasons for their remarkable ability to generalize are not well understood yet. When class labels in the training set are shuffled to varying degrees, it is known that deep networks can still reach perfect training accuracy at the detriment of generalization to true labels -- a phenomenon that has been called memorization. It has, however, been unclear why the poor generalization to true labels that accompanies such memorization, comes about. One possibility is that during training, all layers of the network irretrievably re-organize their representations in a manner that makes generalization to true labels difficult. The other possibility is that one or more layers of the trained network retain significantly more latent ability to generalize to true labels, but the network somehow "chooses" to readout in a manner that is detrimental to generalization to true labels. Here, we provide evidence for the latter possibility by demonstrating, empirically, that such models possess information in their representations for substantially-improved generalization to true labels. Furthermore, such abilities can be easily decoded from the internals of the trained model, and we build a technique to do so. We demonstrate results on multiple models trained with standard datasets. Our code is available at: https://github.com/simranketha/MASC_DNN.
arxiv_record.authors: Simran Ketha and Venkatakrishnan Ramaswamy
arxiv_record.title: Decoding Generalization from Memorization in Deep Neural Networks

D1.justification: v2 provides a code-repository link and implementation details for the new experiments, including ResNet-18 training settings, logistic regression's optimizer, learning rate, batch size and epochs, KNN's neighbor count and distance, and the retraining pipeline. E2.justification: v2 adds evaluated comparisons against logistic regression, K-nearest neighbors, linear discriminant analysis, quadratic discriminant analysis, and nearest class mean (Section 5 and Appendix C). v1 compares principally against network predictions, early-stopping performance, and random-initialization controls; those existing comparisons are retained.

E3.justification: New retraining experiments reserve 20% of the original test set for layer selection and validation, evaluate on the remaining 80%, and use up to 30 additional epochs with patience 3; a separate experiment uses 10 epochs without early stopping. v2 also adds ResNet-18 layer evaluations, probe-training protocols, and computational-cost and relabeling-error metrics. These additions do not establish changes to the retained experiments' protocols.

E4.justification: v2 replaces the Tiny ImageNet-focused PCA variance sweeps with comparisons of 99%, 75%, 50%, 25%, and one principal component across multiple model-dataset pairs. arxiv_record.abstract: Large Language Models (LLMs) have demonstrated remarkable abilities in tackling a wide range of complex tasks. However, their huge computational and memory costs raise significant challenges in deploying these models on resource-constrained devices or efficiently serving them. Prior approaches have attempted to alleviate these problems by permanently removing less important model structures, yet these methods often result in substantial performance degradation due to the permanent deletion of model parameters. In this work, we tried to mitigate this issue by reducing the number of active parameters without permanently removing them. Specifically, we introduce a differentiable dynamic pruning method that pushes dense models to maintain a fixed number of active parameters by converting their MLP layers into a Mixture of Experts (MoE) architecture. Our method, even without fine-tuning, consistently outperforms previous structural pruning techniques across diverse model families, including Phi-2, LLaMA-2, LLaMA-3, and Qwen-2.5.

Detailed analysis becomes an additional stated contribution. The original claims about uncovering experts without updating pretrained weights and jointly learning routing and expert configurations remain.

C2.justification: v2 adds explanations linking the modest VO-routing benefit to small head dimensions and poor head-pruning performance to distorted attention features. It also discusses temperature robustness, recommends fewer than 16 experts, and qualifies comparable throughput by sufficiently large batch size. Existing interpretations of expert semantics and width allocation are retained.

D1.justification: The abstract adds a code-availability statement and repository address. New comparisons disclose training-token budgets and the matched-iteration fine-tuning setting for LLaMA-MoE. The detailed module configurations, optimizer settings, GPU allocations, and data-processing instructions already present in v1 remain substantially unchanged.

E1.justification: v2 adds evaluated BoolQ, SciQ, TruthfulQA, and MMLU benchmarks in Tables 5–6 and Figure 10, substantially broadening task coverage beyond the original language-modeling and five commonsense benchmarks. The original training datasets and evaluation coverage are retained.

E2.justification: Tables 4–6 add evaluated LLaMA-MoE, G-MoEfication, LLaMA-MoE-v2, and CMoE comparators, including multiple configurations and fine-tuned variants. This introduces a substantial direct MoE-construction comparison group. The original structural and semi-structured pruning comparators remain represented.

E3.justification: Alongside the retained zero-shot protocols, v2 introduces 32-shot BoolQ, 5-shot WinoGrande and MMLU, 25-shot ARC-c, and 10-shot HellaSwag evaluations. It also introduces throughput measurements at batch sizes 512, 1024, and 1536. These are additional evaluation designs; the original default 10,000-iteration training setup remains unchanged.

E4.justification: Beyond the retained loss, dataset, and expert-count analyses, Table 13 tests local embeddings, head pruning, removal of VO routing, and temperature sensitivity. Figure 4 adds aggregate expert-utilization analysis, Figure 10 examines the MMLU accuracy–parameter trade-off, and Table 15 examines throughput scaling with batch size.

E5.justification: Neither version reports experimental seed counts, repeated-run summaries, confidence intervals, or significance tests. The retained expert-width boxplots describe variation among experts rather than uncertainty across experimental runs.

E6.justification: Original benchmark values are retained, including LLaMA-2 rows relocated from Table 3 to Table 12. v2 adds substantial MoE, MMLU, ablation, and throughput results: Table 13 reports 56.07 for full ToMoE versus 44.99 for head pruning, and Table 15 reports 2360.38–2919.45 tokens/s across batch sizes. Section 4.3 also incorrectly redescribes the unchanged 3.14-point advantage over ModeGPT-Alpaca as '3.14 times'.

M1.justification: The core architecture, expert construction, routing, and frozen-weight training remain the same. However, Section 3.4 changes the load-balancing probability calculation from explicitly defined softmax in v1 to GSmax in v2 without explaining whether this represents a changed calculation or inconsistent notation. An actual loss modification cannot be established reliably.

P1.justification: v2 rewrites the abstract, condenses the introductory background, edits method explanations and notation, updates author information, and removes the Impact Statement. The main section sequence and much of the existing method and appendix prose remain intact.

P2.justification: The main paper changes from a two-column conference layout to a single-column journal layout with substantially different front matter and table placement. v2 adds comparison and ablation tables and new plots, moves part of Table 3 into appendix Table 12, and combines v1 Figures 5–6 into v2 Figure 6.

R1.justification: v2 expands positioning against contextual sparsity through Deja Vu, CATS, and structured-sparsity work, and broadens dense-to-MoE discussion and comparisons through MoEfication, generalized MoEfication, LLaMA-MoE-v2, and CMoE. T1.justification: New Appendix F derives the effective query–key width from overlapping binary pruning masks, showing that it reaches the allocated width K only when the masks coincide. This adds a focused mathematical justification to the qualitative concern already stated in v1 Appendix A.2.

improvement.justification: v2 addresses an important gap in v1: a dense-to-MoE method was evaluated mainly against pruning. arxiv_record.abstract: From implicit differentiation to probabilistic modeling, Jacobian and Hessian matrices have many potential use cases in Machine Learning (ML), but they are viewed as computationally prohibitive. Fortunately, these matrices often exhibit sparsity, which can be leveraged to speed up the process of Automatic Differentiation (AD). This paper presents advances in sparsity detection, previously the performance bottleneck of Automatic Sparse Differentiation (ASD). Our implementation of sparsity detection is based on operator overloading, able to detect both local and global sparsity patterns, and supports flexible index set representations. It is fully automatic and requires no modification of user code, making it compatible with existing ML codebases. Most importantly, it is highly performant, unlocking Jacobians and Hessians at scales where they were considered too expensive to compute. On real-world problems from scientific ML, graph neural networks and optimization, we show significant speed-ups of up to three orders of magnitude. Notably, using our sparsity detection system, ASD outperforms standard AD for one-off computations, without amortization of either sparsity detection or matrix coloring.
arxiv_record.authors: Adrian Hill and Guillaume Dalle
arxiv_record.title: Sparser, Better, Faster, Stronger: Sparsity Detection for Efficient Automatic Differentiation

improvement.justification: v1's efficiency evidence centers on derivative construction. v2 addresses the important downstream-use gap through Newton and GNN solver comparisons, adds bottleneck diagnostics, corrects central mathematical statements, and documents concrete failure conditions while preserving the Hessian evidence. arxiv_record.abstract: Fine-tuning large language models (LLMs) using low-rank adaptation (LoRA) has become a highly efficient approach for downstream tasks, particularly in scenarios with limited computational resources. However, applying LoRA techniques to quantized LLMs poses unique challenges due to the reduced representational precision of quantized weights. In this paper, we introduce CLoQ (Calibrated LoRA initialization for Quantized LLMs), a simplistic initialization strategy designed to overcome these challenges. Our approach focuses on minimizing the layer-wise discrepancy between the original LLM and its quantized counterpart with LoRA components during initialization. By leveraging a small calibration dataset, CLoQ quantizes a pre-trained LLM and determines the optimal LoRA components for each layer, ensuring a strong foundation for subsequent fine-tuning. A key contribution of this work is a novel theoretical result that enables the accurate and closed-form construction of these optimal LoRA components. We validate the efficacy of CLoQ across multiple tasks such as language generation, arithmetic reasoning, and commonsense reasoning, demonstrating that it consistently outperforms existing LoRA fine-tuning methods for quantized LLMs, especially at ultra low-bit widths.

arxiv_record.title: CLoQ: Enhancing Fine-Tuning of Quantized LLMs via Calibrated LoRA Initialization

arxiv_record.abstract: We introduce a novel inference-time alignment approach for LLMs that aims to generate safe responses almost surely, i.e., with probability approaching one. Our approach models the generation of safe responses as a constrained Markov Decision Process (MDP) within the LLM's latent space. We augment a safety state that tracks the evolution of safety constraints and dynamically penalize unsafe generations to ensure the generation of safe responses. Consequently, we demonstrate formal safety guarantees w.r.t. the given cost model upon solving the MDP in the latent space with sufficiently large penalties. Building on this foundation, we propose InferenceGuard, a practical implementation that safely aligns LLMs without modifying the model weights. Empirically, we demonstrate that InferenceGuard effectively balances safety and task performance, outperforming existing inference-time alignment methods in generating safe and aligned responses. Our findings contribute to the advancement of safer LLM deployment through alignment at inference-time, thus presenting a promising alternative to resource-intensive, overfitting-prone alignment techniques like RLHF.

arxiv_record.abstract: Dense process rewards have proven a more effective alternative to the sparse outcome-level rewards in the inference-time scaling of large language models (LLMs), particularly in tasks requiring complex multi-step reasoning. While dense rewards also offer an appealing choice for the reinforcement learning (RL) of LLMs since their fine-grained rewards have the potential to address some inherent issues of outcome rewards, such as training efficiency and credit assignment, this potential remains largely unrealized. This can be primarily attributed to the challenges of training process reward models (PRMs) online, where collecting high-quality process labels is prohibitively expensive, making them particularly vulnerable to reward hacking. To address these challenges, we propose PRIME (Process Reinforcement through IMplicit rEwards), which enables online PRM updates using only policy rollouts and outcome labels through implict process rewards. PRIME combines well with various advantage functions and forgoes the dedicated reward model training phrase that existing approaches require, substantially reducing the development overhead. We demonstrate PRIME's effectiveness on competitional math and coding. Starting from Qwen2.5-Math-7B-Base, PRIME achieves a 15.1% average improvement across several key reasoning benchmarks over the SFT model. Notably, our resulting model, Eurus-2-7B-PRIME, surpasses Qwen2.5-Math-7B-Instruct on seven reasoning benchmarks with 10% of its training data.

The headline performance and data-efficiency claims remain unchanged.

C2.justification: v2 substantially expands interpretation of the method through Appendix C's discussion of reward parameterization, loss normalization and reward shaping. It adds interpretations concerning limited benefits from larger PRMs and reduced relative overhead for long responses. Appendix A newly states the 32B experimental boundary and shorter ablation budgets; the earlier Zero-training saturation discussion is retained.

D1.justification: v2 adds hardware specifications, component-level timing, CPU-offloading information and resource budgets for new comparisons. Existing training hyperparameters and preprocessing instructions remain. v1's public project/model/data link is removed, while v2 instead states that code is provided in supplementary material.

E1.justification: v2 adds AIME 2025 evaluation in Table 5. Additional comparisons use MATH training data and the DeepScaleR training setting in Appendices B.6–B.7. The original seven benchmarks and documented SFT/RL data collections remain, with coverage still centered on mathematical and coding reasoning.

E2.justification: v2 adds a reproduced VinePPO comparison and comparisons with DeepScaleR checkpoints in Tables 6–7, substantially extending the evaluated alternatives beyond the existing RL algorithms. VinePPO was only cited in v1. DeepScaleR comparisons use reported results and an estimated training curve; the original comparator sets are retained.

E3.justification: New experiments introduce 800 rollout steps, 16 responses per prompt instead of four, and 3B/7B/14B reward models with a fixed 7B policy. Additional protocols include matched 96-step RhoMath-1.1B training, 330-step training with an 8k response limit under the DeepScaleR setting, and avg@16 evaluation at temperature 0.3. The original main-experiment settings are retained.

E4.justification: v2 adds substantial tests of whether gains persist with more training and rollouts, whether reward-model capacity matters, and whether CE versus DPO PRM training changes performance. Runtime profiling also examines computational overhead. Earlier filtering, initialization, reference-model, single/double-forward and Zero analyses are retained, including relocated appendix material.

E5.justification: Table 12 newly reports avg@16 evaluation, adding explicit averaging over 16 sampled responses for AIME 2024 and AMC. This does not establish repeated independent RL training runs. The disclosed SFT seed remains 42, and no new confidence-interval or significance-testing procedure is documented.

E6.justification: The original main and RL-algorithm tables retain their scores, but v2 adds substantial scaling, timing, model-size, loss-choice and avg@16 results. For example, Table 6 reports 18.8% versus 18.4% validation accuracy and 1.22 versus 13.94 hours for PRIME versus VinePPO at 96 steps. These are newly reported experiments, not improvements to the unchanged original scores.

M1.justification: Algorithm 1 and the default implicit-reward, advantage-estimation and policy-update procedures remain unchanged. Appendix C.2 introduces and tests an alternative DPO loss for updating the PRM, while retaining CE as the default.

P1.justification: The document is extensively reorganized: imitation warmup moves into Appendix D; reference-model, single/double-forward and Zero studies move into Appendix B; detailed alternative advantage formulas also move out of the main text. v2 adds limitations, ethics, reproducibility and theoretical-discussion sections, alongside prose compression and author-list changes.

P2.justification: Numerous displays are relocated and resized, including v1 Figure 1 becoming appendix Figure 12 and v1 Table 3 becoming appendix Table 4. v2 adds scaling plots, runtime and comparison tables, and loss-ablation displays. Figure 17 presents the existing dense-versus-sparse comparison against wall time; retained plots also receive caption and legend revisions.

R1.justification: v2 adds references to DeepScaleR, Rho-1, potential-based reward shaping and maximum-entropy RL, and removes the Meta 2024 reference. Appendix C clarifies relationships to DPO and entropy-regularized RL. The main positioning around scalable online dense rewards remains substantially unchanged.

T1.justification: Appendix C adds a soft-Q expression, mathematical reasoning about cancellation of prompt-dependent reward offsets, and a potential-based reward-shaping argument at gamma=1. These extend the justification of the existing formulation; the original advantage equations remain, and no substantial new theorem-and-proof development is supplied.

improvement.justification: v2 materially strengthens the central efficiency argument, which in v1 relied mainly on training-step counts, through runtime profiling and a matched VinePPO comparison. A1.justification: Both PDFs describe PRIME. Their text, equations, tables, figures and appendices are readable and support reliable comparison, including matching material moved between the main text and appendices.

after.justification: v2 retains the original experiments and adds original scaling, runtime, reward-model-size, loss-function and baseline-comparison results.

before.justification: v1 reports original RL training results, seven-benchmark evaluations and ablations, including Tables 2–3 and Figures 3–13.

arxiv_record.abstract: As the general capabilities of artificial intelligence (AI) agents continue to evolve, their ability to learn to master multiple complex tasks through experience remains a key challenge. Current LLM agents, particularly those based on proprietary language models, typically rely on prompts to incorporate knowledge about the target tasks. This approach does not allow the agent to internalize this information and instead relies on ever-expanding prompts to sustain its functionality in diverse scenarios. This resembles a system of notes used by a person affected by anterograde amnesia, the inability to form new memories. In this paper, we propose a novel method to train AI agents to incorporate knowledge and skills for multiple tasks without the need for either cumbersome note systems or prior high-quality demonstration data. Our approach employs an iterative process where the agent collects new experiences, receives corrective feedback from humans in the form of hints, and integrates this feedback into its weights via a context distillation training procedure. We demonstrate the efficacy of our approach by implementing it in a Llama-3-based agent that, after only a few rounds of feedback, outperforms advanced models GPT-4o and DeepSeek-V3 in tasksets requiring correct sequencing of information retrieval, tool use, and question answering.
arxiv_record.authors: Minttu Alakuijala, Ya Gao, Georgy Ananov, Samuel Kaski, Pekka Marttinen, Alexander Ilin, Harri Valpola
arxiv_record.title: Memento No More: Coaching AI Agents to Master Multiple Tasks via Hints Internalization

arxiv_record.abstract: In this work, we introduce a novel framework for privately optimizing objectives that rely on Wasserstein distances between data-dependent empirical measures. Our main theoretical contribution is, based on an explicit formulation of the Wasserstein gradient in a fully discrete setting, a control on the sensitivity of this gradient to individual data points, allowing strong privacy guarantees at minimal utility cost. Building on these insights, we develop a deep learning approach that incorporates gradient and activations clipping, originally designed for DP training of problems with a finite-sum structure. We further demonstrate that privacy accounting methods extend to Wasserstein-based objectives, facilitating large-scale private training. Empirical results confirm that our framework effectively balances accuracy and privacy, offering a theoretically sound solution for privacy-preserving machine learning tasks relying on optimal transport distances such as Wasserstein distance or sliced-Wasserstein distance.
