arxiv_record.abstract: Neural operators have shown great potential in surrogate modeling. However, training a well-performing neural operator typically requires a substantial amount of data, which can pose a major challenge in complex applications. In such scenarios, detailed physical knowledge can be unavailable or difficult to obtain, and collecting extensive data is often prohibitively expensive. To mitigate this challenge, we propose the Pseudo Physics-Informed Neural Operator (PPI-NO) framework. PPI-NO constructs a surrogate physics system for the target system using partial differential equations (PDEs) derived from simple, rudimentary physics principles, such as basic differential operators. This surrogate system is coupled with a neural operator model, using an alternating update and learning process to iteratively enhance the model's predictive power. While the physics derived via PPI-NO may not mirror the ground-truth underlying physical laws -- hence the term ``pseudo physics'' -- this approach significantly improves the accuracy of standard operator learning models in data-scarce scenarios, which is evidenced by extensive evaluations across five benchmark tasks and a fatigue modeling application.
arxiv_record.authors: Keyan Chen, Yile Li, Da Long, Zhitong Xu, Wei Xing, Jacob Hochhalter, Shandian Zhe
arxiv_record.title: Pseudo-Physics-Informed Neural Operators: Enhancing Operator Learning from Limited Data

arxiv_record.abstract: Neural networks are fragile when confronted with data that significantly deviates from their training distribution. This is true in particular for simulation-based inference methods, such as neural amortized Bayesian inference (ABI), where models trained on simulated data are deployed on noisy real-world observations. Recent robust approaches employ unsupervised domain adaptation (UDA) to match the embedding spaces of simulated and observed data. However, the lack of comprehensive evaluations across different domain mismatches raises concerns about the reliability in high-stakes applications. We address this gap by systematically testing UDA approaches across a wide range of misspecification scenarios in silico and practice. We demonstrate that aligning summary spaces between domains effectively mitigates the impact of unmodeled phenomena or noise. However, the same alignment mechanism can lead to failures under prior misspecifications - a critical finding with practical consequences. Our results underscore the need for careful consideration of misspecification types when using UDA to increase the robustness of ABI.

arxiv_record.title: Does Unsupervised Domain Adaptation Improve the Robustness of Amortized Bayesian Inference? A Systematic Evaluation

It adds substantive limitations concerning label-free hyperparameter selection, interpretability, and failure of majority-domain alignment to protect rare misspecified observations.

D1.justification: New appendices document Ricker architectures and search ranges, decision-model networks and training budgets, empirical-data selection, cleaning thresholds, and Mahalanobis-based test-set classification. NNPE standardization and image-noise scaling are explicitly documented. One reproducibility inconsistency remains: Gaussian adaptation data number 48,000 in Section 5.2 but 49,000 in Appendix B.4.

E1.justification: v2 adds contaminated Ricker population-dynamics inference and diffusion-model inference on empirical Implicit Association Test data. These introduce temporal ecological simulations and human response-time modeling beyond the retained Gaussian and MNIST/USPS denoising coverage.

E2.justification: The matched benchmarks retain the same comparison participants: NPE, NNPE, NPE-MMD, NPE-DANN, and the analytic posterior for Gaussian inference. The new applications reuse the neural comparator set. NNPE standardization and noise scaling concern experimental settings.

E3.justification: Denoising evaluation changes from observed images seen during adaptation to a separate unseen test set. Gaussian test sets increase from 100 to 1,000, with posterior samples increasing from 100 to 5,000; denoising samples increase from 10 to 100. PPD changes to RMSE with denoised/resimulated references, and v2 adds NLL, C2ST diagnostics, and a 50-trial-per-method tuning protocol.

E4.justification: v2 adds systematic Ricker hyperparameter sensitivity analyses, t-SNE examinations of summary-space alignment, and real-data analyses of cleaning and prior–posterior convergence. Conversely, v1 Figures B6–B8, which directly measure approximation distances to the analytic posterior, are removed. The existing Gaussian domain and regularization analyses remain.

E5.justification: Gaussian reporting changes from averages over three runs to medians over ten runs, explicitly because extreme failures distort means. Ricker analyses introduce Gaussian-process trend estimates with 95% predictive intervals. Denoising retains its existing three-run mean and standard-deviation reporting.

arxiv_record.abstract: This paper introduces a cost-efficient active learning (AL) framework for classification, featuring a novel query design called candidate set query. Unlike traditional AL queries requiring the oracle to examine all possible classes, our method narrows down the set of candidate classes likely to include the ground-truth class, significantly reducing the search space and labeling cost. Moreover, we leverage conformal prediction to dynamically generate small yet reliable candidate sets, adapting to model enhancement over successive AL rounds. To this end, we introduce an acquisition function designed to prioritize data points that offer high information gain at lower cost. Empirical evaluations on CIFAR-10, CIFAR-100, and ImageNet64x64 demonstrate the effectiveness and scalability of our framework. Notably, it reduces labeling cost by 48% on ImageNet64x64. The project page can be found at https://yehogwon.github.io/csq-al.
arxiv_record.authors: Yeho Gwon, Sehyun Hwang, Hoyoung Kim, Jungseul Ok, Suha Kwak
arxiv_record.title: Enhancing Cost Efficiency in Active Learning with Candidate Set Query

arxiv_record.abstract: Early Classification of Time Series (ECTS) is vital in fields like industrial monitoring and medical triage, where quick and accurate predictions are essential. One of the core challenges lies in the trigger function, which decides when to make a prediction, independently of the classifier itself. Most existing methods rely on handcrafted rules, but can data-driven approaches outperform them? This paper introduces Alert, a Deep-RL framework that learns trigger functions from any state representation. Systematic comparisons on 30 datasets show that the design of the state space significantly influences performance. Building on this, we propose Alert+, a simple yet effective variant that consistently outperforms traditional methods in balancing accuracy and delay within an imbalanced misclassification and exponential delay cost setting. Alert and Alert+ are released to support reproducible research and practical applications.
arxiv_record.authors: Aur\'elien Renault, Alexis Bondu, Antoine Cornu\'ejols, Vincent Lemaire
arxiv_record.title: Alert: Learning Trigger Functions for Early Classification of Time Series using Deep-RL

arxiv_record.abstract: Feature importance measures are widely studied and are essential for understanding model behavior, guiding feature selection, and enhancing interpretability. However, many machine learning fitted models involve complex interactions between features. Existing feature importance metrics fail to capture these pairwise or higher-order effects, while existing interaction metrics often suffer from limited applicability or excessive computation; no methods exist to conduct statistical inference for feature interactions. To bridge this gap, we first propose a new model-agnostic metric, interaction Leave-One-Covariate-Out (iLOCO), for measuring the importance of pairwise feature interactions, with extensions to higher-order interactions. Next, we leverage recent advances in LOCO inference to develop distribution-free and assumption-light confidence intervals for our iLOCO metric. To address computational challenges, we also introduce an ensemble learning method for calculating the iLOCO metric and confidence intervals that we show is both computationally and statistically efficient. We validate our iLOCO metric and our confidence intervals on both synthetic and real data sets, showing that our approach outperforms existing methods and provides the first inferential approach to detecting feature interactions.
arxiv_record.authors: Camille Little, Lili Zheng, Genevera Allen
arxiv_record.title: iLOCO: Distribution-Free Inference for Feature Interactions

The cocktail study changes from 15,972 records and 200 ingredients with a kernel regressor and 30,000 minipatches to 5,934 records and 100 ingredients with a three-hidden-layer MLP and 20,000 minipatches. The appendix also revises the stated autoregressive parameter from 0.9 to 0.8; this documents a setting change without establishing that retained curves were rerun.

E4.justification: Figures 1A and A1A substantially expand validation by comparing second- and third-order iLOCO across feature dimensionalities, replacing the earlier isolated third-order demonstration. E5.justification: Section 4.2 and Figure 4 change from marginal intervals described as controlling false coverage rate to reported Bonferroni-adjusted intervals, retaining alpha=0.1. T1.justification: Proposition 1 replaces v1's claim that population iLOCO equals the isolated interaction function with expected squared contributions from all terms containing the selected pair, using MSE for regression and absolute error for Bernoulli classification. arxiv_record.abstract: This paper challenges the recent paradigm in atomic property prediction that links progress to growing dataset sizes and computational resources. We show that pretraining on a carefully selected task-aligned dataset can match or even surpass large-scale joint pretraining while using only 1/24th of the pretraining budget. We introduce the Chemical Similarity Index (CSI), a simple metric for molecular graphs inspired by the Fr\'echet Inception Distance in computer vision, which quantifies the alignment between upstream pretraining datasets and downstream tasks. By selecting the most aligned dataset with minimal CSI distance, we show that models pretrained on a smaller, focused dataset consistently achieve better performance on downstream tasks than those pretrained on massive, mixed datasets such as JMP. This holds even when the mixed dataset includes the upstream dataset most aligned with the downstream task. Counterintuitively, we also find that indiscriminately adding more data can degrade model performance when the additional data is poorly aligned with the target task. Our findings highlight that quality often outperforms quantity in pretraining for atomic property prediction.
arxiv_record.authors: Yasir Ghunaim, Hasan Abed Al Kader Hammoud, Bernard Ghanem
arxiv_record.comments: Published in Transactions on Machine Learning Research (TMLR), 2026

The central claims that aligned dataset selection can outperform mixtures and that misaligned additions can harm performance are retained.

C2.justification: v2 interprets alignment as transferable across backbone types and supervised/denoising objectives, and adds an effective-rank explanation for information loss through pooling. Section 5 changes the ID/OOD distinction from domain-or-label differences to target-property differences. Appendix B documents feature-extractor-dependent QM9 ranking exceptions, while Appendix A softens the earlier blanket assertion that additional epochs cannot compensate for fewer samples on misaligned datasets.

D1.justification: Appendix D newly specifies the classes used for balanced sampling: molecular formulas for ANI-1x/Transition-1x and bulk structures for OC20/OC22, with equal sampling per class. Table 3 adds configuration-specific A100 GPU-day measurements. Existing GemNet batch sizes, learning rates, checkpoint selection, validation-subset size, and code-access information remain essentially unchanged.

E1.justification: v2 adds inorganic-material force prediction on OMat24's rattled-300-subsampled split, extending the energy/force evaluations beyond the earlier molecular targets. It also adds a denoising pretraining task on the existing upstream data. The four upstream datasets and earlier molecular and OOD benchmarks remain.

E2.justification: v2 Table 2 adds budget-matched Joint (Balanced) and Joint (Temperature) comparators to the large GemNet-OC-L experiment; these were absent from v1 Table 3. The original JMP references and small-backbone comparator membership are retained. Changing 'Mixed' to 'Joint' is a rename.

E3.justification: v2 adds a 0.5M-sample point to the budget sweep, evaluates 31M- and 87M-parameter EquiformerV2 configurations, and introduces a paired effective-rank protocol using 5k, 10k, and 15k graphs with standardized node-level and pooled features (Appendix C). The original main budget of 2M samples over five epochs and existing GemNet settings are retained.

E4.justification: v2 adds backbone-type and pretraining-objective analyses, replaces the single alternative JMP feature-extractor check with a multi-checkpoint EquiformerV2 study, and adds effective-rank evidence about pooling. v1's random-sampling CSI plot and JMP-extractor plot are removed. The pooling comparison, class-coverage analysis, and epoch-versus-data experiment are retained or expanded.

E5.justification: Compared with v1's point estimates in Table 1, v2 reports means and standard deviations over three random seeds for the limited-budget rows. Appendix C also introduces a ten-repeat bootstrap procedure reporting mean effective ranks. These are substantial additions to statistical reporting; v1 does not specify a previous seed count from which an increase could be established.

E6.justification: Table 1 replaces earlier scores with multi-seed estimates: ANI-1x changes from 5.4 to 5.2 ± 0.2 on rMD17, 5.13 to 5.39 ± 0.26 on SPICE, and 2.9 to 3.1 ± 0.1 on QM9. New OMat24 results favor OC20 over ANI-1x, with MAEs of 87.4 versus 98.1. Additional joint-pretraining, EquiformerV2, DeNS, and appendix results substantially expand the evidence. The OOD and epoch-versus-data tables retain their numerical results.

M1.justification: v1 trains GemNet-OC models using energy/force supervision. v2 additionally trains EquiformerV2 backbones and introduces a DeNS denoising-pretraining variant using noisy atomic coordinates (Sections 4.4 and 4.6). These substantially expand the model and training-objective variants, while the central CSI-based dataset-selection procedure remains intact.

P1.justification: The paper is retitled around pretraining alignment, with substantial rewrites of related work, experimental explanations, and takeaways. CSI design discussion moves from Section 3.2 into reorganized appendices devoted to feature extractors, representations, and class balancing. Terminology is revised throughout, including 'relevance' toward 'alignment' and 'mixed' toward 'joint' pretraining.

P2.justification: The main text changes from two columns to one column, and figures and tables are extensively reformatted. The budget table becomes a multi-panel curve figure, Figure 1 changes from a grid to a horizontal arrangement, and Table 1 gains an OMat24 column and uncertainty entries. New architecture/objective tables and appendix plots accompany removal or replacement of earlier metric-design displays.

R1.justification: Section 2 adds substantial distribution-similarity positioning, including KL, JS, MMD, Fréchet ChemNet Distance, and GuacaMol. It explicitly distinguishes CSI's 3D cross-domain alignment purpose from earlier chemistry applications of FID. The pretraining discussion also develops distinctions between 2D, equilibrium-focused, and non-equilibrium methods, including DeNS.

T1.justification: The formal optimization equations, computational-budget definition, and Fréchet-distance formulation are substantively unchanged. Appendix C states the standard entropy-based effective-rank formula for an empirical diagnostic; it does not introduce a new theoretical result, proof, or derivation.

improvement.justification: v1's central evidence relied on one trained backbone family and molecular ID tasks that all favored ANI-1x. v2 meaningfully tests dataset selection through OMat24, where OC20 wins, and extends validation to EquiformerV2 and denoising pretraining. Three-seed uncertainty reporting, stronger representation analyses, and discussion of closely related chemical-distance metrics substantially improve credibility and positioning. Some earlier metric ablations disappear, and Appendix A retains errors such as calling 5.4 better than 5.1, but the overall evidential gains are substantial.

A1.justification: Both PDFs describe the same CSI-based pretraining dataset-selection study, despite the changed title and formatting. Their complete main texts, equations, tables, figures, and appendices support reliable comparison.

after.justification: v2 retains original experiments and adds OMat24 evaluation, EquiformerV2 and denoising-pretraining results, and feature-representation analyses.

before.justification: v1 reports original pretraining and fine-tuning experiments in Tables 1–5, alongside CSI, sampling, and representation analyses.

arxiv_record.abstract: Recent advances in long-term time series forecasting have introduced numerous complex supervised prediction models that consistently outperform previously published architectures. However, this rapid progression raises concerns regarding inconsistent benchmarking and reporting practices, which may undermine the reliability of these comparisons. In this study, we first perform a broad, thorough, and reproducible evaluation of the top-performing supervised models on the most popular benchmark and additional baselines representing the most active architecture families. This extensive evaluation assesses eight models on 14 datasets, encompassing $\sim$5,000 trained networks for the hyperparameter (HP) searches. Then, through a comprehensive analysis, we find that slight changes to experimental setups or current evaluation metrics drastically shift the common belief that newly published results are advancing the state of the art. Our findings emphasize the need to shift focus away from pursuing ever-more complex models, towards enhancing benchmarking practices through rigorous and standardized evaluations that enable more substantiated claims, including reproducible HP setups and statistical testing. We offer recommendations for future research.
arxiv_record.authors: Lorenzo Brigato, Rafael Morand, Knut Str{\o}mmen, Maria Panagiotou, Markus Schmidt, and Stavroula Mougiakakou
arxiv_record.title: There are no Champions in Supervised Long-Term Time Series Forecasting

arxiv_record.abstract: Continual learning requires models to integrate new classes or domains over time while preserving previously acquired knowledge. Within this paradigm, foundation models often achieve strong performance, but they still remain subject to the stability-plasticity trade-off, where excessive plasticity leads to forgetting of prior knowledge, and excessive stability constrains the adaptation. This necessitates an effective post-training strategy that introduces minimal yet functional modifications. To address this challenge, we first introduce a new parameter-efficient fine-tuning module 'Learn and Calibrate', or LuCA, designed to acquire task-specific knowledge through an adapter-calibrator couple, enabling well-refined feature representations. Then, for each task, we deploy a sparse LuCA module on top of the last classification token [CLS] just before the classifier, which we refer to as 'Token-level Sparse Calibration and Adaptation', or TOSCA. By leaving the generalization capabilities of the foundation models intact and adapting exclusively via the last token, our approach achieves a harmonious balance between stability and plasticity while reducing both training and inference complexity. We demonstrate that TOSCA yields state-of-the-art performance while introducing ~8 times fewer parameters compared to prior methods.

C2.justification: v2 adds substantive explanations connecting sparsity to reduced feature overlap and explaining why adaptation before calibration improves class geometry. It interprets task-wise and EuroSAT findings as evidence of plasticity and robustness. Appendix A.2 newly discusses lower IN1K average accuracies as an efficiency–adaptability tradeoff; dependence on pretrained-model generalization was already acknowledged in v1.

D1.justification: v2 supplies a code-repository link, explicitly identifies sigmoid calibration, and clarifies classifier optimization in Algorithm 1. Hardware and principal hyperparameters are retained. Conversely, it omits v1's explicit class-shuffling seed and statement that all methods use identical training/testing splits.

E1.justification: v2 adds a dedicated EuroSAT satellite-imagery classification scenario with ten classes, extending evaluation to an explicitly different image domain while retaining the six original benchmarks. Table 3 and Figure 5 report this additional coverage.

E2.justification: Tables 1 and A add RanPAC across all six retained benchmarks and HiDePrompt on CIFAR, CUB and ImageNet-R with both backbones. Both also enter the runtime comparison. RanPAC was cited but not evaluated in v1; HiDePrompt is not evaluated on the other benchmark columns, which contain dashes.

E3.justification: v2 adds per-task accuracy evaluation, module-selection accuracy against ground-truth task identities, cosine-similarity comparisons and feature-separation diagnostics. EuroSAT uses B0 Inc2. Existing backbone choices, training budgets and hyperparameters remain unchanged. The stated VTAB class count changes from 100 to 50, matching v1's plotted range without establishing that experiments were rerun.

E4.justification: v2 adds direct investigations of single-token plasticity, satellite-domain robustness, module decorrelation under different regularization strengths, feature geometry and entropy-based routing reliability (Tables 2, 3 and B; Figures 5–7). The original hyperparameter and component-order ablations remain; LuCA_r becoming TOSCA_r is a rename.

E5.justification: Both versions state five random-seed runs and retain mean-plus-standard-deviation reporting in the main benchmark tables. However, v2 removes v1's explicit class-order seed of 1993. There is no documented increase in repeated runs or addition of confidence intervals or significance tests.

E6.justification: Substantial new results include CUB task-wise average accuracy of 97.6% and EuroSAT task-wise average accuracy of 99.3% for TOSCA, alongside new baseline and diagnostic results. Other shared table entries remain unchanged.

M1.justification: Both versions use an adapter followed by a calibrator, one sparse module per task on the final CLS representation, a frozen backbone, cross-entropy plus l1 regularization, and entropy-based module selection. P2.justification: v2 adds Tables 2, 3 and B and Figures 5–7, expands existing benchmark tables and plots with additional comparators, and revises legends and captions. The LuCA diagram is redrawn, and the document adopts journal typography, headers and wider layouts. These are substantial display changes beyond numerical updates.

R1.justification: v2 adds HiDePrompt, EuroSAT and two sparse/online continual-learning references, and expands discussion of the already-cited RanPAC. arxiv_record.abstract: Implicit Neural Representations (INRs) have been recently garnering increasing interest in various research fields, mainly due to their ability to represent large, complex data in a compact, continuous manner. Past work further showed that numerous popular downstream tasks can be performed directly in the INR parameter-space. Doing so can substantially reduce the computational resources required to process the represented data in their native domain. A major difficulty in using modern machine-learning approaches, is their high susceptibility to adversarial attacks, which have been shown to greatly limit the reliability and applicability of such methods in a wide range of settings. In this work, we perform an in-depth security analysis of the behavior of weight-space classifiers under adversarial attacks. Our study reveals that parameter-space models trained for classification exhibit increased robustness to standard white-box adversarial attacks compared to standard classifiers that operate in the original signal space. This is achieved without the need of any robust training. We source this robust behavior to the phenomenon of gradient-obfuscation promoted during the INR optimization process, and pinpoint the limitations of this robustness under alternative adversarial approaches. To support our claims, we develop a novel suite of adversarial attacks targeting parameter-space classifiers, and furthermore analyze practical considerations of such attacks.
arxiv_record.authors: Tamir Shor, Ethan Fetaya, Chaim Baskin, Alex Bronstein
arxiv_record.title: Adversarial Attacks in Weight-Space Classifiers

C1.justification: V1's abstract and conclusion emphasize inherent adversarial robustness without robust training. V3 reframes the contribution as a security analysis, narrows the abstract's robustness claim to standard white-box attacks, attributes the behavior to gradient obfuscation, and makes vulnerability under alternative attacks an explicit contribution.

C2.justification: V1 already discusses attenuation and vanishing gradients, but v3 interprets the new attack failures as evidence of gradient masking rather than general security. It adds a spectral-bias/low-pass scrubbing hypothesis and explains implicit differentiation's fixed-point versus finite-trajectory mismatch. Applicability limitations are revised, while the conclusion's explicit clean-accuracy tradeoff is dropped.

D1.justification: V3 replaces the promise of future code release with a repository location and an availability statement. It newly documents L2 gradient clipping at 1, damped inverse-Hessian calculations, and classifier depths in the runtime discussion. These are additional disclosures; the PDFs do not establish that the retained experiments changed accordingly.

E1.justification: Both versions evaluate MNIST, Fashion-MNIST and voxelized ModelNet10 classification under the same image and voxel perturbation domains. AutoAttack and BPDA extend testing on existing data without introducing new datasets, populations, modalities or task requirements.

E2.justification: V3 adds AutoAttack to the MNIST/Fashion-MNIST accuracy comparison in Table 1 and evaluates BPDA in Table 2. Table 3 also compares AutoAttack component timings with the proposed attacks. The existing ViT, CNN, autoencoder and voxel-classifier baselines remain.

E3.justification: V3 extends the evaluation design with BPDA's identity approximation for the backward derivative of the INR optimization mapping and sequential AutoAttack testing. Section 4.5 introduces cumulative component-runtime comparisons against 100-step suite attacks. These are new testing procedures; the previously stated training, preprocessing and perturbation-budget settings are retained.

E4.justification: Section 4.4.2 adds a diagnostic BPDA experiment testing whether apparent robustness survives bypassing gradient masking. Section 4.5 adds a detailed AutoAttack efficiency comparison. The existing activation-amplification, attack-bound sensitivity and latent-space analyses remain; moving Figure 6 into the main text does not constitute a new analysis.

E5.justification: V3 specifies five random restarts for the new BPDA evaluation, adding randomized repetition information absent from v1. These are attack restarts, not reported independent training runs or uncertainty estimates. No new confidence intervals or significance tests are introduced, and the existing shaded amplification plots are retained.

E6.justification: The original Table 1 scores and ModelNet10 table values are unchanged. New results include AutoAttack accuracies of 0.44 and 0.05, and BPDA accuracies of 0.076 and 0.159, for MNIST and Fashion-MNIST respectively at a 32/256 bound, plus Table 3 timings. V1 Appendix B.1.1's autoencoder accuracies of 98.8% clean and 11.28% robust are omitted.

M1.justification: The five original attacks—Full PGD, TMO, BOTTOM, ICOP and implicit differentiation—and BVA are retained. Expanded threat-model explanations and newly disclosed implementation details do not establish procedural changes to these methods. AutoAttack and BPDA enter as additional evaluations; the implicit-gradient formula correction is addressed under T1.

P1.justification: V3 retitles the paper and extensively rewrites the abstract, introduction, implicit-differentiation explanation and discussion. It introduces dedicated threat-model and mechanism sections, consolidates the conclusion and limitations, and relocates much of the computational analysis to Appendix C. These constitute substantial narrative and structural revisions.

P2.justification: The main text changes from two columns to one, with widespread figure resizing and relocation. Figure 1 replaces duplicated parameter-space panels with the intended parameter-versus-signal-space comparison. Table 1 gains AutoAttack columns, new BPDA and runtime tables appear, and Figure 6 moves from the appendix into the main text. Figures 2–10 otherwise retain their graphical content.

R1.justification: Related work expands substantially beyond weight-space learning to gradient obfuscation, equilibrium models and adversarial purification. V3 positions the work against Athalye et al., Yang et al., DiffPure and robustness-trained INRs from Luo et al., while adding AutoAttack references and newer neural-functional learning work. This materially changes the security context and novelty positioning.

T1.justification: V3 Section 3.4.5 adds a Taylor-expansion derivation and an explicit Hessian-invertibility assumption. Equation 5 corrects the inverse-Hessian and mixed-derivative multiplication order shown in v1 Equation 3. This is a localized mathematical correction and expansion of the existing implicit-differentiation analysis; Section 4.4 supplies empirical reasoning rather than a new robustness theorem.

improvement.justification: V1's central robustness claim relied on its proposed attack suite. V3 adds AutoAttack and especially BPDA results exposing severe vulnerabilities, then narrows the abstract's claim and explicitly identifies gradient masking. This substantially improves the evidence underlying the paper's central security assessment, supported by the corrected derivation and additional reproducibility information. The discussion still mislabels BPDA as gradient-free despite defining a gradient approximation, and retains some overbroad robustness wording, so the improvement does not resolve every interpretive problem.

A1.justification: Both PDFs describe the same INR classifier attack study despite the changed title and format. Their text, equations, tables, figures and complete appendices support reliable comparison.

after.justification: V3 retains the original empirical results and adds AutoAttack accuracy, BPDA robustness and comparative runtime measurements in Tables 1–3.

before.justification: V1 reports original adversarial classification experiments on MNIST, Fashion-MNIST and ModelNet10, activation and latent-space analyses, and computational measurements in Section 4 and the appendices.

arxiv_record.abstract: Mathematical formulas are a fundamental and widely used component in various scientific fields, serving as a universal language for expressing complex concepts and relationships. While state-of-the-art transformer models excel in processing and understanding natural language, they encounter challenges with mathematical notation, which involves a complex structure and diverse representations. This study focuses on the development of specialized training datasets to enhance the encoding of mathematical content. We introduce Math Mutator (MAMUT), a framework capable of generating equivalent and falsified versions of a given mathematical formula in LaTeX notation, effectively capturing the mathematical variety in notation of the same concept. Based on MAMUT, we have generated four large mathematical datasets containing diverse notation. Experiments show that models trained on these datasets exhibit new SoTA performance on mathematical retrieval tasks. We publish our code, generated datasets, and pretrained mathematical models: https://github.com/aieng-lab/math-mutator.
arxiv_record.authors: Jonathan Drechsel, Anja Reusch, Steffen Herbold
arxiv_record.title: MAMUT: A Novel Framework for Modifying Mathematical Formulas for the Generation of Specialized Datasets for Language Model Training

C1.justification: v1 principally claims a framework and four datasets suitable for mathematical language-model training. v2 adds claims of state-of-the-art mathematical retrieval performance and demonstrated benefits even for previously mathematically pretrained BERT models, alongside pretrained-model releases.

C2.justification: Sections 7–9 and Appendix C add interpretations of complementary pretraining benefits and challenging-negative effects, while acknowledging the advantage of task-related pretraining. Beyond v1's parsing caveats, v2 discusses unsupported notations, LaTeX-only applicability, possible incorrect falsifications and the need for systematic output-error analysis.

D1.justification: Appendix C adds software versions, hyperparameters, eight-A100 hardware, training-time estimates, checkpoint identifiers, and training/evaluation code locations. Appendix B.1 newly specifies SymPy filtering calls. An MT upvote criterion is also newly documented, although Sections 6 and 8.2 inconsistently apply it to answers versus questions; the PDFs do not establish that the existing datasets were regenerated.

E1.justification: Using the retained MF, MT, NMF and MFR datasets, v2 adds actual training on masked-token and formula-pair tasks and evaluation of name-to-formula and formula-to-formula retrieval. v1 reports dataset generation and corpus analysis, with these learning applications only proposed. The source corpora and 71-identity collection remain unchanged.

E2.justification: v1 contains no model-baseline experiment. v2 evaluates BERT, MathBERT from Shen et al. (2021), and MPBERT against MAMUT-pretrained variants in Table 6, with checkpoints identified in Table 16. Table 21 additionally compares MPBERT variants using random or fixed negative examples.

E3.justification: v2 introduces retrieval protocols with 250 positive examples per identity, ten times as many negatives, ten-epoch fine-tuning, validation-F1 model selection, and classification and ranking metrics. It adds MLM-only pretraining controls and an NMF-Split evaluation using 49/11/11 training/validation/test identities with a frozen encoder. These are new experimental designs, not revisions to v1 model experiments.

E4.justification: Beyond the retained NMF generation analysis, Appendix C.4 adds evaluations by falsification count, substitution type, text versus formula input, and mathematical identity. It also tests challenging versus random negatives, changing versus fixed negatives, and generalization across identities excluded from fine-tuning.

E5.justification: v2 newly reports averaging five fine-tuning runs with different seeds and using different identity partitions across the five NMF-Split runs. This adds repeated-run reporting, but no standard deviations, confidence intervals or significance tests.

E6.justification: The original dataset counts and Figure 5 findings are retained, while extensive model results are added. In v2 Table 6, MAMUT-MPBERT-MLM achieves NMF-FT/MFR-FT F1 scores of 87.6/80.6, compared with MPBERT's 79.9/74.0. Table 21 reports NMF-FT F1 of 79.9 with changing challenging negatives, 24.6 with random negatives and 74.4 with fixed challenging negatives. These are newly reported comparisons, not improvements over v1 scores.

arxiv_record.abstract: Transformers have achieved remarkable success across multiple fields, yet their impact on 3D medical image segmentation remains limited with convolutional networks still dominating major benchmarks. In this work, (A) we analyze current Transformer-based segmentation models and identify critical shortcomings, particularly their over-reliance on convolutional blocks. Further, we demonstrate that in some architectures, performance is unaffected by the absence of the Transformer, thereby demonstrating their limited effectiveness. To address these challenges, we move away from hybrid architectures and (B) introduce Transformer-centric segmentation architectures, termed Primus and PrimusV2. Primus leverages high-resolution tokens, combined with advances in positional embeddings and block design, to maximally leverage its Transformer blocks, while PrimusV2 expands on this through an iterative patch embedding. Through these adaptations, Primus surpasses current Transformer-based methods and competes with a default nnU-Net while PrimusV2 exceeds it and is on par with the state-of-the-art CNNs such as ResEnc-L and MedNeXt architectures across nine public datasets. In doing so, we introduce the first competitive Transformer-centric model, making Transformers state-of-the-art in 3D medical image segmentation. The code is available here: https://github.com/MIC-DKFZ/nnUNet/blob/master/documentation/primus.md.

E4.justification: New tokenizer ablations compare four alternatives with and without Transformers, testing the tradeoff between accuracy and Transformer dependence (Table 6). v2 also extends dataset-size analysis to Primus-L, adds qualitative segmentation examples, and investigates memory and inference-time feasibility. M1.justification: v2 introduces PrimusV2 alongside Primus. P1.justification: Substantial portions of the introduction, diagnostic discussion, method description, and conclusions are rewritten. R1.justification: Appendix B's historical review is largely retained. v2 extends positioning to state-space and xLSTM competitors and adds references including UNETR++, DINOv3, V-JEPA, Chameleon, and clinical-timing work. improvement.justification: v2 substantially strengthens the central empirical argument through tokenizer-removal controls and comparisons against stronger, newer baselines (Tables 6–7). arxiv_record.abstract: While advances in large language models (LLMs) have greatly improved the quality of synthetic text data in recent years, synthesizing tabular data has received relatively less attention. We address this disparity with Tabby, a simple but powerful post-training modification to the standard Transformer language model architecture, enabling its use for tabular dataset synthesis. Tabby enables the representation of differences across columns using Gated Mixture-of-Experts, with column-specific sets of parameters. Empirically, Tabby results in data quality near or equal to that of real data. By pairing our novel LLM table training technique, Plain, with Tabby, we observe up to a 44% improvement in quality over previous methods. We also show that Tabby extends beyond tables to more general structured data, reaching parity with real data on a nested JSON dataset as well.
arxiv_record.authors: Sonia Cromp, Satya Sai Srinath Namburi GNVV, Mohammed Alkhudhayri, Catherine Cao, Samuel Guo, Nicholas Roberts, Frederic Sala
arxiv_record.title: Tabby: A Language Model Architecture for Tabular and Structured Data Synthesis

arxiv_record.abstract: Emergent Language (EL) focuses on the emergence of communication among artificial agents. Although symbolic communication channels more closely mirror the discrete nature of human language, learning such protocols remains fundamentally difficult due to the non-differentiability of symbol sampling. Existing approaches typically rely on high-variance gradient estimators such as REINFORCE or on continuous relaxations such as Gumbel-Softmax, both of which suffer from limitations in training stability and scalability. Motivated by cognitive theories that emphasize intrapersonal processes preceding communication, we explore self-play as a substrate for language emergence prior to mutual interaction. We introduce Vector Quantized Emergent Language (VQEL), a novel architecture that incorporates vector quantization into the message generation process. VQEL enables agents to perform self-play using discrete internal representations derived from a learned codebook while preserving end-to-end differentiability. Moreover, the resulting vector-quantized codebook naturally induces a symbolic vocabulary that can be directly transferred and aligned during subsequent mutual play with other agents. Empirical results show that agents pretrained via VQEL self-play achieve more consistent symbol alignment and higher task success when later engaged in mutual interaction. These findings position self-play as a principled and effective mechanism for learning discrete communication protocols, addressing key optimization and representational challenges in emergent language systems.
arxiv_record.authors: Mohammad Mahdi Samiei Paqaleh, Mehdi Jamalkhah, Mahdieh Soleymani Baghshah
arxiv_record.title: VQEL: Enabling Self-Play in Emergent Language Games via Agent-Internal Vector Quantization

C1.justification: The central VQ-based self-play contribution remains. However, v2's conclusion adds substantive claims that self-play itself drives the gains beyond the VQ architecture, that VQEL achieves complete vocabulary use and lower concept-message entropy, and that performance compares favorably with both REINFORCE and Gumbel-Softmax. V1 primarily claimed REINFORCE superiority, controllability and reduced collapse without isolating self-play's contribution.

C2.justification: V1's explanations connecting commitment weight and channel capacity to exploration difficulties are removed. V2 introduces explanations based on sender codebook initialization, attributes the CelebA sender-only shortfall to the frozen pretrained encoder, and identifies receiver-only pretraining as a failure condition in Appendix B. It also qualifies the relationship between communication accuracy and topographic similarity.

D1.justification: V2 newly specifies GRUs, baseline temperature implementation, search ranges and a 100-epoch baseline versus 50+50-epoch VQEL schedule; v1 provided only an illustrative equal-budget example. However, v2 removes v1's EMA decay, stale-code threshold, selected commitment weights, 100-step reward-baseline description and validation-checkpoint selection rule. Reproducibility documentation therefore changes substantially in both directions.

E1.justification: V2 retains Synthetic Objects, dSprites and CelebA and adds ShapeWorld, including evaluation on held-out color-shape combinations. This is a focused extension of synthetic visual and compositional coverage within the retained referential-game task.

E2.justification: V1 evaluates only REINFORCE as an external baseline, although it discusses Gumbel-Softmax. V2 actually evaluates straight-through Gumbel-Softmax with learned temperature alongside REINFORCE throughout Tables 1–5. Adding this central alternative substantially strengthens the comparator set.

E3.justification: V2 adds active vocabulary fraction, topographic similarity and conditional concept entropy to the evaluation. It retains only vocabulary size 10 and message length 4, removing the smaller-channel setting, and changes candidate-count evaluations from the original table settings to curves spanning 2–512 candidates. The stated fixed sampling temperature becomes a searched parameter, and new freezing and no-self-play controls expand the evaluation design.

E4.justification: V2 adds a direct test of self-play versus VQ architecture alone (Table 3), sender update and agent-role comparisons, and cosine-versus-Euclidean analysis (Appendix A). arxiv_record.abstract: Gaussian Splatting has become a popular technique for various 3D Computer Vision tasks, including novel view synthesis, scene reconstruction, and dynamic scene rendering. However, the challenge of natural-looking object insertion, where the object's appearance seamlessly matches the scene, remains unsolved. In this work, we propose a method, dubbed D3DR, for inserting a 3DGS-parametrized object into a 3DGS scene while correcting its lighting, shadows, and other visual artifacts to ensure consistency. We reveal a hidden ability of diffusion models trained on large real-world datasets to implicitly understand correct scene lighting, and leverage it in our pipeline. After inserting the object, we optimize a diffusion-based Delta Denoising Score (DDS)-inspired objective to adjust its 3D Gaussian parameters for proper lighting correction. We introduce a novel diffusion personalization technique that preserves object geometry and texture across diverse lighting conditions, and utilize it to achieve consistent identity matching between original and inserted objects. Finally, we demonstrate the effectiveness of the method by comparing it to existing approaches, achieving 2.0 dB PSNR improvements in relighting quality.
arxiv_record.authors: Vsevolod Skorokhodov, Nikita Durasov, Pascal Fua
arxiv_record.title: Diffusion Models are Secretly Zero-Shot 3DGS Harmonizers

arxiv_record.abstract: While cryptographic algorithms such as the ubiquitous Advanced Encryption Standard (AES) are secure, *physical implementations* of these algorithms in hardware inevitably 'leak' sensitive data such as cryptographic keys. A particularly insidious form of leakage arises from the fact that hardware consumes power and emits radiation in a manner that is statistically associated with the data it processes and the instructions it executes. Supervised deep learning has emerged as a state-of-the-art tool for carrying out *side-channel attacks*, which exploit this leakage by learning to map power/radiation measurements throughout encryption to the sensitive data operated on during that encryption. In this work we develop a principled deep learning framework for determining the relative leakage due to measurements recorded at different points in time, in order to inform *defense* against such attacks. This information is invaluable to cryptographic hardware designers for understanding *why* their hardware leaks and how they can mitigate it (e.g. by indicating the particular sections of code or electronic components which are responsible). Our framework is based on an adversarial game between a classifier trained to estimate the conditional distributions of sensitive data given subsets of measurements, and a budget-constrained noise distribution which probabilistically erases individual measurements to maximize the loss of this classifier. We demonstrate our method's efficacy and ability to overcome limitations of prior work through extensive experimental comparison on 6 publicly-available power/EM trace datasets from AES, ECC and RSA implementations. Our PyTorch code is available at https://github.com/jimgammell/learning_to_localize_leakage.
arxiv_record.authors: Jimmy Gammell, Anand Raghunathan, Abolfazl Hashemi, Kaushik Roy
arxiv_record.comments: Accepted to TMLR (Transactions on Machine Learning Research), 2026. Camera-ready version. 65 pages, 21 figures. Code available at https://github.com/jimgammell/learning_to_localize_leakage
arxiv_record.title: Learning to Localize Leakage of Cryptographic Sensitive Variables

C2.justification: V2 substantially expands v1's scattered qualifications into explicit limitations of oracle assessments, DNN tests, template attacks, computational cost, tuning, synchronization and evaluation on cropped traces (Appendix F). New ablations also support interpretations concerning regularization, smoothing and the mixed usefulness of mask conditioning, materially refining explanations of ALL's gains and applicability.

D1.justification: V1 already supplied code access and hyperparameter tables. V2 adds ALL and evaluation pseudocode, a linked self-contained implementation, detailed comparator adaptations, dataset sizes and DPAv4/OTP processing disclosures, and A6000 runtime measurements. These substantially expand reproducibility information, although Algorithm 4's mask expression conflicts with its stated unocclusion convention.

E1.justification: The six real datasets and four simulated AES perturbation scenarios remain. V1's separate mixed-order and redundant first-order toy experiments are replaced by a scenario combining redundancy with multiple second-order leaking pairs (v2 Section 5.1 and Appendix E.1), changing a limited part of the synthetic coverage.

E2.justification: V2 adds actual evaluations of OccPOI, m-Occlusion and second-order m-Occlusion, including tuned-window variants, alongside the retained statistical and attribution baselines. V1 discussed the related Yap and Schamberger methods but did not benchmark them. These additions substantially expand comparison with closely related approaches.

E3.justification: V2 replaces oGMM agreement with an SNR-based oracle and adds template-attack evaluation using selected features. Training settings and selection procedures also change: supervised ASCAD training increases from 10k steps to 20k/40k, and ALL selection changes from reverse occlusion alone to a composite criterion. These are substantive protocol revisions, not merely additional documentation.

E4.justification: Beyond v1's toy demonstrations and synthetic parameter sweeps, v2 adds controlled ablations of heavy input dropout, cooperative versus adversarial training, mask conditioning and smoothing (Appendix E.3.7). It also adds real-data learning-rate and budget sensitivity analyses and hyperparameter-search distributions. The earlier joint synthetic budget sweeps are replaced by fixed-budget simulations.

E5.justification: Both versions report benchmark means and standard deviations over five seeds. V2 adds median, quartile and whisker summaries of hyperparameter-search outcomes (Figures 20–21) and explicitly describes error-bar-based grouping of best results. These extend statistical reporting without establishing an increase in repeated-run counts.

E6.justification: Numerical results are extensively revised and expanded. For example, ALL's ASCAD-fixed reverse-occlusion score changes from 125.5 ± 0.4 in v1 Table 6 to 126.4 ± 0.2 in v2 Table 13. V2 additionally reports template-attack results, new toy outcomes, ablations and runtimes. Changed methods and settings prevent interpreting these as controlled version-to-version performance gains.

M1.justification: The constrained mutual-information objective and adversarial classifier/mask framework remain. V2 replaces the unbiased REBAR gradient estimator with biased CONCRETE at fixed temperature 1 (Section 4.2 and Appendix D.4), a localized but substantive change to the training procedure.

P1.justification: V2 extensively rewrites the introduction, background, method explanation and experimental narrative, including a clearer attacker/defender explanation. It reorganizes the appendices around notation, background, related work, derivations, experiments and limitations. This exceeds renumbering or expansion solely through new scientific content.

P2.justification: The main text changes from two columns to a single-column layout. V2 redraws the method and causal diagrams, adds notation and architecture displays, introduces a consolidated main results table, and substantially reorganizes experimental graphics. Many of v1's individual baseline and occlusion-curve grids are replaced by summary tables and diagnostic plots.

R1.justification: Sections 3 and 4.3 and Appendix C substantially develop the relationship to prior methods, including their differing objectives and computational costs. Newly cited Egger et al. (2022) informs the white-box oracle and positioning of ALL as complementary to expert analysis. Yap and Schamberger were already cited in v1; their expanded treatment is not a new citation.

improvement.justification: V2 addresses important weaknesses in v1's validation by evaluating closely related methods and testing whether regularization, smoothing or particular ALL components explain the gains. The biased gradient relaxation, acknowledged comparator contamination and Algorithm 4's inconsistent mask convention remain drawbacks, but the expanded controls and transparency provide a substantial net improvement.

A1.justification: Both PDFs describe the same ALL research work. Their text, equations, tables, figures and complete appendices support reliable comparison, including matching retained material across substantial reorganization.

arxiv_record.abstract: In this paper, we study when we might expect the optimization curve induced by gradient descent to be \emph{convex} -- precluding, for example, an initial plateau followed by a sharp decrease, making it difficult to decide when optimization should stop. Although such undesirable behavior can certainly occur when optimizing general functions, might it also occur in the benign and well-studied case of smooth convex functions? As far as we know, this question has not been tackled in previous work. We show, perhaps surprisingly, that the answer crucially depends on the choice of the step size. In particular, for the range of step sizes which are known to result in monotonic convergence to an optimal value, we characterize a regime where the optimization curve will be provably convex, and a regime where the curve can be non-convex. We also extend our results to gradient flow, and to the closely-related but different question of whether the gradient norm decreases monotonically.
arxiv_record.authors: Guy Barzilai, Ohad Shamir and Moslem Zamani
arxiv_record.title: Are Convex Optimization Curves Convex?

arxiv_record.abstract: Simulating the long-term dynamics of multi-scale and multi-physics systems poses a significant challenge in understanding complex phenomena across science and engineering. The complexity arises from the intricate interactions between scales and the interplay of diverse physical processes, which manifest in PDEs through coupled, nonlinear terms that govern the evolution of multiple physical fields across scales. Neural operators have shown potential in short-term prediction of such complex spatio-temporal dynamics; however, achieving stable high-fidelity predictions and providing robust uncertainty quantification over extended time horizons remains an open and unsolved area of research. These limitations often lead to stability degradation with rapid error accumulation, particularly in long-term forecasting of systems characterized by multi-scale behaviors involving dynamics of different orders. To address these challenges, we propose an autoregressive Spatio-temporal Fourier Transformer (StFT), in which each transformer block is designed to learn the system dynamics at a distinct scale through a dual-path architecture that integrates frequency-domain and spatio-temporal representations. By leveraging a structured hierarchy of \ours blocks, the resulting model explicitly captures the underlying dynamics across both macro- and micro- spatial scales. Furthermore, a generative residual correction mechanism is introduced to learn a probabilistic refinement temporally while simultaneously quantifying prediction uncertainties, enhancing both the accuracy and reliability of long-term probabilistic forecasting. Evaluations conducted on three benchmark datasets (plasma, fluid, and atmospheric dynamics) demonstrate the advantages of our approach over state-of-the-art ML methods.

arxiv_record.abstract: Following the introduction of Dynamic Mode Decomposition and its numerous extensions, many neural autoencoder-based implementations of the Koopman operator have recently been proposed. This class of methods appears to be of interest for modeling dynamical systems, either through direct long-term prediction of the evolution of the state or as a powerful embedding for downstream methods. In particular, a recent line of work has developed invertible Koopman autoencoders (IKAEs), which provide an exact reconstruction of the input state thanks to their analytically invertible encoder, based on coupling layer normalizing flow models. We identify that the conservation of the dimension imposed by the normalizing flows is a limitation for the IKAE models, and thus we propose to augment the latent state with a second, non-invertible encoder network. This results in our new model: the Augmented Invertible Koopman AutoEncoder (AIKAE). We demonstrate the relevance of the AIKAE through a series of long-term time series forecasting experiments, on satellite image time series as well as on a benchmark involving predictions based on a large lookback window of observations.

E2.justification: Corresponding comparisons retain the same competing methods: iTransformer, PatchTST, TimesNet and DLinear in Table 1, persistence in the extended table, and the existing comparator sets in the lookback, RevIN and satellite experiments. E3.justification: V1 reports fixed training hyperparameters, with batch sizes 4 for ETT and 32 otherwise. For example, Weather at horizon 720 changes from AIKAE MSE/MAE 0.363/0.354 to 0.317/0.333; this is not a same-setting method improvement. V2 also adds substantial sensitivity and ablation results. External baseline scores, satellite Table 2 and the original RevIN ablation scores are retained.

M1.justification: The main AIKAE architecture, delay embedding and assimilation procedure remain unchanged. Limited methodological additions include an explicitly untested stochastic IKAE variant with a variance encoder in Appendix B and weighted linearity-loss variants evaluated in F.2. These do not replace the principal deterministic method or its default loss.

P1.justification: The seven-section main narrative and much of its wording are retained. V2 makes targeted explanatory and grammatical revisions, moves stochastic-modeling discussion into Appendix B, and reorganizes the expanded appendices. The added scientific material does not amount to a wholesale rewrite of the existing paper.

P2.justification: V2 adds multi-step and delay-embedding schematics, a hyperparameter-sensitivity figure, two forecasting case-study figures, and tables for dataset characteristics, seed variability and satellite ablations. Existing displays are retained or relocated under new numbering. These additions substantially expand the visual explanation and presentation of evidence.

R1.justification: V2 adds references on flow conditioning, linear forecasting and channel independence, including Lee et al., Toner and Darlow, and Han et al., plus activation-function references. The overall research positioning remains stable. Several other reference changes are publication metadata updates for already cited works.

T1.justification: Appendix B extends the existing change-of-variables discussion with Gaussian uncertainty propagation and a stochastic latent formulation. F.2 introduces the weighted linearity objective in Equation 23, and Section 3.1 adds a nullspace condition to the augmentation discussion. improvement.justification: V2 substantially improves reproducibility through Appendices C–D and strengthens evidence for the augmentation mechanism through capacity and loss ablations, sensitivity studies and five-seed uncertainty reporting. arxiv_record.abstract: Building trust in reinforcement learning (RL) agents requires understanding why they make certain decisions, especially in high-stakes applications like robotics, healthcare, and finance. Existing explainability methods often focus on single states or entire trajectories, either providing only local, step-wise insights or attributing decisions to coarse, episodelevel summaries. Both approaches miss the recurring strategies and temporally extended patterns that actually drive agent behavior across multiple decisions. We address this gap by proposing a fully offline, reward-free framework for behavior discovery and segmentation, enabling the attribution of actions to meaningful and interpretable behavior segments that capture recurring patterns appearing across multiple trajectories. Our method identifies coherent behavior clusters from state-action sequences and attributes individual actions to these clusters for fine-grained, behavior-centric explanations. Evaluations on four diverse offline RL environments show that our approach discovers meaningful behaviors and outperforms trajectory-level baselines in fidelity, human preference, and cluster coherence. Our code is publicly available.
arxiv_record.authors: Rishav Rishav, Somjit Nath, Vincent Michalski, Samira Ebrahimi Kahou
arxiv_record.title: Behaviour Discovery and Attribution for Explainable Reinforcement Learning

It also distinguishes geometric clustering quality from human interpretability and expands limitations concerning hand-crafted similarity measures. The earlier noisy-transition and ambiguous-cluster limitations remain.

D1.justification: v2 Appendix B adds batch sizes, A100 hardware, explicit decay schedules, sequence padding/truncation, three-layer MLP/CNN behavior-cloning architectures, neighboring-label smoothing, and per-cluster training sample counts. E1.justification: v2 retains HalfCheetah, Seaquest, and MiniGridTwoGoalsLava while adding pen-expert-v1, extending coverage to dexterous manipulation. E2.justification: Deshmukh et al. (2024), discussed but not experimentally compared in v1, becomes an evaluated comparator in v2 Tables 3–5. v2 also adds random-segment and random-cluster controls, raw state-action clustering, and direct k-means on learned embeddings as evaluated alternatives.

E3.justification: v2 introduces human-study protocols with 15 participants, description-similarity and preference metrics, structural clustering metrics, and fidelity evaluation over 200 actions from 20 episodes. arxiv_record.abstract: The robustness of algorithms against covariate shifts is a fundamental problem with critical implications for the deployment of machine learning algorithms in the real world. Current evaluation methods predominantly measure robustness through the lens of standard generalization, relying on task performance measures like accuracy. This approach lacks a theoretical justification and underscores the need for a principled foundation of robustness assessment under distribution shifts. In this work, we set the desiderata for a robustness measure, and we propose a novel principled framework for the robustness assessment problem that directly follows the Posterior Agreement (PA) theory of model validation. Specifically, we extend the PA framework to the covariate shift setting and propose a measure for robustness evaluation. We assess the soundness of our measure in controlled environments and through an empirical robustness analysis in two different covariate shift scenarios: adversarial learning and domain generalization. We illustrate the suitability of PA by evaluating several models under different nature and magnitudes of shift, and proportion of affected observations. The results show that PA offers a reliable analysis of the vulnerabilities in learning algorithms across different shift conditions and provides higher discriminability than accuracy-based measures, while requiring no supervision.

arxiv_record.abstract: Modern reinforcement learning (RL) systems have demonstrated remarkable capabilities in complex environments, such as video games. However, they still fall short of achieving human-like sample efficiency and adaptability when learning new domains. Theory-based reinforcement learning (TBRL) is an algorithmic framework specifically designed to address this gap. Modeled on cognitive theories, TBRL leverages structured, causal world models - "theories" - as forward simulators for use in planning, generalization and exploration. Although current TBRL systems provide compelling explanations of how humans learn to play video games, they face several technical limitations: their theory languages are restrictive, and their planning algorithms are not scalable. To address these challenges, we introduce TheoryCoder, an instantiation of TBRL that exploits hierarchical representations of theories and efficient program synthesis methods for more powerful learning and planning. TheoryCoder equips agents with general-purpose abstractions (e.g., "move to"), which are then grounded in a particular environment by learning a low-level transition model (a Python program synthesized from observations by a large language model). A bilevel planning algorithm can exploit this hierarchical structure to solve large domains. We demonstrate that this approach can be successfully applied to diverse and challenging grid-world games, where approaches based on directly synthesizing a policy perform poorly. Ablation studies demonstrate the benefits of using hierarchical abstractions.

arxiv_record.abstract: Image classification models trained on clean data often degrade sharply when exposed to corrupted test or deployment data, such as images with impulse noise, Gaussian noise, or environmental noise. This degradation reduces overall performance and disproportionately affects demographic subgroups, raising algorithmic bias concerns. Although robust learning algorithms such as Sharpness-Aware Minimization improve overall robustness and generalization, they do not address biased performance degradation across demographic subgroups. Existing fairness-aware machine learning methods reduce performance disparities but struggle to maintain robust and equitable accuracy across demographic subgroups under data corruption. This limitation reveals an inherent tension between robustness and fairness under corrupted data. To address these challenges, we introduce a metric to assess performance degradation across subgroups under data corruption. We propose FairSAM, a framework that integrates Fairness-oriented strategies into SAM to equalize performance across demographic groups under corrupted conditions. Experiments on multiple real-world datasets and prediction tasks show that FairSAM balances robustness and fairness in corrupted image classification. The framework yields a structured solution for fair and robust image classification in the presence of data corruption.

arxiv_record.abstract: While text-to-image generative models can synthesize diverse and faithful content, subject variation across multiple generations limits their application to long-form content generation. Existing approaches require time-consuming fine-tuning, reference images for all subjects, or access to previously generated content. We introduce Contrastive Concept Instantiation (CoCoIns), a framework that effectively synthesizes consistent subjects across multiple independent generations. The framework consists of a generative model and a mapping network that transforms input latent codes into pseudo-words associated with specific concept instances. Users can generate consistent subjects by reusing the same latent codes. To construct such associations, we propose a contrastive learning approach that trains the network to distinguish between different combinations of prompts and latent codes. Extensive evaluations on human faces with a single subject show that CoCoIns performs comparably to existing methods while maintaining greater flexibility. We also demonstrate the potential for extending CoCoIns to multiple subjects and other object categories.

arxiv_record.abstract: Finding deletion-correcting codes of maximum size has been an open problem for over 70 years, even for a single deletion. We adapt FunSearch, a large language model (LLM)-guided evolutionary search, to discover functions that construct deletion-correcting codes at short code lengths. For a single deletion, our search finds a function that we prove constructs the conjectured-optimal Varshamov-Tenengolts code. For multiple deletions and quaternary edit codes, the discovered functions improve on prior explicit, search-based, and neural constructions but remain empirical heuristics without new theoretical insights. We study design choices for LLM-guided evolutionary search and find that, for our problem, compute is better allocated to sampling more functions than to longer reasoning traces per function, and that co-evolving natural language descriptions with code hurts search quality. We propose deduplicating logically identical functions during evolution, which we find critical for search diversity. Our results demonstrate the potential of LLM-guided evolutionary search for information theory and code design and represent the first application of such methods for constructing error-correcting codes. However, in our current formulation, evaluating a function scales exponentially with code length, limiting the approach to short codes.
arxiv_record.authors: Franziska Weindel and Reinhard Heckel
arxiv_record.title: LLM-Guided Search for Deletion-Correcting Codes

C1.justification: V1 headlines new best-known two-deletion sizes at lengths 12, 13 and 16 and previously unknown optimal constructions. V2 emphasizes a proof of concept and VT rediscovery, acknowledges known non-uniqueness of short optimal codes, and qualifies multiple-deletion superiority against stronger graph solvers. Compute allocation, harmful summary-code co-evolution, deduplication's importance and quaternary-code construction become central contributions.

C2.justification: V2 distinguishes VT complements from constructions outside every VT class and discusses rediscovery versus memorization. It adds explanations for reasoning and co-evolution failures, interprets joint optimization as regularization, and analyzes the contributions of discovered heuristics. The retained exponential-scaling limitation is developed into specific encoder requirements, limited theoretical understanding and potential use as short inner codes.

D1.justification: V2 adds model-specific hyperparameters, computational-cost tables, batching and prefetch settings, immutable-graph documentation and graph statistics. Appendix A revises evaluator allocation from two CPU cores to one and timeout from five minutes to 30 seconds. The code-access statement changes from a promised FunDCC release to a stated DistributedFunSearch release. Conversely, v1's extensive verbatim prompt appendix is removed.

E1.justification: V1 evaluates binary deletion-correcting codes. V2 adds quaternary single-edit-correcting codes covering insertions, deletions and substitutions, searching lengths 6–9 and reporting results through length 11. Binary two- and three-deletion evaluation extends through length 18. Three-deletion evaluation and single-deletion checks through length 25 already existed in v1.

E2.justification: V2 adds evaluated OnlineMIS, ReduMIS and Gurobi comparisons, explicit Helberg–Ferreira construction results, and DoDo-Code for quaternary codes. V1 principally compares against VT sizes, Landjev–Haralambiev search results, a trivial lexicographic baseline and cited minimum-degree results. Random greedy existed in v1 Appendix J but now participates in the principal benchmark tables.

E3.justification: Main single-deletion searches change from a 400K-function limit with early stopping and 20K additional functions to 500K iterations. V2 introduces $120 inference-budget comparisons, a primary top-50 mean normalized-gap metric, and held-out evaluation of a function selected on search instances instead of per-length maxima across functions. Qwen3/Gemma 4 configurations and direct three-deletion optimization add further protocols; three-deletion testing itself is retained.

E4.justification: V2 adds extensive reasoning-on/off and code/summary/reflection/co-evolution ablations across Qwen3 and Gemma 4, plus individual removal of six heuristics from a discovered two-deletion function (Appendix F). Existing deduplication, graph-input, scoring and prompt analyses are revised. The GPT-4o mini comparison and random-greedy code-size distribution analysis from v1 are removed.

E5.justification: V1 already includes three repeated default runs, variability across islands and min-max ranges across discovered functions. V2 makes three seeded runs standard and reports across-run mean/min-max bands, including pooled 12-run and 9-run reasoning comparisons. Appendix A adds throughput mean ± SD over four measurement windows and run-level variability in computational costs.

E6.justification: Results are substantially replaced and expanded. For two deletions at length 16, v1 Table 4 reports a maximum of 204 across joint-search functions; v2 Table 2 reports 200 for its selected joint function and 215 for both KaMIS solvers. Changed selection and search conditions prevent interpreting 204 versus 200 as a same-setting decline. New results include quaternary size 40,604 versus DoDo-Code's 36,368 at length 11, and findings against reasoning and summary-code co-evolution.

M1.justification: The core greedy construction, island-based evolution, output-hash deduplication and reset scheme remain. V2 adds per-instance normalized-gap feedback to few-shot docstrings and implements summary, reflection and joint summary-code evolution variants with reasoning enabled or disabled (Section 5.2). These are procedural adaptations within the existing framework.

P1.justification: The abstract, introduction and experimental narrative are extensively rewritten. Method steps become numbered subsections, experiments are reorganized around correction tasks and ablations, Limitations becomes Scalability, and a Conclusion is added. Several separate appendices are consolidated, with much of the earlier hyperparameter evidence retained in condensed prose.

P2.justification: The presentation is substantially redesigned: solver-oriented comparison tables, cost-versus-gap plots with uncertainty bands, and computational-cost, hyperparameter and graph-statistics tables replace much of the earlier display structure. Overlap histograms, numerous prompt listings and several tuning plots disappear. The existing VT-equivalent function listing moves from v1 Figure 6 to v2 Figure 3.

R1.justification: V2 substantially repositions the work around scientific program discovery and inference-compute allocation. It adds discussion and citations concerning AlphaEvolve, ShinkaEvolve, OpenEvolve/CodeEvolve, classical graph solvers, DoDo-Code and low-redundancy deletion constructions. It also explicitly contrasts its distributed implementation with existing systems and develops the connection to inner codes, while pruning much of v1's broader application survey.

T1.justification: VT equivalence was already argued in v1 Appendix H. V2 Appendix E substantially rewrites the proof into separate priority and lexicographic-order claims: a conflicting VT word can have equal or one-higher priority, replacing v1's equal-priority argument. This changes mathematical reasoning, not merely presentation. V2 Appendix C also adds verification costs to the retained exhaustive-search complexity analysis.

improvement.justification: V2 substantially strengthens empirical credibility. Its graph-solver comparisons expose limitations missing from v1's record-size claims, while selected-function held-out evaluation and repeated-run ablations provide stronger support for generalization and search-design conclusions. Appendix F also supplies direct evidence about discovered mechanisms. Removing detailed prompt listings weakens self-contained reproducibility, but the improved comparisons, uncertainty reporting and more carefully qualified claims outweigh that loss.

A1.justification: Both PDFs describe the same work by Weindel and Heckel. All 40 pages of v1 and 31 pages of v2, including their appendices, provide readable text, equations, figures and tables supporting a reliable comparison.

after.justification: V2 reports original code-construction experiments, graph-solver comparisons, reasoning and prompting ablations, component analyses and computational measurements.

before.justification: V1 reports original evolutionary-search experiments, constructed code sizes, prompt and hyperparameter comparisons, throughput measurements and repeated-run results.

arxiv_record.abstract: We present a method to dynamically deform 3D garments, in the form of a 3D polygon mesh, based on body shape, motion, and physical cloth material properties. Considering physical cloth properties allows to learn a physically grounded model, with the advantage of being more accurate in terms of physically inspired metrics such as strain or curvature. Existing work studies pose-dependent garment modeling to generate garment deformations from example data, and possibly data-driven dynamic cloth simulation to generate realistic garments in motion. We propose D-Garment, a learning-based approach trained on new data generated with a physics-based simulator. Compared to prior work, our 3D generative model learns garment deformations conditioned by physical material properties, which allows to model loose cloth geometry, especially for large deformations and dynamic wrinkles driven by body motion. Furthermore, the model can be efficiently fitted to observations captured using vision sensors such as 3D point clouds. We leverage the capability of diffusion models to learn flexible and powerful generative priors by modeling the 3D garment in a 2D parameter space independently from the mesh resolution. This representation allows to learn a template-specific latent diffusion model. This allows to condition global and local geometry with body and cloth material information. We quantitatively and qualitatively evaluate D-Garment on both simulations and data captured with a multi-view acquisition platform. Compared to recent baselines, our method is more realistic and accurate in terms of shape similarity and physical validity metrics. Code and data are available for research purposes at https://dumoulina.github.io/d-garment/
