It acknowledges that SPIDER's vector library performs best in that comparison. Conversely, v1 Appendix D.2's explanation of declining Darcy GP success through overfitting is removed.

D1.justification: v2 specifies the previously unspecified Boussinesq domain length and filtering cutoff, supplies Darcy initialization, boundary conditions and integration settings, and adds reaction-diffusion initialization and solver details. It also documents new invariant libraries and 3D simulation settings. These disclosures substantially expand reproducibility information, although v1's CPU and runtime statement disappears, and the newly stated zero-flux Darcy boundaries conflict with the claimed steady state under positive constant forcing.

E1.justification: Beyond the retained three systems, v2 evaluates a scalar 3D reaction-diffusion equation with SO(3) symmetry (Appendix C.4) and turbulent channel flow with velocity and pressure fields from the Johns Hopkins Turbulence Database (Appendix D.2). These materially extend spatial dimensionality, equation types, and physical settings.

E2.justification: v2 adds the compact-library PySINDy** comparator to the existing Boussinesq and reaction-diffusion comparisons (Table 4), D-CIPHER on Darcy flow (Table 6), and scalar- and vector-library SPIDER comparisons on channel flow (Table 10). The SPIDER results are reused from the cited work, not reported as new baseline runs. The original comparators remain.

E3.justification: The noisy-data protocol changes from comparing K=100 versus K=1000 test functions to default versus auto-tuned WSINDy configurations involving function counts, support widths, and polynomial degrees. New protocols include a 32-cubed 3D simulation with 1% noise and a temporal training/test split, plus a six-threshold filtering sweep. Newly specified settings for retained simulations are additional disclosure, not evidence that those experiments changed.

E4.justification: v2 adds auto-tuned WSINDy tests under imperfect symmetry (Appendix C.3, Figure 7) and a Boussinesq filtering-threshold sensitivity study measuring retained samples, success, and error (Appendix E.2, Table 11). Appendix D.2 also examines spurious channel-flow terms. The GP iteration-budget analysis already existed in v1; its relocation is not a new experiment.

E5.justification: v1 reports success probabilities and median prediction errors over 100 runs without dispersion intervals. v2 adds 25th–75th percentile ranges for the existing errors in Table 3 and uses that practice in new experiments. These are interquartile ranges, despite being called confidence intervals; the stated repeat count remains 100.

E6.justification: Table 1 revises PySR's Darcy prediction error from 0.187 to 0.114 and SI's Boussinesq complexity from 13 to 15. Substantial new results include 3D SINDy success probabilities of 0.51 versus 1.00 for SI, D-CIPHER and channel-flow equations, and filtering success ranging from 0.36 to 1.00. Noisy-data curves also change under revised parameter-selection settings, so they are not same-setting performance gains.

M1.justification: Appendix C.5 adds a concrete D-CIPHER adaptation: invariant differential operators construct its derivative dictionary, while fundamental invariants constrain its learned right-hand side. P1.justification: The main-text and appendix organization is substantially reworked: related work moves into Section 2, Sparse PCA explanations and GP-budget discussion move into the main narrative, and broader impacts move before the references. The appendices are reorganized around expanded experiments and a dedicated comparison section. Much original mathematical prose remains, but the explanatory structure changes considerably.

P2.justification: v2 adopts a different journal layout and adds a prolongation illustration, an auto-tuned WSINDy figure, and tables for uncertainty ranges, 3D results, D-CIPHER, channel flow, and filtering sensitivity. Existing tables gain comparator rows. The GP-budget plot moves from v1 Figure 5 to v2 Figure 3; several other figures are retained with renumbering.

R1.justification: Section 2 adds substantial coverage of neural operators, surrogate models, and coarse-grained dynamics. New Appendix D positions the framework against EquivSINDy, symmetry regularization, and SPIDER, explaining restricted equivalence and differences in symmetry and algorithm scope. improvement.justification: v2 substantially strengthens support for the framework's generality through higher-dimensional experiments and broader comparisons. after.justification: v2 retains these original experiments and adds results on 3D reaction-diffusion, channel flow, D-CIPHER integration, and parameter sensitivity. Its SPIDER comparison numbers are explicitly attributed to prior work.

before.justification: v1 reports original equation-discovery experiments on Boussinesq, Darcy flow, and reaction-diffusion data, including repeated trials, prediction errors, and noise and symmetry-breaking studies.

arxiv_record.abstract: Pre-trained vision-language models, such as contrastive language-image pre-training (CLIP), have demonstrated a remarkable generalizability, enabling a wide range of applications, including zero-shot classification. However, vision-language models still struggle to handle distribution shifts, where input samples have large gaps from training ones. We found that CLIP is especially vulnerable to image corruption, a type of realistic distribution shift caused by sensor conditions such as weather, light, or noise. Collecting a new dataset from a test distribution for fine-tuning is highly costly since image corruption occurs unexpectedly and has a wide variety of types. Thus, we investigate test-time adaptation (TTA) of zero-shot classification, which enables on-the-fly adaptation to the test distribution with unlabeled test data. Existing TTA methods for CLIP mainly focus on modifying image and text embeddings or predictions to address distribution shifts. Although these methods can adapt to domain shifts, such as out-of-distribution or different renditions in input images, they fail to adapt to distribution shifts beyond domain shifts, e.g., image corruption. We found that uniformity of image embeddings, which is related to the amount of information, is a key factor that differentiates domain shifts and other distribution shifts. To enable adaptation to image corruption, we propose a novel method called uniformity-aware information-balanced TTA (UnInfo). To address distribution shifts, we introduce uniformity-aware confidence maximization, information-aware loss balancing, and knowledge distillation from the exponential moving average (EMA) teacher. Through experiments, we demonstrate that our UnInfo improves accuracy under image corruption by retaining information in terms of uniformity. The code is available at https://github.com/kzkadc/uninfo.

snapshot_arxiv_record.abstract: Pre-trained vision-language models, such as contrastive language-image pre-training (CLIP), have demonstrated a remarkable generalizability, enabling a wide range of applications, including zero-shot classification. Although these methods can adapt to domain shifts, such as out-of-distribution or different renditions in input images, they fail to adapt to distribution shifts beyond domain shifts, e.g., image corruption. To enable adaptation to image corruption, we propose a novel method called uniformity-aware information-balanced TTA (UnInfo). To address distribution shifts, we introduce uniformity-aware confidence maximization, information-aware loss balancing, and knowledge distillation from the exponential moving average (EMA) teacher. Through experiments, we demonstrate that our UnInfo improves accuracy under image corruption by retaining information in terms of uniformity. arxiv_record.abstract: We present a neural framework for learning conditional optimal transport (OT) maps between probability distributions. Our approach introduces a conditioning mechanism capable of processing both categorical and continuous conditioning variables simultaneously. At the core of our method lies a hypernetwork that generates transport layer parameters based on these inputs, creating adaptive mappings that outperform simpler conditioning methods. Comprehensive ablation studies demonstrate the superior performance of our method over baseline configurations. Furthermore, we showcase an application to global sensitivity analysis, offering high performance in computing OT-based sensitivity indices. This work advances the state-of-the-art in conditional optimal transport, enabling broader application of optimal transport principles to complex, high-dimensional domains such as generative modeling and black-box model explainability.

arxiv_record.abstract: In this work, we evaluate the potential of Large Language Models (LLMs) in building Bayesian Networks (BNs) by approximating domain expert priors. LLMs have demonstrated potential as factual knowledge bases; however, their capability to generate probabilistic knowledge about real-world events remains understudied. We explore utilizing the probabilistic knowledge inherent in LLMs to derive probability estimates for statements regarding events and their relationships within a BN. Using LLMs in this context allows for the parameterization of BNs, enabling probabilistic modeling within specific domains. Our experiments on eighty publicly available Bayesian Networks, from healthcare to finance, demonstrate that querying LLMs about the conditional probabilities of events provides meaningful results when compared to baselines, including random and uniform distributions, as well as approaches based on next-token generation probabilities. We explore how these LLM-derived distributions can serve as expert priors to refine distributions extracted from data, especially when data is scarce. Overall, this work introduces a promising strategy for automatically constructing Bayesian Networks by combining probabilistic knowledge extracted from LLMs with real-world data. Additionally, we establish the first comprehensive baseline for assessing LLM performance in extracting probabilistic knowledge.

arxiv_record.abstract: Prompt tuning has become a key mechanism for adapting pre-trained Graph Neural Networks (GNNs) to new downstream tasks. However, existing approaches are predominantly supervised, relying on labeled data to optimize the prompting parameters and typically fine-tuning a task-specific prediction head -- practices that undermine the promise of parameter-efficient adaptation. We propose Unsupervised Graph Prompting Problem (UGPP), a challenging new setting where the pre-trained GNN is kept entirely frozen, labels on the target domain are unavailable, the source data is inaccessible, and the target distribution exhibits covariate shift. To address this, we propose UGPrompt, the first fully unsupervised GNN prompting framework. UGPrompt leverages consistency regularization and pseudo-labeling to train a prompting function, complemented with diversity and domain regularization to mitigate class imbalance and distribution mismatch. Our extensive experiments demonstrate that UGPrompt consistently outperforms state-of-the-art supervised prompting methods with access to labeled data, demonstrating the viability of unsupervised prompting as a practical adaptation paradigm for GNNs.
arxiv_record.authors: Peyman Baghershahi, Sourav Medya
arxiv_record.title: Freeze, Prompt, and Adapt: A Framework for Source-free Unsupervised GNN Prompting

snapshot_arxiv_record.abstract: Prompt tuning has become a key mechanism for adapting pre-trained Graph Neural Networks (GNNs) to new downstream tasks. However, existing approaches are predominantly supervised, relying on labeled data to optimize the prompting parameters and typically fine-tuning a task-specific prediction head -- practices that undermine the promise of parameter-efficient adaptation. We propose Unsupervised Graph Prompting Problem (UGPP), a challenging new setting where the pre-trained GNN is kept entirely frozen, labels on the target domain are unavailable, the source data is inaccessible, and the target distribution exhibits covariate shift. To address this, we propose UGPrompt, the first fully unsupervised GNN prompting framework. UGPrompt leverages consistency regularization and pseudo-labeling to train a prompting function, complemented with diversity and domain regularization to mitigate class imbalance and distribution mismatch. Our extensive experiments demonstrate that UGPrompt consistently outperforms state-of-the-art supervised prompting methods with access to labeled data, demonstrating the viability of unsupervised prompting as a practical adaptation paradigm for GNNs.

C1.justification: The central UGPP formulation and fully unsupervised frozen-GNN prompting contributions remain. v2's introduction strengthens the comparative claim from outperforming baselines 'in most cases' to consistently outperforming methods with full label access. Its conclusion also explicitly qualifies applicability to a shared source/target label space.

C2.justification: v2 explicitly interprets adversarial regularization as target-side stabilization, with source compatibility supplied indirectly by the frozen model and confidence filtering. It adds substantive discussion of confirmation bias, calibration, access to unlabeled data, computational tradeoffs, and the distinction from LLM reasoning. The new limitations paragraph explains why a frozen head cannot generally accommodate new target classes.

D1.justification: v2 adds measured training and inference times with evaluated node counts in Table 21 and clarifies validation-based disabling of ineffective regularizers. The PyTorch implementation, RTX 3090 hardware, principal hyperparameter grids, and code-access statement are retained. These are limited additions to technical documentation.

E1.justification: v2 adds BBBP and BACE molecular graph datasets and Cornell, Texas, and Wisconsin node datasets while retaining the original coverage. It also adds cross-dataset transfer, a stress test with reindexed target categories, and evaluation without distribution shift (Section 4.5 and Appendix A.6.3), substantially broadening the tested populations and scenarios.

E2.justification: Beyond the retained comparators, v2 evaluates DAGPrompt, PRONOG, and GCOPE in Tables 9–10 and SOGA and GraphCTA in Table 14. The SFDA comparators are explicitly adapted to freeze their encoders and train their prediction heads; these are not evaluations of unrestricted full-model adaptation.

E3.justification: v2 introduces sorted source/target partitions with graded shift severity, category reindexing with a three-output frozen head, GraphGPS and GATv2 backbones, and an additional comparison allowing supervised baselines to fine-tune their decoders. New diagnostics measure MMD, pseudo-label accuracy, ECE, and runtime. The original main-experiment splits and tuning grids are retained.

E4.justification: Beyond the retained ablations and embedding analysis, v2 adds graded-shift sensitivity, cross-dataset and category-transfer stress tests, source-performance retention, no-shift controls, computational-cost analysis, MMD diagnostics, and confidence-threshold/calibration analysis. These test robustness and mechanism questions largely unexamined in v1.

E5.justification: Both versions specify 10 dataset seeds and five model initializations per seed, totaling 50 runs, and mix results with ± reporting and point estimates. No new confidence intervals, significance tests, or uncertainty-estimation procedures are specified. The added calibration study evaluates predictive reliability rather than changing sampling-uncertainty reporting.

E6.justification: v2 adds substantial results for new datasets, comparators, transfer settings, runtime, and reliability diagnostics; for example, Table 1 newly reports UGPrompt's GCN BACE F1 as 64.6±1.9. Most original scores remain. One retained entry changes: GraphPrompt's 50%-label CiteSeer clustering-shift IMP moves from +1.6 in v1 Table 7 to -1.6 in v2 Table 12 despite unchanged F1 values.

M1.justification: The core unsupervised architecture and three losses remain unchanged. The few-shot pseudo-label loss changes from summing over the full batch B in v1 Equation 8 to unlabeled samples Su in v2 Section 4.4. Algorithm 2's body also switches from returning scores to argmax labels, although its output header still says scores. The PDFs do not establish corresponding implementation changes or reruns.

P1.justification: The title, abstract, and introduction are substantially rewritten around source-free, parameter-efficient adaptation. Related work moves from v1 Section 2 to v2 Appendix A.1, the experimental and appendix organization expands, and terminology systematically distinguishes 'source-trained' from general 'pre-trained' models. These changes substantially revise the narrative and structure.

P2.justification: Tables 1–2 expand with new dataset columns, Figure 2 is redrawn with logarithmic axes, revised legends, and additional datasets, and numerous new comparisons and diagnostics receive dedicated tables. Journal formatting changes typography, margins, headers, and table styling. The original framework, embedding, and higher-label-budget figures are largely retained.

R1.justification: v1 distinguishes UGPP from source-free adaptation mainly in an appendix. v2 explicitly positions it as a restrictive prompting instance within SFDA in the introduction and problem formulation. It substantially expands engagement with recent graph prompting, graph SFDA, and PEFT through DAGPrompt, PRONOG, GCOPE, SOGA, GraphCTA, and LoRA, beyond merely relocating related work.

T1.justification: The few-shot loss definition changes its summation domain from B to Su and its confidence comparison from strict to inclusive (v1 Equation 8; v2 Section 4.4). The formal UGPP assumptions, core unsupervised objectives, and complexity bound otherwise remain equivalent. No new theorem or proof is added.

improvement.justification: v2 substantially strengthens assessment of the central adaptation claim: comparisons with decoder-finetuned prompting and adapted SFDA methods address v1's restricted comparison regime, while MMD and calibration diagnostics test previously mostly intuitive mechanism arguments. Explicit label-space limitations improve applicability guidance. These gains outweigh remaining weaknesses: superiority language exceeds the new evidence—DAGPrompt leads on five of seven datasets in Table 10—and v2 introduces an inconsistent IMP sign in Table 12.

A1.justification: Both PDFs describe the same UGPP problem and UGPrompt framework despite the changed title. Their complete main texts, equations, tables, figures, and appendices are readable and support reliable comparison.

after.justification: v2 retains those original results and adds benchmark comparisons, transfer experiments, runtime measurements, and pseudo-label reliability diagnostics.

before.justification: v1 reports original graph and node classification experiments, distribution-shift evaluations, ablations, and embedding analyses in the main text and appendix.

arxiv_record.abstract: Diffusion probabilistic models have become a cornerstone of modern generative AI, yet the mechanisms underlying their generalization remain poorly understood. In fact, if these models were perfectly minimizing their training loss, they would just generate data belonging to their training set, i.e., memorize, as empirically found in the overparameterized regime. We revisit this view by showing that, in highly overparameterized diffusion models, generalization in natural data domains is progressively achieved during training before the onset of memorization. Our results, ranging from image to language diffusion models, systematically support the empirical law that memorization time is proportional to the dataset size. Generalization vs. memorization is then best understood as a competition between time scales. We show that this phenomenology is recovered in diffusion models learning a simple probabilistic context-free grammar with random rules, where generalization corresponds to the hierarchical acquisition of deeper grammar rules as training time grows, and the generalization cost of early stopping can be characterized. We summarize these results in a phase diagram. Overall, our results support that a principled early-stopping criterion - scaling with dataset size - can effectively optimize generalization while avoiding memorization, with direct implications for hyperparameter transfer and privacy-sensitive applications.
arxiv_record.authors: Alessandro Favero, Antonio Sclocchi, Matthieu Wyart

C1.justification: The introduction adds a theoretical contribution: explaining dataset-size scaling for kernel methods at fixed, low diffusion noise. The abstract and central claims about generalization before memorization, early stopping and the hierarchical phase diagram retain their previous scope.

C2.justification: Section 3.3 adds a spectral interpretation of memorization time, interprets agreement under feature learning as extending beyond fixed kernels, and links batch-size independence to optimization steps rather than repeated exposures. Section 5 distinguishes diffusion memorization from noisy supervised regression. The conclusion removes v1's explicit limitation concerning explanation of the law for deep, time-dependent diffusion architectures.

D1.justification: Appendix E documents the added experiment's ReLU activation, single hidden layer, width 8192, data dimension, initialization regimes and optimization conditions. Existing Appendix A hyperparameters, hardware information and code-access links are retained.

E1.justification: Appendix E adds Gaussian-distributed vectors in 64 dimensions for empirical-score fitting at fixed diffusion noise. This is a limited synthetic extension; the existing image, language and hierarchical-grammar coverage is retained.

E2.justification: Comparator membership in the existing experiments is unchanged. The new NTK and feature-learning initializations are controlled conditions in the scaling analysis; the cited random-feature results are theoretical comparisons, not newly evaluated benchmark baselines.

E3.justification: Appendix E introduces a distinct controlled evaluation protocol: fixed-noise score fitting with a one-hidden-layer network, NTK versus mean-field initialization, noise and dataset-size sweeps, and full-batch versus stochastic gradient descent. Figures 14–16 cover P=128–2048 and batch sizes B=8–128. Existing diffusion-experiment settings remain unchanged.

E4.justification: Figures 14–16 add substantial diagnostic analyses testing the predicted noise and dataset-size scaling, its persistence under feature learning, and sensitivity to batch size. These directly investigate the mechanism and robustness of the central memorization-time law; v1 lacks these analyses.

E5.justification: Existing error-bar displays and statistical reporting are retained. Appendix E adds no reported seed counts, repeated-run summaries, confidence intervals or significance tests.

E6.justification: Figures 14–16 newly report memorization times consistent with linear dependence on dataset size, inverse dependence on noise standard deviation under both initializations, and approximate batch-size independence. These are new findings in the Gaussian setting. Existing results and Figures 1–13 remain unchanged, including CIFAR-10 FID 5.4 with 0% copies.

M1.justification: The early-stopping proposal and existing diffusion-model training and sampling procedures are unchanged. Appendix E introduces analytical and experimental probes of score learning, rather than a revised generative method.

P1.justification: Related work moves from Section 1.1 to Section 5, the conclusion is renumbered, and Section 3.3 gains a theoretical-support discussion. Local wording and explanatory edits accompany these changes, but most existing prose and the main experimental narrative are retained.

P2.justification: v2 adds Figures 14–16 with paired panels, rescaled-axis plots, insets and legends for the new experiments. Existing Figures 1–13 retain their graphical content, with limited caption edits and changes to placement and surrounding text flow.

R1.justification: v2 substantially expands positioning through explicit comparison with Bonnaire et al.'s random-feature analysis, earlier Gaussian-approximation learning, and supervised double descent and benign overfitting. It adds relevant kernel and mean-field references while retaining the earlier cited works.

T1.justification: New Appendix E develops a kernel-operator scaling argument using separated Gaussian components, localized score-mode ansatz functions and Rayleigh quotients, obtaining tau_mem proportional to P/sigma^nu. It distinguishes ReLU NTK and random-feature exponents. Section 2 also corrects the empirical distribution by inserting the missing 1/P normalization.

improvement.justification: v1 explicitly lacked an explanation for its central memorization-time scaling law. v2 substantially strengthens that argument through a kernel scaling derivation and controlled tests of noise, dataset size, initialization and batch size in Appendix E. Removing the explicit deep-architecture limitation weakens qualification, since the new theory addresses a restricted setting. Nevertheless, its assumptions remain stated, and the added explanatory and diagnostic evidence provides a substantial net improvement.

A1.justification: Both PDFs describe the same work, with matching authors, central claims and original experiments. The text, equations, figures and appendices support reliable comparison, including the new Appendix E in v2.

after.justification: v2 retains these original experiments and adds numerical score-learning experiments on Gaussian data in Appendix E, Figures 14–16.

before.justification: v1 reports original diffusion-model experiments on CIFAR-10, CelebA, text8, LAION-10k and Random Hierarchy Model data, including results in Appendices B–D.

arxiv_record.abstract: Modern large reasoning models demonstrate impressive problem-solving capabilities by employing sophisticated reasoning strategies. However, they often struggle to balance efficiency and effectiveness, frequently generating unnecessarily lengthy reasoning chains for simple problems. In this work, we propose AdaCtrl, a novel framework to support both difficulty-aware adaptive reasoning budget allocation and explicit user control over reasoning depth. AdaCtrl dynamically adjusts its reasoning length based on self-assessed problem difficulty, while also allowing users to manually control the budget to prioritize either efficiency or effectiveness. This is achieved through a two-stage training pipeline: an initial cold-start fine-tuning phase to instill the ability to self-aware difficulty and adjust reasoning budget, followed by a difficulty-aware reinforcement learning (RL) stage that refines the model's adaptive reasoning strategies and calibrates its difficulty assessments based on its evolving capabilities during online training. To enable intuitive user interaction, we design explicit length-triggered tags that function as a natural interface for budget control. Empirical results show that AdaCtrl adapts reasoning length based on estimated difficulty, compared to the standard training baseline that also incorporates fine-tuning and RL, it yields performance improvements and simultaneously reduces response length by 10.06% and 12.14% on the more challenging AIME2024 and AIME2025 datasets, which require elaborate reasoning, and by 62.05% and 91.04% on the MATH500 and GSM8K datasets, where more concise responses are sufficient. Furthermore, AdaCtrl enables precise user control over the reasoning budget, allowing for tailored responses to meet specific needs.
arxiv_record.authors: Shijue Huang, Hongru Wang, Wanjun Zhong, Zhaochen Su, Jiazhan Feng, Bowen Cao, Yi R. Fung
arxiv_record.title: AdaCtrl: Towards Adaptive and Controllable Reasoning via Difficulty-Aware Budgeting

C1.justification: The central claims of adaptive budgeting, explicit user control, and difficulty-aware two-stage training are retained. V2 additionally claims robustness under hyperparameter variation in the introduction; its abstract and conclusion otherwise preserve the original contribution scope.

C2.justification: V2 adds localized interpretations: initial Easy-tag bias is attributed primarily to format learning during SFT, prompting failures are linked to instruction-following limitations, and binary difficulty categories are justified by control simplicity and reliability. It also interprets the new ablations and sweeps as supporting reward complementarity and robustness.

D1.justification: V2 newly specifies the default difficulty threshold as 0.625 and supplies exact baseline and difficulty-aware evaluation prompts in Section 4.1. These disclosures do not establish changes to the existing experiments. Software, hardware, optimizer details, and the promised future code release remain unchanged.

E1.justification: DeepMATH training and evaluation on AIME2024, AIME2025, MATH500, and GSM8K are retained. The additional experiments vary model size, rewards, and prompting within the existing mathematical task coverage.

E2.justification: V2 adds the evaluated S1.1-7B-PE prompting baseline in Figure 4(b), reporting response lengths under a requested 500-token limit. The existing comparison methods remain, with renamed rows and corresponding 14B configurations.

E3.justification: V2 adds matched 14B training/evaluation, reward-removal experiments, reward-weight combinations, and difficulty-threshold sweeps over 0.625, 0.5, and 0.375. It also tests prompted 500-token limits and qualitatively reports a 1000-token test. Previously stated data budgets, metrics, and decoding settings remain unchanged.

E4.justification: V2 adds individual reward ablations, hyperparameter sensitivity tests, comparison with prompted length control, and response-length distributions by predicted difficulty. It also expands final difficulty-tag proportions into trajectories during RL, directly examining how difficulty judgments develop.

E5.justification: Both versions average AIME2024 and AIME2025 performance over eight independent runs. V2 adds no seed reporting, confidence intervals, significance tests, or other uncertainty-estimation procedures.

E6.justification: The original 7B results in Tables 1–2 remain unchanged. V2 adds extensive results under new conditions: AdaCtrl-14B achieves 34.58% accuracy with 15173.21 tokens on AIME2024, while 7B reward ablations yield 17.08% without calibration reward and 15.42% without length reward. Hyperparameter, prompting, and distribution analyses add further findings; these are additional results rather than same-setting improvements over v1.

M1.justification: The two-stage training procedure, Easy/Hard control interface, rollout-based difficulty estimation, three reward components, and GRPO objective remain unchanged. The 14B experiments extend model-size settings without introducing a new algorithm or architecture.

P1.justification: The introduction and substantial portions of the method/results narrative are rewritten. The separate tag-interface subsection is integrated into cold-start training, RL subsections are consolidated, and controllability moves from analysis into main results. Terminology shifts from length-trigger tags to difficulty-aware tags.

P2.justification: V2 removes the opening summary chart, redesigns the retained example and training diagrams, expands Tables 1–2, and adds Tables 3–4. Final tag-proportion bars become training trajectories, with new prompting and distribution plots. The retained training curves also change their step-axis scale from 0–640 to 0–80 without explanation.

R1.justification: V2 adds Wei et al.'s chain-of-thought work and two Hongru Wang et al. papers, while removing the ThinkPrune citation. The introduction more explicitly contrasts uniform compression with brittle fine-grained prompting. Most related-work discussion and the overall novelty positioning remain intact; duplicate-reference consolidation does not remove those works.

T1.justification: Equations 1–7 retain their mathematical substance. Renaming reasoning traces from r to p and distinguishing the KL coefficient as beta-prime are notation refinements. Neither version supplies theoretical propositions or proofs.

improvement.justification: V1 lacked individual reward ablations and sensitivity tests and evaluated only a 7B backbone. V2 substantially strengthens validation through separate reward-removal controls, threshold/weight sweeps, and matched 14B comparisons, while disclosing previously missing prompts and the default threshold. Reporting weaknesses remain: some mode-comparison claims overgeneralize Table 2, and the training-step axis changes unexplained. These issues limit precision but do not outweigh the substantial gains in testing the method's components and robustness.

A1.justification: Both PDFs describe the same AdaCtrl research. All pages, equations, tables, and figures support comparison. Neither supplied PDF contains an appendix.

after.justification: V2 retains these original results and adds 14B experiments, hyperparameter sweeps, reward ablations, and further analyses.

before.justification: V1 reports original model-training and evaluation results, including accuracy, response lengths, controllability experiments, and training dynamics.

arxiv_record.abstract: Internal representations are crucial for understanding deep neural networks, such as their properties and reasoning patterns, but remain difficult to interpret. While mapping from feature space to input space aids in interpreting the former, existing approaches often rely on crude approximations. We propose using a conditional diffusion model - a pretrained high-fidelity diffusion model conditioned on spatially resolved feature maps - to learn such a mapping in a probabilistic manner. We demonstrate the feasibility of this approach across various pretrained image classifiers from CNNs to ViTs, showing excellent reconstruction capabilities. Through qualitative comparisons and robustness analysis, we validate our method and showcase possible applications, such as the visualization of concept steering in input space or investigations of the composite nature of the feature space. This approach has broad potential for improving feature space understanding in computer vision models.

arxiv_record.abstract: Discrete normalizing flows are promising generative models with advantages such as analytical log-likelihood computation and end-to-end training. However, the architectural constraints to ensure invertibility and tractable Jacobian computation limit their expressive power and practical usability. Recent advancements utilize autoregressive modeling, significantly enhancing expressive power and generation quality. Nevertheless, such sequential modeling inherently restricts parallel computation during inference, leading to slow generation that impedes practical deployment. In this paper, we first identify that strict sequential dependency in inference is unnecessary to generate high-quality samples. We observe that sub-variables in sequential modeling can also be approximated without strictly conditioning on all preceding sub-variables. Moreover, the models tend to exhibit low dependency redundancy in the initial layer and higher redundancy in subsequent layers. Leveraging these observations, we propose to selectively use Jacobi decoding strategy that accelerates its autoregressive inference through parallel iterative optimization. Theoretical analyses demonstrate the method's superlinear convergence rate and guarantee that the number of iterations required is no greater than the original sequential approach. Empirical evaluations across multiple datasets validate the generality and effectiveness of our acceleration technique, achieving up to 4.7 times faster inference on modern normalizing flow models while preserving generation quality.
arxiv_record.authors: Jiaru Zhang, Juanwu Lu, Xiaoyu Wu, Ziran Wang, Ruqi Zhang
arxiv_record.title: Accelerating Inference of Discrete Autoregressive Normalizing Flows by Selective Jacobi Decoding

arxiv_record.abstract: Noisy labelled datasets are generally inexpensive compared to clean labelled datasets, and the same is true for graph data. In this paper, we propose a denoising technique DeGLIF: Denoising Graph Data using Leave-One-Out Influence Function. DeGLIF uses a small set of clean data and the leave-one-out influence function to make label noise robust node-level prediction on graph data. Leave-one-out influence function approximates the change in the model parameters if a training point is removed from the training dataset. Recent advances propose a way to calculate the leave-one-out influence function for Graph Neural Networks (GNNs). We extend that recent work to estimate the change in validation loss, if a training node is removed from the training dataset. We use this estimate and a new theoretically motivated relabelling function to denoise the training dataset. We propose two DeGLIF variants to identify noisy nodes. Both these variants do not require any information about the noise model or the noise level in the dataset; DeGLIF also does not estimate these quantities. For one of these variants, we prove that the noisy points detected can indeed increase risk. We carry out detailed computational experiments on different datasets to show the effectiveness of DeGLIF. It achieves better accuracy than other baseline algorithms
arxiv_record.authors: Pintu Kumar and Nandyala Hemachandra
arxiv_record.title: DeGLIF for Label Noise Robust Node Classification using GNNs

arxiv_record.abstract: Decentralized training of large language models offers the opportunity to pool computational resources across geographically distributed participants, but is often bottlenecked by network communication, particularly under pipeline parallel settings. While pipeline parallelism partitions model layers across devices to handle large-scale models, it necessitates frequent communication of intermediate activations, creating challenges when network bandwidth is limited. To address these issues, we propose TAH-Quant (Tile-wise Adaptive Hadamard Quantization), a novel activation quantization framework for pipeline parallelism. TAH-Quant integrates fine-grained tile-wise quantization, entropy-guided tile-wise adaptive bit allocation for optimal bit usage, and a Hadamard-based transformation with pivot swapping to effectively suppress outliers. Compared with token-level allocation, the tile-wise allocator assigns precision at the granularity of small channel windows within each token, reducing quantization error under the same bit budget. We prove that pipeline parallel training equipped with TAH-Quant maintains a convergence rate of O(1/sqrt(T)), matching that of vanilla stochastic gradient descent. Extensive experiments demonstrate that TAH-Quant achieves an aggressive activation quantization ratio of 3-4 bits, providing up to 4.3x throughput speedup over uncompressed FP32 and up to 1.33x wall-clock speedup over AQ-SGD, while preserving training convergence, avoiding AQ-SGD's activation-cache overhead, and generalizing well across various training scenarios.
arxiv_record.authors: Guangxin He, Yuan Cao, Yutong He, Tianyi Bai, Kai Chen, Kun Yuan, Binhang Yuan
arxiv_record.title: TAH-QUANT: Effective Activation Quantization in Pipeline Parallelism over Slow Network

snapshot_arxiv_record.abstract: Decentralized training of large language models offers the opportunity to pool computational resources across geographically distributed participants, but is often bottlenecked by network communication, particularly under pipeline parallel settings. While pipeline parallelism partitions model layers across devices to handle large-scale models, it necessitates frequent communication of intermediate activations, creating challenges when network bandwidth is limited. To address these issues, we propose TAH-Quant (Tile-wise Adaptive Hadamard Quantization), a novel activation quantization framework for pipeline parallelism. TAH-Quant integrates fine-grained tile-wise quantization, entropy-guided tile-wise adaptive bit allocation for optimal bit usage, and a Hadamard-based transformation with pivot swapping to effectively suppress outliers. Compared with token-level allocation, the tile-wise allocator assigns precision at the granularity of small channel windows within each token, reducing quantization error under the same bit budget. We prove that pipeline parallel training equipped with TAH-Quant maintains a convergence rate of O(1/sqrt(T)), matching that of vanilla stochastic gradient descent. Extensive experiments demonstrate that TAH-Quant achieves an aggressive activation quantization ratio of 3-4 bits, providing up to 4.3x throughput speedup over uncompressed FP32 and up to 1.33x wall-clock speedup over AQ-SGD, while preserving training convergence, avoiding AQ-SGD's activation-cache overhead, and generalizing well across various training scenarios.

C1.justification: The abstract and contribution statement redefine the allocator as a strict refinement of token-level allocation and newly claim lower quantization error under the same bit budget. They explicitly extend the contribution to from-scratch pretraining. The abstract also recasts 4.3× as throughput speedup over FP32, adds a 1.33× wall-clock claim over AQ-SGD, and narrows the memory claim to avoiding activation-cache overhead. The 3–4-bit and SGD-rate claims remain.

C2.justification: v2 adds substantive explanations involving within-token heterogeneity, group-size/metadata tradeoffs, and pipeline bubbles. v1's dedicated early-pretraining limitation is removed, while Appendix D qualifies the 8B run through its limited tokens-per-parameter budget. Appendices G–H add low-bit applicability boundaries and attribute the long-horizon NaN event to backward fixed-point precision, reporting recovery at 10 bits.

D1.justification: v2 substantially expands reproducibility information: default allocation/group sizes and the 80/20 precision split, contiguous uint8 packing, approximately 4.41 transmitted bits per element including metadata, profiling settings, and detailed pretraining architecture and optimizer parameters. Appendix H documents gradient scaling and checkpoint recovery. These disclosures go well beyond v1's short training-settings appendix, although no new code-access resource is provided.

E1.justification: v1's C4 pretraining experiment is replaced by SlimPajama-6B pretraining, and Appendix D adds mathematical-corpus pretraining on Proof-Pile. HellaSwag and MBPP evaluation disappear. MMLU is removed from the main downstream comparison but remains in the group-size ablation, so its coverage is not wholly removed. The four fine-tuning/instruction-tuning datasets and Math-7K verification remain.

E2.justification: The main FP32/FP16, AQ-SGD, and original-Qwen comparators remain. Appendix H newly evaluates NAIVE-4bit against TAH-Quant-4bit for backward gradients. Newly cited methods such as QuaRot and SpinQuant are not evaluated baselines; likewise, Appendix D explicitly says AQ-SGD is only included in the legend, not executed.

E3.justification: The pretraining protocol changes from Qwen2.5-3B/C4 for 6,000 iterations to LLaMA-3.2-1B/SlimPajama training through approximately 6B tokens, with PP=4, sequence length 4096, batch size 256, and held-out perplexity checkpoints. A separate 8B-model protocol and controlled micro-batch/precision sweeps are added. v2 also reports four or eight pipeline stages instead of uniformly eight, changes the downstream average's benchmark composition, and documents an actual backward-precision increase from 8 to 10 bits after instability.

E4.justification: The original group-size, adaptive-allocation, and Hadamard ablations remain. Appendices E–H add throughput sensitivity to micro-batch size and bandwidth, outlier-threshold sensitivity, INT4/INT3 ratio comparisons, an INT2 failure test, and backward-gradient stress tests. The long-horizon NaN investigation adds a concrete failure analysis absent from v1.

E5.justification: v2 adds curves labelled ePDF to the existing quantization-error histograms and specifies a 300-step rolling-mean estimator for pretraining loss in Table 1. These are limited additions to statistical summaries. Neither version supplies repeated-run counts, seeds, confidence intervals, or a significance test supporting v2's statistically indistinguishable wording.

E6.justification: New results include 6B-token validation perplexities of 20.64 versus 20.67 for TAH-QUANT and FP16, and step-600 backward-quantization losses of 2.52 versus 6.04 for TAH-Quant-4bit and NAIVE-4bit. C4 and several downstream result entries disappear. Retained downstream scores and GPT-2 throughput values are unchanged; the SFT average changes from 60.9 to 59.32 because benchmark membership changes. The unchanged throughput table gives 4045/751, approximately 5.39× at 100 Mbps, inconsistent with v2's stated maximum of 4.3×.

M1.justification: Section 3.2 changes a central component: v1 assigns one precision to every tile belonging to a token, whereas v2 ranks channel-window allocation tiles and permits different precisions within one token. The new allocation size A defaults to the quantization group size G; A=C recovers token-level allocation. This changes the allocation procedure, while retaining group quantization and the pivot-Hadamard transform.

P1.justification: The main section sequence and much existing prose remain. Targeted rewrites affect the abstract, contributions, allocation explanation, evaluation discussion, and conclusion; computational overhead receives its own subsection. Evaluation instructions move from the table caption into Appendix B, additional appendices are organized by study, and writing/impact disclosures and an additional author are introduced.

P2.justification: v2 consolidates the retained convergence and runtime panels into Figure 2 and merges the two component-ablation figures into Figure 3. It redraws Figure 1 with density overlays and revised axes, narrows the downstream table, and adds a pretraining table, a two-panel pretraining figure, and six supplementary experimental tables. This substantially changes the presentation of the evidence beyond renumbering.

R1.justification: Section 2 adds positioning against Subspace Networks, QuaRot, and SpinQuant, distinguishing parameterization constraints and inference rotations from activation communication during training. Additional citations support slow-network settings and the pretraining token-budget discussion. MMLU, HellaSwag, and MBPP references are removed. The broader research positioning remains intact.

T1.justification: The convergence assumptions, theorem, corollary, and Appendix C proofs remain substantively unchanged after matching renumbering. v2 adds computational-complexity bounds for pivot selection, entropy ranking, and Hadamard application in Section 3.4, and formalizes allocation tiles and the A=C special case. These are limited mathematical additions, not a new convergence proof.

improvement.justification: v2 substantially addresses v1's explicitly acknowledged weak pretraining validation through a 6B-token from-scratch experiment with held-out perplexity and an additional 8B-model check. The sensitivity tests, disclosed backward-gradient failure, and implementation details materially improve evidence about applicability and reproducibility. These gains outweigh the narrower downstream comparison, although unsupported statistical-equivalence language and the throughput-speedup inconsistency limit the strength of some claims.

A1.justification: Both PDFs describe TAH-QUANT. Their text, equations, figures, tables, and complete appendices are readable and support reliable matching despite substantial additions and reorganization.

after.justification: v2 retains original empirical results and reports additional pretraining, throughput-sensitivity, low-bit quantization, and numerical-stability experiments in the main text and Appendices D–H.

before.justification: v1 reports original training-loss curves, throughput measurements, downstream benchmark scores, quantization-error measurements, and component ablations.

arxiv_record.abstract: Differential privacy (DP) has become an essential framework for privacy-preserving machine learning. Existing DP learning methods, however, often have disparate impacts on model predictions, e.g., for minority groups. Gradient clipping, which is often used in DP learning, can suppress larger gradients from challenging samples. We show that this problem is amplified by adaptive clipping, which will often shrink the clipping bound to tiny values to match a well-fitting majority, while significantly reducing the accuracy for others. We propose bounded adaptive clipping, which introduces a tunable lower bound to prevent excessive gradient suppression. Our method improves worst-class accuracy by over 10 percentage points on Skewed and Fashion MNIST compared to unbounded adaptive clipping, 7 points compared to Automatic clipping, and 5 points compared to constant clipping. The code is available at https://github.com/TrustworthyMLHelsinki/adaptive-clipping-fairness.
arxiv_record.authors: Linzh Zhao, Aki Rehn, Mikko A. Heikkil\"a, Razane Tajeddine, Antti Honkela

D1.justification: v1 promises a future code release; v2 supplies a repository link. v2 newly identifies the BoTorch sampler, AUTO's stability constant, and model-specific runtimes, including revised tabular timing. E1.justification: v2 retains the four original datasets and adds CelebA eyeglasses classification with gender-specific evaluation (Section 4.1, Figure 3). This extends coverage from handwritten digits, clothing, and census records to natural face images and demographic disparities in attribute prediction.

E2.justification: v2 adds AUTO to the retained image and tabular comparisons, including DP-HPO experiments. Appendix C.1 additionally evaluates FairDP against the existing methods on Adult and Dutch using group accuracy and demographic parity. Constant and unbounded adaptive clipping remain.

E3.justification: v2 adds demographic-parity evaluation and fixed-lower-bound controls. E4.justification: Beyond v1's illustrative trajectories and hyperparameter heatmaps, v2 adds an Adult accuracy-sensitivity analysis (Figure A1), tests fixed CLB = 0.1 against tuning (Appendix C.2), and adds Skewed MNIST/CelebA training trajectories (C.4). P1.justification: v2 reorganizes Methodology, moves dataset preprocessing from Appendix A into Section 4.1, restructures the experimental appendices, and substantially rewrites results discussion and conclusion. P2.justification: The principal accuracy-versus-budget line plots are redesigned as joint-performance scatter panels, with expanded line-plot comparisons appearing in the appendix. v2 adds CelebA, demographic-parity, sensitivity, and trajectory displays, expands result tables, and revises heatmap captions and axes. R1.justification: v2 substantially broadens positioning through AUTO and FairDP comparisons and reconciles its findings with prior small-clipping results using bias–variance reasoning. New discussion cites Rehn et al. (2026), Barocas et al. (2023), and Defrance and De Bie (2025) to contextualize clipping regimes and fairness trade-offs.

T1.justification: Lemma 3.1 expands Gaussian-mechanism composition from unit sensitivities to arbitrary sensitivities Delta1 and Delta2, retaining the original formula as a special case. The applied privacy theorem remains unchanged, and no substantial new proof development is added.

improvement.justification: v2 substantially strengthens validation through alternative clipping/fairness baselines, demographic-parity evaluation, CelebA, and direct tests of tuning sensitivity and a fixed lower bound. arxiv_record.abstract: We introduce Temporal Variational Implicit Neural Representations (TV-INRs), a probabilistic framework for modeling irregular multivariate time series that enables efficient and accurate individualized imputation and forecasting. By integrating implicit neural representations with latent variable models, TV-INRs learn distributions over time-continuous generator functions conditioned on signal-specific covariates. Unlike existing INR approaches that require extensive training, fine-tuning or meta-learning, our method achieves accurate individualized predictions through a single forward pass. Our experiments demonstrate that with a single TV-INRs instance, we can accurately solve diverse imputation and forecasting tasks, offering a computationally efficient and scalable solution for real-world applications. TV-INRs performs particularly well in low-data regimes, where on several datasets it achieves substantially lower imputation error, including order-of-magnitude improvements.
arxiv_record.authors: Batuhan Koyuncu, Rachael DeVries, Ole Winther, Isabel Valera

The conclusion replaces the broad inference-efficiency advantage with the more specific claim of fixed inference time independent of gradient adaptation.

C2.justification: v1 already discussed stronger competitors in some settings and long-horizon outliers. v2 substantially extends interpretation through architectural-complexity tradeoffs, calibration behavior, decoder and likelihood explanations, and explicit limitations concerning informative missingness and a single global latent representation. It also distinguishes evaluated in-distribution generalization from unevaluated foundation-model and out-of-distribution settings.

D1.justification: v2 adds an anonymous code link and repository-based data/dependency instructions in its reproducibility statement. It newly specifies the Laplace output parameterization, covariate binning, temporal pooling, AdamW use and configurations for added experiments. The existing detailed split, hyperparameter and hardware disclosures largely remain unchanged.

E1.justification: The underlying datasets are retained, but v2 adds joint multivariate forecasting on Electricity, Traffic and Solar-H, requiring multiple series to be modeled together (Section 4.1.5). Appendix B.3 also adds Electricity forecasting with partially observed history, extending the previously fully observed forecasting scenario.

E2.justification: CSDI is added to univariate and multivariate imputation comparisons and downstream HAR classification. Appendix A.13 introduces evaluated TV-VAE decoder baselines, while A.8 adds a TimeFlow variant trained with randomly sampled observation ratios. The original comparison methods remain.

E3.justification: Existing splits and principal univariate settings are retained. Added protocols include enlarged networks for joint forecasting, randomized TimeFlow training, decoder and likelihood controls, and NLL/90% coverage evaluation. Missing-history forecasting uses shared test masks but different training exposure: TV-INRs receives a missing-history curriculum while baselines train on full histories. B.3 lists a 0.2 observation ratio where Table 29 lists 0.3.

E4.justification: v2 adds Fourier-frequency ablations, comparisons against direct MLP decoders, predictive calibration analysis, forecasting-error histograms, missing-history robustness tests and Laplace-versus-Gaussian sensitivity analysis (A.12–A.13 and B.1–B.4). These test architectural necessity and failure mechanisms beyond v1's existing covariate and TimeFlow missingness analyses.

E5.justification: v2 introduces quantitative predictive-uncertainty evaluation, explicitly labeled 5th–95th percentile bands and detailed best-model-versus-comparator significance tables. Welch's test at alpha=0.05 was already documented in v1. Conversely, v1's explicit three-training-seed statement disappears; this is a loss of reporting detail, not evidence that fewer runs were performed.

P1.justification: The introduction, contributions, related-work passages, method instructions and experimental narrative undergo substantial rewriting. v2 adds an explicit pipeline summary, reorganizes appendix material and introduces dedicated reproducibility and limitations sections. These changes materially reshape the explanation and navigation beyond simply appending results.

P2.justification: v2 expands comparison tables and the classification figure with CSDI, adds numerous analytical tables and an error-distribution figure, and redraws prediction examples with percentile bands. Main-table highlighting changes from significance/comparability to best/second-best means, the dataset summary moves to the appendix, and the document adopts journal formatting.

R1.justification: v2 adds discussion and citations for CSDI, LSCD and temporal INR foundation models, plus references supporting missing-data mechanisms, masked training and Fourier features. This broadens and qualifies the existing research positioning without replacing its central relationship to INR, hypernetwork and amortized-inference work.

T1.justification: Appendix A.9 adds componentwise complexity reasoning under the assumption L is much larger than embedding and latent dimensions, yielding stated time and memory bounds of O(NL²E) and O(ML²). v2 also removes the earlier equality that incorrectly defined the absent-index set as all indices. These are bounded analytical additions and corrections, without new central theorems or proofs.

improvement.justification: v1 lacked direct validation of the INR decoder's contribution and quantitative assessment of its probabilistic predictions. v2's targeted decoder/Fourier ablations, calibration measurements and explicit failure analyses substantially strengthen architectural justification and expose applicability limits, including serious interval undercoverage. Different training curricula and inconsistent ratios weaken the missing-history comparison, and the lost seed-count statement reduces transparency, but these shortcomings do not outweigh the broader gains in validation and qualification.

A1.justification: Both PDFs describe Temporal Variational Implicit Neural Representations by the same authors. All 22 pages of v1 and 36 pages of v2, including appendices, tables, equations and figures, support comparison despite substantial additions and reorganization.

after.justification: v2 retains those empirical results and adds baseline comparisons, multivariate forecasting, ablations, uncertainty evaluation and missing-history experiments.

arxiv_record.abstract: Most existing safe reinforcement learning (RL) benchmarks focus on robotics and control tasks, offering limited relevance to high-stakes domains that involve structured constraints, mixed-integer decisions, and industrial complexity. This gap hinders the advancement and deployment of safe RL in critical areas such as energy systems, manufacturing, and supply chains. To address this limitation, we present SafeOR-Gym, a benchmark suite of nine operations research (OR) environments tailored for safe RL under complex constraints. Each environment captures a realistic planning, scheduling, or control problems characterized by cost-based constraint violations, planning horizons, and hybrid discrete-continuous action spaces. The suite integrates seamlessly with the Constrained Markov Decision Process (CMDP) interface provided by OmniSafe. We evaluate several state-of-the-art safe RL algorithms across these environments, revealing a wide range of performance: while some tasks are tractable, others expose fundamental limitations in current approaches. SafeORGym provides a challenging and practical testbed that aims to catalyze future research in safe RL for real-world decision-making problems.

snapshot_arxiv_record.abstract: Most existing safe reinforcement learning (RL) benchmarks focus on robotics and control tasks, offering limited relevance to high-stakes domains that involve structured constraints, mixed-integer decisions, and industrial complexity. This gap hinders the advancement and deployment of safe RL in critical areas such as energy systems, manufacturing, and supply chains. To address this limitation, we present SafeOR-Gym, a benchmark suite of nine operations research (OR) environments tailored for safe RL under complex constraints. Each environment captures a realistic planning, scheduling, or control problems characterized by cost-based constraint violations, planning horizons, and hybrid discrete-continuous action spaces. The suite integrates seamlessly with the Constrained Markov Decision Process (CMDP) interface provided by OmniSafe. We evaluate several state-of-the-art safe RL algorithms across these environments, revealing a wide range of performance: while some tasks are tractable, others expose fundamental limitations in current approaches. SafeORGym provides a challenging and practical testbed that aims to catalyze future research in safe RL for real-world decision-making problems.

C1.justification: Both versions retain the same central contributions: nine OR environments, Gym/OmniSafe integration, and empirical diagnosis of safe RL limitations under complex constraints. v2 explicitly calls the work a benchmarking and diagnostic study, clarifying rather than changing its original contribution.

C2.justification: v2 replaces the brief overall discussion with extensive interpretations by algorithm class, linking behavior to trust-region updates, replay-based estimation, and discontinuous constraint landscapes. It adds qualifications about scalarization favoring high-violation policies and deterministic coverage. ASU is now interpreted as failing feasibility despite reasonably competitive rewards.

D1.justification: New Section 4 documents the small CMDP wrapper, external JSON instance specifications, and extension through inheritance. Further details include stochastic failure sampling, inventory-policy trigger bounds, and runtimes for added methods and scenarios. The repository access information and hardware remain the same.

E1.justification: The nine task families remain. Evaluation adds stochastic compressor failures through SchedMaintEnv-v1 and removes the GTEP scenario without transmission lines. Standard GTEP, multi-bus unit commitment, and ASU evaluations are retained despite changes in placement.

E2.justification: FOCOPS, SACLag, and SACPID join the original five algorithms in the retained comparisons. Appendix C.3 also evaluates classical (s, S) and (r, Q) inventory policies against the RL reward results, substantially broadening the comparison methods.

E3.justification: Section 5.1 replaces v1's cost-filtered best/worst selection with Pareto identification and normalized scalarization over 101 preference weights. It specifies a cost threshold of 25 for reasonable optimality and introduces a perfect-information optimization upper bound for stochastic maintenance. Evaluation remains based on 10 episodes.

E4.justification: v2 adds reward–safety preference sensitivity analyses in Figures 3 and 13 and compares deterministic versus stochastic maintenance behavior. Constraint-wise diagnostics expand to eight algorithms. Conversely, v1's blending disable/none ablations and generation-expansion analysis without transmission are removed.

E5.justification: Both versions describe standard-deviation bands for training curves. Unlike v1's mean-only evaluation tables, v2 Table 4 explicitly reports standard deviations for selected stochastic-maintenance results. The 10-episode evaluation count is unchanged; additional independent training runs are not established.

E6.justification: The original algorithms' retained deterministic evaluation values are unchanged, but substantial results are added for three algorithms, stochastic maintenance, and inventory heuristics. New SACLag results on GridStorageEnv are reward −68690.5 and cost 0.03, supporting its revised solvability classification. The (r, Q) policy obtains reward 10948.9 versus OnCRPO's retained 7598.66. Results for the removed variants disappear.

M1.justification: The benchmark gains a localized environment-model extension: SchedMaintEnv-v1 uniformly samples compressor failure times from MTTF, MTTF−1, and MTTF−2 at episode initialization (Appendix A.8). The deterministic version remains, and no new learning algorithm is proposed.

P1.justification: The environment overview is reorganized to cover all nine families, a dedicated implementation section is introduced, and the results discussion is extensively rewritten around multi-objective evaluation and algorithm classes. Evaluation tables and supplementary discussions are reorganized into separate appendices.

P2.justification: v2 adds eight environment schematics, evaluation bar charts, Pareto-score plots, and comparison and summary tables. Earlier evaluation tables are consolidated into a rotated appendix table, existing plots expand to eight algorithms, and several variant plots are removed. These substantially change the visual presentation.

R1.justification: v2 adds references for SAC, PID constraint control, FOCOPS, and Powell's sequential-decision framework. Table 1 and Appendix D expand comparisons with OR-Gym and SustainGym, including interfaces and observation/action dimensions. The central positioning around industrial constraints beyond existing benchmarks remains unchanged.

T1.justification: v2 introduces a formal normalized scalarized score for Pareto comparisons and a stochastic failure-time assumption. Appendix A also revises state-set definitions, including equipment in STN and restricting observed inventory to main supply-chain nodes. Most environmental equations remain equivalent, and no new theorem or proof appears.

improvement.justification: v2 substantially strengthens the benchmark's evidential value through broader algorithm comparisons, an evaluated stochastic scenario, and classical inventory reward references that challenge the learned policies. Explicit reward–safety analysis and implementation documentation address important evaluation and usability gaps. Removing blending and topology ablations reduces diagnostic coverage, scalarized winners can remain highly infeasible, and classical-policy costs are unreported. These limitations temper, but do not outweigh, the substantial gains.

A1.justification: Both PDFs describe SafeOR-Gym and the same nine core environment families. Their main text, appendices, equations, tables, and figures support reliable comparison, including matching relocated and renamed material.

after.justification: v2 retains original empirical results and adds evaluations of further RL algorithms, stochastic maintenance, and classical inventory policies.

before.justification: v1 reports original training curves, evaluation rewards and costs, constraint-violation analyses, and runtimes for five safe RL algorithms.

arxiv_record.abstract: Contrastive language-image pre-training aligns features of text-image pairs in a common latent space via distinct encoders for each modality. While this approach achieves impressive performance in several zero-shot tasks, it cannot natively handle multimodal inputs, i.e., encoding image and text into a single feature vector. As a remedy, it is common practice to use additional modules to merge the features extracted by unimodal encoders. In this work, we present FuseLIP, a new architecture for multimodal embedding. Leveraging recent progress in discrete image tokenizers, we propose to use a single transformer model operating on a unified vocabulary of text and image tokens. This early fusion approach allows the different modalities to interact at each depth of encoding and obtain richer representations compared to common late fusion. We collect new datasets for multimodal pre-training and evaluation, designing challenging tasks for multimodal encoders. We show that FuseLIP outperforms late fusion approaches in several multimodal and unimodal embedding tasks.
arxiv_record.authors: Christian Schlarmann, Francesco Croce, Nicolas Flammarion, Matthias Hein
arxiv_record.comments: TMLR 2026. Code and models available at https://github.com/chs20/fuselip

arxiv_record.abstract: Vision Language Models (VLMs) have shown remarkable capabilities in multimodal understanding, yet their susceptibility to adversarial perturbations poses a significant threat to their reliability in real-world applications. Despite often being imperceptible to humans, these perturbations can drastically alter model outputs, leading to erroneous interpretations and decisions. This paper introduces DiffCAP, a novel diffusion-based purification strategy that can effectively neutralize adversarial corruptions in VLMs. We theoretically establish a provable recovery region in the forward diffusion process and meanwhile quantify the convergence rate of semantic variation with respect to VLMs. These findings manifest that adversarial effects monotonically fade as diffusion unfolds. Guided by this principle, DiffCAP leverages noise injection with a similarity threshold of VLM embeddings as an adaptive criterion, before reverse diffusion restores a clean and reliable representation for VLM inference. Through extensive experiments across six datasets with three VLMs under varying attack strengths in three task scenarios, we show that DiffCAP outperforms existing defense techniques by a substantial margin. Notably, DiffCAP significantly reduces both hyperparameter tuning complexity and the required diffusion time, thereby accelerating the denoising process. Equipped with theorems and empirical support, DiffCAP provides a robust and practical solution for securely deploying VLMs in adversarial environments. The source code is available at https://github.com/JasonFu1998/DiffCAP.

D1.justification: v2 adds a source-code access link, detailed BPDA identity-gradient implementation and EOT averaging instructions, calibration and component timing, and further experimental configuration information. It specifies A100 40G hardware and H100 use for hallucination/jailbreaking, replacing v1's blanket A100 description. Previously disclosed diffusion hyperparameters are mainly relocated into the main text.

E1.justification: v2 adds MNIST and ImageNet-Sketch evaluations, resolution/long-tail distribution-shift scenarios, targeted-caption attacks on MiniGPT-4, and L2-bounded threats. E2.justification: Matched comparisons retain TeCoA, FARE, JPEG-DL, DiffPure, and CLIPure. Additional evaluations use existing defenses or no-defense controls, sometimes restricting the comparator subset for new settings. AttackVLM supplies additional attacks, rather than a new competing defense.

arxiv_record.abstract: We propose a novel, flexible, and efficient framework for designing Concept Bottleneck Models (CBMs) that enables practitioners to explicitly encode and extend their prior knowledge and beliefs about the concept-concept ($C-C$) and concept-task ($C \to Y$) relationships within the model's reasoning when making predictions. The resulting $\textbf{C}$oncept $\textbf{REA}$soning $\textbf{M}$odels (CREAMs) architecturally encode arbitrary types of $C-C$ relationships such as mutual exclusivity, hierarchical associations, and/or correlations, as well as potentially sparse $C \to Y$ relationships. Moreover, CREAM can optionally incorporate a regularized side-channel to complement the potentially {incomplete concept sets}, achieving competitive task performance while encouraging predictions to be concept-grounded. To evaluate CBMs in such settings, we introduce a $C \to Y$ agnostic metric that quantifies interpretability when predictions partially rely on the side-channel. In our experiments, we show that, without additional computational overhead, CREAM models support efficient interventions, can avoid concept leakage, and achieve black-box-level performance under missing concepts. We further analyze how an optional side-channel affects interpretability and intervenability. Importantly, the side-channel enables CBMs to remain effective even in scenarios where only a limited number of concepts are available.

arxiv_record.abstract: Neural rendering has advanced significantly in 3D reconstruction and novel view synthesis, and integrating physics into these frameworks opens new applications such as physically accurate digital twins for robotics and XR. However, the inverse problem of estimating physical parameters from visual observations remains challenging. Existing physics-aware neural rendering methods typically require dense multi-view videos, making them impractical for scalable, real-world deployment. Under sparse-view settings, the sequential optimization strategies employed by current approaches suffer from severe error accumulation: inaccuracies in initial 3D reconstruction propagate to subsequent stages, degrading physical state and material parameter estimates. On the other hand, simultaneous optimization of all parameters fails due to the highly non-convex and often non-differentiable nature of the problem. We propose ProJo4D, a progressive joint optimization framework that gradually expands the set of jointly optimized parameters. This design enables physics-informed gradients to refine geometry while avoiding the instability of direct joint optimization over all parameters. Evaluations on synthetic and real-world datasets demonstrate that ProJo4D substantially outperforms prior work in 4D future state prediction and physical parameter estimation, achieving up to 10x improvement in geometric accuracy while maintaining computational efficiency. Please visit the project webpage: https://daniel03c1.github.io/ProJo4D/
arxiv_record.authors: Daniel Rho and Jun Myeong Choi and Biswadip Dey and Roni Sengupta
arxiv_record.title: ProJo4D: Progressive Joint Optimization for Sparse-View Inverse Physics Estimation

arxiv_record.abstract: Sequence modeling tasks across domains such as natural language processing, time series forecasting, and control require learning complex input-output mappings. Nonlinear recurrence is theoretically required for universal approximation of sequence-to-sequence functions, yet linear recurrent models often prove surprisingly effective. This raises the question of when nonlinearity is truly required. We present a framework to systematically dissect the functional role of nonlinearity in recurrent networks, identifying when it is computationally necessary and what mechanisms it enables. We address this using Almost Linear Recurrent Neural Networks (AL-RNNs), which allow recurrence nonlinearity to be gradually attenuated and decompose network dynamics into analyzable linear regimes, making computational mechanisms explicit. We illustrate the framework across diverse synthetic and real-world tasks, including classic sequence modeling benchmarks, a neuroscientific stimulus-selection task, and a multi-task suite. We demonstrate how the AL-RNN's piecewise linear structure enables identification of computational primitives such as gating, rule-based integration, and memory-dependent transients, revealing that these operations emerge within predominantly linear backbones. Across tasks, sparse nonlinearity improves interpretability by reducing and localizing nonlinear computations, promotes shared representations in multi-task settings, and reduces computational cost. Moreover, sparse nonlinearity acts as a useful inductive bias: in low-data regimes or when tasks require discrete switching between linear regimes, sparsely nonlinear models often match or exceed fully nonlinear architectures. Our findings provide a principled approach for identifying where nonlinearity is functionally necessary, guiding the design of recurrent architectures that balance performance, efficiency, and interpretability.

arxiv_record.abstract: Recent progress in text-to-music generation has enabled models to synthesize high-quality musical segments, full compositions, and even respond to fine-grained control signals, e.g. chord progressions. State-of-the-art (SOTA) systems differ significantly in many dimensions, such as training datasets, modeling paradigms, and architectural choices. This diversity complicates efforts to evaluate models fairly and identify which design choices influence performance the most. While factors like data and architecture are important, in this study we focus exclusively on the modeling paradigm. We conduct a systematic empirical analysis to isolate its effects, offering insights into associated trade-offs and emergent behaviors that can guide future text-to-music generation systems. Specifically, we compare the two arguably most common modeling paradigms: auto-regressive decoding and conditional flow-matching. We conduct a controlled comparison by training all models from scratch using identical datasets, training configurations, and similar backbone architectures. Performance is evaluated across multiple axes, including generation quality, robustness to inference configurations, scalability, adherence to both textual and temporally aligned conditioning, and editing capabilities in the form of audio inpainting. This comparative study sheds light on distinct strengths and limitations of each paradigm, providing actionable insights that can inform future architectural and training decisions in the evolving landscape of text-to-music generation. Audio sampled examples are available at: https://huggingface.co/spaces/ortal1602/ARvsFM
arxiv_record.authors: Or Tal and Felix Kreuk and Yossi Adi
arxiv_record.title: Auto-Regressive vs Flow-Matching: a Comparative Study of Modeling Paradigms for Text-to-Music Generation

E6.justification: Tables 2–5 and the original Euler-sampling results retain their values. v3 adds extensive results, including MusicCaps 25 Hz FAD scores of 4.10 for AR, 5.53 for EnCodec-based FM, and 4.58 for VAE-based FM, plus reconstruction, duration, entropy and model-depth measurements. P1.justification: The principal section order and much of the original prose remain. v3 makes focused language and explanation edits, reorganizes the conclusion under explicit subheadings, adds a broader-impact paragraph, and renumbers existing appendices around new material.
