arxiv_record.abstract: Tree-based ensembles such as random forests remain the go-to for tabular data over deep learning models due to their prediction performance and computational efficiency. These advantages have led to their widespread deployment in high-stakes domains, where interpretability is essential for ensuring trustworthy predictions. This has motivated the development of popular local feature importance methods such as LIME and TreeSHAP. However, these approaches rely on approximations that ignore the model's internal structure and instead depend on potentially unstable perturbations. These issues are addressed in the global setting by MDI+, a global feature importance method which combines tree-based and linear feature importances by exploiting an equivalence between decision trees and least squares on a transformed node basis. However, the global MDI+ scores are not able to explain predictions when faced with heterogeneous individual characteristics. To address this gap, we propose Local MDI+ (LMDI+), a novel extension of the MDI+ framework that quantifies feature importances for each particular sample. Across twelve real-world benchmark datasets, LMDI+ outperforms existing baselines at identifying instance-specific predictive features, yielding an average 10% improvement in predictive performance when using only the selected features. It further demonstrates greater stability by consistently producing similar instance-level feature importance rankings across repeated model fits with different random seeds. Ablation experiments show that each component of LMDI+ contributes to these gains, and that the improvements extend beyond random forests to gradient boosting models. Finally, we show that LMDI+ enables local interpretability use cases by identifying closely matched counterfactuals for each classification benchmark and discovering homogeneous subgroups in a housing dataset case study.
arxiv_record.authors: Zhongyuan Liang, Zachary T. Rewolinski, Abhineet Agarwal, Tiffany M. Tang, Bin Yu
arxiv_record.title: Local MDI+: Local Feature Importances for Tree-Based Models

T1.justification: Equation 3 replaces threshold-only indicators with explicit membership in the left and right child nodes. improvement.justification: v1 lacked quantitative runtime comparisons and experimental validation beyond its default RF configuration and capped real-data evaluations. v2's ensemble checks, full-dataset evaluations, and timing studies substantially strengthen evidence for practical applicability while revealing computational tradeoffs with TreeSHAP and LIME. arxiv_record.abstract: Cross-view masked autoencoding has emerged as a powerful pretext task for learning dense correspondences, which are essential for applications such as video label propagation. The cross-view pretext task is modeled with a masked autoencoder, where a masked target view is reconstructed from an anchor view. However, acquiring effective training data remains a challenge - collecting diverse video datasets is costly, while simple image crops lack the necessary pose variations, underperforming video-based methods. This paper introduces CDG-MAE, a novel MAE-based self-supervised method that uses diverse synthetic views generated from static images via an image-conditioned diffusion model. We present a quantitative method to evaluate the local and global consistency of the generated views to choose the right diffusion model for cross-view self-supervised pretraining. These generated views exhibit substantial changes in pose and perspective, providing a rich training signal that overcomes the limitations of video and crop-based anchors. Furthermore, we enhance the standard single-anchor MAE setting to a multi-anchor masking strategy to increase the difficulty of the pretext task. CDG-MAE substantially narrows the gap to video-based MAE methods, while maintaining the data advantages of image-only MAEs.

C1.justification: The core contributions remain diffusion-generated views for cross-view MAE, consistency metrics, and multi-anchor masking, with improvements over CropMAE and a narrower gap to video-based methods. v2 emphasizes diffusion-model selection in its headline contribution, but that use was already claimed and demonstrated in v1 Appendix A.4.1.

C2.justification: v2 adds substantive qualifications concerning Lumos pretraining and possible data leakage, the comparability of 3D-pretrained CroCo, and the computational impracticality of video diffusion. New analyses motivate hypotheses about parameter-scaling difficulties and why classifier filtering may sacrifice useful diversity. These extend the original limitation concerning uncontrolled generated variations.

D1.justification: v2 supplies a project-code link, specifies the feature space for nearest-neighbor image selection and the 4–48-frame sampling interval, and documents synthetic-image resolution and storage. It also adds detailed optical-flow training settings and expanded resource comparisons. Existing optimizer, hardware, and default training disclosures are retained; the new compute reporting inconsistently labels eight-GPU elapsed hours as GPU hours.

E1.justification: v1 evaluates downstream representations only through video label propagation on DAVIS, VIP, and JHMDB. v2 Appendix A.4.5 adds optical-flow estimation, training WAFT on FlyingChairs and FlyingThings and evaluating transfer to KITTI. This substantially extends task and data coverage.

E2.justification: v2 Table 6 adds evaluated CroCo v1 and v2 baselines, including different model sizes; v1 cited CroCo but did not report these comparisons. Table 10 also adds a CropMAE Real+Synthetic control. These additions broaden comparison to 3D-pretrained methods and directly test a synthetic-data alternative, while retaining the original baselines.

E3.justification: Table 1 increases the stated consistency-evaluation sample from 500 to 5,000 images and video-frame pairs. New protocols include two-stage WAFT training with 50K/100K iterations and zero-shot KITTI evaluation, larger-model experiments, and bag sizes of six and eight. The filtering experiment removes 20.4% of training instances while holding training iterations fixed. Original default pretraining and label-propagation settings remain unchanged.

E4.justification: v2 adds synthetic-data CropMAE controls, parameter-versus-patch scaling, DINOv2-based consistency checks, classifier-based quality assessment and filtering, and bag-size/masking sensitivity studies. The existing Gen-SIS/RCG analysis is extended with Lumos rather than newly introduced. The comparative pose visualization in v1 Figure 3 is removed, although CDG-MAE-only qualitative examples remain.

E5.justification: The original three-seed means and standard deviations, and the single-seed four-anchor results, are retained unchanged in v2 Table 5. Table 15 reuses existing uncertainty estimates and extends the single-seed exploratory reporting practice. No increased repeated-run budget, new uncertainty estimator, confidence interval, or significance test is reported.

E6.justification: Original headline label-propagation scores are retained, but substantial new results cover CroCo, Lumos, scaling, filtering, robustness, and optical flow. For example, v2 Table 12 reports Stage-2 KITTI endpoint error/F1 of 3.70/11.50 for CDG-MAE versus 3.81/11.75 for CropMAE. Table 14 reports slightly lower scores after filtering. Table 1 consistency values also change under the enlarged sampling protocol, rather than establishing same-setting performance gains.

M1.justification: The proposed procedure retains offline diffusion-generated views, a shared ViT encoder, masked multi-anchor cross-attention, and pixel reconstruction loss. Additional generators, filtering experiments, and downstream WAFT evaluation test configurations or applications without revising the default CDG-MAE algorithm.

P1.justification: The abstract, introduction, and related-work prose are substantially revised and tightened. Diffusion-model selection and computational analysis move into dedicated main-text sections, while the appendix is reorganized around expanded supplementary studies. The title and publication presentation also change.

P2.justification: v2 redraws the overview diagrams, removes the comparative pose figure, consolidates earlier diffusion-selection and multi-anchor tables, and adds displays for resource comparisons and new analyses. Previously adjacent tables and appendix visualizations are redistributed and resized within a different document layout. Retained plots and examples are distinguishable from genuinely new displays.

R1.justification: v2 adds references and discussion for Lumos, video-diffusion alternatives, optical-flow pipelines, and classifier-based analysis. It also explains CroCo's distinct 3D-pretraining context. The principal positioning relative to CropMAE, SiamMAE, and self-supervised diffusion remains stable; citation-format changes and duplicate-reference cleanup do not constitute substantive additions.

T1.justification: The GS, LS, and NPS definitions and the substantive encoder, decoder, and reconstruction equations remain unchanged. Distinguishing mask-token notation in Equation 8 clarifies the existing procedure. Neither version introduces theoretical propositions or proofs.

improvement.justification: v2 substantially strengthens empirical support: the synthetic-data CropMAE control addresses a previously untested alternative explanation, optical-flow transfer extends validation beyond label propagation, and backbone, filtering, and scaling studies test important assumptions and limits. Added access and implementation information improves reproducibility. The inconsistent compute units and single-seed exploratory results limit some conclusions, but do not outweigh the substantial gain in controlled and diagnostic evidence.

A1.justification: Both PDFs describe the same CDG-MAE research despite the revised title. The complete main texts and appendices, including equations, tables, and figures, are readable and support reliable comparison.

after.justification: v2 retains these original experiments and adds optical-flow evaluation, synthetic-data controls, scaling experiments, and generated-view quality and robustness analyses.

before.justification: v1 reports original view-consistency measurements, CDG-MAE training experiments, ablations, and evaluations on DAVIS, VIP, and JHMDB, including additional appendix experiments.

arxiv_record.abstract: Public datasets, crucial for modern machine learning and statistical inference, often contain low-quality or contaminated samples that can harm model performance. This creates a need for principled prefiltering procedures that a data provider can apply to protect the accuracy of a range of potential downstream statistical and learning procedures simultaneously. In this work, we formalize and analyze Learner-Agnostic Robust data Prefiltering (LARP), the problem of designing prefiltering procedures with guarantees on the worst-case loss over a pre-specified set of learners. We establish the feasibility of LARP in two theoretical settings, by providing upper-bound guarantees on the worst-case loss. Our theoretical results indicate that protecting heterogeneous learner sets via LARP comes at the price of some performance loss compared to individual, learner-specific prefiltering; we call this gap the price of LARP. To assess this gap in performance, we empirically measure the price of LARP across image and tabular tasks. We further explore potential benefits of LARP from the perspective of saving on repeated data curation efforts, in a game-theoretic model where the downstream learners can split the cost of the single prefiltering.
arxiv_record.authors: Kristian Minchev, Dimitar I. Dimitrov, Nikola Konstantinov
arxiv_record.comments: Published in Transactions on Machine Learning Research (06/2026). URL: https://openreview.net/forum?id=gI6VOV3jfO

C1.justification: v1 emphasizes scalar Gaussian mean estimation and algorithm heterogeneity. v4 explicitly claims feasibility in two theoretical settings and adds heterogeneous downstream risk functions as a contribution. Its abstract frames large-dataset benefits more cautiously as potential savings in repeated curation within a cost-sharing model.

C2.justification: v4 adds explanations for nonmonotonic dependence on contamination and filter effectiveness, and conjectures why Tiny ImageNet shows a weaker price signal. It expands the applicability discussion for cost-sharing conditions and identifies sample modification, particularly token editing in language modeling, as outside the current sample-removal framework.

D1.justification: v4 adds a stated public code link, filtering pseudocode, and model/scoring-function mappings in Appendix E. It documents new experimental configurations, replaces Adult tuning tables with defaults and neural-network settings, and revises reported GPU usage from 200 to 250 hours. Appendix G expands dataset access/licensing information and changes the CIFAR-10 license statement.

E1.justification: v4 adds CIFAR-10N with human annotation errors, Tiny ImageNet with 200 image classes, and BAF fraud classification with fairness objectives (Section 5.2; Appendices D.3 and D.6). Adult and CIFAR-10 label-noise and shortcut coverage remain, with shortcut experiments moved to the appendix.

E2.justification: v4 Table 1 adds evaluated Confident Learning-based and oracle filters alongside the default filter. Figure 5a adds a no-prefiltering comparator to the Gaussian experiment, absent from v1 Figure 1a. The quantile, z-score, SDO, and earlier alternative shortcut filters remain.

E3.justification: Adult changes from 14 tuned robust/brittle model instances to seven models using library defaults and a fixed neural-network configuration; its label-noise metric changes from accuracy to macro-F1. New protocols include a wider CNN and different regularization range for Tiny ImageNet, and seven Random Forest learners with different fairness weights for BAF.

E4.justification: v4 adds sensitivity analyses for oracle effectiveness and Confident Learning-based filtering, and extends learner-diameter analysis to label noise (Appendices D.4, D.5, D.8). Existing shortcut diameter, alternative-filter, and loss-reweighting studies are retained. The original default-filter learner-specific shortcut profiles in v1 Figures 6 and 7b are omitted.

E5.justification: Both versions specify eight repetitions and standard errors for Gaussian mean estimation, and repeated-run averages with error bars for classification. v4 extends uncertainty reporting to new comparisons, including Table 1, without introducing a changed run count, seed policy, or statistical testing procedure.

E6.justification: v4 adds substantial benchmark and filter-comparison results. For example, Table 1 reports CIFAR-10 high-heterogeneity prices of 2.2% (s.e. 0.2) for default filtering and 2.0% (s.e. 0.2) for CL-based filtering. Adult results are replaced under revised settings. Gaussian-risk values and the plotted quantile/z-score ordering also change between v1 Figure 1a and v4 Figure 5a without an explained protocol change.

M1.justification: The original minimax framework remains, but v4 adds learner-specific accuracy/fairness objectives and integrates subgroup sampling controlled by three parameters (Section 5.2, Algorithm 2). Section 4.2 also introduces an oracle filter parameterized by removal fraction and effectiveness. These extend the objectives and procedures; Algorithm 1 primarily formalizes existing filtering.

P1.justification: The abstract, introduction, and conclusion are substantially rewritten. Theory is reorganized with major proofs in the main text; Gaussian experiments and shortcut descriptions move into Appendix D. The supplementary material is extensively restructured, and new algorithm and applicability discussions reshape the narrative beyond simple renumbering.

P2.justification: v1's twelve-panel Figure 2 is split and rearranged into v4 Figures 2 and 6. Selected learner-specific plots move into main-text Figure 1, while new comparison tables, benchmark plots, sensitivity plots, and pseudocode displays are added. Adult hyperparameter tables and some shortcut profiles disappear, alongside extensive journal-format layout changes.

R1.justification: Section 2 adds substantive comparisons with distributionally robust optimization, multi-distribution learning, and the price of robustness. Appendix E connects LARP's filtering structure to LAION and C4 curation. New Confident Learning and fairness references support additional methodological relationships; the original first-framework novelty claim remains.

T1.justification: The Gaussian/Huber-contamination result becomes a theorem for strictly smooth distributions under strong contamination, retaining the Gaussian bound as Corollary 4.5. v4 adds the oracle PAC-style Theorem 4.6 and general utility conditions in Corollary 5.2, replacing v1's mean-specific Appendix D argument. The original cost-sharing lemma is retained as Theorem 5.1.

improvement.justification: v4 substantially strengthens support for LARP's generality beyond v1's narrow theoretical setting and synthetic-corruption benchmarks. Broader guarantees, natural annotation errors, alternative filters, and conflicting fairness objectives test important aspects of the central argument. Explicit cost-sharing conditions, pseudocode, and a stated code release also improve scrutiny and reproducibility. Unexplained Gaussian-result revisions and omitted shortcut profiles limit parts of the evidence, but do not outweigh these substantial gains.

A1.justification: Both PDFs describe the same LARP framework and share identifiable methods, experiments, and theoretical results. All 24 pages of v1 and 34 pages of v4, including appendices, were readable; figures and equations could be checked visually.

after.justification: v4 reports original experiments throughout Section 5 and Appendix D, including retained studies and new BAF, CIFAR-10N, Tiny ImageNet, and filtering comparisons.

before.justification: v1 reports original Gaussian mean-estimation simulations and Adult/CIFAR-10 experiments, including learner-specific results and supplementary analyses in Appendix C.

arxiv_record.abstract: Anomaly detection in multivariate time series is essential across domains such as healthcare, cybersecurity, and industrial monitoring, yet remains fundamentally challenging due to high-dimensional dependencies, the presence of cross-correlations between time-dependent variables, and the scarcity of labeled anomalies. We introduce mTSBench, the largest benchmark to date for multivariate time series anomaly detection and model selection, consisting of 344 labeled time series across 19 datasets from a wide range of application domains. We comprehensively evaluate 24 anomaly detectors, including the only two publicly available large language model-based methods for multivariate time series. Consistent with prior findings, we observe that no single detector dominates across datasets, motivating the need for effective model selection. We benchmark three recent model selection methods and find that even the strongest of them remain far from optimal. Our results highlight the outstanding need for robust, generalizable selection strategies. We open-source the benchmark at https://plan-lab.github.io/mtsbench to encourage future research.
arxiv_record.authors: Xiaona Zhou, Constantin Brif, Ismini Lourentzou
arxiv_record.title: mTSBench: Benchmarking Multivariate Time Series Anomaly Detection and Model Selection at Scale

arxiv_record.abstract: The integration of Large Language Model (LLM) blocks with Vision Transformers (ViTs) holds significant promise for vision-only tasks by leveraging the rich semantic knowledge and reasoning capabilities of LLMs. However, a fundamental challenge lies in the inherent modality mismatch between the text-centric pre-training of LLMs and the vision-centric training of ViTs. Direct fusion often fails to fully exploit the LLM's potential and suffers from unstable finetuning. Consequently, prior works typically keep LLM blocks frozen while learning only the vision components. To address these challenges, we introduce Language-Adapted Vision Enhancer (LAVIE), a novel framework that bridges this modality gap through a synergistic pre-training strategy. LAVIE co-adapts a ViT backbone and an LLM fusion block by (1) employing Masked Auto-Encoding (MAE) to pre-train the ViT for richer visual representations, and (2) concurrently training Low-Rank Adaptation (LoRA) layers within the LLM block using the same MAE objective. This joint optimization guides the ViT to produce LLM-aligned features and the LLM to effectively interpret visual information. We demonstrate through extensive experiments that LAVIE significantly improves performance in various downstream vision tasks, offering an effective and efficient way to enhance visual understanding using frozen LLM knowledge. Code is available at https://github.com/selimkuzucu/LAVIE
arxiv_record.authors: Selim Kuzucu, Muhammad Ferjad Naeem, Anna Kukleva, Federico Tombari, Bernt Schiele
arxiv_record.comments: Published in Transactions on Machine Learning Research (TMLR), 32 pages, 7 figures
arxiv_record.title: Enhancing Self-Supervised Visual Representation Learning via Low-Rank Adapted LLMs

LAVIE co-adapts a ViT backbone and an LLM fusion block by (1) employing Masked Auto-Encoding (MAE) to pre-train the ViT for richer visual representations, and (2) concurrently training Low-Rank Adaptation (LoRA) layers within the LLM block using the same MAE objective. This joint optimization guides the ViT to produce LLM-aligned features and the LLM to effectively interpret visual information. We demonstrate through extensive experiments that LAVIE significantly improves performance in various downstream vision tasks, offering an effective and efficient way to enhance visual understanding using frozen LLM knowledge. Code is available at https://github.com/selimkuzucu/LAVIE

arxiv_record.abstract: Traditional continual learning methods prioritize knowledge retention and focus primarily on mitigating catastrophic forgetting, implicitly assuming that the data distribution of previously learned tasks remains static. This overlooks the dynamic nature of real-world data streams, where concept drift permanently alters previously seen data and demands both stability and rapid adaptation. We introduce a holistic framework for continual learning under concept drift that simulates realistic scenarios by evolving task distributions. As a baseline, we consider Full Relearning (FR), in which the model is retrained from scratch on newly labeled samples from the drifted distribution. While effective, this approach incurs substantial annotation and computational overhead. To address these limitations, we propose Adaptive Memory Realignment (AMR), a lightweight alternative that equips rehearsal-based learners with a drift-aware adaptation mechanism. AMR selectively removes outdated samples of drifted classes from the replay buffer and repopulates it with a small number of up-to-date instances, effectively realigning memory with the new distribution. This targeted resampling matches the performance of FR while reducing the need for labeled data and computation by orders of magnitude. To enable reproducible evaluation, we introduce four concept drift variants of standard vision benchmarks, where previously seen classes reappear with shifted representations. Comprehensive experiments on these datasets using several rehearsal-based baselines show that AMR consistently counters concept drift, maintaining high accuracy with minimal overhead. These results position AMR as a scalable solution that reconciles stability and plasticity in non-stationary continual learning environments. Full implementation of our framework and benchmark datasets is available at: github.com/AlifAshrafee/CL-Under-Concept-Drift.

arxiv_record.abstract: Understanding the locus of semantic representation in large language models (LLMs) is crucial for interpretability and architectural innovation. The dominant paradigm posits that trainable input embeddings serve as foundational "meaning vectors." This paper challenges that view. We construct Transformer models where the embedding layer is entirely frozen, with vectors derived not from data, but from the visual structure of Unicode glyphs. These non-semantic, precomputed visual embeddings are fixed throughout training. Our method is compatible with any tokenizer, including a novel Unicode-centric tokenizer we introduce to ensure universal text coverage. Despite the absence of trainable, semantically initialized embeddings, our models converge, generate coherent text, and, critically, outperform architecturally identical models with trainable embeddings on the MMLU reasoning benchmark. We attribute this to "representational interference" in conventional models, where the embedding layer is burdened with learning both structural and semantic features. Our results indicate that high-level semantics are not inherent to input embeddings but are an emergent property of the Transformer's compositional architecture and data scale. This reframes the role of embeddings from meaning containers to structural primitives. We release all code and models to foster further research.

arxiv_record.abstract: Understanding how different AI models encode the same high-level concepts, such as objects or attributes, remains challenging because each model typically produces its own isolated representation. Existing interpretability methods like Sparse Autoencoders (SAEs) produce latent concepts individually for each model, resulting in incompatible concept spaces and limiting cross-model interpretability. To address this, we introduce SPARC (Sparse Autoencoders for Aligned Representation of Concepts), a new framework that learns a single, unified latent space shared across diverse architectures and modalities (e.g., vision models like DINO, and multimodal models like CLIP). SPARC's alignment is enforced through two key innovations: (1) a Global TopK sparsity mechanism, ensuring all input streams activate identical latent dimensions for a given concept; and (2) a Cross-Reconstruction Loss, which explicitly encourages semantic consistency between models. On Open Images, SPARC dramatically improves concept alignment, achieving a Jaccard similarity of 0.80, more than tripling the alignment compared to previous methods. SPARC creates a shared sparse latent space where individual dimensions often correspond to similar high-level concepts across models and modalities, enabling direct comparison of how different architectures represent identical concepts without requiring manual alignment or model-specific analysis. As a consequence of this aligned representation, SPARC also enables practical applications such as text-guided spatial localization in vision-only models and cross-model/cross-modal retrieval. Code and models are available at https://github.com/AtlasAnalyticsLab/SPARC
arxiv_record.authors: Ali Nasiri-Sarvi, Hassan Rivaz, Mahdi S. Hosseini

arxiv_record.abstract: The general trace reconstruction problem seeks to recover an original sequence from its noisy copies independently corrupted by insertions, deletions, and substitutions. This problem arises in applications such as DNA data storage, a promising storage medium due to its high information density and longevity. However, errors introduced during DNA synthesis, storage, and sequencing require correction through algorithms and codes, with trace reconstruction often used as part of data retrieval. In this work, we propose TReconLM, a decoder-only transformer that solves trace reconstruction as a next-token prediction task. TReconLM outperforms state-of-the-art trace reconstruction algorithms, including prior deep-learning approaches, recovering a substantially higher fraction of sequences without error. We pretrain on synthetic data generated from a simple error model and fine-tune on real-world data to adapt to technology-specific error patterns. Code is available at https://github.com/MLI-lab/TReconLM.
arxiv_record.authors: Franziska Weindel, Michael Girsch and Reinhard Heckel
arxiv_record.title: Trace Reconstruction with Language Models

arxiv_record.abstract: Machine learning interatomic potentials trained on first-principles reference data are becoming valuable tools for computational physics, biology, and chemistry. Equivariant message-passing neural networks, including transformers, achieve state-of-the-art accuracy but rely on cutoff-based graphs, limiting their ability to capture long-range effects such as electrostatics or dispersion, as well as electron delocalization. While long-range correction schemes based on inverse power laws of interatomic distances have been proposed, they are unable to communicate higher-order geometric information and are thus limited in applicability. To address this shortcoming, we propose the use of equivariant, rather than scalar, charges for long-range interactions, and design a graph neural network architecture, LOREM, around this long-range message passing mechanism. We consider several datasets specifically designed to highlight non-local physical effects, and compare short-range message passing with different receptive fields to invariant and equivariant long-range message passing. Even though most approaches work for careful dataset-specific choices of their model hyperparameters, LOREM works consistently without such changes, with excellent benchmark performance.
arxiv_record.authors: Egor Rumiantsev, Marcel F. Langer, Tulga-Erdene Sodjargal, Michele Ceriotti, Philip Loche
arxiv_record.title: Learning Long-Range Representations with Equivariant Messages

C2.justification: V2 explicitly frames the work as a proof of concept and explains why aggregate errors on heterogeneous datasets can obscure contributions from long-range physics. Appendix D adds qualifications about numerical precision and the imperfect relationship between validation error and qualitative cumulene curves. The earlier limitations concerning distance decay, naive quadratic evaluation, and inadequate benchmarks remain.

D1.justification: V1 promises a future code and data release; v2 states that code, data, configurations, and trained models are available in a specified Zenodo archive. V2 also supplies float32 training information, more detailed PET settings and model counts, tuning procedures, and hardware and training-time information for the added experiments. These substantially expand documented reproducibility.

E1.justification: The five original benchmarks are retained. Appendix J adds ADAPT silicon point-defect configurations with 24 dopant elements and 52 dopant pairs, substantially extending the evaluated materials coverage. Appendix E also introduces periodic NaCl, CsCl, and Cu2O supercells for runtime evaluation.

E2.justification: SpookyNet is added to the MgO and NaCl comparisons in Table 1. The new ADAPT comparison includes ADAPT Small/Large, MatterSim, and several pretrained MACE variants alongside retrained MACE. CACE's renaming to CACE-LES represents the same retained comparator.

E3.justification: V1 specifies LAMB throughout; v2 specifies ADAM except for cumulene and changes the MgO energy-loss weight from 100 to 1000. PET's cumulene settings also change, including batch size 32 to 16, attention layers, and learning-rate scheduling. New protocols include the inner 4000/500 tuning split, runtime scaling measurements, additional error metrics, and ADAPT evaluation on 100 held-out trajectory starting structures.

E4.justification: Beyond the retained cutoff, message-passing-depth, and SN2 analyses, Appendix F systematically compares no long-range block and long-range orders l=0,1,2 across four benchmarks. Appendix E analyzes runtime scaling and long-range overhead, while Appendix H tests whether tuning and early stopping on the reported validation set affect conclusions. These address substantial new questions about mechanism, efficiency, and evaluation robustness.

E5.justification: V2 newly discloses two LOREM training seeds, reporting the better run in the main table and the alternative run in Tables 11–12. arxiv_record.abstract: We propose a new framework for generating tabular synthetic datasets via disjoint generative models. In this paradigm, a dataset is partitioned into disjoint subsets that are supplied to separate instances of generative models. The results are then combined post hoc by a joining operation that works in the absence of common variables/identifiers. The success of the framework is demonstrated through several case studies and examples on tabular data that help illuminate some of the design choices that one may make. The advantages achieved by the disjoint generation include: i) An observed increase in the empirical measurement of privacy. ii) Increased computational feasibility of certain model types. iii) Ability to generate synthetic data using a mixture of different generative models. Specifically, mixed-model synthesis bridges the gap between privacy and utility performance, providing highly competitive performance on Accuracy and Area Under the Curve for downstream tasks while significantly lowering the empirical re-identification risk.

arxiv_record.abstract: Large Language Models (LLMs) have demonstrated remarkable capabilities across diverse tasks but remain fundamentally static, unable to adapt their internal parameters to novel tasks, evolving knowledge domains, or dynamic interaction contexts. As LLMs are increasingly deployed in open-ended, interactive environments, this static nature has become a critical bottleneck, necessitating agents that can adaptively reason, act, and evolve in real time. This paradigm shift -- from scaling static models to developing self-evolving agents -- has sparked growing interest in architectures and methods enabling continual learning and adaptation from data, interactions, and experiences. This survey provides the first systematic and comprehensive review of self-evolving agents, organizing the field around three foundational dimensions: what, when, and how to evolve. We examine evolutionary mechanisms across agent components (e.g., models, memory, tools, architecture), categorize adaptation methods by stages (e.g., intra-test-time, inter-test-time), and analyze the algorithmic and architectural designs that guide evolutionary adaptation (e.g., scalar rewards, textual feedback, single-agent and multi-agent systems). Additionally, we analyze evaluation metrics and benchmarks tailored for self-evolving agents, highlight applications in domains such as coding, education, and healthcare, and identify critical challenges and research directions in safety, scalability, and co-evolutionary dynamics. By providing a structured framework for understanding and designing self-evolving agents, this survey establishes a roadmap for advancing more adaptive, robust, and versatile agentic systems in both research and real-world deployments, and ultimately sheds light on the realization of Artificial Super Intelligence (ASI) where agents evolve autonomously and perform beyond human-level intelligence across tasks.

arxiv_record.abstract: Text embeddings, i.e. vector representations of entire texts, play an important role in many NLP applications, such as retrieval-augmented generation, clustering, or visualizing collections of texts for data exploration. Currently, top-performing embedding models are derived from pre-trained language models via supervised contrastive fine-tuning. This fine-tuning strategy relies on an external notion of similarity and annotated data for generation of positive pairs. Here we study self-supervised fine-tuning and systematically compare the two most well-known augmentation strategies used for fine-tuning text embeddings models. We assess embedding quality on MTEB and additional in-domain evaluations and show that cropping augmentation strongly outperforms the dropout-based approach. We find that on out-of-domain data, the quality of resulting embeddings is substantially below the supervised state-of-the-art models, but for in-domain data, self-supervised fine-tuning can produce high-quality text embeddings after very short fine-tuning. Finally, we show that representation quality increases towards the last transformer layers, which undergo the largest change during fine-tuning; and that fine-tuning only those last layers is sufficient to reach similar embedding quality.
arxiv_record.authors: Rita Gonz\'alez-M\'arquez, Philipp Berens, Dmitry Kobak
arxiv_record.title: Cropping outperforms dropout as an augmentation strategy for self-supervised training of text embeddings

arxiv_record.abstract: We consider the problem of online regret minimization in linear bandits with access to prior observations (offline data) from the underlying bandit model. There are numerous applications where extensive offline data is often available, such as in recommendation systems, online advertising. Consequently, this problem has been studied intensively in recent literature. Our algorithm, Offline-Online Phased Elimination (OOPE), effectively incorporates the offline data to substantially reduce the online regret compared to prior work. To leverage offline information prudently, OOPE uses an extended D-optimal design within each exploration phase. OOPE achieves an online regret is $\tilde{O}(\sqrt{\deff T \log \left(|\mathcal{A}|T\right)}+d^2)$. $\deff \leq d)$ is the effective problem dimension which measures the number of poorly explored directions in offline data and depends on the eigen-spectrum $(\lambda_k)_{k \in [d]}$ of the Gram matrix of the offline data. The eigen-spectrum $(\lambda_k)_{k \in [d]}$ is a quantitative measure of the \emph{quality} of offline data. If the offline data is poorly explored ($\deff \approx d$), we recover the established regret bounds for purely online setting while, when offline data is abundant ($\Toff >> T$) and well-explored ($\deff = o(1) $), the online regret reduces substantially. Additionally, we provide the first known minimax regret lower bounds in this setting that depend explicitly on the quality of the offline data. These lower bounds establish the optimality of our algorithm in regimes where offline data is either well-explored or poorly explored. Finally, by using a Frank-Wolfe approximation to the extended optimal design we further improve the $O(d^{2})$ term to $O\left(\frac{d^{2}}{\deff} \min \{ \deff,1\} \right)$, which can be substantial in high dimensions with moderate quality of offline data $\deff = \Omega(1)$.

arxiv_record.abstract: We consider the problem of designing constraint-aware flow matching (FM) models that address the issue of constraint violations commonly observed in vanilla generative models. We consider two scenarios, viz.: (a) when a differentiable distance function to the constraint set is given, and (b) when the constraint set is only available via queries to a membership oracle. For case (a), we propose a simple adaptation of the FM objective with an additional term that penalizes the distance between the constraint set and the generated samples. For case (b), we propose to employ randomization and learn a mean flow that is numerically shown to have a high likelihood of satisfying the constraints. This approach deviates significantly from existing works that require simple convex constraints, knowledge of a barrier function, or a reflection mechanism to constrain the probability flow. Furthermore, in the proposed setting we show that a two-stage approach, where both stages approximate the same original flow but with only the second stage probing the constraints via randomization, is more computationally efficient than the corresponding one-stage approach. Through several synthetic cases of constrained generation, we numerically show that the proposed approaches achieve significant gains in terms of constraint satisfaction while matching the target distributions. As a showcase for a practical oracle-based constraint, we show how our approach can be used for training an adversarial example generator, using queries to a hard-label black-box classifier. We conclude with several future research directions. Our code is available at https://github.com/ZhengyanHuan/FM-RE.
arxiv_record.authors: Zhengyan Huan, Jacob Boerma, Li-Ping Liu, Shuchin Aeron

arxiv_record.abstract: Dimensionality reduction techniques are widely used for visualizing high-dimensional data in two dimensions. Existing methods are typically designed to preserve either local (e.g., $t$-SNE, UMAP) or global (e.g., MDS, PCA) structure of the data, but none of the established methods can represent both aspects well. In this paper, we present DREAMS (Dimensionality Reduction Enhanced Across Multiple Scales), a method that combines the local structure preservation of $t$-SNE with the global structure preservation of PCA via a simple regularization term. Our approach generates a spectrum of embeddings between the locally well-structured $t$-SNE embedding and the globally well-structured PCA embedding, efficiently balancing both local and global structure preservation. We benchmark DREAMS across eleven real-world datasets, showcasing qualitatively and quantitatively its superior ability to preserve structure across multiple scales compared to previous approaches.
arxiv_record.authors: No\"el Kury, Dmitry Kobak, Sebastian Damrich
arxiv_record.title: DREAMS: Preserving both Local and Global Structure in Dimensionality Reduction

The central contribution of combining t-SNE locality with PCA global structure and the claim of superior benchmark performance remain.

C2.justification: v2 adds explicit qualifications concerning absent theoretical guarantees, runtime overhead, CIFAR10 difficulties, and UMAP's strengths under clustering-based metrics not evaluated here. Appendix B also explains the scaling choice and gradient-induced shrinkage. Earlier limitations concerning reference-embedding bias and dataset-dependent regularization remain.

D1.justification: Appendix A documents the added datasets' sampling and preprocessing, including Mammoth coloring through agglomerative clustering and Fashion MNIST rescaling before PCA. Code links now identify the tmlr branches. Hardware and the reported CNE training budget remain unchanged.

E1.justification: Table 1 expands coverage from seven to eleven datasets, retaining all previous datasets and adding Mammoth, Landsat Satellite, Fashion MNIST, and CIFAR10. E2.justification: The main benchmark retains the same competing algorithms. E3.justification: Reported initialization changes from unit-standard-deviation PCA or approximately scale-10 MDS coordinates to first-coordinate standard deviation 10^-4. New protocols include alignment controls, runtime accounting including reference-embedding computation, and a k sweep from 1 to 200.

E4.justification: Beyond the retained CNE-versus-decoder analysis, v2 adds tests of scaling, translation, rotation, and gradient propagation in Appendix B; runtime comparisons in Appendix C; and sensitivity to the neighborhood size used for evaluation in Appendix F. These directly examine previously untested design choices and evaluation robustness.

E5.justification: Both versions specify means and uncertainties across four random seeds. v2 additionally identifies the runtime error bars as standard deviations in Figure S2, whereas v1 does not identify its uncertainty statistic. This is a limited reporting clarification, not evidence of increased run counts.

E6.justification: v2 adds results for four datasets and the new supplementary analyses, while replacing several retained-dataset scores: for example, DREAMS on Tasic changes from 0.91 to 0.88 in Table 2 under revised settings. These are not same-setting performance changes. Some new results have unexplained cross-display differences: FMNIST DREAMS-MDS scores 0.87 in Table 2 but 0.83 in Figure S14.

M1.justification: Equation 2 changes the reported regularization penalty from lambda times the squared discrepancy to lambda/n times that discrepancy. The underlying t-SNE-plus-global-reference framework, norm-ratio scaling, and CNE/decoder variants remain. This is a limited objective revision; the PDFs do not establish whether it corrects documentation or changes implementation.

P1.justification: The main section sequence and most explanatory prose remain recognizable. v2 makes local language corrections, expands selected explanations, adds publication and affiliation text, and reorganizes the appendix into separately titled sections rather than v1's three subsections.

P2.justification: Figure 3 and the CNE comparison expand into two-row displays, and Tables 1–2 accommodate the added datasets. R1.justification: Related work adds EmbedOR, UMATO, and Cluster and Embed, alongside new references supporting Procrustes analysis, evaluation qualifications, and dataset sources. These extend the context without substantially changing DREAMS' positioning relative to StarMAP and SQuadMDS-hybrid.

T1.justification: Appendix B adds a focused mathematical analysis: an alternative least-squares scaling factor, its relationship to norm-ratio scaling through Cauchy–Schwarz, and gradients with and without differentiating through the scale factor (Equations 6–9). improvement.justification: v2 substantially strengthens support for the method beyond v1's predominantly biological benchmark. A1.justification: Both PDFs describe the same DREAMS method and retain identifiable corresponding experiments. Their text, equations, tables, figures, and complete appendices support a reliable comparison despite the expanded scope in v2.

arxiv_record.abstract: Combinatorial optimization problems are ubiquitous in science and engineering. Still, learning-based approaches to accelerate combinatorial optimization often require solving a large number of difficult instances to collect training data, incurring significant computational cost. Existing learning-based methods require training dedicated models for each problem distribution, for each downstream task, severely limiting their scalability and generalization. We introduce Forge: Foundational Optimization Representations from Graph Embeddings, a framework that pre-trains a vector-quantized graph autoencoder on a large, diverse collection of mixed-integer programming (MIP) instances in an unsupervised manner, without relying on optimization solvers or optimal solutions. Vector quantization produces discrete code assignments that serve as a vocabulary for representing optimization instances. We evaluate Forge in both unsupervised and supervised settings. In the unsupervised setting, Forge embeddings effectively cluster unseen instances across problem domains and sizes. In the supervised setting, we fine-tune Forge embeddings and show that a single pre-trained model helps predicting both the integrality gap for cut-generation and variable hints for search guidance across multiple problem and size distributions. In both tasks, we improve the performance of a commercial optimization solver and outperform state-of-the-art learning-based methods. Finally, we open-source our training code, pre-trained Forge weights, and embeddings for multiple MIP distributions to foster further research in representation learning for optimization problems https://skadio.github.io/forge/
arxiv_record.authors: Zohair Shafi and Serdar Kadioglu
arxiv_record.title: FORGE: Foundational Optimization Representations from Graph Embeddings

C1.justification: The central claim—solver-independent unsupervised MIP representations supporting multiple downstream tasks—remains. v5's conclusion extends claimed applicability to preliminary MIP-to-SAT transfer and qualifies FORGE as a step toward a foundational model. Replacing 'warm-start prediction' with 'search guidance' largely clarifies the existing variable-hint application rather than introducing a different central contribution.

C2.justification: Section 7 adds specific limitations concerning training scale, unexplored code semantics, solver integration and untested downstream applications. The appendices add interpretations of codebook insensitivity, covering/packing directions and cross-domain transfer. v5 also discusses the accuracy/computation tradeoff against strong hand-crafted features and distinguishes FORGE's sharing across problems from Cai et al.'s sharing across tasks, substantially refining the account of generalization.

D1.justification: Most hardware, learning rates, epochs and solver budgets were already disclosed and move to A.7. New details include Gurobi v12.0.3, equal BCE/triplet weighting, explicit PS-Gurobi retraining, and GPU-driven exclusion of very large training instances. A.1 and A.6 document baseline and SAT features. The stated release expands from code/pretrained weights to datasets, fine-tuned models and ready-made benchmark embeddings; availability is not independently verified.

E1.justification: v5 adds strIPlib evaluation across ten named optimization families, solver-configuration prediction using SCIP, and SAT/UNSAT-aware clustering on G4SATBench (A.2, A.5–A.6). This substantially expands task and domain coverage beyond the original optimization experiments. Figure 3 also changes the displayed difficulty groups, although its legend disagrees with the retained category list in Section 4.

E2.justification: v5 adds the Hutter et al. (2014) hand-crafted feature baseline to clustering and directly evaluates Cai et al. (2025a)'s multitask model for solver configuration (Figure 8; Table 3). These introduce substantive external comparisons absent from v1's experiments. The original mean-readout, label-propagation, Gurobi, Li et al. and PS-Gurobi comparisons remain; the random-feature PS-Gurobi control moves to Appendix A.8.

E3.justification: Section 4 changes the reported clustering test size from 1,050 to 1,000 instances. Added protocols include 500 strIPlib instances, codebooks ranging from 500 to 10,000 entries, embedding-arithmetic controls fixing graph size and solving difficulty, SCIP configuration evaluation, and 1,400 Hard SAT formulas grouped by problem type and feasibility. These substantially extend evaluation design; the original Gurobi time limits and principal training budgets are retained.

E4.justification: Appendix A.3 adds codebook-size sensitivity analysis, A.4 tests whether embedding arithmetic reflects covering/packing relationships, and A.6 compares unchanged MIP features with SAT-adapted features to isolate feature specialization. These address new questions about representation behavior and transfer. The pretraining-versus-scratch comparison and PS-Gurobi random-feature control already existed in v1; relocating the latter is not a new ablation.

E5.justification: Both versions average clustering NMI over ten k-means runs, and v1 Figure 3 already displays ± uncertainty terms. v5 extends that reporting convention to additional results without documenting a new uncertainty-estimation procedure, increased run count or seed policy. Appendix A.3's significance statement supplies no identifiable new test procedure.

E6.justification: Figure 3 changes mean-readout NMI from 0.087 to 0.726 and FORGE NMI from 0.843 to 0.953; changed sample counts and plotted categories prevent treating these as same-setting gains. New results include static-feature NMI 0.991, codebook sensitivity, SAT-transfer NMIs 0.76 and 0.77, and configuration runtimes—for example, 801.21 seconds for Cai et al. versus 670.95 for FORGE on CA. Original integrality-prediction errors and displayed solver-gain percentages are retained.

M1.justification: The GraphSAGE/vector-quantization backbone and pretraining losses remain unchanged. The reported search-guidance procedure changes from top-5% positive candidates to top-decile candidates and describes separate negative-anchor neighborhoods; hard-negative selection changes from proximity to the positive variable to proximity to the anchor. Appendices A.5–A.6 add configuration-prediction heads and a SAT-specific input-feature variant using unchanged pretrained weights. These are limited adaptations of the existing framework.

P1.justification: v5 extensively rewrites the introduction and experimental narrative, consistently reframes warm starts as search guidance, merges numerical-results subsections into task descriptions, moves setup details to A.7, and splits related work between Section 6 and A.9. The former conclusion becomes a structured limitations/future-work discussion. These are substantial changes to the existing document's organization and exposition.

P2.justification: v5 adds static-feature, strIPlib, embedding-arithmetic and SAT plots plus three tables. Existing diagrams and solver plots are enlarged or relabeled, and Figure 3 is replotted with changed categories and axis labels. The original three-way PS-Gurobi plot is retained as Figure 14 while a two-method view appears in Figure 7. Typography, margins and figure placement are extensively revised.

R1.justification: Beyond relocating existing related work, v5 substantially expands positioning around GNN expressivity and foldable MILPs, hand-crafted instance features, algorithm selection and portfolios, online neighborhood search, and optimization-to-SAT transfer. New relevant works include Hutter et al.'s feature studies, Chen et al.'s MILP representation analysis, G4SATBench and Pal and Kadıoğlu's transfer work. Bibliographic duplicates and publication updates do not account for this substantive expansion.

T1.justification: Appendix A.4 adds explicit covering/packing problem formulations, the vertex-cover/independent-set complement relation, and mathematical definitions of embedding centroids, difference vectors and translations in Equations 6–9. The original model losses and triplet-loss equation remain unchanged. No new theorem or proof establishing FORGE's capabilities is supplied; the GNN expressivity discussion summarizes prior work.

improvement.justification: v5 substantially strengthens evaluation of the central general-purpose representation claim. The strong hand-crafted comparator, additional optimization and SAT domains, third downstream task and codebook ablation address important gaps in v1's validation; explicit limitations also better qualify the foundational-model framing. The revised clustering account remains insufficiently reconciled: Section 4 reports 1,000 instances and 21 groups, Figure 3 lists 20 groups, and A.3 uses 1,050 instances. Despite this reporting weakness and sparse statistical-test details, the broader, more discriminating evidence provides a substantial net quality improvement.

A1.justification: Both PDFs describe the same FORGE research. Their text, equations, figures and tables support reliable comparison, including all nine appendix subsections in v5. v1 has no appendix.

after.justification: v5 retains original empirical evaluations and adds appendix experiments on static features, strIPlib, codebook size, embedding arithmetic, solver configuration and SAT transfer.

before.justification: Sections 4–5 report original clustering, integrality-gap prediction, solver-guidance and PS-Gurobi augmentation experiments.

arxiv_record.abstract: Large language models demonstrate impressive results across diverse tasks but are still known to hallucinate, generating linguistically plausible but incorrect answers to questions. Uncertainty quantification has been proposed as a strategy for hallucination detection, requiring estimates for both global uncertainty (attributed to a batch of responses) and local uncertainty (attributed to individual responses). While recent black-box approaches have shown some success, they often rely on disjoint heuristics or graph-theoretic approximations that lack a unified geometric interpretation. We introduce a geometric framework to address this, based on archetypal analysis of batches of responses sampled with only black-box model access. At the global level, we propose Geometric Volume, which measures the convex hull volume of archetypes derived from response embeddings. At the local level, we propose Geometric Suspicion, which leverages the spatial relationship between responses and these archetypes to rank reliability, enabling hallucination reduction through preferential response selection. Unlike prior methods that rely on discrete pairwise comparisons, our approach provides continuous semantic boundary points which have utility for attributing reliability to individual responses. Experiments show that our framework performs comparably to or better than prior methods on short form question-answering datasets, and achieves superior results on medical datasets where hallucinations carry particularly critical risks. We also provide theoretical justification by proving a link between convex hull volume and entropy.
arxiv_record.authors: Edward Phillips, Sean Wu, Soheila Molaei, Danielle Belgrave, Anshul Thakur, David Clifton
arxiv_record.comments: Revision. Clarified positioning as a unified geometric framework for global and local uncertainty in LLMs. Added baselines (Degree, Eccentricity) and expanded comparison to related methods. Included ablations (PCA dimension, number of archetypes, number of samples) and complexity analysis. Extended discussion of medical QA results and model-specific behaviour
arxiv_record.title: Geometric Uncertainty for Detecting and Correcting Hallucinations in LLMs

C1.justification: v1 claims that no existing black-box approach supplies both global and local uncertainty and presents Geometric Suspicion as the first sampling-based black-box local method. v2 removes these broad priority claims and emphasizes a unified geometric alternative to existing graph-based approaches. This substantially narrows the claimed novelty, while retaining the overall detection and correction contributions.

C2.justification: v1 emphasizes deferral for high-dispersion batches and correction for intermediate hallucination rates. v2 substantially reframes the discussion around semantic distributions, limitations of single-vector representations, and confidently wrong models with little response diversity. It interprets Qwen3-8B/TriviaQA failure through the scarcity of correct alternatives and adds explanations connecting the component metrics to Degree and Eccentricity.

D1.justification: Appendix B.3 newly identifies the adapted UQ-NLG baseline code, the entailment variant using DeBERTa-Large, and an eigenvalue threshold of 0.7. Appendix C documents reproduction details for the new ablations, including PCA handling and archetype-count constraints. The original embedding model, optimization steps, and main hyperparameters are retained.

E1.justification: Both versions use CLAMBER, TriviaQA, text-only ScienceQA, MedicalQA, and K-QA for the same ambiguity-detection and question-answering tasks. The new analyses reuse this coverage; sample-size sweeps and changes to filtered-subset reporting concern evaluation design rather than new datasets or tasks.

E2.justification: v1 Table 2 compares Geometric Suspicion selection with default greedy responses. v2 adds Degree and Eccentricity as competing local uncertainty methods across four QA benchmarks and four LLMs, substantially expanding direct comparative evaluation. The global comparators—Semantic Volume, Semantic Entropy, and p(true)—are retained.

E3.justification: v2 adds per-question AUARC evaluation and replaces Table 2's absolute hallucination rates and separate mid-valid subset reporting with ΔH/AUARC comparisons. Appendix C introduces controlled sample-count, PCA-dimension, and archetype-count sweeps, including subset-specific PCA refitting and fixed-basis truncation. The original dataset construction, default hyperparameters, and validation split remain unchanged.

E4.justification: New Appendix C tests sensitivity to response count, embedding dimension, and archetype count for local and global uncertainty. Appendix E adds an analysis relating correction performance to available correct responses. Figure 3 replaces two illustrative cases, while the earlier mid-valid performance breakdown disappears. The existing Appendix D component-selection analysis is retained.

E5.justification: Table 2 changes its stated uncertainty convention from standard errors to standard deviations across runs. Appendix C introduces 30 within-question subset resamples for the sample-count analysis and explains aggregation; Figure 5 adds a quadratic fit with a 95% confidence interval. Both versions retain three main experimental runs, so this does not establish an increase in that run count.

E6.justification: v2 adds baseline and AUARC results, ablation results, and the corrective-potential relationship, while removing absolute hallucination rates and mid-valid results from Table 2. Some proposed-method values change: Qwen3-8b/MedicalQA ΔH is 7.4 percentage points in v1 and 8.0 in v2 under the revised scoring rule. Global Table 1 and the Appendix D Mann–Whitney results remain numerically unchanged.

M1.justification: The final Geometric Suspicion aggregation changes from summing component ranks in v1 Eq. 6 to combining empirical right-tail probabilities using Fisher's method in v2 Eqs. 7–8. This changes the response-ranking rule but is a localized refinement: the three component metrics, archetypal analysis, global volume score, and minimum-score selection remain.

P1.justification: The abstract, contribution statements, local-method explanations, and discussion are substantially rewritten. The theorem moves from the appendix into the methodology, case-study interpretation moves into the results, and the proof and experimental appendices are reorganized. These alter the narrative structure beyond simply appending new experiments.

P2.justification: Table 2 is reorganized from dataset-grouped hallucination-rate breakdowns into model-grouped method comparisons. Figure 3 is redrawn using UMAP instead of t-SNE, with new annotations and two replacement examples. v2 also adds five ablation tables and Figure 5's regression plot; the earlier appendix tables are retained as Tables 8–9.

R1.justification: The new Semantic Space Confidence discussion positions the method against Semantic Density and the already-cited Lin et al. work's Degree/Eccentricity methods, substantially revising its relationship to prior local uncertainty research. Bhardwaj et al. and Han et al. are newly cited for long-form representation and factuality limitations. Lin's changed citation year does not represent a newly added work.

T1.justification: The entropy–volume theorem, assumptions, corollary, and proof retain their mathematical substance; moving the theorem into Section 3.3 is not new theory. v2 revises the formal suspicion-score definition and adds Appendix F's time and memory complexity arguments, O(Tnd'K) and O(nd'+nK+Kd').

improvement.justification: v2 addresses v1's lack of established local-method comparisons through Degree/Eccentricity evaluations, adds parameter-sensitivity and corrective-potential evidence, and narrows the first-of-kind novelty claim. These substantially strengthen validation and clarify the main contribution's scope. Removing absolute hallucination rates and the mid-valid breakdown loses useful detail, and no direct ablation establishes that Fisher fusion improves on rank summation, but the overall gain in evidential support and qualification is substantial.

A1.justification: Both PDFs describe the same research work. All 17 pages of v1 and 20 pages of v2, including appendices, are readable, and the methods, equations, tables, and figures can be matched across revisions and relocations.

after.justification: v2 retains original benchmark experiments and adds local-method comparisons, parameter ablations, and an empirical analysis of corrective potential in Appendices C and E.

before.justification: Tables 1–2 report original hallucination-detection and response-selection experiments across four LLMs. Appendix D reports original analyses supporting the component metrics.

arxiv_record.abstract: Harnessing parallelism in seemingly sequential models is a central challenge for modern machine learning. Several approaches have been proposed for evaluating sequential processes in parallel using iterative fixed-point methods, like Newton, Picard, and Jacobi iterations. In this work, we show that these methods can be understood within a common framework based on linear dynamical systems (LDSs), where different iteration schemes arise naturally as approximate linearizations of a nonlinear recursion. Moreover, we theoretically analyze the rates of convergence of these methods, and we verify the predictions of this theory with several case studies. This unifying framework highlights shared principles behind these techniques and clarifies when particular fixed-point methods are most likely to be effective. By bridging diverse algorithms through the language of LDSs, the framework provides a clearer theoretical foundation for parallelizing sequential models and points toward new opportunities for efficient and scalable computation.

C1.justification: The abstract and introduction add convergence-rate analysis as an explicit central contribution, linking rates to approximation fidelity and LDS stability. Case studies are now presented as validation of theoretical predictions, extending v1's central claims beyond unification and heuristic guidance.

C2.justification: v2 removes v1's broad dismissal of Jacobi for Markovian models and replaces Table 1's convergence-based ordering with approximation order. Interpretations now accommodate Jacobi's favorable GRU behavior and distinguish approximation accuracy from LDS stability. Appendix C.2 adds explicit local-basin conditions and limitations of the convergence bound.

D1.justification: Appendix E documents the new diagonal experiment's zero trajectory initialization and dimensions, the GRU diagnostic configuration, and the Langevin step-size settings. These are limited reproducibility additions. The existing JAX/Equinox implementation, H100 hardware disclosure, stochastic diagonal estimator, and code-access information are retained.

E1.justification: v2 adds the synthetic diagonal-LDS scenario x(t+1) = alpha x(t), testing contraction dynamics distinct from the retained permutation, GRU, and Langevin settings (Appendix C.4). The existing application coverage remains; the additional Langevin parameter sweep stays within that coverage.

E2.justification: Jacobi is newly evaluated alongside sequential evaluation, Picard, quasi-Newton, and Newton in all three main case studies (v1 Figures 1–3 versus v2 Figures 2–4). Previously it was discussed theoretically but omitted from these comparisons. This substantially expands the central solver comparisons.

E3.justification: Existing experiments retain the residual tolerance of 5e-4 and batch size 16. New protocols include a D=2, T=100 diagonal-LDS test measuring iterations to trajectory error below 1e-5, D=8/T=1000 GRU diagnostics, and Langevin step sizes 1e-5, 1e-4, and 1e-3 at D=2, 4, and 8.

E4.justification: v2 adds controlled Jacobi-versus-Picard contraction analysis (Figure 7), diagnostics connecting GRU Jacobians and convergence factors to solver behavior (Figure 8), and Langevin step-size sensitivity (Figure 10). These substantially strengthen mechanism and sensitivity analysis. v1's mixture-component analysis is retained as v2 Figure 9.

E5.justification: Figure 8 newly shows cross-seed distributions of inverse-Jacobian norms and convergence factors, exposing variability beyond v1's median performance curves. The existing ten-seed reporting and five timed repetitions per seed remain unchanged; no increased replication, confidence intervals, or significance tests are reported.

E6.justification: New results show Jacobi achieving GRU speedups while requiring approximately T iterations for S5 and Langevin problems (Figures 2–4). Figures 7, 8, and 10 add contraction trajectories, Jacobian diagnostics, and a Picard/Newton timing reversal as Langevin step size increases. These materially extend the reported findings.

M1.justification: Algorithm 1 and the intended Newton, diagonal quasi-Newton, Picard, and Jacobi procedures are retained. Hutchinson diagonal estimation and clip-ELK already appear in v1 and remain in v2. Expanded explanations and convergence analysis do not introduce a new algorithm.

P1.justification: The introduction, method explanations, case-study narratives, and related-work discussion are substantially rewritten. The former Section 2.5 summary is condensed, and the narrative becomes framework, convergence analysis, then empirical validation. Existing experimental and related-work appendices move to E and F, alongside new C and D; author and publication information also changes.

P2.justification: v2 adds a parallel-scan schematic and three substantial analytical figures (Figures 1, 7, 8, and 10). Table 1 gains a parallelization column, and the main experimental plots gain Jacobi curves, revised legends, captions, and some axis ranges. Existing appendix illustrations and the mixture-component plot are retained and renumbered.

R1.justification: v2 substantially expands historical and theoretical positioning through Bellen and Zennaro, Gander and Vandewalle, Kelley, and Lu et al., among others. It acknowledges earlier parareal frameworks, narrows the LDS-unification novelty claim to the machine-learning community, and explicitly positions its convergence analysis as extending prior results.

T1.justification: v2 adds a Lipschitz-based error bound and proof (Proposition 3), a Jacobian-difference norm identity (Lemma 1), and an exact Picard inverse-norm formula and proof (Lemma 2), with supporting Appendices C–D. Existing group-word and R-convergence propositions are retained and renumbered. The Picard summation's lower index is also corrected from 1 to 0.

improvement.justification: v1's method-selection advice was largely heuristic and broadly dismissed Jacobi without evaluating it. v2 adds an explicit convergence bound with limitations, direct comparisons correcting that guidance, and diagnostic and sensitivity experiments supporting more conditional recommendations. These changes substantially improve scientific support and practical reliability, although the bounds remain conservative and do not establish exact wall-clock rankings.

A1.justification: Both PDFs describe the same LDS framework and core case studies. Their main text, equations, figures, tables, and complete appendices are readable and can be matched despite substantial expansion and reorganization.

after.justification: v2 retains original simulation results and adds Jacobi comparisons, a diagonal-LDS simulation, GRU Jacobian diagnostics, and Langevin step-size experiments.

before.justification: v1 reports original simulations measuring convergence iterations and wall-clock time for S5 word problems, randomly initialized GRUs, and Gaussian-mixture Langevin dynamics, including an appendix experiment varying mixture components.

arxiv_record.abstract: The reliability of large language models (LLMs) during test-time scaling is often assessed with \emph{external verifiers} or \emph{reward models} that distinguish correct reasoning from flawed logic. Prior work has studied both outcome reward models (ORMs), which assess only the final answer, and process reward models (PRMs), which score intermediate reasoning steps. Although PRMs are often viewed as advantageous due to their finer-grained supervision, much of the supporting evidence comes from math-adjacent settings, and their relative benefits across broader domains remain unclear. We present the first unified evaluation of four reward model variants, discriminative ORM and PRM (dORM, dPRM) and generative ORM and PRM (gORM, gPRM), across 14 diverse domains. Contrary to conventional wisdom, we find that (i) dORM performs on par with dPRM, (ii) gPRM is not competitive, and (iii) overall, gORM is the most robust, yielding significant and consistent gains across every tested domain. We attribute the worse performance of gPRM to the stepwise scoring process, which inherits label noise from LLM-based automatic labeling, leading to difficulties in evaluating long reasoning trajectories, including those involving self-correcting reasoning. Both our theoretical analysis and empirical observations indicate that stepwise aggregation compounds errors as reasoning length increases. These findings challenge the common assumption that fine-grained supervision is always better and support generative outcome verification for multi-domain deployment. Our \href{https://github.com/db-Lee/Multi-RM}{\underline{code}} is publicly available to facilitate future research in multi-domain settings.

C1.justification: The central contributions remain a controlled four-variant evaluation across 14 domains, comparable multi-domain performance of dORM and dPRM, gORM's overall robustness, and length/noise explanations for PRM weaknesses. The added benchmarks and controls principally supply further evidence for these retained claims.

C2.justification: v3 clarifies that outcome supervision still allows ORMs to use intermediate reasoning, adds an annotation-reliability qualification to the 'aha' analysis, and interprets refinement and relaxed filtering as insufficient to resolve gPRM's weakness. It also removes v1's explicit limitation that verifiable-outcome results may not generalize to open-ended generation.

D1.justification: v3 adds seed-specific and Qwen3-8B checkpoint listings, access entries for the new evaluation datasets, blank-category prompt instructions, label-refinement details, and inference timings. Existing prompts and most training hyperparameters remain. The explicit 750/650-token sequence-limit statement in v1 is removed, without establishing an actual change to those limits.

E1.justification: v3 adds evaluation on graduate-level science questions in GPQA-Diamond and specialized medical and legal examination questions in MedQA and LEXam. Testing MMLU-Pro-trained verifiers on these datasets substantially expands coverage beyond the retained mathematical benchmarks and MMLU-Pro evaluation.

E2.justification: The four verifier variants and majority voting remain the principal comparisons. Tables 7–12 additionally compare label-refined or relaxed-filtering PRMs and product, mean, and last-step dPRM aggregation against the existing methods. Pass@N is added as an oracle reference.

E3.justification: v3 adds cross-dataset transfer evaluation with N=16, restricts MedQA/LEXam comparisons to two generators, introduces a Qwen3-8B verifier backbone, and evaluates additional learning rates, LoRA ranks, and aggregation settings. Some Appendix F backbone identifications and the length-bin boundaries in v1 Figure 38/v3 Figure 9b also change; these reported revisions do not establish that the corresponding experiments were rerun.

E4.justification: New analyses test whether PRM weaknesses depend on distilled backbones, hyperparameter choices, aggregation rules, label quality, or strict consensus filtering (Figure 37 and Tables 3, 5–12). v1 Figure 39's per-dataset 'aha' breakdown is removed. The complete label-noise study moves from v1 Figure 40 to v3 Figure 11 and is not a new analysis.

E5.justification: Appendix D changes the reported replication from three independent runs for mathematics and one for multi-domain experiments to five independent runs, except experiments using R1-Distill-Llama-8B or Qwen3-8B. v3 also lists checkpoints for seeds 1–5. This is an explicit expansion of reported replication.

E6.justification: v3 adds specialized-benchmark, backbone, tuning, filtering, aggregation, and timing results, and revises several retained curves. Newly reported Table 7 gives N=16 gPRM accuracy of 64.26%, 64.84% with label refinement, and 64.82% with relaxed filtering, versus 70.02% for gORM. These are additional comparisons within v3, not version-to-version performance gains. The per-dataset 'aha' results in v1 Figure 39 disappear.

M1.justification: The four core formulations, losses, and default inference procedures remain unchanged. v3 adds tested procedural variants involving Gemini-refined process labels, relaxed gPRM consensus filtering, and alternative dPRM aggregation rules (Appendix G). These are limited adaptations within the existing framework.

P1.justification: The main section sequence and Appendix A–G organization are retained. v3 edits the abstract, introduction, and method explanations, presents informal theorem summaries in the main text, expands the practical-guidance discussion, and removes Appendix H's LLM-use disclosure. These refine the existing narrative.

P2.justification: v3 substantially reorganizes the displays and adopts a different publication layout. Figure 6 combines multiple benchmarks, existing 'aha' and shuffled-reasoning plots are merged, length analyses are combined, and detailed MMLU-Pro plots move to Appendix F. New and expanded tables present tuning, filtering, and aggregation comparisons.

R1.justification: v3 adds references for GPQA, MedQA, LEXam, Gemini, and She et al.'s R-PRM. It also expands discussion of the already-cited Uesato et al. work to acknowledge strong outcome-supervision results while distinguishing policy training from test-time verification. The broader research positioning remains intact.

T1.justification: Appendix A replaces per-step variance floors with average variance floors and replaces the aggregate anti-correlation assumption with finite-window dependence bounded by rho. The resulting bounds use 2k rho instead of 2 gamma, with revised derivations. The mean-gPRM proof also removes unexplained sigma_A-squared and gamma_A terms present in v1. The overall length-growth conclusion remains.

improvement.justification: v3 substantially strengthens the evidence behind the recommendations through cross-dataset evaluations, reported five-run replication, and controls addressing backbone, tuning, aggregation, and filtering explanations. These address v1's reliance on one multi-domain benchmark and single-run multi-domain results. Appendix A also improves proof consistency. Removing the detailed 'aha' breakdown and open-ended-generation limitation reduces transparency, but the stronger validation provides a substantial net improvement.

A1.justification: Both PDFs describe the same four-variant reward-model study. Their main text, figures, tables, equations, and appendices are readable and support comparison, including matching relocated material.

after.justification: v3 retains original empirical results and adds GPQA-Diamond, MedQA, and LEXam evaluations, additional model and training controls, and filtering experiments.

before.justification: v1 reports original reward-model training and evaluation on mathematical benchmarks and MMLU-Pro, together with noise, reasoning-length, and single-domain training analyses.
