arxiv_record.abstract: The linear representation hypothesis states that language models (LMs) encode concepts as directions in their latent space, forming organized, multidimensional manifolds. Prior work has largely focused on identifying specific geometries for individual features, limiting its ability to generalize. We introduce Supervised Multi-Dimensional Scaling (SMDS), a model-agnostic method for evaluating and comparing competing feature manifold hypotheses. We apply SMDS to temporal reasoning as a case study and find that different features instantiate distinct geometric structures, including circles, lines, and clusters. SMDS reveals several consistent characteristics of these structures: they reflect the semantic properties of the concepts they represent, remain stable across model families and sizes, actively support reasoning, and dynamically reshape in response to contextual changes. Together, our findings shed light on the functional role of feature manifolds, supporting a model of entity-based reasoning in which LMs encode and transform structured representations.
arxiv_record.authors: Federico Tiblias, Irina Bigoulaeva, Jingcheng Niu, Simone Balloccu, Iryna Gurevych
arxiv_record.title: Hypothesis-Driven Feature Manifold Analysis in LLMs via Supervised Multi-Dimensional Scaling

C1.justification: The abstract and conclusion narrow the headline methodological claim from automatic manifold discovery to evaluating supplied geometric hypotheses, making explicit a restriction already implicit in v1's model-selection formulation. The three principal empirical claims about shared geometry, contextual adaptation and reasoning remain.

C2.justification: v2 explicitly discusses dependence on the quality and breadth of candidate geometries and the need for suitable labels. It newly acknowledges that logarithmically spaced synthetic labels could explain apparent temporal compression, and proposes contextual reconstruction as an explanation for weaker later-layer interventions. These materially qualify applicability and interpretation.

D1.justification: Section 4 newly specifies that manifold visualizations use the best-scoring layer and a 50/50 train/test split. Figure 21 clarifies that the geographic visualization uses the flat hypothesis. The code-access pointer changes from arxiv2025-shape-happens to tmlr2026-manifold-analysis; the PDFs do not establish changes to repository contents.

E1.justification: The eight temporal tasks and geographic reasoning task remain. Appendix B.1 newly evaluates prior numeric-property and weekday/month datasets for variability. The stated US/Canada city eligibility also broadens from populations above 100,000 to above 10,000, although the PDFs do not establish that the geographic experiments were rerun.

E2.justification: v2 adds a randomized-label SMDS comparator specifically to the two-dimensional duration experiment (Table 4); v1's corresponding experiment lacked this comparison. The PCA/LDA/PLS illustration and random-subspace/full-space intervention comparators remain.

E3.justification: The principal validation changes from five-fold cross-validation to ten-fold validation, and a separate bootstrap protocol trains on resampled data and evaluates out-of-bag samples. Added analyses vary dimensionality over {2,3,4,5,10} and measure BERTScore F1 over 5,000 sampled text pairs. These substantially extend the evaluation design.

E4.justification: Appendix D.4 supplies a dimensionality sensitivity study where v1 only stated that higher dimensionalities gave similar results. Appendix B.1 adds dataset variability analysis, and Section 5.4 adds controlled evidence for the two-dimensional manifold. Section 5.3 also newly reports weaker effects from interventions at later layers.

E5.justification: Beyond v1's five-fold averages, error bars and correlation tests, v2 reports ten-fold validation repeated five times, 500 bootstrap iterations, Friedman/Nemenyi rank tests and Wilcoxon comparisons for the two-dimensional control. Tables 3, 4 and 9 report standard errors, and intervention figures newly display and identify standard-error bands.

E6.justification: v2 Table 3 replaces v1 Tables 5 and 8 with revised validation scores and some changed rankings: base Llama-3.2-3B's duration result changes from linear/euclidean at 1.899 to log_linear at 2.879. These use different validation protocols and are not same-setting gains. v2 also adds bootstrap, variability, sensitivity and controlled two-dimensional results, and revises intervention curves.

M1.justification: The SMDS distance-based objective, MDS construction, regularized linear projection, candidate geometries and default dimensionality remain unchanged. Appendix C already documented the fitting procedure in v1; v2's expanded explanation and statistical validation do not establish a changed projection algorithm.

P1.justification: The title, abstract, headings and several explanatory passages adopt hypothesis-driven analysis terminology. v2 adds a contents page and reorganizes supplementary material into additional subsections. The main section order, F1–F3 narrative and much of the original prose remain.

P2.justification: v2 switches from two-column to single-column journal formatting, redraws the overview figure and adds rank-comparison and sensitivity plots. It consolidates the original model-result tables, moves geographic results and the two-dimensional visualization into the main text, and adds uncertainty bands to intervention plots.

R1.justification: Appendix A substantially expands the probing literature, covering linguistic and structural probes, sparsity, truthfulness and the distinction between decodability and mechanistic use. It also adds topology-preserving methods and newer SAE research. Sections 2 and 6 explicitly position SMDS as complementary to existing dimensionality-reduction methods.

arxiv_record.abstract: Web agents powered by large language models (LLMs) must process lengthy web page observations to complete user goals; these pages often exceed tens of thousands of tokens. This saturates context limits and increases computational cost processing; moreover, processing full pages exposes agents to security risks such as prompt injection. Existing pruning strategies either discard relevant content or retain irrelevant context, leading to suboptimal action prediction. We introduce FocusAgent, a simple yet effective approach that leverages a lightweight LLM retriever to extract the most relevant lines from accessibility tree (AxTree) observations, guided by task goals. By pruning noisy and irrelevant content, FocusAgent enables efficient reasoning while reducing vulnerability to injection attacks. Experiments on WorkArena and WebArena benchmarks show that FocusAgent matches the performance of strong baselines, while reducing observation size by over 50%. Furthermore, a variant of FocusAgent significantly reduces the success rate of prompt-injection attacks, including banner and pop-up attacks, while maintaining task success performance in attack-free settings. Our results highlight that targeted LLM-based retrieval is a practical and robust strategy for building web agents that are efficient, effective, and secure.

New failure analyses identify missing navigation cues, omitted chart values, loops, and premature termination; the latency analysis identifies the additional retrieval call as a major practical limitation. Discussion also qualifies pruning's usefulness by model capability and explains model-dependent responses to security warnings. The original Appendix A and popup-blocking limitations remain.

D1.justification: v2 adds API-call timing and retry-aggregation details, deterministic task-template sampling pseudocode, and pricing/local-deployment information. Its code pointer changes from the general AgentLab repository to a dedicated FocusAgent repository. E1.justification: WorkArena L1 and the 381-task WebArena coverage remain unchanged. v2 adds similar-goal diversion attacks on the existing 114-task Reddit security subset, creating a bounded new adversarial scenario in which banners substitute a related task goal for the legitimate goal.

E2.justification: Table 1 replaces v1's text-embedding-3-small comparator with text-embedding-3-large and Qwen3-Embedding-8B comparisons. Table 3 also adds DefenseGenericAgent, a warning-only security baseline, alongside the retained regular and guard-based agents. These materially expand the retrieval and defense comparisons.

E3.justification: v2 adds Qwen backbone/retriever configurations and evaluates 200- and 400-token retrieval chunks with 2000/4000-token observation caps; v1 reported the selected 200-token configuration after describing a different candidate-size sweep. It introduces input-token cost accounting, a sequential 33-task latency evaluation, and template-based goal-drift attack construction. E4.justification: v2 adds systematic analysis of tasks where GenericAgent succeeds but FocusAgent fails: 15 GPT-4.1 cases and 18 Claude cases in Appendix B. It also adds latency decomposition, explicit retrieval-budget comparisons, cost breakdowns, and goal-drift robustness testing. Existing prompt, history, formatting, and pruning-distribution analyses are retained.

E5.justification: The new latency study specifies a fixed seed and reports means, 95th percentiles, and ± dispersion, labeled 'standard deviation of the mean' in Table 11. E6.justification: v2 adds substantial results for new comparators, Qwen configurations, GPT-5-mini on WebArena, costs, latency, and goal-drift attacks; the latter report 0.9% ASR and 47.4% TSR for GPT-4.1 DefenseFocusAgent. P1.justification: v2 combines experimental setup and results within Section 4, subdivides the security section, and adds appendix contents. P2.justification: Main comparison tables gain extensive rows, backbone groups, and cost columns, while new tables and plots present security, failure, latency, and cost evidence. v1 Figure 4 moves to the appendix as v2 Figure 7; the ASR-versus-TSR plot in v1 Figure 5b is removed. R1.justification: Section 2 adds substantive comparisons with Prune4Web and Read More, Think More, positioning FocusAgent relative to programmatic DOM pruning and stronger models using richer observations. improvement.justification: v2 substantially strengthens evaluation of the central efficiency and security claims through stronger retrieval comparisons, a warning-only defense control, and goal-drift testing. arxiv_record.abstract: Large time series foundation models often adopt channel-independent architectures to handle varying data dimensions, but this design ignores crucial cross-channel dependencies. Meanwhile, existing cross-modal methods predominantly rely on textual modalities, leaving the spatial pattern recognition capabilities of vision models underexplored for time series analysis. To address these limitations, we propose VFEM, a cross-modal forecasting model that leverages pre-trained large vision models (LVMs) to capture complex cross-variable patterns. VFEM transforms multivariate time series into visual representations, enabling LVMs to perceive spatial relationships that are not explicitly modeled by channel-independent models. Through a dual-branch architecture, visual and temporal features are independently extracted and then fused via cross-modal attention, allowing complementary information from both modalities to enhance forecasting. By freezing the LVM and training only 7.45% of the total parameters, VFEM achieves competitive performance on multiple benchmarks, offering a new perspective on multivariate time series forecasting.

arxiv_record.abstract: Time series reasoning is crucial to decision-making in diverse domains, including finance, energy, and scientific discovery. While existing time series foundation models (TSFMs) can capture low-level dynamic patterns and provide accurate forecasting, further analysis usually requires additional background knowledge and sophisticated reasoning, which are lacking in most TSFMs but can be achieved through Large Language Models (LLMs). On the other hand, without expensive post-training, LLMs often struggle with the numerical understanding of time series data. Although it is intuitive to integrate the two types of models, developing effective training recipes that align the two modalities for reasoning tasks is still an open challenge. To this end, we propose TS-Reasoner that aligns the latent representations of TSFMs with the textual inputs of LLMs for downstream understanding/reasoning tasks. Specifically, we propose a simple yet effective method to curate diverse, synthetic pairs of time series and textual captions for alignment training. We then develop a two-stage training recipe that applies instruction fine-tuning after the alignment pretraining. Unlike existing works that train an LLM to take time series as inputs, we leverage a pretrained TSFM and freeze it during training. Experiments on several benchmarks demonstrate that TS-Reasoner not only outperforms a wide range of open-source LLMs, Vision-Language Models (VLMs), and Time Series LLMs of comparable scale, but also does so with remarkable data efficiency, e.g., using less than half the training data.
arxiv_record.authors: Fangxu Yu, Hongyu Zhao, Tianyi Zhou
arxiv_record.comments: Accepted to Transactions on Machine Learning Research, 2026
arxiv_record.title: TS-Reasoner: Aligning Time Series Foundation Models with LLM Reasoning

arxiv_record.abstract:
Spatio-temporal sensor data in real-world systems is often sparse, noisy, and irregular, making latent field reconstruction fundamentally underconstrained. Under extreme sparsity, multiple physically plausible fields may remain consistent with the same observations, requiring models to rely on inductive biases about locality, transport, and spatial regularity. In such regimes, reliable reconstruction is concentrated around the observational support induced by the sensor network, making sensor-space modeling a more identifiable objective than unconstrained global field recovery.
  We introduce FieldFormer, a mesh-free transformer architecture for locality-aware sensor-space modeling in persistent sensor networks. For each query, FieldFormer aggregates local evidence using learnable velocity-scaled offsets that adapt neighborhood geometry to spatio-temporal dependencies. Neighborhoods are constructed as fixed maximal sparse contexts over nearby sensors and bounded temporal windows, enabling stable and scalable inference under extreme sparsity. A local transformer encoder integrates neighborhood information, while a coordinate-based neural field formulation supports mesh-free prediction.
  We evaluate FieldFormer on five synthetic and real-world benchmarks, including anisotropic heat diffusion, shallow-water dynamics, atmospheric transport, and pollution monitoring datasets. Results show that locality-aware reconstruction provides strong advantages when local domains of dependence remain observed, enabling FieldFormer to consistently outperform state-of-the-art baselines on sparse sensor-space prediction tasks.

arxiv_record.abstract: Accurate predictions on tabular data rely on capturing complex, dataset-specific feature interactions. Attention-based methods and graph neural networks, referred to as graph-based tabular deep learning (GTDL), aim to improve predictions by modeling these interactions as a graph. In this work, we analyze how these methods model the feature interactions. Current GTDL approaches primarily focus on optimizing predictive accuracy, often neglecting the accurate modeling of the underlying graph structure. Using synthetic datasets with known ground-truth graph structures, we find that current GTDL methods fail to recover meaningful feature interactions, as their edge recovery is close to random. This suggests that the attention mechanism and message-passing schemes used in GTDL do not effectively capture feature interactions. Furthermore, when we impose the true interaction structure, we find that the predictive accuracy improves. This highlights the need for GTDL methods to prioritize accurate modeling of the graph structure, as it leads to better predictions.
arxiv_record.authors: Elias Dubbeldam, Reza Mohammadi, Marit Schoonhoven, S. Ilker Birbil
arxiv_record.title: The Role of Feature Interactions in Graph-based Tabular Deep Learning

arxiv_record.abstract: Flow matching models generate high-fidelity molecular geometries but incur significant computational costs during inference, requiring hundreds of network evaluations. This inference overhead becomes the primary bottleneck when such models are employed in practice to sample large numbers of molecular candidates. This work discusses a training-free caching strategy that accelerates molecular geometry generation by predicting intermediate hidden states across solver steps. The proposed method operates directly on the SE(3)-equivariant backbone, is compatible with pretrained models, and is orthogonal to existing training-based accelerations and system-level optimizations. Experiments on the GEOM-Drugs dataset demonstrate that caching achieves a twofold reduction in wall-clock inference time at matched sample quality and a speedup of up to 3x compared to the base model with minimal sample quality degradation. Because these gains compound with other optimizations, applying caching alongside other general, lossless optimizations yield as much as a 7x speedup.
arxiv_record.authors: Johanna Sommer and John Rachwan and Nils Fleischmann and Stephan G\"unnemann and Bertrand Charpentier
arxiv_record.comments: Accepted at the AI for Science Workshop @ NeurIPS 2025

arxiv_record.abstract: Out-of-distribution (OOD) detection plays a crucial role in ensuring the robustness of machine learning systems deployed in real-world applications. Recent approaches have explored the use of unlabeled data, showing potential for enhancing OOD detection capabilities. However, effectively utilizing unlabeled in-the-wild data remains challenging due to the mixed nature of both in-distribution (InD) and OOD samples. The lack of a distinct set of OOD samples complicates the task of training an optimal OOD classifier. In this work, we introduce Medix, a novel framework designed to identify potential outliers from unlabeled data using the median-based robust gradient statistics. We use the median because it provides a stable estimate of the central tendency, as an OOD detection mechanism, due to its robustness against noise and outliers. Using these identified outliers, along with labeled InD data, we train a robust OOD classifier. From a theoretical perspective, we derive error bounds that demonstrate Medix achieves a low error rate. Empirical results further substantiate our claims, as Medix outperforms existing methods across the board in open-world settings.
arxiv_record.authors: Momin Abbas and Ali Falahati and Hossein Goli and Mohammad Mohammadi Amiri
arxiv_record.title: Medix: Out-of-Distribution Detection from Unlabeled Wild Data via Robust Gradient Statistics

P1.justification: The theoretical exposition and Appendix C are extensively rewritten and reorganized into explicit setup, assumptions, scoped statements and compact proofs. v2 also retitles the paper, condenses introductory contributions, expands the experimental roadmap and adds explanatory appendix subsections. P2.justification: v2 adds an overview diagram, three experimental tables and two gradient-diagnostic figures, and substantially revises the notation table. arxiv_record.abstract: Instance-level recognition (ILR) focuses on identifying individual objects rather than broad categories, offering the highest granularity in image classification. However, this fine-grained nature makes creating large-scale annotated datasets challenging, limiting ILR's real-world applicability across domains. To overcome this, we introduce a novel approach that synthetically generates diverse object instances from multiple domains under varied conditions and backgrounds, forming a large-scale training set. Unlike prior work on automatic data synthesis, our method is the first to address ILR-specific challenges without relying on any real images. Fine-tuning foundation vision models on the generated data significantly improves retrieval performance across seven ILR benchmarks spanning multiple domains. Our approach offers a new, efficient, and effective alternative to extensive data collection and curation, introducing a new ILR paradigm where the only input is the names of the target domains, unlocking a wide range of real-world applications. The code and pretrained models are publicly available at https://github.com/yankungou/ILGen.
arxiv_record.authors: Yankun Wu, Zakaria Laskar, Giorgos Kordopatis-Zilos, Noa Garcia, Giorgos Tolias
arxiv_record.title: Instance-Level Generation for Representation Learning

arxiv_record.abstract: Researchers have pursued neurosymbolic artificial intelligence (AI) applications for nearly three decades. A marriage of the neural and symbolic components can lead to rapid advancements in AI. Yet, the field has not realized this promise since most neurosymbolic AI frameworks fail to scale. In addition, the implicit representations and approximate reasoning of purely neural approaches limit interpretability and trust. Knowledge graphs (KGs), a gold-standard representation of explicit semantic knowledge, can address the symbolic side of the problem. However, automatically deriving reliable KGs from text corpora remains an open problem. We address these challenges by introducing GraphMERT, a tiny graphical encoder-only model that distills high-quality KGs from unstructured text corpora and its own internal representations. GraphMERT and its equivalent KG form a modular neurosymbolic stack: neural learning of abstractions; symbolic KGs for verifiable reasoning. GraphMERT + KG is the first efficient and scalable neurosymbolic model to achieve state-of-the-art benchmark accuracy along with superior symbolic representations relative to baselines. Concretely, we target reliable domain-specific KGs that are both (1) factual (with provenance) and (2) valid (ontology-consistent relations with domain-appropriate semantics). When a large language model (LLM), e.g., Qwen3-32B, generates domain-specific KGs, it falls short on reliability due to prompt sensitivity, shallow domain expertise, and hallucinated relations. On text obtained from PubMed papers on diabetes, our 80M-parameter GraphMERT yields a KG with a 69.8% FActScore; a 32B-parameter baseline LLM yields a KG that achieves only 40.2% FActScore. The GraphMERT KG also attains a higher ValidityScore of 68.8%, versus 43.0% for the LLM baseline.

E1.justification: The PubMed diabetes corpus and diabetes-filtered ICD-Bench, MedMCQA, MedQA, and medical MMLU coverage remain unchanged. arxiv_record.abstract: Modern weather forecasting has increasingly transitioned from numerical weather prediction (NWP) to data-driven machine learning forecasting techniques. While these new models produce probabilistic forecasts to quantify uncertainty, their training and evaluation may remain hindered by conventional scoring rules, primarily MSE, which are designed for single time point predictions and ignore the highly correlated data structures present in weather behaviour. This work introduces the signature kernel scoring rule to the domain of weather forecasting, which reframes weather variables as continuous paths to encode temporal and spatial dependencies through iterated integrals. Validated as strictly proper through the use of path augmentations to guarantee uniqueness, the signature kernel provides a theoretically robust metric for forecast verification and model training. Empirical evaluations through weather scorecards on WeatherBench 2 models demonstrate the signature kernel scoring rule's high discriminative power and unique capacity to capture path-dependent interactions. Following previous demonstration of successful adversarial-free probabilistic training, we train sliding window generative neural networks using a predictive-sequential scoring rule on ERA5 reanalysis weather data. Using a lightweight model, we demonstrate that signature kernel based training outperforms climatology for forecast paths of up to fifteen timesteps.
arxiv_record.authors: Archer Dodson, Ritabrata Dutta
arxiv_record.title: Signature Kernel Scoring Rule: A Spatio-Temporal Diagnostic for Probabilistic Weather Forecasting

arxiv_record.abstract: This note reconciles two seemingly distinct approaches to policy gradient optimization for the Pass@K objective in reinforcement learning with verifiable rewards: (1) direct REINFORCE-style methods, and (2) advantage-shaping techniques that directly modify GRPO. We show that these are two sides of the same coin. By reverse-engineering existing advantage-shaping algorithms, we reveal that they implicitly optimize surrogate rewards. We specifically interpret practical "hard-example up-weighting" modifications to GRPO as reward-level regularization. Conversely, starting from surrogate reward objectives, we provide a simple recipe for deriving both existing and new advantage-shaping methods. This perspective provides a lens for RLVR policy gradient optimization beyond our original motivation of Pass@K.
arxiv_record.authors: Christos Thrampoulidis, Sadegh Mahdavi, Wenlong Deng
arxiv_record.title: Advantage Shaping as Surrogate Reward Maximization: Unifying Pass@K Policy Gradients

E3.justification: Appendix D introduces new experimental protocols: Qwen2.5-0.5B synthetic training with a 50,000/500/500 split and eight epochs, and Qwen2.5-Math-1.5B training for 40 steps with dynamic sampling. arxiv_record.abstract: Large language models (LLMs) are increasingly used as raters for evaluation tasks. However, their reliability is often limited for subjective tasks, when human judgments involve subtle reasoning beyond annotation labels. Thinking traces, the reasoning behind a judgment, are highly informative but challenging to collect and curate. We present a human-LLM collaborative framework to infer thinking traces from label-only annotations. The proposed framework uses a simple and effective rejection sampling method to reconstruct these traces at scale. These inferred thinking traces are applied to two complementary tasks: (1) fine-tuning open LLM raters; and (2) synthesizing clearer annotation guidelines for proprietary LLM raters. Across multiple datasets, our methods lead to significantly improved LLM-human agreement. Additionally, the refined annotation guidelines increase agreement among different LLM models. These results suggest that LLMs can serve as practical proxies for otherwise unrevealed human thinking traces, enabling label-only corpora to be extended into thinking-trace-augmented resources that enhance the reliability of LLM raters.

E3.justification: V2 substantially expands experimental conditions through a DeepSeek-R1-Distill-Llama-8B base model, ratings-only training, GPT-4o trace generation, sampling coverage at k values from 1 to 32, and four instruction/rubric trace-budget combinations. E4.justification: V2 adds an ablation testing whether traces contribute beyond SFT alone (Table 4), sampling-coverage analysis (Figure 5), and trace-quantity sensitivity analysis (Table 8). P1.justification: Most prose and the main section sequence are retained. P2.justification: V2 replaces the two-column draft layout with a single-column publication layout, redraws Figure 3 with concrete examples, adds the sampling plot and five tables, and reorders metric columns. R1.justification: Section 2 adds reasoning-distillation references covering medical questions, software engineering, finance, cybersecurity, and general-purpose trace datasets such as Synthetic-1 and OpenThoughts. improvement.justification: The added ratings-only SFT control addresses an important missing comparison in v1, substantially strengthening evidence that thinking traces contribute beyond generic fine-tuning. before.justification: Sections 4.3–4.5 and Tables 1–5 report original fine-tuning, codebook-refinement, inter-rater agreement, and ablation results.

arxiv_record.abstract: Foundation models for time series imputation remain largely unexplored. Recently, two such models, TabPFN-TS and MoTM, have emerged. These models share a common philosophy that places them within the family of time-indexed foundation models. This paper presents the first large-scale empirical study of these models for zero-shot imputation, which enables missing value recovery without retraining across a wide range of scenarios. We conduct extensive univariate experiments across 33 out-of-domain datasets (approximately 1.3M imputation windows) and evaluate their ability to integrate covariates at inference time to improve accuracy without fine-tuning. Our results demonstrate that time-indexed foundation models are a powerful and practical step toward achieving general-purpose, zero-shot imputation for real-world time series.

arxiv_record.abstract: Model merging combines multiple fine-tuned checkpoints into a single model without additional training, offering an attractive approach to reusing models and efficiently improving performance. However, it remains unclear whether the advantages reported for settings where all merged experts have distinct roles and are tuned on clearly separated tasks also hold in settings where the merged experts do not have clearly distinct roles, but are trained on overlapping or even conflicting objectives. To evaluate this setting, we present a large-scale, systematic evaluation of "in-the-wild" model merging of heterogeneous experts, that may have been trained on overlapping or conflicting objectives. Concretely, we evaluate six state-of-the-art merging methods, including recent subspace methods, across four open-weight LLMs, twelve fine-tuned checkpoints per base model, and sixteen standard LLM benchmarks. Evaluating through standardized benchmarks, we measure both the probability that a model merged from a heterogeneous set of experts outperforms the base model and we measure relative gains over the best individual checkpoint. Our results show that the oldest and simplest method, Task Arithmetic, is the only approach that reliably yields performance gains on LLMs in this "in-the-wild" setting. Other interference-aware and subspace merging methods typically do not result in notable improvements over the base model. Our findings indicate that current merging techniques mostly do not enable extracting useful weight updates from heterogeneous and potentially conflicting versions. This motivates the design of LLM-specific merging algorithms and merging-aware fine-tuning methods.
arxiv_record.authors: O\u{g}uz Ka\u{g}an Hitit, Leander Girrbach, Zeynep Akata
arxiv_record.title: A Systematic Study of In-the-Wild Model Merging for Large Language Models

C1.justification: The abstract, introduction, and conclusion narrow the central claim from merging methods generally failing to transfer to LLMs to difficulty improving general capabilities through heterogeneous, potentially conflicting checkpoints. TIES is recast from catastrophic degradation to limited gains under tuning. Task Arithmetic remains the preferred approach.

C2.justification: New explanations attribute Task Arithmetic’s stability to normalized averaging and TIES’s sensitivity to trimming and sign consensus limiting cancellation. Section 5 interprets the domain controls as evidence about heterogeneity, while Section 3.1 explicitly frames Model Stock’s use as a stress test beyond its intended setting. These materially revise mechanisms and applicability boundaries.

D1.justification: v1’s promised code release becomes a repository link in v2. Appendices C and F newly disclose normalization, float16 evaluation, automatic batching, absence of chat templates, and exact few-shot counts. Appendix E supplies specialist checkpoint identifiers and task lists. These materially improve documentation without establishing that newly disclosed inference settings changed.

E1.justification: Appendix E adds a distinct evaluation scenario using curated medical and mathematical specialists for Qwen3-4B and Qwen3-8B. It tests preservation of domain capabilities through within-domain and joint-domain merging. The original checkpoint pools and sixteen-benchmark coverage remain; the new task suites draw on subsets of existing benchmarks.

E2.justification: Matched comparisons retain Task Arithmetic, TIES-Merging, Model Stock, TSV-Merge, Iso-C, TA+SB, and TIES+SB. Appendix E reuses these methods with base-model and individual-expert references. Newly cited works do not become additional evaluated merging algorithms.

E3.justification: New protocols include a joint TIES density–scaling grid, normalization-disabled Task Arithmetic controls, extension of the normalized scaling sweep to λ=10, and three-expert domain merges versus six-expert joint merges. Revised main TIES/TIES+SB evaluations specify λ=0.1; v1 did not separately state their scaling coefficient.

E4.justification: Appendices C–E substantially expand tests of why merging succeeds or fails: normalization controls, scaling-versus-update-norm analyses, global and layerwise task-vector alignment, and structured domain-mixing comparisons. The original density and boosting-threshold sweeps are retained as Figures 17 and 18, rather than newly introduced.

E5.justification: Both versions use fifteen matched checkpoint subsets at intermediate merge sizes, one all-twelve merge, and standard deviations across sampled subsets. No new seed-reporting practice, confidence intervals, significance tests, or repeated-run uncertainty procedure is introduced.

E6.justification: TIES and TIES+SB results are substantially replaced. At n=12, the average success-rate/reported-improvement entries change from 0/-4.32 to 75/+0.13 in Table 1 and from 0/-8.67 to 100/+0.36 in Table 3. These are revised evaluations, not established gains under identical settings. Appendices C–E also add normalization, alignment, and domain-retention findings.

M1.justification: The evaluated merging algorithms and their principal procedures remain unchanged. Appendix C documents normalization as an existing configuration and tests normalization/scaling variants; it does not introduce a new merging algorithm or establish a change to the original method implementation.

P1.justification: The abstract and much of the introduction are rewritten, research questions are reformulated, and results, discussion, and conclusion narratives are revised around in-the-wild merging. Appendix C becomes a structured explanation with four subsections, and new appendices and a broader-impact statement extend the document structure.

P2.justification: v2 adds normalization and joint-sensitivity plots, global and layerwise alignment heatmaps, domain-comparison bar charts, and Tables 4–6. Figure 11 gains an extended scaling axis; retained displays are resized or relocated, and Table 2’s caption is expanded. Earlier density and boosting figures remain under new numbering.

R1.justification: v2 removes the assertion that merging methods had not been evaluated on LLMs and distinguishes its general-capability objective from prior domain-specialist retention studies. New references include He et al.’s MergeBench, Cohere et al.’s Command A, and Roth et al. This substantially changes positioning; publication updates to retained references are bibliographic changes only.

T1.justification: Equations (1)–(11) are retained. Equation (12) spells out the weighted-average normalization that v2 says was already enabled. This implementation explanation and the qualitative cancellation arguments do not introduce a substantive theoretical derivation, formal assumption, theorem, or proof.

improvement.justification: v2 substantially strengthens the central comparison by investigating scaling and normalization behind the earlier TIES failures, reporting tuned results, and narrowing broad LLM-failure claims to heterogeneous merging. Domain controls and explicit implementation/evaluation details improve evidential support and reproducibility. Section 5 still overstates causal certainty when attributing failures specifically to heterogeneity, but the correction of the central comparison and its interpretation provides a substantial net improvement.

A1.justification: Both PDFs describe the same model-merging study. The original experiments, equations, checkpoint lists, and appendix figures can be matched despite retitling and substantial additions. Text extraction and visual inspection support reliable comparison, including the appendices.

after.justification: v2 reports retained and revised benchmark results, plus new normalization controls, task-vector alignment measurements, and domain-specific merging experiments in Appendices C–E.

before.justification: v1 reports original evaluations across four base models and sixteen benchmarks, including merge-size comparisons, taskwise results, and hyperparameter ablations in Tables 1–3 and Appendices B–C.

arxiv_record.abstract: Large Language Models (LLMs) encode factual knowledge within hidden parametric spaces that are difficult to inspect or control. While Sparse Autoencoders (SAEs) can decompose hidden activations into more fine-grained, interpretable features, they often struggle to reliably align these features with human-defined concepts, resulting in entangled and distributed feature representations. To address this, we introduce AlignSAE, a method that aligns SAE features with a predefined ontology through a "pre-train, then post-train" curriculum. After an initial unsupervised training phase, we apply supervised post-training to bind specific concepts to dedicated latent slots while preserving the remaining capacity for general reconstruction. This separation creates an interpretable interface where specific concepts can be inspected and controlled without interference from unrelated features. Empirical results demonstrate that AlignSAE enables precise causal interventions, such as reliable "concept swaps", by targeting single, semantically aligned slots, and further supports multi-hop reasoning and a mechanistic probe of grokking-like generalization dynamics.

C1.justification: The alignment and causal-swap claims remain, but v2's abstract and conclusion add multi-hop applicability and a mechanistic account of grokking. Section 6.3 claims the first SAE-based step-wise binding probe of multi-hop grokking. The conclusion replaces v1's broad world-model, agent, and robotics framing with relation completion and representation-learning dynamics.

C2.justification: v2 introduces the interpretation that stable concept binding precedes observable generalization, and uses ablations to distinguish the roles of supervision, decorrelation, and pretraining. Its limitations replace v1's single-hop restriction with explicit boundaries concerning GPT-2 scale, synthetic templates, small ontologies, indirect-question failures, and uncertain transfer to symbolic-ID settings.

D1.justification: v2 adds Code & Data access information, the full paraphrase-generation prompt, two-hop construction and training details, hyperparameter-selection disclosures, and the 1,000-example swap sample size. However, it removes earlier specifics about decoder initialization and value-head dimensions. The PDFs establish the added resource pointers, not their external availability.

E1.justification: v2 adds two-hop relation composition over 20 relations and 60 entities, extending v1's six-relation biography recall to intermediate-entity prediction and sequential reasoning. Appendix A.4 also reports an exploratory test of indirect LLM-generated paraphrases, excluded from the main evaluation. The reported biography birth-city inventory expands from 8 to 50 cities.

E2.justification: The traditional unsupervised SAE comparator is retained. v2 additionally evaluates supervised linear-probe steering in the two-hop comparison in Figure 8. G-SAE is discussed as related work but is not an evaluated baseline.

arxiv_record.abstract: Video world models have attracted significant attention for their ability to produce high-fidelity future visual observations conditioned on past observations and navigation actions. However, achieving temporally and spatially consistent generation over long horizons remains an open challenge: existing approaches either compress past frames without explicitly accounting for 3D viewpoint geometry or retrieve only a handful of spatially relevant frames without increasing the total amount of retained history. In this paper, we propose WorldPack, a video world model that introduces spatially-aware compressed memory to address both limitations simultaneously. The key insight is that compression rates should not be uniform or temporally determined, but should instead be dynamically allocated based on 3D spatial relevance to the current viewpoint. WorldPack achieves this through two tightly coupled mechanisms: trajectory packing, which fits substantially more historical frames into a fixed-length context through hierarchical frame compression, and geometric selection, which leverages camera pose information and field-of-view overlap to assign lower compression to spatially important frames and higher compression to less relevant ones. Together, these mechanisms expand the effective context from 4 to 22 frames with moderate computational overhead: trajectory packing increases diffusion-model inference time by 16%, while FoV-based geometric selection introduces an additional cost. We evaluate WorldPack on LoopNav, a Minecraft benchmark for long-horizon spatial consistency, and conduct comprehensive experiments on the RECON, real-world navigation dataset, across multiple metrics. WorldPack outperforms strong baselines, including Oasis, Mineworld, DIAMOND, and NWM, with pronounced gains on spatial reasoning tasks that require recall of distant observations.
arxiv_record.authors: Yuta Oshima, Yusuke Iwasawa, Masahiro Suzuki, Yutaka Matsuo, Hiroki Furuta
arxiv_record.title: WorldPack: Dynamic Frame Compression for Long-context Video World Modeling

arxiv_record.abstract: Domain shift remains a key challenge in deploying machine learning models to the real world. Unsupervised domain adaptation (UDA) aims to address this by minimising domain discrepancy during training, but the discrepancy estimates suffer from high variance in stochastic settings, which can stifle the theoretical benefits of the method. This paper proposes Variance-Reduced Domain Adaptation via Stratified Sampling (VaRDASS), the first specialised stochastic variance reduction technique for UDA. We consider two specific discrepancy measures -- correlation alignment and the maximum mean discrepancy (MMD) -- and derive ad hoc stratification objectives for these terms. We then present expected and worst-case error bounds, and prove that our proposed objective for the MMD is theoretically optimal (i.e., minimises the variance) under certain assumptions. Finally, a practical k-means style optimisation algorithm is introduced and analysed. Experiments on four domain shift datasets demonstrate improved discrepancy estimation accuracy and target domain performance.
arxiv_record.authors: Andrea Napoli, Paul White
arxiv_record.title: Variance Matters: Improving Domain Adaptation via Stratified Sampling

arxiv_record.abstract: Ensuring safety in autonomous systems requires controllers that aim to satisfy state-wise constraints without relying on online interaction.While existing Safe Offline RL methods typically enforce soft expected-cost constraints, they struggle to ensure strict state-wise safety. Conversely, Control Barrier Functions (CBFs) offer a principled mechanism to enforce forward invariance, but often rely on expert-designed barrier functions or knowledge of the system dynamics. We introduce Value-Guided Offline Control Barrier Functions (V-OCBF), a framework that learns a neural CBF entirely from offline demonstrations. Unlike prior approaches, V-OCBF does not assume access to the dynamics model; instead, it derives a recursive finite-difference barrier update, enabling model-free learning of a barrier that propagates safety information over time. Moreover, V-OCBF incorporates an expectile-based objective that avoids querying the barrier on out-of-distribution actions and restricts updates to the dataset-supported action set. The learned barrier is then used with a Quadratic Program (QP) formulation to synthesize real-time safe control. Across multiple case studies, V-OCBF yields substantially fewer safety violations than baseline methods while maintaining strong task performance, highlighting its scalability for offline synthesis of safety-critical controllers without online interaction or hand-engineered barriers.

C1.justification: v1 presents the framework as learning formally safe, safety-certified controllers. v2 restricts the invariance guarantee to an idealized setting without approximation errors and explicitly states that the learned barrier is not formally verified. This materially narrows the central safety claim while retaining the offline-learning and empirical-performance contributions.

C2.justification: v2 explains how function approximation, finite data, and learned dynamics can invalidate closed-loop guarantees, and discusses relaxing safety constraints for QP feasibility. It also qualifies v1's favorable interpretation of tau approaching one: optimistic stochastic outcomes can make extreme expectiles brittle, with the new MuJoCo evidence supporting tau=0.9.

D1.justification: v2 explicitly identifies tau=0.9 for main experiments, documents the boat dynamics and constraints, and names implementation sources for the additional baselines. Conversely, Table 11 removes v1 Table 8's shared Adam, learning-rate 10^-3, and ReLU specification. Existing hardware and architecture details are retained.

E1.justification: Appendix D adds boat navigation with state-dependent river drift, static obstacles, and bounded actuation. AGV collision avoidance and all five existing MuJoCo velocity-constrained tasks remain, making this a limited extension of domain coverage.

E2.justification: The new boat comparison in Table 9 evaluates CPQ, WSAC, CDT, and C2IQL alongside several retained competitors. These four additional methods substantially broaden the evaluated comparator set; the original AGV and MuJoCo comparator sets remain unchanged.

E3.justification: New protocols sweep four expectile values on three MuJoCo tasks and evaluate dynamics models trained for 50% and 25% of the standard budget, measuring prediction error on sampled state-action pairs. Existing dataset sizes, architectures, rollout metrics, and main evaluation sample counts are retained.

E4.justification: Beyond the retained AGV ablations, v2 adds learned-barrier geometry across six expectiles, reward/cost sensitivity to expectiles on MuJoCo, and direct dynamics-underfitting tests with measured prediction errors. These substantially strengthen analysis of the central learning mechanism and sensitivity to model inaccuracies, previously investigated mainly through action noise.

E5.justification: Existing five-seed evaluations, reported uncertainties, standard-error description, and rollout percentile bands are retained. The boat comparison follows the existing five-seed practice; no new uncertainty estimator, significance test, or increased repeated-run count is reported.

E6.justification: Existing main results and Tables 1–6 are unchanged, but substantial new findings appear. Table 7 favors tau=0.9 over 0.99 on three MuJoCo tasks; Table 8 reports 96.32% safety with quarter-trained dynamics; Table 9 reports boat safety of 97.56±0.13% versus 88.43±0.59% for the strongest listed baseline, BC+NCBF. These are additional results, not demonstrated improvements over v1 under identical settings.

M1.justification: Equations 9–10 and Algorithm 1 replace separate behavior-barrier training and explicit action-support gathering with direct expectile updates using a target bootstrapped from B_theta at the observed next state. Appendix A.3 also introduces a slack-penalized QP. These substantially revise the specified training and control procedures; the PDFs do not establish that retained experiments were rerun.

P1.justification: There are targeted rewrites of the abstract, positioning, methodology, and limitations, plus new appendix subsections and a boat appendix that shifts Experimental Details from D to E. Affiliations and publication information change, but most prose and the overall narrative structure are retained.

P2.justification: v2 adds the six-panel expectile visualization and Tables 7–9. The environment illustration moves from main-text Figure 2 to appendix Figure 5, while existing plots and tables are retained and reflowed. Publication headers and the shortened Algorithm 1 alter presentation without a comprehensive redesign.

R1.justification: v2 adds references for WSAC, C2IQL, and conformal-prediction-based verification. Section 2.3 refines positioning around offline policy learning and using learned dynamics only during inference. The broader related-work survey remains largely unchanged.

T1.justification: The mathematical target/loss definitions in Equations 9–10 are revised, and Equation 22 introduces a formally specified relaxed QP. The finite-difference lemma and proof and the expectile definitions in Appendices A.1–A.2 are retained; no new learned-controller certification theorem is supplied.

improvement.justification: v2 addresses a central credibility problem: v1's formally safe-controller framing becomes an explicit distinction between idealized invariance and empirical safety of an unverified learned controller. The revised training specification and targeted expectile and model-fidelity experiments substantially improve assessment of the method's behavior and limitations. Additional boat comparisons strengthen empirical support. Missing slack-penalty settings and removed baseline optimization details leave reproducibility gaps, but these do not outweigh the substantial gains in claim accuracy and validation.

A1.justification: Both PDFs describe the same V-OCBF study. Their complete main texts and appendices are readable, and equations, tables, and figures can be matched across relocation and renumbering.

after.justification: v2 retains these empirical results and adds boat-navigation comparisons, MuJoCo expectile experiments, and dynamics-model accuracy analyses.

before.justification: v1 reports original AGV and five MuJoCo simulation evaluations, controller comparisons, and network-size, disturbance, and expectile ablations.

arxiv_record.abstract: Selecting compact and informative gene subsets from single-cell transcriptomic data is essential for biomarker discovery, improving interpretability, and cost-effective profiling. However, most existing feature selection approaches either operate as multi-stage pipelines or rely on post hoc feature attribution, making selection and prediction weakly coupled. In this work, we present YOTO (you only train once), an end-to-end framework that jointly identifies discrete gene subsets and performs prediction within a single differentiable architecture. In our model, the prediction task directly guides which genes are selected, while the learned subsets, in turn, shape the predictive representation. This closed feedback loop enables the model to iteratively refine both what it selects and how it predicts during training. Unlike existing approaches, YOTO enforces sparsity so that only the selected genes contribute to inference, eliminating the need to train additional downstream classifiers. Through a multi-task learning design, the model learns shared representations across related objectives, allowing partially labeled datasets to inform one another, and discovering gene subsets that generalize across tasks without additional training steps. We evaluate YOTO on two representative single-cell RNA-seq datasets, showing that it consistently outperforms state-of-the-art baselines. These results demonstrate that sparse, end-to-end, multi-task gene subset selection improves predictive performance and yields compact and meaningful gene subsets, advancing biomarker discovery and single-cell analysis.

C1.justification: The abstract and introduction retreat from prominent claims about benefiting from partially labeled datasets, and the conclusion explicitly leaves experimental validation of that benefit to future work. Resource-efficiency wording is also softened. The central contributions of discrete, end-to-end selection and joint multi-task prediction remain.

C2.justification: v2 adds substantive qualifications about generalization to unseen cells rather than unseen patients, patient-specific confounding, sparse-panel task tradeoffs and the need for shared biological structure. It acknowledges that multi-task learning is not always optimal and partial-label benefits remain untested. New stability discussions interpret variable gene identities through functional redundancy and stabilization of a core panel.

D1.justification: New Appendix A.3 documents software packages, SMOTE, Random Forest settings, optimizers, architectures, batch sizes, learning rates, temperature schedules and sparsification schedules, including Tables 11-15. v2 also clarifies split granularity and F1 averaging and supplies a code-access link. These are substantial disclosures, not evidence that previously reported experiments were changed or rerun.

E1.justification: Both versions evaluate VISp and COVID-PBMC with the same supervised targets and gene-panel size ranges. The added classifier, stability and marker/GO analyses examine the existing data and selected panels, without introducing a new prediction population, domain or input scenario.

E2.justification: The main comparisons add YOTO (FS only), which predicts with a Random Forest trained on YOTO-selected genes, while retaining all six original baselines. Appendix A.2.1 additionally evaluates multi-task Random Forest variants of Seurat and Seurat v3.

E3.justification: v2 substantially extends the evaluation design with isolated panel evaluation, matched-architecture single-task versus multi-task controls, a larger-capacity condition, and multi-task Random Forest comparisons. It also introduces gene-overlap, GO-rank concordance and cross-size containment protocols. The original 80-20 split and 1000-epoch budget remain; cell-level splitting and macro-F1 are newly clarified, not demonstrated protocol changes.

E4.justification: Beyond the retained selection-module ablation, v2 tests panel quality separately from classifier choice and multi-task learning separately from model capacity. Sections 4.4.6-4.4.7 add seed stability, known-marker enrichment, functional concordance and panel nestedness analyses; Appendix A.2.1 examines single-task versus multi-task baseline classifiers.

E5.justification: Existing benchmark reporting retains means and standard deviations across seeds 0, 1 and 2. Section 4.4.6 newly introduces Fisher's exact test, with an odds ratio and p-value for marker enrichment. This adds inferential reporting without establishing an increase in repeated runs.

E6.justification: v2 adds substantial results for FS-only prediction, controlled multi-task comparisons, baseline classifier variants and biological stability. Most matched benchmark entries remain unchanged, but VISp F1 at 32 genes changes from 84.8 ± 0.0 in v1 Table 5 to 82.7 ± 2.7 in v2 Table 6. New Tables 2-3 show FS-only YOTO outperforming integrated YOTO on VISp, but not COVID-PBMC, contrary to the added prose.

M1.justification: The learned gene scores, differentiable ranking, straight-through binary selection, progressive sparsification, shared encoder and task-specific losses remain unchanged. The added Random Forest evaluation and architecture controls test the existing method; the implementation appendix does not establish a revised core algorithm.

P1.justification: The main section order and much existing prose are retained, with targeted rewrites, expanded explanations and additional experimental and implementation subsections. Author/publication information expands and acknowledgments disappear. v2 also introduces a duplicated abstract sentence and an unfinished '[...]' phrase in Section 4.4.6.

P2.justification: Figure 1 adds a feedback arrow, Figure 2 adds the FS-only series, and new Figures 4-5 visualize overlap, GO concordance and nestedness. Comparative tables gain pipeline columns, FS-only rows and revised highlighting; new ablation and implementation tables substantially expand the displays. The original class-distribution figure is retained as Figure 6.

R1.justification: v2 adds references supporting multi-task learning, SMOTE and biological marker validation, including Kurin, Liu, He, Chawla and Tasic. It qualifies PERSIST's end-to-end status in Table 1 and clarifies the relationship to Grover et al.'s ranking operator. The main related-work narrative and nearest comparison remain unchanged.

T1.justification: Appendix A.3 adds an explicit mathematical specification of the exponential subset-size annealing schedule in Equations 8-9, where v1 described progressive annealing qualitatively. This is a limited formalization: the core ranking, masking and loss equations remain unchanged, and no theorem or proof is added.

improvement.justification: v2 substantially addresses v1's missing implementation specifications and limited evidence isolating gene-panel quality and stability through Appendix A.3, classifier controls and new robustness analyses. These gains outweigh localized reporting and editing problems, including the duplicated abstract text and the COVID-PBMC FS-only claim contradicted by Table 2.

A1.justification: Both PDFs describe the same YOTO research work. Their complete main texts and appendices, including equations, tables and figures, support reliable comparison; retained material can be matched across renumbering.

after.justification: v2 retains those empirical results and adds classifier controls, multi-task ablations, gene-selection stability analyses and biological enrichment results.

arxiv_record.abstract: Flow Matching (FM) has emerged as a powerful paradigm for continuous normalizing flows, yet standard FM implicitly performs an unweighted $L^2$ regression over the entire ambient space. In high dimensions, this leads to a fundamental inefficiency: the vast majority of the integration domain consists of low-density ``void'' regions where the target velocity fields are often chaotic or ill-defined. In this paper, we propose {$\gamma$-Flow Matching ($\gamma$-FM)}, a density-weighted variant that aligns the regression geometry with the underlying probability flow. While density weighting is desirable, naive implementations would require evaluating the intractable target density. We circumvent this by introducing a Dynamic Density-Weighting strategy that estimates the \emph{target} density directly from training particles. This approach allows us to dynamically downweight the regression loss in void regions without compromising the simulation-free nature of FM. Theoretically, we establish that $\gamma$-FM minimizes the transport cost on a statistical manifold endowed with the $\gamma$-Stein metric. Spectral analysis further suggests that this geometry induces an implicit Sobolev regularization, effectively damping high-frequency oscillations in void regions. Empirically, $\gamma$-FM significantly improves vector field smoothness and sampling efficiency on high-dimensional latent datasets, while demonstrating intrinsic robustness to outliers.
arxiv_record.authors: Shinto Eguchi
arxiv_record.title: Implicit geometric regularization in flow matching via density weighted Stein operators

C1.justification: V1 claims variance-optimal estimation, transport minimization in γ-Stein geometry, and improved efficiency without sacrificing generation quality. V2's abstract, contributions and conclusion narrow these to a variance-suppression bound, idealized geometric/spectral mechanisms, and empirical evaluation under an explicit protocol. This materially reduces the claimed guarantees and generality.

C2.justification: V2 extends the existing continuum-analogy caveat to its double-well, geodesic and NFE interpretations, and treats GSC as a heuristic rather than an optimality certificate. It explains rank weights as an ordering device rather than calibrated density estimates, acknowledges fidelity costs, and limits practical benefits in light of the weak clean-target results.

D1.justification: V2 Appendix D supplies substantially more reproducibility information: training-mixture composition, autoencoder and flow architectures, optimizer and training duration, weighting and Jacobian parameters, solver settings, retrieval-bank size, and metric sample counts. It also adds a code-availability statement. Most are newly disclosed details; the PDFs do not establish that previously unspecified settings changed.

E1.justification: The principal CIFAR-10 task shifts from v1's stated clean-data training to a robust-target task using an inlier/outlier-class mixture and evaluation against held-out inlier-class images. This substantially changes the represented training population and generation target. The double-well, 20D ring, and Gaussian-contamination scenarios remain; v2 also reports a complementary clean-target rerun.

E2.justification: V2 adds one targeted comparator, FM+Jac, to the main quantitative comparison and decoded-sample gallery. V1 compares standard FM with γ-FM variants without this explicit-smoothing control. The optional γ-FM+Jac combination is mentioned but has no reported comparison results.

E3.justification: V2 introduces a matched-budget comparison with decoded-image FID, Recall and Coverage, fixed-step midpoint sampling, and validation-FID-informed selection instead of GSC alone. New experiments vary batch size from 128 to 1024 and dimension from 32 to 256. The main γ sweep drops γ=4. Newly disclosed architecture and training details do not establish changes to previously unspecified settings.

E4.justification: V2 adds diagnostics of distance concentration and weight stability across dimensions and batch sizes (Appendix C.1), trained-model minibatch ablations and clean-target checks (Appendix D.1), and density/weight/radial analysis of the ring example. The existing neighbor-count ablation and contamination stress plot remain. The original autoencoder reconstruction diagnostic is removed.

E5.justification: V2 first reports three-seed means and standard deviations in Table 4, identifies seeds 42, 1042 and 2042, and adds error-bar plots. E6.justification: Table 1 is replaced: v1 reports γ=1 achieving inlier MMD 0.0126 versus FM's 0.0481, whereas v2 reports γ=1 with worse FID than FM (61.198 versus 59.063) and higher inlier MMD (0.000773 versus 0.000609). These are different settings, not cross-version performance changes. V2 also adds proxy/batch results and reports little clean-target advantage; the γ=4 result disappears.

M1.justification: The weighted-CFM framework remains, but v2's experimental implementation uses rank-based, quantile-scaled and clipped weights rather than v1's exponential distance-based proxy (Appendices C.1 and D). Shared-time batching is now explicit; v1 does not establish whether its batches mixed times. V2's Algorithm 1 still displays the exponential rule, leaving an implementation-description inconsistency.

P1.justification: The abstract, contribution list, experimental narrative and conclusion are substantially rewritten. V2 separates latent-flow setup from a new evaluation subsection, reorganizes and expands the experimental appendices, and revises theoretical explanations to distinguish formal results from mechanisms. Cross-references and supporting document sections are also updated.

P2.justification: V2 redesigns Table 1, adds Tables 3–4 and Figures 3 and 7, replaces the ring visualization with density/weight/speed/radial panels, redraws the GSC curve, and replaces the sample gallery to include FM+Jac. Margins and figure placement change substantially. The double-well, contamination and NFE graphics are retained despite renumbering or revised captions.

R1.justification: V2 adds Eguchi (2025) and explicitly identifies prior density-powered Stein-operator work in Section 3.4. The broader positioning relative to flow matching, optimal transport and escort geometry remains. Added bibliography entries for spectral-bias papers already cited in v1 complete references rather than introduce new research coverage.

T1.justification: The propositions, proofs, and Appendix A largely remain. V2 changes the diffusion flux from p∇p^γ to p^γ∇p and restores the density factor in the final roughness functional (v1 Eq. 20 to v2 Eq. 21). The flux revision fixes the double-well equation's γ=0 limit, but v2 Eq. 9 retains an incompatible 1/γ prefactor.

improvement.justification: V2 substantially improves the paper's experimental scrutiny and transparency through an explicit smoothing comparator, fidelity/diversity metrics, three-seed sensitivity results, and detailed implementation reporting. Its acknowledgement of fidelity trade-offs and weak clean-target gains corrects important overstatements in v1. The weighting-rule inconsistency and newly introduced diffusion-prefactor error remain material weaknesses, but the clearer evidence and narrower claims provide a substantial net improvement.

A1.justification: Both PDFs describe the same γ-Flow Matching work. Their text, equations, figures, tables, and appendices are readable and support comparison, including material moved or renumbered between versions.

after.justification: V2 reports original synthetic and CIFAR-10 results, including FM+Jac comparisons, decoded-image metrics, and additional proxy and minibatch sensitivity experiments.

before.justification: V1 reports original synthetic-flow and latent CIFAR-10 experiments, contamination tests, sampling-efficiency results, and a neighbor-count ablation.

arxiv_record.abstract: In recurrent neural networks (RNNs) used to model biological neural networks, noise is typically introduced during training to emulate biological variability and regularize learning. The expectation is that removing the noise at test time should preserve or improve performance. Contrary to this intuition, we find that continuous-time RNNs (CTRNNs) often perform best at or near the training noise level. This noise preference typically arises when noise is injected inside the neural activation function; networks trained with noise injected outside the activation function perform best with zero noise. The phenomenon arises robustly in diverse tasks for large enough training noise; we also show the phenomenon arising in feedforward neural networks, not just in RNNs. Our analyses show that the phenomenon stems from noise-induced shifts of fixed points (stationary distributions) in the underlying stochastic dynamics of the RNNs. These fixed point shifts are noise-level dependent and bias the network outputs when the noise is removed, degrading performance. Analytical and numerical results show that the bias arises when neural states operate near activation-function nonlinearities, where noise is asymmetrically attenuated, and that performance optimization incentivizes operation near these nonlinearities; such performance incentives exist for networks with noise inside, but not outside, the activation function, explaining why only noise-in networks show the preference. Thus, networks can overfit to the training noise itself rather than just to the input-output data. The phenomenon is distinct from stochastic resonance, wherein nonzero noise enhances signal processing. Our findings reveal that training noise can become an integral part of the computation learned by neural networks, with implications for understanding neural population dynamics and for the design of robust artificial RNNs.
arxiv_record.authors: Noah Eckstein, Manoj Srinivasan
arxiv_record.comments: Published in Transactions on Machine Learning Research (TMLR), 2026 21 pages, 8 figures
arxiv_record.title: Paradoxical noise preference in RNNs

C1.justification: The abstract expands the contribution beyond the original CTRNN demonstrations to diverse cognitive tasks, path integration, and feedforward networks. It also qualifies preference for the training noise as approximate and dependent on sufficiently large training noise, refining the original emphasis on matching the training level.

C2.justification: Sections 3.5 and 4 substantially expand the saturation-versus-coupling explanation and distinguish training stabilization from generalization benefits. v2 discusses applicability beyond rectifying, fixed-point networks and updates the remaining limitations to include unexplored limit-cycle dynamics and the unquantified relative regularization effectiveness of noise-in versus noise-out.

D1.justification: Appendices A-B add MLP architecture, regularization and optimizer settings, cognitive-task sampling and encoding choices, and path-generation distributions, boundary handling, and trial lengths. Appendix A also newly states that experimental code is supplied as Supplementary Material, although its availability cannot be verified from the PDFs alone.

E1.justification: v2 retains function computation, maze navigation, and regulation, while adding six cognitive tasks: ReactPro/ReactAnti, MemoryPro/MemoryAnti, and DelayPro/DelayAnti. It also adds two-dimensional path integration, extending coverage to stimulus-response rules, memory, delayed responses, and position estimation from movement cues (Sections 2.2.3-2.2.4).

E2.justification: The corresponding function-computation comparisons retain noise-in and noise-out networks and their noise-level controls. The added MLP and tanh experiments investigate architectural dependencies rather than introduce competing benchmark methods. Cited task implementations are not newly evaluated baselines.

E3.justification: v2 adds training-noise sweeps beyond the original function-computation setting (Figures 2b and A2), plus protocols for the new experiments. These include 15,000 cognitive-task training batches with doubled sampling of memory tasks, 100-step path-integration trials, and 20,000 MLP training batches (Appendices A-B). Settings for the retained experiments are largely unchanged.

E4.justification: New analyses test dependence on training-noise magnitude, rectification through ReLU versus tanh, recurrence through feedforward MLPs, and initialization through repeated training runs (Figures 2b, 3e, 6b, A1-A2). These substantially extend the original fixed-point prediction and ReLU regulator analyses.

E5.justification: Figure A1 newly reports four independent training runs with different initializations and noise seeds, displaying their individual error curves. v1 already reported error standard deviations and 300-sample Monte Carlo estimation, but lacked this across-training-run evidence. No confidence intervals or significance tests are introduced.

E6.justification: v2 adds cognitive-task, path-integration, MLP, tanh-regulator, training-noise, and replication results. New findings include zero-noise preference at sufficiently low training noise and sharper preference but worse optimal error as training noise increases (Figure 2b). The original principal curves are retained; these are additional results under expanded conditions, not same-setting performance improvements.

M1.justification: The central CTRNN update rules, noise-in/noise-out formulations, and fixed-point procedure are retained. v2 adds a feedforward adaptation with two 100-unit hidden layers and extends the single-neuron regulator from ReLU to tanh (Appendices A and B.5), introducing model variants without redesigning the central approach.

P1.justification: v2 reworks the abstract, several Results passages, and Future work, substantially expanding the mechanistic explanation. The Discussion is reorganized from two subsections into four covering regularization, broader relevance, stochastic resonance, and future work. The overall Methods/Results and Appendix A-C framework is retained.

P2.justification: Figure 2 gains a training-noise panel, Figure 3 expands from two to five panels, and Figure 6 gains a full tanh comparison. New appendix Figures A1-A2 display replication and noise-out sweeps. Figures 4-5 are rearranged, and Figure 4's noise-axis label is corrected from variance to standard deviation.

R1.justification: v2 adds literature on path integration and noise-dependent biological computation. Noise-out models are now grounded in prior neuroscience work rather than introduced solely for didactic purposes, and Koren et al. (2025) motivates an energy-efficiency qualification. The central positioning relative to stochastic resonance remains.

T1.justification: Equation 4 corrects its first branch condition from x >= 0 to x <= 0, repairing the overlapping conditions in the piecewise Ornstein-Uhlenbeck example. The principal fixed-point reasoning and Appendix C objectives remain unchanged; no substantial new proof framework is added.

improvement.justification: v2 substantially addresses v1's limited evidence for generality and repeatability through path-integration, cognitive-task, feedforward, tanh, training-noise, and repeated-run tests. These additions establish meaningful applicability boundaries and qualify the training-noise-matching claim. Expanded implementation details and discussion improve assessability. The gains outweigh localized reporting problems, including Section 4.1's reversed noise-in/noise-out label and Appendix B.5's nonnegative setpoint range despite negative tanh setpoints in Figure 6b.

A1.justification: Both PDFs describe the same noise-preference study and retain identifiable methods, experiments, and analyses. Their complete text, figures, equations, and Appendices A-C are readable and support comparison.

after.justification: v2 retains those original results and adds cognitive-task, path-integration, feedforward-network, activation-function, and training-run experiments.

before.justification: v1 reports original trained-network experiments on function computation, maze navigation, and single-neuron regulation, together with numerical fixed-point analyses.

arxiv_record.abstract: This paper provides a fresh view of the neural network (NN) pruning problem through the lens of graph theory. To achieve effective pruning, we aim to identify the main NN data flows and the corresponding NN connections that are most and least important for the performance of the full model. Unlike the standard approach to NN data flow analysis, which is based on information theory, we employ the notion of graph curvature, specifically Ollivier-Ricci curvature (ORC). ORC has been successfully used to identify important graph edges in various domains such as road traffic analysis, biological networks, and social networks. In particular, edges with negative ORC are considered bottlenecks and are therefore critical to the graph's overall connectivity, whereas positive-ORC edges are less essential. We use this intuition for NNs to (1) construct a graph induced by the NN structure and introduce the notion of neural curvature (NC) based on ORC; (2) calculate curvatures based on activation patterns for a set of input examples; and (3) demonstrate that NC can be used to rank edges according to their importance for overall NN functionality. We evaluate our method through pruning experiments on a variety of small and medium size models trained on three image datasets: MNIST, CIFAR-10, and CIFAR-100. The results indicate that our method can identify a larger number of unimportant edges compared to existing pruning methods.
arxiv_record.authors: Shuhang Tan, Jayson Sia, Paul Bogdan, Radoslav Ivanov
arxiv_record.title: Post-Training Neural Network Pruning using Graph Curvature
