C2.justification: v2 adds explanations linking SparseGPT's uneven performance to convolutional spatial coupling and training objectives, interprets the seed experiments as evidence of stability, and questions the suitability of the standard SynFlow iteration budget. Its expanded discussion addresses measured computational costs and hybrid mitigation. It also explains that CIFAR-100 adversarially trained models were excluded because of substantial accuracy loss.

D1.justification: v1 refers to training details in an appendix absent from the supplied PDF. v2 Appendices A.2-A.4 provide optimizer, learning-rate, weight-decay, PGD, normalization, and layer-level architecture details. v2 also adds a project code URL, a SparseGPT implementation pointer, and runtime/memory information. These improve documented reproducibility without establishing that previously unspecified settings changed.

E1.justification: Both versions evaluate image classification on MNIST, CIFAR-10, and CIFAR-100. Additional training configurations and sensitivity experiments retain these datasets and task requirements.

E2.justification: v1 compares against magnitude pruning, SNIP, and SynFlow. v2 adds the post-training Hessian-based SparseGPT baseline to the benchmark and weight-decay comparisons, including the Tanh plots whose legends show its participation. SynFlow is removed from the Tanh comparisons, substantially revising the comparator set across existing experiments.

E3.justification: The stated calibration sizes and pruning without retraining are retained. v2 expands CIFAR-100 evaluation from one ReLU model to three configurations, explicitly covering two CE learning rates and WD. New protocols compare aggregation rules, test SynFlow with 5, 50, and 100 iterations, measure computational resources, and evaluate hybrid pre-pruning with an accuracy-loss threshold of 0.025.

E4.justification: v2 adds minimum/mean/maximum ranking ablation (Figure 5b), calibration-selection and model-initialization sensitivity (Figure 8), hybrid scalability analysis (Figure 9), and SynFlow iteration sensitivity (Appendix A.10). Existing component, calibration-size, weight-decay, and per-layer analyses are retained or relocated. Additional appendix panels supply evidence that v1 sometimes mentions without including.

E5.justification: v1 provides no repeated-run or uncertainty reporting. v2 Section 6.3.5 tests three calibration sets and three model initializations, reporting mean pruning curves with minimum-to-maximum envelopes across the three models. This introduces an explicit uncertainty-reporting practice, although its coverage is limited to the CIFAR-10 CE ReLU setting.

E6.justification: v2 adds SparseGPT results, an expanded CIFAR-100 configuration comparison, aggregation and seed findings, and computational measurements; it removes Tanh SynFlow curves. New findings favor minimum aggregation and report improved SynFlow performance with five iterations. Within v2, Table 1 reports 1060.574 seconds per example for curvature versus 675.012 for the hybrid, with peak memory increasing from 13493.0 to 17201.2 MB.

M1.justification: The core inverse-weight graph, activation-dependent curvature, and minimum-based parameter ranking are retained. Section 7 adds an evaluated hybrid variant that first performs magnitude pruning to an accuracy-loss threshold and then applies curvature pruning to the remaining parameters.

P1.justification: The title, abstract, introduction, related work, and conclusion are extensively rewritten around pruning. Implementation becomes Section 5.5; Algorithm 1 and the proof move to Appendices A.5-A.6; Tanh comparisons and per-layer discussion move into organized appendix sections. These are substantial narrative and structural changes beyond the added experiments.

P2.justification: The original combined benchmark Figure 3 is reorganized into a ReLU comparison and appendix Tanh Figure 10, with revised legends and comparator curves. Per-layer and Tanh weight-decay displays move to the appendix. v2 adds aggregation, seed-variation, hybrid, and iteration-sensitivity plots, additional supplementary panels, and the runtime/memory Table 1.

R1.justification: Related work is substantially refocused around pruning at initialization versus post-training pruning, adding SparseGPT, Kumar et al.'s information-theoretic pruning barriers, and Wang et al.'s gradient-flow pruning work. The earlier robustness/OOD motivation and several information-flow and learning-based pruning references are removed. This accompanies a substantive repositioning as a graph-based post-training pruning approach.

T1.justification: The background probability definition changes from proportional weighting in v1 Definition 3 to explicit exponential normalization in v2 Definitions 2 and 4. Section 5.5 also corrects v1's self-referential shortest-path recurrence with a layer-recursive min-plus expression. Proposition 1 and its proof are retained, with the proof moved to Appendix A.6 and its probability distributions explained more explicitly.

improvement.justification: Relative to the supplied v1, v2 substantially strengthens assessability by supplying missing training and architecture details, adding a relevant post-training comparator, testing ranking and baseline-budget choices, reporting variation across runs, and quantifying computational costs. These address important reproducibility and validation gaps. The seed study remains narrow, and the hybrid reduces runtime while increasing peak memory, but these limitations do not outweigh the substantial gains in evidence and transparency.

A1.justification: The authors, neural-curvature construction, proposition, and overlapping experiments identify the same research despite the title change. Both PDFs are readable, but v1 ends with references on page 21 despite referring to appendices. Earlier supplementary details therefore cannot be fully compared with v2's Appendix A.

after.justification: v2 retains original pruning results and reports additional baseline comparisons, aggregation and seed experiments, and runtime and memory measurements.

before.justification: v1 reports original pruning experiments on MNIST, CIFAR-10, and CIFAR-100, together with component, calibration-size, weight-decay, and per-layer analyses.

arxiv_record.abstract: Sampling configurations at thermodynamic equilibrium is a central challenge in statistical physics. Boltzmann Generators (BGs) tackle it by combining a generative model with a Monte Carlo (MC) correction step to obtain asymptotically unbiased samples from an unnormalized target. Most current BGs use classic MC mechanisms such as importance sampling, which both require tractable likelihoods from the backbone model and scale poorly in high-dimensional, multi-modal targets. We study BGs built on annealed Monte Carlo (aMC), which is designed to overcome these limitations by bridging a simple reference to the target through a sequence of intermediate densities. Diffusion models (DMs) are powerful generative models and have already been incorporated into aMC-based recalibration schemes via the diffusion-induced density path, making them appealing backbones for aMC-BGs. We provide an empirical meta-analysis of DM-based aMC-BGs on controlled multi-modal Gaussian mixtures (varying mode separation, number of modes, and dimension), explicitly disentangling inference effects from learning effects by comparing (i) a perfectly learned DM and (ii) a DM trained from data. Even with a perfect DM, standard integrations using only first-order stochastic denoising kernels fail systematically, whereas second-order denoising kernels can substantially improve performance when covariance information is available. We further propose a deterministic aMC integration based on first-order transport maps derived from DMs, which outperforms the stochastic first-order variant at higher computational cost. Finally, in the learned-DM setting, all DM-aMC variants struggle to produce accurate BGs; we trace the main bottleneck to inaccurate DM log-density estimation. Code available at https://github.com/h2o64/dabg.
arxiv_record.authors: Louis Grenioux, Maxence Noble
arxiv_record.title: Diffusion-based Annealed Boltzmann Generators : benefits, pitfalls and hopes

C1.justification: The central contributions remain the same: diffusion paths benefit annealed sampling; first-order stochastic transitions offer limited gains; deterministic maps can approach second-order performance; and inaccurate learned log-densities undermine practical BGs. V2 changes their implementation and supporting evidence without replacing these core claims.

C2.justification: V2 strengthens the density-bottleneck interpretation using controlled experiments and revises the mode-blindness discussion to distinguish target-dependent tSM behavior and DiffCLF's partial success. Appendix C.1 newly qualifies the correction through Gaussianity, truncation error, and possible failure at dimensions at most 10. These are substantive mechanism and applicability qualifications.

D1.justification: V2 newly provides code-access information. Tables 2–4 document expanded search grids, initialization schemes, and selected hyperparameters, while Appendix D.2 explains shared-model selection. Appendices B.4 and C.1 add detailed scheduling and shared-probe estimator instructions. These materially expand reproducibility information beyond v1's smaller parameter table and general descriptions.

E1.justification: V2 adds non-Gaussian ManyWell targets in dimensions 16, 32, and 64, extending evaluation beyond v1's Gaussian mixtures. The 32-dimensional ManyModes benchmark also changes from 16/32/64 modes to 4/16/64 modes. Both versions retain the one-dimensional density-path case studies.

E2.justification: V2 adds DiffCLF+DSM to the evaluated density-learning objectives. Across the main AIS/SMC/RE comparisons, first-order stochastic baselines switch from EI to DDPM beta kernels; Figure 18 additionally compares both. V1's second-order DDPM is renamed DDPM-2, which alone is not a new comparator.

E3.justification: Fixed logarithmic tempering schedules become target-specific Lambda-optimal schedules, K=16 is dropped, and RE defaults to base rather than score-informed initialization. Training changes from K-specific networks and sampling-based hyperparameter selection to shared networks selected using density diagnostics; standalone DSM receives 2,000 rather than 1,000 epochs. V2 also adds log-normalizer evaluation and replaces TwoModes absolute weight error with direct weight estimates.

E4.justification: Figure 4 introduces exact-density/learned-score controls. Appendix D.4 adds scheduling, EI-versus-DDPM, and multi-step-transition comparisons, plus direct VP/VE invertibility and penalty-estimator diagnostics. These substantially revise the analysis suite: v1's local-MCMC-step and swap-period studies disappear, and its final-sampling hyperparameter sweeps are replaced by component-error investigations.

E5.justification: The main sampling experiments still use eight runs. V2 adds a dedicated metric-calibration experiment with 128 independent repetitions and explicit mean-plus-standard-deviation reporting (Figure 8). It also introduces boxplots for direct mode-weight and log-normalizer estimates, expanding distributional reporting without establishing an increase in the main experiment run counts.

E6.justification: V2 adds ManyWell, DiffCLF, log-normalizer, and diagnostic results while removing many detailed Gaussian-mixture panels and runtime results. Under its revised procedures, Figure 3 reports much closer agreement between Hutchinson-based and Hessian-based RE than v1. The RE-initialization findings also change from broadly beneficial score-informed initialization to mostly neutral or mixed effects. These are revised results under changed conditions, not isolated same-setting performance gains.

M1.justification: The implicit-midpoint framework remains, but v2 substantially revises its stochastic Jacobian treatment: ordinary Hutchinson estimation becomes Hutch++, and a penalty correction modifies importance weights and MH acceptance probabilities. Appendix C.1 also specifies shared probes for RE swaps. These change the implemented sampling procedure, rather than merely explaining v1.

P1.justification: The abstract is rewritten, several experimental discussions are clarified and streamlined, and discrete-time material moves from Appendix A.2 to B.4. Supplementary results are organized more thematically. Nevertheless, the seven-section main structure and much of the background, related-work exposition, and existing proofs remain recognizable.

P2.justification: Figure 3 combines TwoModes and ManyModes panels and removes its runtime row. Figure 4 expands the objective panels and changes control hatching. Extensive appendix grids give way to consolidated plots, boxplots, and new diagnostic figures; hyperparameter tables are expanded substantially. These are extensive display changes beyond renumbering or numerical updates.

R1.justification: V2 adds substantive references and discussion for DiffCLF, Hutch++, penalty corrections, and concurrent work by Hoffmann et al., while removing the pseudo-marginal justification cited in v1. Most of the related-work framework remains intact. Publication-year and venue updates for retained works do not constitute new research positioning.

T1.justification: New Appendix C.1 develops Gaussian-noise assumptions, a Bessel penalty transform, and variance-symmetry conditions for corrected MH transitions. This replaces v1's unsupported inference that unbiased log-determinant estimates automatically preserve sampling guarantees. Appendix B.4 also revises discretization formulas and introduces communication-barrier reasoning. The original implicit-midpoint lemmas and proofs are largely retained.

improvement.justification: V2 substantially strengthens the empirical foundation: optimized tempering improves baseline fairness, exact-density/learned-score controls better test the proposed failure mechanism, and ManyWell addresses the Gaussian-only scope. Reproducibility information also improves. Important caveats remain: the runtime panel and detailed result grids are removed, and v2 Equation (35) gives gamma^2/N where the preceding penalty definition implies gamma^2/2. That inconsistency limits confidence in the mathematical repair, but does not outweigh the substantial improvement in experimental support.

A1.justification: Both PDFs describe the same research work. Their main texts, equations, figures, tables, and appendices A–D support reliable comparison, including matching relocated material and renamed methods.

after.justification: V2 reports original Gaussian-mixture and ManyWell experiments, controlled density-error investigations, and additional numerical diagnostics.

before.justification: V1 reports original sampling experiments on TwoModes and ManyModes, learned-density evaluations, and extensive appendix ablations.

arxiv_record.abstract: Unsupervised neural combinatorial optimization (NCO) enables learning powerful solvers without access to ground-truth solutions. Existing approaches fall into two disjoint paradigms: models trained for generalization across instances, and instance-specific models optimized independently at test time. While the former are efficient during inference, they lack effective instance-wise adaptability; the latter are flexible but fail to exploit learned inductive structure and are prone to poor local optima. This motivates the central question of our work: how can we leverage the inductive bias learned through generalization while unlocking the flexibility required for effective instance-wise adaptation? We first identify a challenge in bridging these two paradigms: generalization-focused models often constitute poor warm starts for instance-wise optimization, potentially underperforming even randomly initialized models when fine-tuned at test time. To resolve this incompatibility, we propose TACO, a model-agnostic test-time adaptation framework that unifies and extends the two existing paradigms for unsupervised NCO. TACO applies strategic warm-starting to partially relax trained parameters while preserving inductive bias, enabling rapid and effective unsupervised adaptation. Crucially, compared to naively fine-tuning a trained generalizable model or optimizing an instance-specific model from scratch, TACO achieves better solution quality while incurring negligible additional computational cost. Experiments on the canonical problems of minimum vertex cover, maximum clique, maximum independent set, and max cut demonstrate the effectiveness and robustness of TACO across static, distribution-shifted, and dynamic combinatorial optimization problems, establishing it as a practical bridge between generalizable and instance-specific unsupervised NCO.
arxiv_record.authors: Yiqiao Liao, Farinaz Koushanfar, Parinaz Naghizadeh
arxiv_record.title: Test-Time Adaptation for Unsupervised Combinatorial Optimization

Experiments on the canonical problems of minimum vertex cover, maximum clique, maximum independent set, and max cut demonstrate the effectiveness and robustness of TACO across static, distribution-shifted, and dynamic combinatorial optimization problems, establishing it as a practical bridge between generalizable and instance-specific unsupervised NCO.

arxiv_record.abstract: Neural visual decoding is a central problem in brain-computer interface research, aiming to reconstruct human visual perception and to elucidate the structure of neural representations. Recent contrastive neural visual decoding methods commonly align neural signals with the final embeddings of pretrained vision encoders. However, such representations are optimized for high-level semantic invariance, whereas EEG/MEG signals contain information spanning multiple levels of visual abstraction, potentially creating a representational granularity mismatch. Motivated by prior evidence that brain representations correspond to multiple levels of the DNN hierarchy, we propose Shallow Alignment, a granularity-calibration framework that systematically explores intermediate visual representations as alignment targets for neural decoding. Extensive experiments across multiple benchmarks demonstrate that Shallow Alignment significantly outperforms standard final-layer alignment, with performance gains ranging from 22% to 58% across diverse vision backbones. Notably, our approach reveals a positive scaling trend in neural visual decoding, enabling decoding performance to improve consistently with the capacity of pre-trained vision backbones. We further conduct systematic empirical analyses to shed light on the mechanisms underlying the observed performance gains. Code is available at https://github.com/yangdu-neuroai/shallow-alignment.

arxiv_record.abstract: Predicting generalization from quantities available before target-test evaluation remains a central challenge in deep learning. The systematic benchmark of Jiang et al. (2020) evaluated many generalization measures, but it focused on independent and identically distributed (IID) settings. We revisit this problem for image classifiers evaluated under controlled corruptions and perturbations. Our study uses CIFAR-10-C/P, where the label space and task remain fixed while the input images are degraded or perturbed. This setting also allows us to revisit the robustness concerns raised by Dziugaite et al. (2020), who showed that the apparent reliability of generalization measures can depend strongly on experimental conditions. Our experiments show that the usefulness of generalization measures is strongly regime-dependent. In our exploratory decision analysis across three CNN-style architectures, sharpness- and input-gradient-based measures are among the leading individual signals, whereas family results are close and architecture dependent. Optimization-based measures, Information Criteria, and Sharpness-based measures provide additional regime-dependent signals in correlation or local-reliability analyses. Together, these findings suggest that model selection should not rely only on measures favored by IID evaluation. Instead, within the evaluated CIFAR-10-C/P setting and architectures, generalization measures should be treated as regime-dependent ranking signals whose utility must be evaluated for the intended corruption or perturbation setting.

arxiv_record.abstract: A key challenge in autoregressive image generation is to efficiently sample independent locations in parallel, while still modeling mutual dependencies with serial conditioning. Some recent works have addressed this by conditioning between scales in a multiscale pyramid. Others have looked at parallelizing samples in a single image using regular partitions or randomized orders. In this work we examine a flexible, fixed ordering based on progressive checkerboards for multiscale autoregressive image generation. Our ordering draws samples in parallel from evenly spaced regions at each scale, maintaining full balance in all levels of a quadtree subdivision at each step. This enables effective conditioning both between and within scales. snapshot_arxiv_record.abstract: A key challenge in autoregressive image generation is to efficiently sample independent locations in parallel, while still modeling mutual dependencies with serial conditioning. Some recent works have addressed this by conditioning between scales in a multiscale pyramid. Others have looked at parallelizing samples in a single image using regular partitions or randomized orders. Our ordering draws samples in parallel from evenly spaced regions at each scale, maintaining full balance in all levels of a quadtree subdivision at each step. This enables effective conditioning both between and within scales. Intriguingly, we find evidence that in our balanced setting, a wide range of scale-up factors lead to similar results, so long as the total number of serial steps is constant. On class-conditional ImageNet, our method achieves competitive performance compared to recent state-of-the-art autoregressive systems with like model capacity, using fewer sampling steps.

arxiv_record.abstract: We introduce Variational Joint Embedding (VJE), a reconstruction-free latent-variable framework for non-contrastive self-supervised learning in representation space. VJE maximizes a symmetric conditional evidence lower bound (ELBO) on paired encoder embeddings by defining a conditional likelihood directly on target representations, rather than optimizing a pointwise compatibility objective. The likelihood is instantiated as a heavy-tailed Student--\(t\) distribution on a polar representation of the target embedding, where a directional--radial decomposition separates angular agreement from magnitude consistency and mitigates norm-induced pathologies. The directional factor operates on the unit sphere, yielding a valid variational bound for the associated spherical subdensity model. An amortized inference network parameterizes a diagonal Gaussian posterior whose feature-wise variances are shared with the directional likelihood, yielding anisotropic uncertainty without auxiliary projection heads. Across ImageNet-1K, CIFAR-10/100, and STL-10, VJE is competitive with standard non-contrastive baselines under linear and \(k\)-NN evaluation, while providing probabilistic semantics directly in representation space for downstream uncertainty-aware applications. We validate these semantics through out-of-distribution detection, where representation-space likelihoods yield strong empirical performance. These results position the framework as a principled variational formulation of non-contrastive learning, in which structured feature-wise uncertainty is represented directly in the learned embedding space.

arxiv_record.abstract: Neural scaling laws -- power-law relationships between loss, model size, and data -- have been extensively documented for language and vision transformers, yet their existence in single-cell genomics remains largely unexplored. We present the first systematic study of scaling behaviour for masked-reconstruction transformers trained on single-cell RNA sequencing (scRNA-seq) data. Using expression profiles from the CELLxGENE Census, we construct two experimental regimes: a data-rich regime (512 highly variable genes, 200,000 cells) and a data-limited regime (1,024 genes, 10,000 cells). Across seven model sizes spanning three orders of magnitude in parameter count (533 to 3.4 x 10^8 parameters), we fit the parametric scaling law to validation mean squared error (MSE). The data-rich regime exhibits clear power-law scaling with an irreducible loss floor of c ~ 1.44, while the data-limited regime shows negligible scaling, indicating that model capacity is not the binding constraint when data are scarce. These results establish that scaling laws analogous to those observed in natural language processing do emerge in single-cell transcriptomics when sufficient data are available, and they identify the data-to-parameter ratio as a critical determinant of scaling behaviour. A preliminary conversion of the data-rich asymptotic floor to information-theoretic units yields an estimate of approximately 2.30 bits of entropy per masked gene position. We discuss implications for the design of single-cell foundation models and outline the additional measurements needed to refine this entropy estimate.
arxiv_record.authors: Ihor Kendiukhov
arxiv_record.title: Scaling Laws for Masked-Reconstruction Transformers on Single-Cell Transcriptomics

arxiv_record.abstract: Models based on partial differential equations (PDEs) are powerful for describing a wide range of complex phenomena in the natural sciences. Accurately identifying the PDE model, which represents the underlying physical law, is essential for a proper understanding of the problem. This reconstruction typically relies on indirect and noisy measurements of the system's state and, without specifically tailored methods, rarely yields symbolic expressions, thereby limiting interpretability. In this work, we address this limitation by considering neural network architectures based on rational functions for the symbolic representation of physical laws. These networks combine the approximation power of rational functions with the flexibility to represent arithmetic operations, and generalize ParFam and EQL-type architectures used in symbolic regression for physical law learning. We further establish regularity results for these symbolic networks. Our main contribution is a reconstruction result showing that, if there exists an admissible physical law that is expressible within the symbolic network architecture, then in the limit of noiseless and complete measurements, symbolic networks recover a physical law within the PDE model that is representable by the architecture. Moreover, the recovered law corresponds to a regularization-minimizing parameterization, promoting interpretability and sparsity in case of $L^1$-regularization. Under an additional identifiability condition, the unique true physical law is recovered. These reconstruction and regularity results are derived at the continuous level prior to discretization due to a formulation in function space. Empirical results using the ParFam architecture are consistent with the theoretical findings and suggest the feasibility of reconstructing interpretable physical laws in practice.
arxiv_record.authors: Erion Morina, Philipp Scholl, Martin Holler
arxiv_record.title: Symbolic recovery of PDEs from measurement data

C1.justification: v1's abstract claims unique reconstruction of the simplest physical law. v2 instead states reconstruction of a representable, regularization-minimizing admissible law, with recovery of the unique true law requiring an additional identifiability condition. The conclusion likewise qualifies statements about network limits, substantially narrowing the headline guarantee to match the retained theory.

C2.justification: Section 4.1.2 substantially expands discussion of regularity, measurement injectivity and applicability beyond the earlier brief remarks. New experiments motivate explanations involving architectural misspecification, enlarged search spaces and local minima. The conclusion explicitly acknowledges limited numerical performance and distinguishes the analytical contribution from a mature numerical framework.

D1.justification: v2 adds substantial reproducibility information: early-stopping patience, regularization strength, derivative estimation, per-system architectures, restart and time budgets, forward solvers, grids and initial-condition generation. Tables 1, 3 and 6 organize these details. The documented code-access link also changes from an anonymous repository to a named GitHub repository.

E1.justification: Coverage expands from two linear 1D PDE examples to seven Strogatz ODE systems, the 2D Brusselator and a 2D membrane-transport system. These introduce coupled nonlinear dynamics, Laplacian-dependent laws, and polynomial, rational, trigonometric and exponential recovery tasks.

E2.justification: Neither version evaluates separate competing recovery algorithms. The new comparisons vary ParFam architecture and structural constraints as ablations; cited approaches such as SINDy and EQL do not become evaluated baselines.

E3.justification: New experiments introduce 10–80 ODE trajectories, system-specific architectures and optimization budgets, 64×64 and 32×32 PDE grids, and distinct measurement-resolution sweeps. They also introduce Savitzky–Golay derivative estimation and coefficient thresholding at 0.015 for error evaluation. These are additional protocols, not evidence that the original linear-PDE settings changed.

E4.justification: Beyond the original domain-dependent error analysis, v2 tests underspecified, default and extended architectures, and compares unconstrained recovery with additive diffusion constraints. Figures 3–7 also examine errors around trajectories and document difficult regimes, diffusion-coefficient recovery failures and variability across optimization runs.

E5.justification: v1 provides no repeated-run counts or uncertainty bands. v2 reports medians and interquartile ranges over 10 seeds for Figure 2, 15 seeds for the ODE experiments, and repeated-seed reporting for the 2D experiments. This establishes substantially stronger uncertainty reporting, without establishing how many runs underlay v1.

E6.justification: Figure 2 contains revised median curves, although the two displayed linear-PDE reconstruction formulas remain unchanged. Table 4 adds recovered ODE formulas and errors, including Lotka–Volterra errors of 0.14 and 0.11. Figures 4–7 add substantial PDE results, including unsuccessful diffusion recovery in the hard Brusselator regime and variable rational-term recovery in membrane transport.

M1.justification: The symbolic-network architecture, objective (Pm) and alternating optimization remain. Section 5.2.3 adds a constrained ParFam variant enforcing additive diffusion and excluding cross-terms between the Laplacian and state variables, a limited procedural extension.

P1.justification: The abstract and introduction are substantially revised, related work becomes a separate section, and scope, novelty and organization receive dedicated subsections. Scattered assumption remarks become a structured discussion, and extensions receive their own subsection. This materially changes the narrative organization beyond simply inserting experiments.

P2.justification: v2 adds Figures 3–7 and Tables 1–6, introducing extensive multipanel results, architecture comparisons and configuration summaries. Figure 2 is redrawn with uncertainty bands and revised captions. Wider text blocks and changed typography also substantially alter the document layout.

R1.justification: Six references are added, covering transport regularity, operator learning, variational regularization and Lasso; the earlier cited works are retained. Section 1.2 sharpens the distinction from existing all-at-once frameworks and ParFam/EQL by emphasizing the nontrivial verification of symbolic networks' function-space properties.

T1.justification: The principal definitions, assumptions, reconstruction theorem, identifiability corollary and Appendix A–C proofs are retained after renumbering. However, v2 drops v1 Remark 8's assertion that the sampling operators satisfy condition (5) while failing the stronger convergence conditions discussed there, removing a limited mathematical assertion.

improvement.justification: v2 substantially addresses v1's narrow validation on two linear examples through nonlinear ODE and 2D PDE experiments, architecture and structure tests, and explicit uncertainty reporting. Expanded implementation details improve reproducibility, while the abstract and conclusion better distinguish reconstruction from unique identification. The experiments still expose numerical failures, but reporting those failures and their variability makes the paper's practical scope considerably better supported.

A1.justification: Both PDFs describe the same symbolic PDE recovery framework. Their text, equations, figures, tables and Appendices A–C are readable and support comparison despite substantial reorganization and expanded experiments.

after.justification: Section 5 retains the linear-PDE experiments and reports original simulations and reconstruction results for seven nonlinear ODE systems and two 2D PDE systems.

before.justification: Section 4 and Figure 2 report original numerical reconstructions of two linear PDEs from simulated incomplete, noisy measurements.

arxiv_record.abstract: Uncertainty quantification has emerged as an effective approach to closed-book hallucination detection for LLMs, but existing methods are largely designed for short-form outputs and do not generalize well to long-form generation. We introduce a taxonomy for fine-grained uncertainty quantification in long-form LLM outputs that distinguishes methods by design choices at three stages: response decomposition, unit-level scoring, and response-level aggregation. We formalize several families of consistency-based black-box scorers, providing generalizations and extensions of existing methods. We also introduce FactScore-STEM-Geo, a new 400-question long-form QA dataset spanning four categories across STEM and Geography. In our experiments across multiple LLMs and datasets, we find 1) claim-response entailment consistently performs better or on par with more complex claim-level scorers, 2) claim-level scoring generally yields better results than sentence-level scoring, and 3) uncertainty-aware decoding is highly effective for improving the factuality of long-form outputs. Our framework clarifies relationships between prior methods, enables apples-to-apples comparisons, and provides practical guidance for selecting components for fine-grained UQ.

arxiv_record.abstract: Missing data problems, such as missing modalities in multi-modal brain MRI and missing slices in cardiac MRI, pose significant challenges in clinical practice. Existing methods rely on external guidance to supply detailed missing-state information for instructing generative models to synthesize missing MRIs. However, manual indicators are not always available or reliable in real-world scenarios due to the unpredictable nature of clinical environments. Moreover, these explicit masks are not informative enough to provide guidance for improving semantic consistency. In this work, we argue that generative models should infer and recognize missing states in a self-perceptive manner, enabling them to better capture subtle anatomical and pathological variations. Towards this goal, we propose CoPeDiT, a shared completeness-perception framework for 3D MRI synthesis, following a common conditioning strategy with task-specific instantiations for different missing-data scenarios. Specifically, we incorporate dedicated pretext tasks into our tokenizer, CoPeVAE, empowering it to learn completeness-aware discriminative prompt tokens, and design MDiT3D, a specialized diffusion transformer architecture for 3D MRI synthesis that effectively uses the completeness-aware prompt tokens as guidance to enhance semantic consistency in 3D space. Comprehensive evaluations on three large-scale MRI datasets demonstrate that CoPeDiT consistently improves upon state-of-the-art methods across diverse missing patterns, yielding high-fidelity and structurally consistent MRI synthesis. Our code is available at https://github.com/JK-Liu7/CoPeDiT.
arxiv_record.authors: Junkai Liu, Nay Aung, Theodoros N. Arvanitis, Joao A. C. Lima, Steffen E. Petersen, Le Zhang
arxiv_record.title: Exploiting Completeness Perception with Diffusion Transformer for Unified 3D MRI Synthesis

Appendix D explicitly states that scanner, institution, protocol, and population shifts were not evaluated. It also explains how prompts complement available latents, while Appendix C.7 links completeness-prediction errors to contrast drift, modality bias, and blurred structures.

E1.justification: The same brain and cardiac datasets are used. Downstream BraTS segmentation coverage expands from three real modalities plus one synthesized modality to one real modality plus three synthesized modalities (v3 Appendix C.8/Table 21), adding a more severely incomplete input scenario within the existing task.

These methods also enter the retained single-synthetic-modality segmentation comparison (v3 Table 7 versus v1 Table 12). APT was cited in v1 but was not evaluated there.

E3.justification: v3 adds MAE and FVD, lesion-restricted metrics, frozen nnU-Net anatomical evaluation with Dice/HD95, and pretext-task accuracy/macro-F1. E4.justification: Beyond v1's existing component, injection-position, backbone, and prompt-corruption analyses, v3 adds position-prompt replacement with mask codes, structured prompt interventions, unseen-combination robustness, lesion/anatomical fidelity, computational-cost analysis, perception accuracy, and synthesis errors grouped by prediction correctness. arxiv_record.abstract: Medical image analysis depends on accurate segmentation and controllable synthesis, but both tasks face severe spatial imbalance: lesions occupy small regions against large backgrounds. We study adaptive spatial weighting as a task-level design principle and instantiate it in two adapters. LAW learns per-pixel loss weights for mask-conditioned diffusion by modulating a ratio prior with a feature-dependent delta map, with normalization, clamping, and Dice regularization for stability. ORDER improves lightweight segmentation by adding selective bidirectional skip attention with stage-wise confidence gating. On held-out diffusion test sets, LAW lowers FID from 158.13$\pm$0.15 to 108.43$\pm$0.71 on Polyps, from 144.13$\pm$0.31 to 89.51$\pm$0.96 on KiTS19, and from 139.22$\pm$0.38 to 112.58$\pm$0.68 on BRISC, while improving held-out mask-recovery Dice from 0.681$\pm$0.013 to 0.825$\pm$0.003 on Polyps. When the resulting images are added to nnUNet training, downstream Polyps mDice rises from 71.7$\pm$0.4 to 74.1$\pm$0.8. On the cleaned Polyps segmentation protocol, the reported ORDER configuration reaches 76.3$\pm$1.9 mDice and 67.2$\pm$2.0 mIoU at 42K parameters and 0.11 GFLOPs, versus 70.3$\pm$1.5 mDice and 59.9$\pm$1.7 mIoU for matched MK-UNet. On BRISC under the same training recipe, ORDER reaches 77.4$\pm$0.8 mDice and 68.1$\pm$0.7 mIoU. These results position adaptive spatial weighting as a practical design idea for both medical diffusion and efficient segmentation.

arxiv_record.abstract: Modern predictive systems combine predictors, sequential monitors, prediction sets, and online strategies, each with a different certificate of optimality. We study four criterion-relative geometries: Blackwell risk dominance, anytime-valid admissibility, fixed-level marginal coverage with expected-length efficiency within a declared rank-indexed family, and choice-based approachability (CApp) boundary-feasibility. We embed the four procedure types in a common product space and prove witness-based pairwise non-nesting: for every ordered pair of criterion classes, an explicit predictive system is active in both relevant coordinates, belongs to one class, and fails the other. The result records non-nesting across different object spaces and partial orders; it does not assert practical incompatibility. We separate three measure-relative coherence notions. In conditionally i.i.d. models, posterior predictive means under a single prior are martingales under the prior predictive law. For a point null, anytime-valid admissibility within e-processes is equivalent to the nonnegative martingale property. Self-consistency under a predictor's own predictive law does not imply Blackwell admissibility, as shown by a Bernoulli log-loss counterexample. Coverage admissibility is certified by exchangeability ranks within the declared rank-indexed family, while CApp boundary-feasibility uses Cesaro steering. A constrained-Bayes design schema organizes the four paradigms without collapsing their distinct decision spaces, partial orders, or risk functionals. Admissibility is criterion-relative.
arxiv_record.authors: Nicholas G. Polson and Daniel Zantedeschi

C1.justification: v1 claims incompatible geometries, no common refinement and no procedure satisfying all four criteria. v3 instead claims non-nesting of componentwise classes, explicitly permits compatible guarantees and replaces 'No universal procedure' with 'No universal certificate.' The abstract also withdraws martingale necessity for general Blackwell admissibility and qualifies the coverage and approachability claims.

C2.justification: v3 distinguishes empirical calibration from self-predictive martingale coherence and explains why calibration does not imply log-loss optimality. It interprets constrained Bayes as separate criterion-specific optimization problems and explains compatibility despite non-nesting. Applications become motivations, Gaussian extensions require further verification, and covariate-shift overcoverage is explicitly interpreted outside the exchangeability guarantee.

D1.justification: v3 supplies the clipping transformation and epsilon=10^-6, identifies simulated versus theoretical table quantities, and documents initialization and split-conformal rank/tie-breaking details. These improve technical specification; they do not establish how v1's computations were implemented. No code or data-access resource is added.

E1.justification: Both versions evaluate the same Bernoulli prediction and testing tasks and the same heteroskedastic Gaussian conformal scenarios involving Uniform and Beta covariates. The removed Gaussian location laboratory was analytical, not an additional empirical dataset or simulation.

E2.justification: The simulations retain Bayes versus plug-in MLE and likelihood-ratio e-process versus five-look z-testing. Clipping is presented as numerical handling of the MLE comparison. KT, discounted e-processes and dogmatic-prior predictors are theoretical witnesses, not new experimental baseline competitors.

E3.justification: The reported log-loss evaluation separates clipped numerical loss from theoretical unclipped risk, and the boundary diagnostic changes from an empirical frequency to an exact model probability. Sample sizes, testing thresholds, peeking schedule and conformal calibration/test sizes remain unchanged. The PDFs do not establish whether v1 already used clipping internally.

E4.justification: v3 adds an analytical failure check for fixed clipping: Table 2 states that it destroys plug-in martingale self-consistency and permits CApp feasibility only on the restricted parameter interval. Section 8.1 also quantifies boundary events below Monte Carlo resolution. The existing conformal covariate-shift analysis is retained.

E5.justification: Both versions state 10,000 Monte Carlo replications. Neither reports seeds, confidence intervals, standard errors or significance tests, and v3 establishes no increase in repeated runs or new uncertainty-reporting practice.

E6.justification: The central risk table is substantially corrected: v1 Table 4 reports finite MLE risk, including 2.368 at n=5; v3 Table 3 reports clipped risk 1.286 and theoretical unclipped risk infinity at every n. These are differently specified quantities, not a same-setting performance gain. Under retained settings, e-process/peeking rejection rates change from 0.034/0.169 to 0.031/0.165, and conformal coverages change from 0.897/0.964/0.888 to 0.900/0.946/0.900.

M1.justification: The work remains a theoretical analysis of existing prediction and inference procedures. The predictive-system tuple and new separation witnesses revise the formal framework, without introducing a new predictive algorithm. The experimental Bayes predictor, likelihood-ratio construction and conformal procedure are retained.

P1.justification: The abstract, introduction, contributions and discussion are extensively rewritten. Sections 4–6 gain substantial explanatory structure, terminology and scope remarks; proofs previously deferred to appendices appear alongside revised statements. The Gaussian laboratory and duality subsection disappear, and Applications becomes Motivations and Interpretations.

P2.justification: Several diagrams are redrawn or relabelled, especially the explicitly schematic risk plot and simplified coverage plot. The procedure-to-geometry diagram is removed, and the constrained-Bayes diagram is reorganized. The extended classification table is removed, a separation-witness table is added, and the classification and log-loss tables receive substantial structural revisions.

R1.justification: Positioning shifts from incompatible paradigms and a purported counterexample to martingale posteriors toward qualified, modular certificate transfer. v3 adds an explicit comparison with Choe and Ramdas on filtration transport and draws on Dawid, Krichevsky–Trofimov and misspecification literature. It removes the companion-paper framing and associated citations, alongside the Blackwell lecture framing.

T1.justification: v3 replaces risk-set closedness with upper-hull closedness, adds support/continuity conditions for Bayes admissibility, and replaces v1's varying-prior martingale equivalence under every true law with a single-prior implication under the prior predictive law. It revises AV dominance and restricts the martingale equivalence to point nulls. New definitions and proofs introduce rank-family coverage efficiency, the predictive-system space, active-coordinate separation witnesses and precise CApp feasibility. The Gaussian separation proposition and formal Lagrangian proposition are removed; appendix proofs are partly relocated and substantially superseded.

improvement.justification: v3 substantially improves the alignment of claims, proofs and numerical evidence. It corrects v1's inference from non-nesting to incompatibility, distinguishes the laws supporting martingale statements, supplies missing qualifications for Bayes admissibility, and resolves the finite-versus-infinite MLE risk presentation. The explicit separation witnesses strengthen the central argument. Generality is reduced, including withdrawal of the Gaussian extension, but this trades unsupported breadth for more defensible conclusions.

A1.justification: Both PDFs describe the same work, with readable text, equations, figures and tables. All supplied pages were inspected, including v1 Appendices A–B; their contents were matched to retained, revised or removed material in v3, which has no separate appendices.

after.justification: Section 8 retains the three original Monte Carlo studies and reports revised numerical results in Tables 3–5.

before.justification: Section 8 reports three original Monte Carlo studies of Bernoulli prediction, sequential testing and conformal coverage, with results in Tables 4–6.

arxiv_record.abstract: Brain-wide recordings of large-scale networks of neurons now provide an unprecedented view into how the brain drives behavior. However, brain activity contains both information directly related to behavior as well as the potential for many internal computations. Moreover, observable behavior is executed not only by the brain, but also by the spinal cord and peripheral nervous system. Behavior is a coarse-grained product of neural activity, and we thus take the view that it can be best represented by lower-dimensional latent neural dynamics. Capturing this indirect relationship while disambiguating behavior-generating networks from internal computations running in parallel requires new modeling approaches that can embody the parallel and distributed nature of large-scale neural populations. We thus present behavior-decomposed linear dynamical systems (b-dLDS) to disentangle simultaneously recorded subsystems and identify how the latent neural subsystems relate to behavior. We demonstrate the ability of b-dLDS to decouple behavioral vs. internal computations on controlled, simulated data, showing improvements over a state-of-the-art model that uses behavior to supervise all dynamics based on behavior. We also demonstrate b-dLDS's interpretability benefits on a task-driven RNN dataset featuring a nonlinear relationship between behavior and activations. We then show that b-dLDS can further scale up to tens of thousands of neurons by applying our model to a large-scale recording of a zebrafish hindbrain during the complex positional homeostasis behavior, wherein b-dLDS highlights asymmetry in behavior-related dynamic connectivity networks.
arxiv_record.authors: Eva Yezerets, En Yang, Misha B. Ahrens, Adam S. Charles
arxiv_record.title: Behavior-dLDS: A decomposed linear dynamical systems model for neural activity partially constrained by behavior

arxiv_record.abstract: The use of Vision-Language Models (VLMs) in automated driving applications is becoming increasingly common, with the aim of leveraging their reasoning and generalisation capabilities to handle long-tail scenarios. However, these models often fail on simple visual questions that are highly relevant to automated driving, and the reasons behind these failures remain poorly understood. In this work, we examine the intermediate activations of VLMs and assess the extent to which specific visual concepts are linearly encoded, with the goal of identifying bottlenecks in the flow of visual information. Specifically, we create counterfactual image sets that differ only in a targeted visual concept and then train linear probes to distinguish between them using the activations of five state-of-the-art (SOTA) VLMs, including two training variants for one model. Our results show that concepts such as the presence of an object or agent in a scene are explicitly and linearly encoded, whereas other spatial visual concepts, such as the orientation of an object or agent, are only implicitly encoded by the spatial structure retained by the vision encoder, or are not linearly encoded at all. In parallel, we observe that in certain cases, even when a concept is linearly encoded in the model's activations, the model still fails to answer correctly. This leads us to identify two failure modes. The first is perceptual failure, where the visual information required to answer a question is not linearly encoded in the model's activations. The second is cognitive failure, where the visual information is present but the model fails to align it correctly with language semantics. Finally, we show that increasing the distance of the object in question quickly degrades the linear separability of the corresponding visual concept...

arxiv_record.abstract: Accurate and reliable forecasting of epidemic incidences is critical for public health preparedness, yet it remains a challenging task due to complex nonlinear temporal dependencies and heterogeneous spatial interactions. Often, point forecasts generated by spatiotemporal models are unreliable in assigning uncertainty to future epidemic events. Probabilistic forecasting of epidemics is therefore crucial for providing the best or worst-case scenarios rather than a simple, often inaccurate, point estimate. We present deep spatiotemporal engression methods to generate accurate and reliable probabilistic forecasts on low-frequency epidemic datasets. The proposed methods act as distributional lenses, and out-of-sample probabilistic forecasts are generated by sampling from the trained models. Our frameworks encapsulate lightweight deep generative architectures, wherein uncertainty is quantified endogenously, driven by a pre-additive noise component during model construction. We establish geometric ergodicity and asymptotic stationarity of the spatiotemporal engression processes under mild assumptions on the network weights and pre-additive noise process. Comprehensive evaluations across six epidemiological datasets over three forecast horizons demonstrate that the proposal consistently outperforms several temporal and spatiotemporal benchmarks in both point and probabilistic forecasting. Additionally, we explore the explainability of the proposal to enhance the models' practical application for informed, timely public health interventions.

arxiv_record.abstract: In many time series forecasting settings, the target time series is accompanied by exogenous covariates, such as promotions and prices in retail demand; temperature in energy load; calendar and holiday indicators for traffic or sales; and grid load or fuel costs in electricity pricing. Ignoring these exogenous signals can substantially degrade forecasting accuracy, particularly when they drive spikes, discontinuities, or regime and phase changes in the target series. Most current time series foundation models (e.g., Chronos, Sundial, TimesFM, TimeMoE, TimeLLM, and LagLlama) ignore exogenous covariates and make forecasts solely from the numerical time series history, thereby limiting their performance. In this paper, we develop ApolloPFN, a prior-data fitted network (PFN) that is time-aware (unlike prior PFNs) and that natively incorporates exogenous covariates (unlike prior univariate forecasters). arxiv_record.abstract: Vision-Language Models (VLMs) have been applied to a wide range of reasoning tasks, yet it remains unclear whether they can reason robustly under distribution shifts. In this paper, we study covariate shifts in which the perceptual input distribution changes while the underlying prediction rules do not. To investigate this question, we consider visual deductive reasoning tasks, where a model is required to answer a query given an image and logical rules defined over the object concepts in the image. Empirically, we find that VLMs fine-tuned through gradient-based end-to-end training can achieve high in-distribution accuracy but fail to generalize under such shifts, suggesting that fine-tuning does not reliably induce the underlying reasoning function. This motivates a neuro-symbolic perspective that decouples perception from reasoning. However, we further observe that recent neuro-symbolic approaches that rely on black-box components for reasoning can still exhibit inconsistent robustness across tasks. To address this issue, we propose VLC, a neuro-symbolic method that combines VLM-based concept recognition with circuit-based symbolic reasoning. In particular, task rules are compiled into a symbolic program, specifically a circuit, which executes the rules exactly over the object concepts recognized by the VLM. Experiments on three simple visual deductive reasoning tasks with distinct rule sets show that VLC consistently achieves higher task accuracy on out-of-distribution data than other reasoning paradigms. Code is available at https://github.com/uiuctml/VLC.

arxiv_record.abstract: We develop a 3D aerothermodynamic simulator for the Orion reentry capsule at hypersonic speeds, a timely case study given its role in upcoming lunar missions. The large computational meshes required for these scenarios make traditional computational fluid dynamics impractical for full-mission performance prediction and control. In this work, we propose physics-enhanced 3D neural fields for predicting steady hypersonic flow around aerodynamic bodies. The model maps spatial coordinates and angle of attack to pressure, temperature, and velocity components. We enhance the base model with Fourier positional feature mappings, which allow it to capture the sharp discontinuities typical of hypersonic flows, and further constrain the solution by imposing no-slip and isothermal wall conditions. We compare our proposed approach to other surrogate alternatives, such as graph neural networks, and demonstrate its superior performance in capturing the steep gradients ubiquitous in this regime. Our formulation yields a continuous and computationally efficient aerothermodynamic surrogate that supports rapid exploration of operating conditions based on angle of attack variation under realistic flight profiles. While we focus on Orion, the proposed framework provides a general methodology for data-driven simulation in 3D hypersonic aerothermodynamics.

arxiv_record.abstract: Fragment-level representations provide a natural way to capture recurring molecular substructures and reuse their learned representations across molecules. However, a shared fragment identity alone may not fully describe how a fragment is instantiated in a particular molecule, since the same fragment can exhibit different chemical behavior depending on its surrounding atomic environment. Effective fragment-based molecular learning therefore requires representations that are both reusable across molecules and sensitive to local atomic context. We introduce BiScale-GTR, a self-supervised molecular representation framework built around context-grounded shared fragment tokens. BiScale-GTR constructs a reusable graph Byte Pair Encoding (graph-BPE) vocabulary using Weisfeiler-Lehman (WL)-based fragment identity, chemical validity filtering, and recursive out-of-vocabulary (OOV) decomposition. Each shared fragment token is then grounded with atom-level GNN representations through atom-to-fragment pooling and gated fusion, allowing the same fragment identity to acquire context-dependent representations in different molecular environments. A structure-aware fragment Transformer performs global reasoning over these atom-grounded tokens, capturing reusable substructure identity, local chemical context, and long-range molecular dependencies. Experiments on MoleculeNet, PharmaBench, and the Long Range Graph Benchmark demonstrate strong performance across classification and regression tasks. Attribution analysis further shows that BiScale-GTR highlights chemically meaningful recurring motifs, providing interpretable links between molecular structure and predicted properties.
arxiv_record.authors: Yi Yang and Ovidiu Daescu
arxiv_record.title: BiScale-GTR: Fragment-Aware Graph Transformers for Multi-Scale Molecular Representation Learning

arxiv_record.abstract: We study how depth, finite precision, state dimension, and chain-of-thought (CoT) affect the expressive power of multi-layer state-space models (SSMs). For the explicit-table $K$-function-composition problem, a canonical benchmark for sequential information propagation, we prove that any $L$-layer SSM solving $(L+3)$-function composition must satisfy $d^2p=\Omega(N/L^3)$, where $d$ is the state dimension and $p$ is the per-scalar precision. Conversely, $K$-function composition is solved exactly by a $(K+1)$-layer generalized SSM with $d=1$ and $p=\Theta(\log N)$. This gives a worst-case depth hierarchy for this formal problem family. We then distinguish post-input reasoning, in which all thought tokens are generated after the input, from input-interleaved reasoning, in which thought tokens may be inserted while the input stream is being read. Post-input reasoning does not circumvent our communication-based lower-bound pipeline, whereas input-interleaved reasoning admits bidirectional simulations with general deterministic one-pass streaming algorithms at the granularity of persistent memory. Finally, width and precision are not interchangeable under exact step-preserving simulation in the base affine-state model, but become interchangeable through the streaming-memory characterization once input-interleaved reasoning is allowed.
arxiv_record.authors: Nikola Zubi\'c, Qian Li, Yuyi Wang, Davide Scaramuzza
arxiv_record.title: On the Expressive Power and Limitations of Multi-Layer SSMs

arxiv_record.abstract: This paper presents FairNVT, a lightweight debiasing framework for pretrained transformer-based encoders that improves prediction fairness while preserving task performance. FairNVT is motivated by the intuition that reducing sensitive-attribute information in the representation used by the downstream classifier can facilitate fairer predictions. Our approach learns task-relevant and sensitive embeddings via lightweight adapters, applies calibrated Gaussian noise to the sensitive embedding, and fuses it with the task representation. Together with orthogonality constraints and fairness regularization, these components jointly reduce sensitive-attribute leakage in the learned embeddings and encourage fairer downstream predictions. Across three datasets spanning vision and language, FairNVT reduces sensitive-attribute attacker accuracy, improves fairness metrics such as demographic parity difference and equalized odds, and maintains competitive task performance.
arxiv_record.authors: Qiaoyue Tang, Sepidehsadat Hosseini, Mengyao Zhai, Thibaut Durand, Greg Mori
arxiv_record.title: FairNVT: Fair Classification via Noise Injection in Vision Transformers

arxiv_record.abstract: Accurate and rapid estimation of hemodynamic metrics, such as pressure and wall shear stress (WSS), is important for assessing the severity of Coronary Artery Disease (CAD). Existing approaches, including invasive Fractional Flow Reserve (FFR) measurements and computationally expensive Computational Fluid Dynamics (CFD) simulations, face challenges in invasiveness, cost, and speed. We present a learned surrogate for fast prediction of CFD-simulated coronary hemodynamics from vessel centerline geometry. The model encodes 1D vessel centerlines together with inlet flow rate using a transformer-based encoder, and predicts continuous wall-based fields via an anisotropic Radial Basis Function (RBF) decoder aligned with vessel morphology. To support training and evaluation, we introduce two datasets with paired steady-state OpenFOAM simulations: (i) a synthetic benchmark of $4{,}200$ single-vessel geometries with controlled anatomical variations, and (ii) a multi-vessel dataset derived from ImageCAS including $4{,}800$ cases spanning both right and left coronary arteries, generated by randomly introducing stenoses and varying physiologically plausible flow rates. Across both datasets, our method achieves lower pressure and WSS errors than strong neural-operator baselines (GNOT, Transolver, and ONO) at a fraction of the computational cost of CFD. On the multi-vessel dataset, using $1{,}024$ anisotropic RBF centers our model reduces the mean relative $\ell_2$ error by $52\%$ compared to the best neural-operator baseline, while at $128$ centers it requires $13.8\times$ fewer FLOPs than GNOT and still outperforms all neural-operator baselines. The single-vessel dataset is publicly available at https://huggingface.co/datasets/angioinsight/single-vessel-flow

Section 6 and Appendix A.16 explain untested solver/physics transfer and practical barriers to external evaluation, while adding a literature-based qualification of the steady-state limitation.

D1.justification: Appendix A.1 substantially expands simulation documentation with mesh sizes and quality thresholds, boundary layers, flux allocation, convergence criteria and unit conversion. v2 also documents the CenterlinePointNet++ adaptation and patient-grouped splitting, and updates training times. Section 4 replaces nominal anatomical ranges with measured statistics and revises the source-patient count from 141 to 140.

E1.justification: The two datasets and hemodynamic prediction tasks are retained. v2 adds testing under noisy coordinates, radii and flow rates, and surface/centerline dropout (Figure 5), extending input conditions within the existing task. The patient-disjoint experiment re-splits existing data; Appendix A.16 discusses external evaluation barriers without reporting external-dataset results.

E2.justification: CenterlinePointNet++, previously only cited, becomes an evaluated domain-specific comparator through a documented adaptation (Appendix A.4). It participates in standard multi-vessel accuracy, qualitative, robustness, distribution and efficiency comparisons. This substantially strengthens comparison coverage beyond the retained generic neural operators and Poiseuille baseline, although it is absent from the patient-disjoint and FFR comparisons.

E3.justification: The reported multi-vessel training budget changes from 5,000 to 3,000 epochs, and warmup from 1,000 to 500 epochs. v2 adds a patient-disjoint 3,989/415/396 split with training-only normalization and inference-time perturbation protocols. Appendix A.1 substantively revises the reported meshing, outlet boundary conditions and convergence specification. These documentation changes do not establish that the CFD datasets were regenerated.

E4.justification: v2 adds anatomy-generalization testing, stratification by flow and vascular complexity, input-noise/dropout sensitivity, geometry-correlated failure analysis and failure visualizations, plus encoder/decoder cost decomposition. The original design-choice ablation, GNOT-input comparison, circumferential WSS analysis and Bland-Altman analysis are retained rather than newly introduced.

E5.justification: v1 explicitly reports single runs with seed 1234 and defers multi-seed evaluation. v2 reports means and standard deviations over seeds 42, 1234 and 7890 for principal accuracy, training, validation and FFR results. Noise curves additionally average three perturbation trials. The GNOT-input ablation remains explicitly single-seed.

E6.justification: Tables 1–2 replace the proposed model's single-run test means of 0.107 and 0.309 with 0.116±0.012 and 0.304±0.010 for the corresponding best configurations. Changed training and aggregation prevent interpreting these as same-setting gains or losses. New results include patient-disjoint error 0.558±0.006 and CenterlinePointNet++ mean error 0.393; its WSS error, 0.315, beats the proposed model's 0.355. FFR, training, validation and supplementary findings also change or expand.

M1.justification: The proposed model retains its Fourier-embedded centerline transformer, FiLM flow conditioning, separate anisotropic Gaussian kernels for pressure and WSS, training loss and inference procedure. Sections 3 and A.4 specify the same proposed architecture.

P1.justification: The six-section organization and most methodological prose remain. Targeted edits revise the abstract, introduction, limitations and CFD description; appendix headings and cross-references are reorganized, and publication/header text is added. Much of the expansion documents new scientific content rather than wholesale narrative rewriting.

P2.justification: v2 adds stratification, noise-robustness and failure-case figures, plus patient-disjoint and cost-decomposition tables. Validation columns move from the main accuracy tables into separate appendix tables. The architecture diagram, Bland-Altman plots and error-distribution plots are redrawn, and several comparisons gain CenterlinePointNet++ columns or legend entries.

R1.justification: v2 adds Corral-Acero et al. (2020), Lo et al. (2019), Nannini et al. (2024) and Suk et al. (2021) for application motivation and limitations. improvement.justification: Three-seed reporting addresses v1's acknowledged single-run limitation, while the patient-disjoint evaluation directly examines previously unchecked anatomy overlap. arxiv_record.abstract: Circuit discovery methods identify subgraphs that explain model behaviors, and structural differences between discovered circuits are commonly interpreted as evidence of distinct mechanisms. We test this assumption by varying input-token frequency while holding the task fixed. The discovered circuits appear specialized by frequency when compared structurally, but functional and representational analyses show no reliable evidence of corresponding differences. We term this mismatch phantom specialization. Using the Literal Sequence Copying task across four frequency bands plus a frequency-weighted control, we extract 75 circuits from five Pythia models (70M-1.4B). We find that structurally distinct circuits implement the same computation: band-specific edges transfer broadly across bands, a core shared across most bands recovers at least 99% of circuit performance in models above 70M, and causal interchange interventions confirm that internal representations are interchangeable across frequency bands. A smaller subject-verb agreement replication shows the same pattern: circuits differ structurally but transfer broadly across bands, and the core shared by most bands recovers nearly all circuit accuracy. Repeated extractions within the same band further suggest that discovery algorithms sample from an equivalence class of valid subgraphs rather than recovering a unique mechanism. Standard evaluation practice obscures this pattern: source-level evaluation inflates apparent faithfulness, while edge-level evaluation reveals the many-to-one mapping from structure to function. We do not test specialization at the level of token positions or features inside a component. Our results show that structural differences between circuits are not sufficient evidence for distinct mechanisms, and that exposing this requires edge-level evaluation and cross-condition transfer tests.
arxiv_record.authors: Alireza Bayat Makou, Jingcheng Niu, Subhabrata Dutta, Iryna Gurevych
arxiv_record.title: Many Circuits, One Mechanism: Input Variation and Evaluation Granularity in Circuit Discovery

C1.justification: The central phantom-specialization claim and four main findings remain. The abstract and conclusion add a bounded SVA replication claim and restrict the ≥99% LSC recovery claim to models above 70M. V2 also explicitly excludes claims about specialization at token-position or within-component feature levels.

C2.justification: V2 substantially qualifies interpretation: cross-draw variability no longer establishes that individual edges are causally irrelevant, zero-ablation collapse limits sensitivity, and SVA does not reproduce every LSC pattern. It adds limitations concerning position aggregation, residual token confounds, few-shot applicability, and the synthetic control's scope. The revised logit-lens findings also replace the slower, weaker-core interpretation with nearly matching computation and timing.

D1.justification: V2 supplies extensive SVA construction and filtering details, positive-control architecture and training hyperparameters, qualification thresholds, corruption procedures, and few-shot construction and timing information. It clarifies effective ACDC batch consumption, supplies the missing 1.4B batch size, documents mask nondeterminism, and explains head-role classification thresholds. The code/data access link is retained.

E1.justification: V2 adds subject–verb agreement, a synthetic cue-controlled retrieval versus memorization task, evaluation of the previously excluded very_low LSC population, and few-shot copying scenarios. The reverse-copy and zero-distractor variants already existed in v1 and are retained.

E2.justification: The ACDC, EAP, EAP-IG, and random-edge comparisons are retained. Additional comparisons include LSC circuits evaluated against SVA circuits on their respective tasks (Appendix J) and a length- and token-matched scrambled-prefix comparator in the new few-shot study (Appendix L).

E3.justification: New protocols include SVA two-choice scoring and subject-number corruption, independent qualification of trained positive-control models, position-resolved attribution, and paired few-shot conditions. Appendix C.4 also revises the reported LSC discovery sample counts: v1 states 256 examples per circuit, whereas v2 specifies effective single-batch counts of 256, 256, 128, 96, and 64 across model sizes. This does not establish that retained experiments were rerun.

E4.justification: V2 adds a successful pipeline positive control, independent edge-marginality analysis, position-resolved attribution checks, head-role threshold sensitivity and canonical-induction checks, and explicit mean-ablation analysis. SVA sensitivity checks examine mislabeled noun pairs and differences between ablation protocols. These address substantial questions absent from v1.

E5.justification: V2 adds draw-blocked permutation tests for SVA and positional analyses, paired McNemar tests and blocked permutations for few-shot effects, and variability across qualifying control models. The primary LSC three-draw design remains. Its transfer-test description changes from permutation testing to one-sided paired Wilcoxon testing, while the redrawn boost heatmap drops per-cell standard deviations.

E6.justification: New results include matched SVA transfer efficiencies of 0.940–0.992 (Table 14) and positive-control cross-route transfer efficiency of −0.056 ± 0.047 (Table 13). Retained analyses also change: universal-core convergence shifts move from 0.50–3.34 layers in v1 Table 59 to −0.40–0.00 in v2 Table 60. Some revised values conflict internally: v2 Tables 4 and 5 report different resample-ablation effect sizes.

M1.justification: The primary discovery procedure retains ACDC, KL-based pruning, factorized tree patching, and per-model threshold selection. The new tasks, control models, and attribution checks extend the experiments without replacing or modifying the proposed discovery pipeline.

P1.justification: Extensive paragraph and sentence rewriting spans the abstract, introduction, experimental explanations, interpretations, and appendices. V2 separates the canonical-copy mechanism discussion into its own subsection, reorganizes the positive-control material, and moves the statistical-testing summary from Appendix D to Appendix G. These changes exceed the insertion of new scientific content.

P2.justification: V2 adds the two-route task diagram and several experimental tables, consolidates duplicate displays, and moves key appendix comparisons into the main text. It redraws the transfer-boost heatmaps with a shared color scale, replaces full interchange matrices with an aggregated display, and revises logit-lens plots and captions.

R1.justification: V2 adds Mueller (2024) and connects pruning ambiguity to overdetermination in counterfactual analysis. Fisher's 1966 reference is removed alongside the changed transfer-test description. The principal related-work coverage and positioning remain substantially intact.

T1.justification: Appendix E.6 introduces the normalized edge-marginality definition ρ = r/k and its interpretation relative to the matched-size selection boundary. The principal circuit and transfer equations remain unchanged; no new theorem or proof is introduced.

improvement.justification: V1 explicitly identifies the missing successful pipeline positive control as its most important limitation. V2 directly addresses this with six independently qualified models and adds a carefully bounded SVA replication, substantially strengthening validation beyond LSC. Positional checks, reproducibility corrections, and more cautious causal interpretations further improve credibility. The control remains limited to constructed models, and reporting inconsistencies persist, notably the conflicting effect sizes in Tables 4 and 5, but these do not outweigh the substantial validation gains.

A1.justification: Both PDFs describe the same research work. Their main text, equations, tables, figures, and complete appendices are readable and support comparison across substantial revision and relocation.

after.justification: V2 retains original LSC results and adds SVA experiments, a learned two-route positive control, very-low-frequency evaluation, and few-shot accuracy studies.

before.justification: V1 reports original experiments on 75 LSC circuits across five Pythia models, including transfer, ablation, representational, and causal-intervention results.
